question: Thales watched the sky and announced that the sun would go dark on a certain day in 585 BC. The eclipse arrived on schedule. Why did this matter for philosophy?
answer: It showed the sky followed regular patterns that humans could figure out, not just the moods of the gods.
choices: It showed the sky followed regular patterns that humans could figure out, not just the moods of the gods.
It showed the gods favored Thales personally, granting him secret knowledge none of his rivals could discover.
It showed astronomy needed temple priests, since only their long records made such a prediction possible at all.
It showed fate was fixed in every detail, so human choice could not alter what the stars had already decided.
context: Thales is usually called the first Greek philosopher. The eclipse story — whether or not he really called the date — captures why: he treated the heavens as something to be reasoned about, not just worshipped. The next move was his: maybe the whole world worked that way.

question: Plato pictured people chained in a cave from birth, watching shadows on a wall. They take the shadows for the whole world. What was this picture meant to say about us?
answer: That we mistake mere appearances for reality, and only hard thinking can drag us out into the daylight.
choices: That we mistake mere appearances for reality, and only hard thinking can drag us out into the daylight.
That we are doomed to ignorance forever, since no human can escape the limits the senses set on our minds.
That we cannot trust other people's reports, since each cave-dweller sees a different shadow from others.
That we should never leave familiar surroundings, since the climb out of comfort ruins more lives than it helps.
context: Plato's Cave is the most famous image in Western philosophy. The chained prisoners are us; the shadows are everyday opinion; the painful climb up to the sun is what real understanding feels like. He was warning that most people will never make the climb — and may attack whoever tries.

question: Athens tried Socrates for impiety. Found guilty and offered exile, he refused, then drank the hemlock his jailers handed him. Why did he stay?
answer: He had spent his life telling Athens to live by reason; fleeing its verdict would betray everything he taught.
choices: He had spent his life telling Athens to live by reason; fleeing its verdict would betray everything he taught.
He had grown old and weary of arguing, and the cup looked easier than another long journey into foreign exile.
He had a vision of the gods promising him a better life beyond, and trusted them to keep their end of the bargain.
He had been promised by friends that the city would soon overturn the verdict, so he sat waiting for the pardon.
context: Socrates was about seventy. The dialogues say he treated the trial as one more conversation with his city — and the hemlock as the last move in an argument he had won. The death of Socrates became, for the West, the founding image of the philosopher who pays for his beliefs.

question: Marcus Aurelius ruled Rome at its height. Each night, in army camps along the frontier, he wrote private notes to himself in Greek. What did he keep telling himself?
answer: That power, fame, and the day's troubles are smaller than they feel; only his own character is worth tending.
choices: That power, fame, and the day's troubles are smaller than they feel; only his own character is worth tending.
That the gods had picked him for the throne, so any setback was a test he was bound by duty to overcome.
That the empire's survival hung on his every decision, so the lonely burden of rule could never be set down.
That his enemies in the Senate would soon be punished, so he had only to wait while their plots unraveled.
context: The notebooks survived. We call them the Meditations — and they were never meant for us. A Stoic emperor was reminding himself, day after day, of what mattered while empire flowed past him: not the empire. The job of the Stoic was the inner job, even on the throne.

question: Epicurus bought a plot of land outside Athens and opened a school called the Garden, where men, women, and slaves studied together. What did he teach was the good life?
answer: A quiet life among close friends, free from fear and pain — not wealth, fame, or wild excitement.
choices: A quiet life among close friends, free from fear and pain — not wealth, fame, or wild excitement.
A life of strict duty to the city, putting public service above private comfort and the gods above all.
A life of constant pleasure of every kind, since the body's appetites should be fed whenever they speak.
A life of solitary thought, withdrawn from human company so the mind can grow clear and undistracted.
context: Epicurus did teach that pleasure was the goal — but he meant something gentler than the word now suggests. Hunger met with bread; thirst with water; friends, conversation, a garden. He thought the loudest pleasures were usually the costliest, and that most fears could be argued away.

question: Augustine and his friends stole pears from a neighbor's tree — not for hunger, just for fun. He spent pages of his Confessions worrying about it. What troubled him most?
answer: That he had loved the wrongness itself, not the pears — breaking the rule was the pleasure.
choices: That he had loved the wrongness itself, not the pears — breaking the rule was the pleasure.
That better moral training would have stopped him giving way to a small foolish urge.
That the neighbor lost fruit he had worked to grow, and the loss was never repaid.
That his friends had led the act, and he had failed to stand apart from the group.
context: Confessions Book II. Augustine returns to the pear theft because it puzzles him: there was no hunger, no real desire for the pears (he threw most to the pigs). The pleasure was the trespass itself. This becomes his model for what later thinkers called original sin — not a list of bad acts, but a tilt in the will that wants the wrong thing because it is wrong. Distractors are real rival readings: Stoic, restitutive, peer-pressure.

question: Anselm of Canterbury thought he had found a proof of God using only the meaning of the word. He defined God as that-than-which-no-greater-can-be-thought. Next move?
answer: Such a being must exist in reality, since a real being is greater than one merely imagined.
choices: Such a being must exist in reality, since a real being is greater than one merely imagined.
Such a being must exist in nature, since the order of the world points back to a designer.
Such a being must exist in time, since every chain of causes traces back to a first mover.
Such a being must exist in mind, since every culture forms some idea of a highest divinity.
context: Anselm's Proslogion, c. 1078. The ontological argument — God exists by definition — has fascinated philosophers ever since: Descartes revived it, Kant attacked it, Plantinga rebuilt it in modal form. Distractors are the other three classical arguments for God: design (later Paley), cosmological (later Aquinas's first way), and universal consent (Cicero). Each is a real argument; only the ontological move tries to prove God from meaning alone.

question: A disciple asked Confucius for one word to guide a whole life. Confucius gave a word and a single sentence explaining it. What was the sentence?
answer: Reciprocity — do not impose on others what you yourself would not wish to suffer.
choices: Reciprocity — do not impose on others what you yourself would not wish to suffer.
Sincerity — let your inner intent and your outward action match in every dealing.
Reverence — treat each person above you with the deference owed to a parent.
Mastery — study the old classics until their teaching becomes your own nature.
context: Analects 15.24. The word is shu, often rendered reciprocity or considerateness. The negative form is older than the positive Christian version; some scholars argue it is also more demanding, because it asks only that you refrain from inflicting on others what you yourself would refuse. Distractors are three other genuine Confucian virtues — cheng (sincerity), li (ritual reverence), and the cultivation of the junzi through study of the classics. Every wrong choice is a real Confucian teaching.

question: Legend says Laozi, sick of the failing Zhou state, rode a water buffalo west to disappear. At the last border gate the keeper begged him not to leave without writing something down. What did he leave?
answer: A short book of five thousand characters — the Daodejing — and then he rode on, never seen again.
choices: A short book of five thousand characters — the Daodejing — and then he rode on, never seen again.
A long oral teaching the gatekeeper memorized, which he later wrote down as the Analects of the Way.
A single carved stone tablet inscribed with every spirit named by the older Zhou court rites.
A bundle of letters addressed to rulers he had served, urging them to abandon active rule of any kind.
context: The legend appears in Sima Qian's Records of the Grand Historian (first century BCE). Modern scholars suspect the Daodejing was compiled over time rather than written by a single sage at a border gate — but the story has carried the book for two thousand years. The keeper Yinxi becomes a recurring figure in later Daoist tradition. Distractors are plausible alternative literary forms: oral teaching like the Analects, inscribed religious tablet, collection of political letters.

question: The opening line of the Daodejing is one of the most quoted in Chinese thought: the Dao that can be spoken is not the eternal Dao. Why start a book this way?
answer: Warning the reader that no string of words can fully capture what the book points at.
choices: Warning the reader that no string of words can fully capture what the book points at.
Promising that careful study of the text will at last deliver the true name of the Dao.
Arguing words are useless, so a wise person should give up speaking of philosophy.
Praising the older oral teachings the Zhou ritual masters preserved before writing.
context: Daodejing Ch. 1. The opening is not a counsel of silence — Laozi writes the rest of the book anyway. The move is closer to Wittgenstein's later distinction between showing and saying: language can point at the Dao, but the pointing is not the same as the thing. Distractors are real misreadings — the optimistic-mystic reading (full disclosure later), the linguistic-defeatist reading (give up speaking), and the antiquarian reading (the older oral way was better).

question: Around 520 CE, the Indian monk Bodhidharma arrived at the court of Emperor Wu of Liang — a ruler who had built temples, copied scriptures, and supported monks for years. The emperor asked: how much merit have I earned? What did Bodhidharma say?
answer: None at all — meritorious acts done for the sake of merit miss the point entirely.
choices: None at all — meritorious acts done for the sake of merit miss the point entirely.
Vast merit — your support has carried the dharma further than any other ruler's.
Equal merit — emperor and beggar both gain by the measure of what they offer.
Lasting merit — buildings and books outlive the body and so guard the dharma.
context: The encounter is recorded in The Blue Cliff Record (case 1) and other Chan compilations. Bodhidharma, who would become the legendary founder of Chinese Chan (Japanese Zen), refuses to play the merit-economy game the emperor expects. Action aimed at earning spiritual credit, in this reading, is still grasping — and grasping is what Buddhism is trying to undo. Distractors are real positions held within the broader Buddhist world: merit-transfer doctrine, equal-offering doctrine, longevity-of-works idea.

question: A Zen koan asks: what is the sound of one hand clapping? Beginners hear it as a trick riddle with a clever answer hidden somewhere. Rinzai teachers insist the hunt for a clever answer is exactly the wrong response. Why?
answer: The koan is meant to exhaust thinking, not to be solved — frustration is part of the method.
choices: The koan is meant to exhaust thinking, not to be solved — frustration is part of the method.
The koan has one correct logical answer, but the student must derive it without instruction.
The koan is mainly a memory aid, helping the student keep a doctrinal point in active mind.
The koan is a private signal between master and disciple, used to confirm a stage of training.
context: The one-hand koan is attributed to the eighteenth-century Japanese Rinzai master Hakuin. The Rinzai use of koans (kanna Zen) is to drive the student into a state of intense doubt — the great ball of doubt — until the conceptual mind exhausts itself and direct insight breaks through. Soto Zen tends to emphasize seated meditation (zazen) more than koan practice. Distractors are real but mistaken framings: koan-as-riddle, koan-as-mnemonic, koan-as-credential.

question: In the Chandogya Upanishad the sage Uddalaka teaches his son with simple lessons — salt dissolved in water, the seed of a fig, a clay pot. Each builds toward one short sentence Uddalaka repeats nine times. What sentence?
answer: Tat tvam asi — that thou art — the deepest self in you is the source of all things.
choices: Tat tvam asi — that thou art — the deepest self in you is the source of all things.
Neti neti — not this, not that — the deepest reality cannot be named by any description.
Aham brahmasmi — I am the source — the awakened sage alone is the cause of the world.
Om tat sat — om that is real — the chanted syllable contains all the seeker can need.
context: Chandogya Upanishad 6.8-16. Uddalaka's lesson is the classical statement of non-dual Vedanta: the atman (deepest self) and brahman (underlying reality) are not two things. Shankara built his entire philosophical system on it eight centuries later. Distractors are real Upanishadic and Hindu formulae used by other lineages: neti neti (Brihadaranyaka 2.3.6), aham brahmasmi (Brihadaranyaka 1.4.10), om tat sat (Bhagavad Gita 17.23). Each is canonical — only one is the line Uddalaka teaches.

question: The Bhagavad Gita opens with the warrior Arjuna freezing before a battle he no longer wants to fight — kin stand across the field. He drops his bow. Krishna, his charioteer, spends eighteen chapters answering him. What is the answer?
answer: Do the duty of your role with skill and detachment, leaving the fruits to a higher order.
choices: Do the duty of your role with skill and detachment, leaving the fruits to a higher order.
Refuse the duty of your role, since killing kin cannot be reconciled with enlightenment.
Withdraw from action entirely, since only inward meditation ends the cycle of rebirth.
Choose the duty that the named gods assign, since dharma is their direct command alone.
context: The Bhagavad Gita, set within the larger Mahabharata, is one of the most influential religious-philosophical texts ever written. Krishna's teaching to Arjuna — karma yoga, action without attachment to outcomes — became the keystone of Hindu philosophical practice and influenced Gandhi, Emerson, and many others. Distractors are real positions held by other Indian schools the Gita is in conversation with: Jain non-violence absolutism, ascetic-withdrawal Sramanism, theistic-ritual Vedism.

question: Each spring in Japan, crowds gather under cherry trees for hanami — flower-viewing. The blossoms last only a week. Poets have written about them for a thousand years, and the feeling has a name: mono no aware. What does the phrase point at?
answer: The tender ache of feeling something beautiful precisely because it is about to be gone.
choices: The tender ache of feeling something beautiful precisely because it is about to be gone.
The cheerful pleasure of an annual festival shared with neighbors, family, and friends.
The serious duty of remembering ancestors at the change of each major farming season.
The quiet pride of a culture in treating its native flora as the symbol of the land.
context: Mono no aware — literally something like the pathos of things — was named in the eighteenth century by the scholar Motoori Norinaga, who used it to describe a sensibility running through the Tale of Genji and older Heian poetry. It is not sadness, not nostalgia, not melancholy — it is the bittersweet alertness that the very thing making you happy will not last. Cherry blossoms became its emblem because they are so visibly transient. Distractors are real but flatter readings: social festival, ancestor ritual, nationalist symbol.

question: Descartes sat by a winter fire and tried to doubt everything — his senses, the world, even his body. One thing survived the doubt. What was it?
answer: The fact that he was thinking — even a doubter must exist to do the doubting.
choices: The fact that he was thinking — even a doubter must exist to do the doubting.
The warmth of the fire — direct sensation is the one thing no mind can possibly reject.
The memory of his childhood — past experience grounds every belief the present supplies.
The presence of other minds — selves are known together or they are not known at all.
context: Descartes wrote the Meditations in 1641. He set out to doubt every belief that could possibly be false, looking for one thing certain enough to rebuild on. The famous line — 'I think, therefore I am' — is the bedrock he hit. Even a deceiving demon would need someone to deceive.

question: John Locke argued the newborn mind is what he called a tabula rasa — a blank slate. What did he mean to deny by that image?
answer: That any ideas are born into the mind — every concept must enter through experience.
choices: That any ideas are born into the mind — every concept must enter through experience.
That the mind has any structure at birth — even logic must be learned from a teacher.
That children differ from one another — at birth all minds are alike in every respect.
That memory has any role in learning — slates record nothing but the present moment.
context: Locke wrote against Descartes and the rationalists, who claimed the mind comes stocked with innate ideas like 'God,' 'substance,' or basic logical truths. Locke said: show me one. He thought all content arrives through sensation and reflection — leaving the mind, at birth, an unwritten page.

question: Berkeley claimed that a tree in a forest, with no one looking, does not exist at that moment. Why did he say such a strange thing?
answer: Because to be is to be perceived — without a mind, there is nothing left for the tree to be.
choices: Because to be is to be perceived — without a mind, there is nothing left for the tree to be.
Because trees are too small to exist without a witness — only large things persist unobserved.
Because matter blinks in and out of being randomly, and only steady gaze can stabilize it.
Because language alone gives the tree existence — when no one names it, the tree dissolves.
context: Berkeley, an Irish bishop writing in 1710, was not joking. He thought 'matter' was a confused idea: strip away color, shape, smell — all of which are perceptions in some mind — and nothing is left. To save the unobserved tree, he added that God perceives everything. Esse est percipi: to be is to be perceived.

question: Hobbes said that without a strong central authority, human life would be 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.' What did he conclude people should do?
answer: Surrender most rights to a sovereign powerful enough to enforce peace among them all.
choices: Surrender most rights to a sovereign powerful enough to enforce peace among them all.
Form small voluntary communes guided by elders and bound by shared religious practice.
Trust the gradual softening of human nature through education and moral self-cultivation.
Abolish property — most quarrels arise from goods, and shared ownership would end them.
context: Hobbes published Leviathan in 1651, after watching the English Civil War tear his country apart. He thought the state of nature — humans without a common power — was a war of all against all. The Leviathan, the great sovereign, was the price of peace. Better one feared ruler than a hundred warring neighbors.

question: Rousseau opened The Social Contract with the line 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' What did he claim the chains were?
answer: The artificial inequalities and dependencies that civilized society had built up around natural humans.
choices: The artificial inequalities and dependencies that civilized society had built up around natural humans.
The literal slavery and feudal serfdom that still bound most of Europe in his own lifetime.
The passions and appetites of the body that reason must master before liberty can begin.
The original sin inherited from Adam that chains every soul until grace restores it.
context: Rousseau, writing in 1762, did not think humans were naturally wicked — quite the opposite. He thought civilization, property, and comparison with neighbors had corrupted a freer original state. The Social Contract asked: given that we cannot go back, what political arrangement would let us be both governed and free?

question: Galileo aimed his improved telescope at Jupiter in 1610 and saw four small lights circling it. Why did this discovery shake the old astronomy?
answer: It proved at least some heavenly bodies orbit something other than the Earth itself.
choices: It proved at least some heavenly bodies orbit something other than the Earth itself.
It proved Jupiter itself was a small sun, with its own heat and not just reflected light.
It proved the heavens contained more bodies than the ancients had counted in their charts.
It proved that telescopes could be trusted, since the moons matched naked-eye predictions.
context: Aristotle and Ptolemy had taught that everything in the heavens circles the Earth. Four moons swinging around Jupiter were an obvious counter-example. Galileo named them the Medicean stars to flatter his patron; we call them the Galilean moons. The old picture cracked, then broke.

question: Francis Bacon warned that the mind has built-in habits that distort inquiry — he called them 'idols.' What did he say investigators should do about them?
answer: Notice each idol, resist it, and lean on careful observation and shared method to correct it.
choices: Notice each idol, resist it, and lean on careful observation and shared method to correct it.
Confess them in writing each morning — only daily disclosure could keep the mind honest.
Welcome them as guides — the mind's habits gather wisdom that pure observation misses.
Trust them in the short term and let centuries of inquiry slowly grind their errors away.
context: Bacon's Novum Organum (1620) named four idols: of the tribe (errors built into human nature), of the cave (each person's quirks), of the marketplace (loose words misleading thought), and of the theatre (inherited bad systems). He thought naming distortions was the first step toward a real method.

question: Kant took the same walk through Königsberg every afternoon at exactly the same time — neighbors set their clocks by him. What ethical idea did he formulate from his quiet desk?
answer: Act only on a rule you could will to become a universal law binding every rational being.
choices: Act only on a rule you could will to become a universal law binding every rational being.
Act only when the outcome promises the greatest happiness for the greatest number of people.
Act according to the virtues your community honors — character matters more than abstract rules.
Act only when you have a clear command from God; outside revelation, suspend moral judgment.
context: Kant's daily walk became local legend. His ethics, published in 1785, asked a hard question: can we ground morality in reason alone, without leaning on consequences or commands? The categorical imperative says: test your action by asking whether everyone could do the same thing without contradiction.

question: Kant closed his second Critique with one line: 'Two things fill the mind with awe — the starry sky above and the moral law within.' What did he mean to pair?
answer: The vastness of the outer world and the equally astonishing fact that humans recognize duty.
choices: The vastness of the outer world and the equally astonishing fact that humans recognize duty.
The light of the stars and the inner conscience God places in every soul to guide it home.
The mathematical beauty of astronomy and the elegance of natural law written in plain sight.
The cold indifference of nature and the warm fellow-feeling that binds humans to each other.
context: The line closes the Critique of Practical Reason (1788). Kant thought both the physical universe and the moral law inside us were genuine objects of wonder — and both lay beyond easy explanation. Reason could only point at each, not flatten it. Awe was the right response, not embarrassment.

question: In 1806 Hegel watched Napoleon ride through Jena the day before a battle and called him 'the world-spirit on horseback.' What did Hegel mean by that phrase?
answer: That history was advancing through a single living person at that moment in time.
choices: That history was advancing through a single living person at that moment in time.
That Napoleon's soul had grown vast enough to absorb the spirits of every nation he ruled.
That military genius was a special gift from heaven, granted to one age in every century.
That horses, as the engine of armies, were the true bearers of every great historical change.
context: Hegel was finishing the Phenomenology of Spirit when French troops occupied his town. For him, history was not a string of accidents but the gradual self-unfolding of Geist — spirit or mind — through human cultures. Sometimes that unfolding bunches into one figure. Napoleon, that morning, looked to Hegel like such a moment.

question: Fichte argued that the philosophy a person chooses depends on what kind of person they are. What was his striking claim from that idea?
answer: A lazy mind picks a system where things just happen; a free mind picks one where the self acts.
choices: A lazy mind picks a system where things just happen; a free mind picks one where the self acts.
A young thinker prefers freedom; an aging thinker drifts back to fate and acceptance of necessity.
A poor mind clings to materialism; only the rich can afford the luxury of idealist speculation.
A pious mind sees God in all things; a worldly mind sees only matter pushed about by causes.
context: Fichte, lecturing in Jena around 1797, refused to treat philosophical disagreement as just intellectual variation. To him, choosing dogmatism (the world acts on me) over idealism (I act) revealed something about a thinker's grip on freedom itself. The remark is striking; many readers still find it overreaching.

question: Adam Smith argued that a baker doesn't bake your bread out of love for you. Yet you get bread anyway. What did he say made the system work?
answer: Each person pursues their own interest, and prices guide that effort into others' service.
choices: Each person pursues their own interest, and prices guide that effort into others' service.
Each person feels duty toward neighbors, and reliable bread reflects this widespread civic virtue.
Each person fears the magistrate's whip, and the law forces good behavior on every trader.
Each person learns by long custom, and tradition alone keeps the bakers turning out their loaves.
context: Smith's Wealth of Nations (1776) put the point plainly: 'It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.' He called the coordinating effect of self-interest meeting prices the 'invisible hand.'

question: John Stuart Mill argued in On Liberty that society may restrict an individual's actions only in one specific case. What was it?
answer: When the action causes harm to other people — otherwise the individual is sovereign.
choices: When the action causes harm to other people — otherwise the individual is sovereign.
When the action breaks an old custom — tradition itself names the public boundary line.
When the action offends religious feeling — communities must protect their sacred bonds.
When the action harms the actor — society owes each person protection from their worst self.
context: Mill's 1859 essay drew the line as sharply as he knew how. Drinking yourself ill is your business; driving drunk is everyone's. The 'harm principle' became a cornerstone of liberal political philosophy — and a perennial battleground, since 'harm' is harder to pin down than it sounds.

question: Marx and Engels closed the Communist Manifesto with 'Workers of the world, unite.' Beneath the slogan lay a specific philosophical claim about workers. What was it?
answer: That national borders were less real than class — workers shared an interest across every country.
choices: That national borders were less real than class — workers shared an interest across every country.
That all workers everywhere held identical moral beliefs, formed by their shared labor experience.
That workers alone could think clearly, since manual labor purified judgment in a way books could not.
That every worker was inherently virtuous and every owner inherently corrupt by their social role.
context: The Manifesto appeared in 1848, weeks before revolutions swept several European capitals. Marx and Engels claimed that the modern factory created a working class with no real homeland — its conditions were the same in Manchester, Lyon, and Berlin. Whether the claim was right is one of the long arguments of the next century.

question: In January 1889 Nietzsche saw a cab driver beating a horse in Turin, ran to embrace its neck, and collapsed. He never recovered his sanity. Why is the scene philosophically poignant?
answer: The fierce critic of pity broke down in an act of pity for a suffering animal.
choices: The fierce critic of pity broke down in an act of pity for a suffering animal.
He had predicted his own madness years earlier and walked toward it as a final experiment.
He confused himself with the horse, illustrating a thesis about animal consciousness he had written.
He had argued horses were lower beings — the embrace contradicted his published philosophy.
context: Nietzsche had spent the previous decade attacking what he called Mitleid — pity — as a value invented by the weak to constrain the strong. The breakdown in Turin became the iconic image of his end. He spent his last eleven years in his sister's care, no longer writing, no longer speaking philosophy.

question: Nietzsche announced that 'God is dead' through a madman with a lantern crying in the marketplace. Readers often miss his tone. What did he mean by it?
answer: A warning — Europe had lost its moral foundation and did not yet grasp the abyss ahead.
choices: A warning — Europe had lost its moral foundation and did not yet grasp the abyss ahead.
A triumph — at last reason had defeated the old superstition and humanity could move forward.
A literal news report — Nietzsche believed a real divine being had recently expired from age.
A confession — Nietzsche himself had stopped believing and was sharing his personal doubt.
context: The line appears in The Gay Science (1882). The madman shouts to crowds who do not understand him; he says he has come too early. Nietzsche thought the death of belief in God would shake every value Europe held — duty, truth, dignity. He was not celebrating. He was sounding an alarm about what would have to be built or remade.

question: Kierkegaard wrote of Abraham raising the knife over Isaac and called what Abraham did 'the leap of faith.' What did Kierkegaard mean by 'leap' there?
answer: A commitment that reason cannot guarantee in advance — the believer steps past what argument can show.
choices: A commitment that reason cannot guarantee in advance — the believer steps past what argument can show.
A sudden emotional surge that overcomes doubt — feeling, not thinking, settles the question.
A decision proven correct after the fact — the outcome shows the choice was rational all along.
A retreat into mystical silence — the leap names a turning away from words and concepts entirely.
context: Fear and Trembling (1843) circles the Abraham story for a hundred pages without quite explaining it. Kierkegaard thought genuine faith was not the conclusion of an argument but a venture made without certainty. The leap is not irrational on his view; it is suprarational — a move reason cannot make for you.

question: Russell and Whitehead spent ten years writing three thick volumes — page 379 of volume one is where they finally proved 1+1=2. What were they trying to do?
answer: Build all of mathematics from pure logic, with no math taken for granted in any step
choices: Build all of mathematics from pure logic, with no math taken for granted in any step
Replace ordinary numbers with a faster shorthand notation easier for school children to learn
Find the shortest proof of every theorem that nineteenth-century mathematics already accepted
Catalogue every error working mathematicians had made when they relied on their intuition
context: Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). The wry footnote at the famous page-379 proof reads: 'The above proposition is occasionally useful.' Russell and Whitehead were not slow — they refused to assume any arithmetic before they had derived it. Gödel would later show in 1931 that the full project could not succeed, but their three volumes reshaped logic permanently.

question: In 1920s Vienna a group of scientists and philosophers met weekly in coffee houses to argue about what counts as real knowledge. They became known as the Vienna Circle. What was their guiding test?
answer: A claim has meaning only if some observation could in principle show it true or false
choices: A claim has meaning only if some observation could in principle show it true or false
A claim is trustworthy only if a recognized expert in that field has formally endorsed it
A claim is meaningful only if the speaker is willing to act as though it were truly the case
A claim is acceptable only if it agrees with the older traditions of the European universities
context: The Vienna Circle (Schlick, Carnap, Neurath, Hahn, and others) gathered around 1924 in Vienna cafés and Schlick's seminar. The 'verification principle' was their slogan: meaning equals method of verification. Metaphysics, theology, and traditional ethics all came out (on their reckoning) as literally meaningless. The principle eventually broke on its own teeth — it could not verify itself — but it set the agenda for half a century.

question: A 26-year-old Englishman named A. J. Ayer wrote Language, Truth and Logic in 1936 — a brash little book that shocked British philosophy. What did he claim about every traditional metaphysical sentence?
answer: It is literally meaningless because no possible experience could confirm or refute it
choices: It is literally meaningless because no possible experience could confirm or refute it
It is poetically valuable but should be reserved for personal writing and Sunday sermons
It is probably true but currently lacks the careful evidence a philosopher should demand
It is the foundation of all empirical science and must be defended against modern critics
context: Ayer brought the Vienna Circle to English readers in his 1936 manifesto, written at age 25 after a year in Vienna. The book treated metaphysical claims ('the Absolute enters into evolution,' 'God is love') as neither true nor false but cognitively empty — like a cough. Ayer himself, decades later, called the book 'almost entirely wrong,' but it set the tone of British analytic philosophy for a generation.

question: After his Tractatus made him famous, Wittgenstein gave away a fortune and spent six years teaching primary school in remote Austrian villages. He thought he had solved philosophy. What did he believe was left to do?
answer: Nothing in philosophy — the work was done, and ordinary life was what remained for him
choices: Nothing in philosophy — the work was done, and ordinary life was what remained for him
Translate his book into every European language so its truths could reach all readers
Establish a school where his findings would be taught to every coming generation of thinkers
Apply his system to political reform and persuade governments to adopt its logical standards
context: Between 1920 and 1926 Wittgenstein taught children in Trattenbach, Puchberg, and Otterthal — having concluded that the Tractatus had said everything philosophy could say. He returned to Cambridge in 1929 only because he came to believe he had been wrong, launching the work that became Philosophical Investigations.

question: The later Wittgenstein asked: what do all 'games' have in common? Card games, board games, ball games, ring-a-ring-a-roses. He found no single feature shared by them all. What did he conclude about words?
answer: Many of our words gather their cases by overlapping likenesses, not by a shared essence
choices: Many of our words gather their cases by overlapping likenesses, not by a shared essence
Many of our words refer to private mental images that no other speaker can directly inspect
Many of our words have a hidden logical form that only careful analysis can ever reveal
Many of our words mean whatever each speaker happens to want them to mean in a moment
context: Philosophical Investigations §66–67. Wittgenstein's 'family resemblance' move undid centuries of essence-hunting. Look at the actual uses, he said: chess and tag share little, tag and patience share little, yet a network of similarities runs across the cases. Names of family members carry the metaphor — sisters share a nose with one, a chin with another, a laugh with a third, but no feature with all.

question: Husserl told his students to set aside scientific theories, religious doctrines, and inherited opinions, and go 'back to the things themselves.' What did he mean by 'the things'?
answer: Whatever shows up in conscious experience, examined as it actually appears to us
choices: Whatever shows up in conscious experience, examined as it actually appears to us
Whatever physics says exists when stripped of perception and analyzed by measurement
Whatever ancient Greek thinkers identified as the real entities behind the changing world
Whatever practical interests in daily life force a working person to attend to as urgent
context: Husserl's program: bracket all standing assumptions — what he called the epoché — and describe experience as it presents itself. A coffee cup is not first a chemical aggregate and then 'experienced'; it shows up to consciousness as warm, brown, mine. Phenomenology studies this showing-up structure. Husserl's slogan, 'Zu den Sachen selbst!' is on the masthead of the movement.

question: Heidegger thought one question was deeper than every other in philosophy: why is there anything at all, rather than just nothing? Why did he say most thinkers had walked past it?
answer: We are so used to things existing that we stop noticing existence is itself remarkable
choices: We are so used to things existing that we stop noticing existence is itself remarkable
We are taught from childhood that no answer is possible, so the question is dismissed
We confuse the question with a religious puzzle and leave it to theologians to settle
We assume modern science has answered it and turn our attention to specialist problems
context: Heidegger opens An Introduction to Metaphysics (1935 lectures) with this question, calling it the most fundamental of all. His Sein und Zeit (1927) had argued that the West had forgotten the question of Being — taking it for granted that things exist, and asking only about what they are. The wonder that anything is at all, rather than nothing, is what Heidegger wanted to recover.

question: Camus took up the Greek myth where Sisyphus is condemned forever to roll a boulder uphill, only to watch it roll back down. He told us to imagine Sisyphus happy. Why?
answer: Because Sisyphus knows his task is futile and chooses to keep rolling anyway
choices: Because Sisyphus knows his task is futile and chooses to keep rolling anyway
Because the gods will eventually relent and let Sisyphus rest at the top of the hill
Because each new push of the rock is technically harder than the one before it was
Because in the next life Sisyphus will be rewarded for the labour of this one fully
context: The closing pages of Camus's The Myth of Sisyphus (1942). Suicide, for Camus, would surrender to absurdity by erasing the questioner; religion would surrender by pretending the world answers. Revolt is the third path: keep pushing, keep seeing the rock roll back, refuse both despair and consolation. 'The struggle itself toward the heights is enough to fill a man's heart.'

question: Simone de Beauvoir's 1949 book The Second Sex opens with a famous line: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' What was she claiming?
answer: Womanhood is shaped by upbringing and culture, not given fully by biology at birth
choices: Womanhood is shaped by upbringing and culture, not given fully by biology at birth
Womanhood is a stage all girls must pass through before they reach a deeper humanity
Womanhood is best left undefined, since any definition restricts the women it covers
Womanhood is a divine vocation revealed slowly to those who pay attention to it carefully
context: Beauvoir wrote The Second Sex from existentialist premises she shared with Sartre: humans are not fixed essences but situations interpreted by free choice. The bourgeois nineteenth-century 'woman' was, she argued, a social product — composed of training, expectation, dress, deference — not a biological inevitability. The biological female body is real; what counts as 'feminine' is built on top of it, and could in principle be different.

question: Adorno coined the phrase 'the culture industry' for popular music, films, magazines, and radio shows. Why did he insist on the word 'industry' rather than 'culture'?
answer: The products are made the way cars are — to a pattern, for sale, on a schedule
choices: The products are made the way cars are — to a pattern, for sale, on a schedule
The artists involved hold formal degrees from universities in the industrial arts
The audiences pay close attention as if they were workers learning a serious craft
The critics treat each new film with the rigor that a scientist applies to research
context: Adorno wanted to block a comforting assumption — that popular songs and Hollywood movies were the natural expression of 'the people.' He argued they were industrially produced consumer goods, designed to standard specifications by a few firms, marketed back to the audience as 'their' culture. The word 'industry' was the punch: an honest description of the production line behind the entertainment.

question: Foucault did not begin in libraries — he began in prisons, mental asylums, and the records of medical clinics. He read each of these institutions for the same reason. What was he tracking?
answer: The way societies define normal people by sorting and confining those they call abnormal
choices: The way societies define normal people by sorting and confining those they call abnormal
The way medieval Christian theology survived hidden inside the routines of modern institutions
The way the working classes resisted the laws of bourgeois governments through small rebellions
The way ordinary citizens lost faith in science once they saw what experts actually did in private
context: Madness and Civilization (1961), The Birth of the Clinic (1963), Discipline and Punish (1975). Foucault's claim was that the 'normal' is not a natural fact but a category produced by the institutions that mark its boundary. The asylum makes 'the sane' by confining 'the mad'; the prison makes 'the law-abiding' by isolating 'the criminal.' To study one is to study how a whole society defines itself by exclusion.

question: Derrida said every word in a text leaves behind a 'trace' of the other words it could have been — what was excluded, what almost meant something else. Why does this matter for reading?
answer: No single fixed meaning can be sealed off from the alternatives a word was chosen against
choices: No single fixed meaning can be sealed off from the alternatives a word was chosen against
No reader can ever finish a long book because the words keep multiplying as one reads
No translation between languages is possible since each language uses different sounds
No author can be held responsible for any meaning the text turns out to bear later
context: Derrida's notion of the 'trace' goes with différance — meaning is produced by differences and deferrals, not by any term pointing directly to a thing. 'House' means what it means partly by not being 'home,' 'shed,' 'tent,' 'palace.' Each word carries the marks of what it isn't. Deconstruction reads texts for these marks, often showing that an opposition the author seems to use (speech/writing, nature/culture) leaks at the seams.

question: William James's friends argued: a man circles a tree pursued by a squirrel, which keeps the trunk between them. Has the man 'gone around' the squirrel? How did James settle it?
answer: Both sides are right — they mean different things by 'around,' and the dispute vanishes
choices: Both sides are right — they mean different things by 'around,' and the dispute vanishes
Only one side can be right; geometry settles it and the other speaker is plainly mistaken
Neither side is right; the question is too vague for any answer to count as the correct one
Whichever side speaks loudest wins; in plain speech meaning belongs to the firmest claim
context: The opening anecdote of Pragmatism (1907). James's friends had divided into camps; he proposed that 'go around' could mean 'pass through north, east, south, west of' (yes, the man does) or 'face all sides of in succession' (no, he doesn't — the squirrel keeps its belly to him). Once the ambiguity is named, the dispute dissolves. The pragmatic method: ask what practical difference the disputed claim would make, and you usually find the dispute was verbal.

question: John Dewey insisted that democracy was not just a way of running elections — it was something larger. What did he say democracy actually was?
answer: A whole way of living in which people share inquiry, problems, and decisions together
choices: A whole way of living in which people share inquiry, problems, and decisions together
A constitutional arrangement that protects citizens against the natural overreach of rulers
A market system in which votes for candidates work the way prices do for ordinary goods
A temporary stage of social progress that better forms of government will eventually replace
context: Dewey's Democracy and Education (1916) and The Public and Its Problems (1927). He distinguished democracy-as-institution (elections, courts, parties) from democracy-as-ethic — a habit of treating every person as capable of inquiry and of shared decision. Schools, workplaces, neighborhoods could be more or less democratic in this deeper sense, regardless of formal politics. Dewey's view shaped American progressive education for half a century.

question: Searle imagined a man in a locked room. People slip Chinese questions under the door; he uses a thick rulebook to slip Chinese answers back. He speaks no Chinese. What was Searle trying to show?
answer: Shuffling symbols by rule is not the same as understanding what they mean.
choices: Shuffling symbols by rule is not the same as understanding what they mean.
A mind is whatever passes a careful conversational test, language or no.
Translation between any two languages works if the rulebook is full enough.
The brain is a rulebook; thinking just is orderly shuffling of neural symbols.
context: Searle's Chinese Room (1980) targeted strong AI. The man inside produces fluent Chinese replies but understands nothing. If symbol manipulation alone cannot give him understanding, Searle argued, it cannot give a computer understanding either.

question: Jackson imagined Mary, a scientist who has lived her whole life in a black-and-white room knowing every physical fact about color. One day she steps outside and sees red for the first time. What did Jackson say happens?
answer: Mary learns something new — proving facts about experience that no physics captures.
choices: Mary learns something new — proving facts about experience that no physics captures.
Mary learns nothing new, since she already knew every physical fact about red.
Mary loses her science and must relearn color from scratch, as a child does.
Mary gains an ability — to imagine red — but acquires no new factual knowledge.
context: Jackson's 'Mary the colour scientist' (1982) attacked physicalism. If complete physical knowledge leaves something out — what red looks like — then the world contains facts beyond the physical. Dennett and Lewis reply that Mary gains ability or learns nothing new.

question: Putnam imagined a planet just like Earth except its 'water' is not H2O but XYZ — colorless, drinkable, filling the lakes. Do Earth-Oscar and Twin-Oscar mean the same by 'water'?
answer: Different things — meaning depends on the stuff in the world, not just on what is in the head.
choices: Different things — meaning depends on the stuff in the world, not just on what is in the head.
The same thing, since both grew up using the word in the same way for the same role.
Nothing definite, because no one in 1750 yet knew the actual chemistry of water itself.
The same, but only if both planets share a common ancestor language at some early point.
context: Putnam's 1975 'Twin Earth' argued meaning 'ain't in the head.' Before chemistry, Oscar and Twin-Oscar were psychologically identical, yet (Putnam said) their word 'water' picked out different substances. Externalism about meaning was born.

question: Popper said that no number of white swans confirms 'all swans are white' — but one black swan refutes it. What did he conclude about how science actually advances?
answer: A theory earns its place by surviving real attempts to refute it, not by confirming cases.
choices: A theory earns its place by surviving real attempts to refute it, not by confirming cases.
A theory becomes scientific once enough careful observations have been gathered to confirm it.
A theory is acceptable when it explains familiar phenomena better than its current rivals.
A theory is acceptable as long as no alternative has yet been proposed for the same facts.
context: Popper's falsificationism (1934) reversed the popular picture of science as confirmation-collecting. Black swans were eventually found in Australia. What matters for Popper is what a theory forbids — and whether the forbidden thing can be looked for.

question: For two thousand years, philosophers said knowledge was justified true belief. In 1963, Gettier published a three-page paper that ended the consensus. What did he show?
answer: You can have a justified true belief that is true only by luck — and luck is not knowledge.
choices: You can have a justified true belief that is true only by luck — and luck is not knowledge.
You can have a justified false belief that becomes knowledge once the world matches it.
You can have a true belief without justification, and call it knowledge by convention.
You can have knowledge that you cannot justify, since some truths exceed reasoned argument.
context: Gettier's 1963 paper offered cases where someone believes something true, has good reason for the belief, yet the reason and the truth come together only by accident. The field has spent sixty years trying to repair the definition. Three pages, lasting fallout.

question: Plato in the Theaetetus offered a clean definition of knowledge that stood for most of philosophy's history. What did he say knowledge was?
answer: A belief that happens to be true and that the believer can back up with good reasons.
choices: A belief that happens to be true and that the believer can back up with good reasons.
A direct seeing of the form, with no need of reasons; the seeing is itself the warrant.
Whatever a community of trained inquirers comes to agree on under steady investigation.
A useful belief that lets the holder act, whether or not the belief strictly maps reality.
context: Plato's tripartite definition — justified, true, belief — survived from the Theaetetus until Gettier's 1963 counterexamples. The other choices map onto rival accounts: Platonic intuition (rival within Plato), Peirce/Dewey-style pragmatism, instrumentalism.

question: Foot asked you to imagine a runaway trolley headed for five workers. You can pull a lever to divert it onto a side track, where it will kill one. What puzzle did the case open?
answer: Why intentionally killing one feels different from letting the same number die unaided.
choices: Why intentionally killing one feels different from letting the same number die unaided.
Why people prefer certain death of one to the uncertain risk of five they could save.
Why utilitarian arithmetic loses out, in real judgments, to whatever rule the law enforces.
Why bystanders refuse to act even when acting would clearly save more lives than not.
context: Philippa Foot introduced the trolley case in 1967. Her interest was the doctrine of double effect: intended harm versus foreseen-but-unintended harm. The puzzle deepened when Judith Thomson added the footbridge variant, where pushing a man feels worse than pulling the lever.

question: Someone says: 'this sentence is false.' If it is true, then it is false. If it is false, then it is true. What is this puzzle?
answer: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
choices: The liar paradox — a sentence that can be neither consistently true nor consistently false.
The sorites paradox — small unnoticed changes adding up to a clearly different situation.
Russell's paradox — a set containing exactly the sets that are not members of themselves.
Zeno's dichotomy — any motion must first cover half a distance, then half the rest forever.
context: Attributed to Epimenides in antiquity, the liar paradox forced 20th-century logic to rethink truth. Tarski concluded that a language cannot consistently contain its own truth-predicate. The distractors are three other famous paradoxes the player may have heard named together.

question: Zeno asked you to imagine an arrow in flight. At any instant, it occupies its own length exactly. At that instant, it is not moving. What did he conclude?
answer: Each instant is a snapshot of rest, and a sum of rests is still rest — unmoving frames can never add up to motion.
choices: Each instant is a snapshot of rest, and a sum of rests is still rest — unmoving frames can never add up to motion.
Motion is real, but cannot be made of instants — time must be a single unbroken whole, not a series of frames.
Motion is real and made of instants; at each one the arrow has a definite speed, and those speeds add up.
Motion exists only relative to an observer; without one, the arrow neither moves nor stays still at all.
context: Zeno's arrow paradox defended Parmenides: appearance shows change, but reason proves change incoherent. The puzzle: an instant has zero duration, and within zero duration nothing moves — so motion must somehow be assembled from non-motion, which Zeno took to be impossible. The calculus eventually modeled instantaneous velocity as a limit, dissolving the paradox at a mathematical level. Each distractor is a real philosophical reply — Bergsonian continuity, the modern calculus answer, relationalism.

question: Nagel imagined a bat — flying in the dark, navigating by bouncing echoes off insects. Even with perfect knowledge of bat biology, he said, you would miss something. What?
answer: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be a bat using echolocation to find its way.
choices: What it is actually like, from the inside, to be a bat using echolocation to find its way.
How the bat learned to echolocate, and whether its first attempts at flight ever succeeded.
What ordinary bats would say about being a bat, if only they were taught to use language.
Whether the bat's brain is conscious in any way at all, given how small the brain really is.
context: Nagel's 1974 paper 'What is it like to be a bat?' argued there is a subjective character to experience that objective description leaves out. Echolocation is alien enough that even imagining your way in stalls. Whether bats are conscious (a distractor) is a different question.

question: Chalmers drew a line between the 'easy problems' of consciousness and the 'hard problem.' The easy ones include attention, memory, behavior. What made the hard one hard?
answer: Explaining why any physical process is accompanied by inner experience at all, rather than darkness.
choices: Explaining why any physical process is accompanied by inner experience at all, rather than darkness.
Explaining how neurons firing in patterns produce the rapid behaviors observed in living animals.
Explaining why some animals have consciousness while others with similar brain sizes do not.
Explaining how the brain stores memories long enough for an animal to recognize its own kin.
context: Chalmers's 1995 essay drew the easy/hard distinction. The easy ones may be unsolved but admit familiar scientific treatment. The hard one asks why there is something it is like to be a brain — a question the easy ones never reach. The distractors are real easy-problem questions.

question: Anselm in 1078 offered an argument for God using only the meaning of a word. God, he said, is 'that than which nothing greater can be conceived.' What was his move?
answer: A being that exists in reality is greater than one in thought; so the greatest must exist.
choices: A being that exists in reality is greater than one in thought; so the greatest must exist.
A being so widely worshipped across cultures must reflect a shared object behind the practice.
A being whose works show design and order proves a designer behind the designed world.
A being able to inspire belief at all must have caused that belief by acting on the mind.
context: Anselm's 'ontological argument' in the Proslogion tries to derive God's existence from the concept of God alone. Aquinas rejected it; Descartes revived it; Kant attacked it; Plantinga reformulated it. The distractors are the other classical arguments — consensus, design, and a religious-experience variant.

question: Kant said calling a sunset beautiful is odd. You are not just reporting your private pleasure — you claim, somehow, that others ought to agree. What did he find strange about this?
answer: Beauty judgments demand universal agreement without resting on a rule that could compel it.
choices: Beauty judgments demand universal agreement without resting on a rule that could compel it.
Beauty judgments are pure taste, like preferring strawberries — disagreement is meaningless.
Beauty judgments are moral judgments in disguise — sunsets are beautiful because they are good.
Beauty judgments depend on training, so only the educated few are entitled to make them.
context: Kant's 1790 Critique of Judgment called this the antinomy of taste. We treat 'this is beautiful' as objective enough to argue about, yet we cannot produce the rule that would settle the argument. Hume's relativism, a moralist reading, and aristocratic taste are the distractors.

question: Burke and Kant noticed that standing at the edge of an Alpine cliff produces a feeling unlike ordinary beauty. The view is too vast, almost frightening — yet you cannot look away. What did they call it?
answer: The sublime — pleasure at confronting what overwhelms the senses but not the mind.
choices: The sublime — pleasure at confronting what overwhelms the senses but not the mind.
The picturesque — a beauty depending on variety, roughness, and irregular texture.
The grotesque — beauty mixed with the unsettling, like gargoyles seen up close.
The numinous — the felt presence of the holy, both fascinating and full of dread.
context: Burke (1757) and Kant (1790) gave the sublime its modern form. The sense of being small before something vast — storms, mountains, the starry sky — became central to Romantic art. The distractors are real adjacent categories from Gilpin, Ruskin, and Rudolf Otto.

question: Leopold once shot a wolf and watched the 'fierce green fire' die in its eyes. The county killed the wolves; deer multiplied; the mountains were stripped bare. He called the lesson 'thinking like a mountain.' What did he mean?
answer: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
choices: A piece of land has a long-term welfare that the eye, focused on immediate gain, misses.
Nature is a hierarchy with predators on top; removing one collapses the rank order beneath.
Wilderness has rights of its own that override any human claim to use or improve the land.
Ecology is a science, and political decisions about land belong to the trained ecologist.
context: Leopold's 1949 Sand County Almanac founded modern conservation ethics. The wolf-deer-mountain chain is its central image. Distractors are real rival positions: trophic-cascade ecology without ethics, deep-ecology rights talk, technocratic land management.

question: Turing in 1950 proposed a game. A judge types to a hidden human and a hidden machine. If the judge cannot tell which is which, the machine passes. What did he claim this settled?
answer: Whether to call something a thinker is a question about behavior, not inner mechanism.
choices: Whether to call something a thinker is a question about behavior, not inner mechanism.
Whether a machine truly understands — indistinguishable replies must rest on understanding.
Whether a machine is conscious — fluent conversation could only come from inner experience.
Whether a machine has a soul — any being that could fool a careful judge must possess one.
context: Turing's 'Computing Machinery and Intelligence' (1950) deliberately replaced the metaphysical question with an operational one. Critics — Searle most famously — argue passing the test would not settle understanding, consciousness, or anything else. The distractors are exactly those inflations.

question: Pinker in The Blank Slate (2002) argued against the view that had dominated 20th-century social science: that the mind is born empty, shaped only by environment. What did he claim instead?
answer: The mind comes with structure built by evolution; culture writes onto a slate not really blank.
choices: The mind comes with structure built by evolution; culture writes onto a slate not really blank.
The mind comes from a soul implanted at conception; biology shapes the body, not what is thought.
The mind reflects whichever class the person is born into; material conditions explain the rest.
The mind has no real structure at all — what we call human nature is a name for habit alone.
context: Pinker named the dominant view 'the Blank Slate' (Locke), with 'the Noble Savage' (Rousseau) and 'the Ghost in the Machine' (Descartes) as its companions. The distractors map onto the second and third of those, plus a Marxist-environmentalist variant.

question: Sowell in A Conflict of Visions argued most political fights trace to a deeper disagreement about humans themselves. He named two visions. What was the split?
answer: Whether human nature is fixed (so policy is tradeoffs) or improvable (so policy solves problems).
choices: Whether human nature is fixed (so policy is tradeoffs) or improvable (so policy solves problems).
Whether the individual is wiser than the group, or the group wiser than any individual in it.
Whether the rich are entitled to their gains, or the poor to a share of the rich's surplus.
Whether reason or revelation should settle disputes about how a society ought to be ordered.
context: Sowell's 1987 book named the 'constrained' vision (Burke, Smith, the Founders) and the 'unconstrained' vision (Godwin, Condorcet). For one, every policy choice is a painful tradeoff; for the other, settling for less than the best is failure. The other splits are real, just not Sowell's.

question: Bastiat in 1850 told of a careless boy who breaks a shopkeeper's window. Neighbors said: good news — it gives the glazier work. Bastiat said they were missing something. What?
answer: The shoes, the book, the dinner the shopkeeper would have spent the money on instead.
choices: The shoes, the book, the dinner the shopkeeper would have spent the money on instead.
The damage to the boy's character; petty vandalism in childhood ripens into worse crimes later.
The trust between neighbors, eroded whenever one refuses to pay for what he himself broke.
The role of insurance, which alone makes such accidents bearable without burdening third parties.
context: Bastiat's 'broken window fallacy' shows any visible gain has invisible costs — what would have been done with the same resource. Distractors are real adjacent readings (moral, communitarian, institutional), none of which is Bastiat's economic point. The lesson opens opportunity cost as a moral category.

question: Havel described a Prague greengrocer who hangs in his window the sign Workers of the World, Unite. He does not believe it. The customers know he does not. Havel asked what the sign really says. What is his answer?
answer: It says: I know what I am supposed to do, and I am doing it — please leave me alone.
choices: It says: I know what I am supposed to do, and I am doing it — please leave me alone.
It says the regime is failing; only failing regimes need slogans in every window pane.
It says workers should unite; the man agrees, even if his customers are uncertain too.
It says nothing at all; shop-window slogans are background noise the neighborhood ignores.
context: Havel's 1978 essay The Power of the Powerless called this post-totalitarianism — a regime sustained not by terror but by the ritual self-implication of citizens in a story none of them believes. The distractors include the regime's reading, a sincere reading, and a denial that signs do anything.

question: King in 1963 dreamed of a day when his children would be judged 'not by the color of their skin but by the content of their character.' What older argument was he extending?
answer: The founders' natural-rights claim — Declaration promises must apply to every American.
choices: The founders' natural-rights claim — Declaration promises must apply to every American.
The Marxist class-struggle claim — legal equality is hollow until economics is transformed.
The black-nationalist claim — the rights of black Americans must come from a separate polity.
The progressive social-engineering claim — government must reshape attitudes through policy.
context: King grounded the speech in the American founding documents and the prophets — Lincoln, Jefferson, Isaiah, Amos. The distractors are three real rival traditions of mid-20th-century black political thought (CPUSA-aligned Marxism, Garveyite nationalism, technocratic progressivism), each of which King knew and rejected.

question: Lincoln at Gettysburg in 1863 gave a two-minute speech that listed no battles. He tied the war to a date almost a century older. What text was the war about?
answer: The Declaration of Independence — its claim that all men are created equal had to come true.
choices: The Declaration of Independence — its claim that all men are created equal had to come true.
The Constitution of 1787 — the federal Union must be preserved against any state's secession.
The Northwest Ordinance — new western territories must always enter the Union as free states.
The Mayflower Compact — the Puritan ideal of self-governing community bound by covenant.
context: Lincoln's address opened 'Four score and seven years ago' — back to 1776, not 1787. He read the war as the test of whether a nation founded on the Declaration's promise could endure. The distractors are real founding texts Lincoln could have invoked, but did not — and the difference is the point.

question: Madison, Hamilton, and Jay wrote 85 essays under the name 'Publius' in 1787, urging New Yorkers to ratify the new Constitution. What was the collection arguing for?
answer: That a single extended republic could govern free people better than a loose league of small states.
choices: That a single extended republic could govern free people better than a loose league of small states.
That Britain's unwritten constitution should be the model for a written American one to come.
That elected presidents — not hereditary executives — would protect the rights of the citizen.
That a national bank should be chartered to manage the new federal government's growing debt.
context: The Federalist defended the proposed Constitution against the Anti-Federalists, who feared a strong central government would swallow the states. Madison's Federalist 10 made the famous argument that a large republic, not a small one, best controls faction. The distractors are real period debates.

question: Simone de Beauvoir opened The Second Sex in 1949 with a sentence that became famous: 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman.' What was she pressing?
answer: What it means to be a woman is shaped by social formation, not fixed by biological birth.
choices: What it means to be a woman is shaped by social formation, not fixed by biological birth.
Biological sex itself is a social construction with no underlying biological reality at all.
Adult identity, once formed by experience, can never afterward be revised by new evidence.
Women and men reason in fundamentally different modes no shared education could bridge.
context: Beauvoir's existentialist feminism distinguished sex (the biological fact) from gender (the formed role). She kept the distinction precise. The first distractor pushes her line past where she drew it; the others are real rival positions in 20th-century thought that she explicitly rejected.

question: Across many Southern African languages runs the saying: 'a person is a person through other persons.' Tutu and Ramose called it Ubuntu and read it as a philosophical claim. What is the claim?
answer: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
choices: A self comes into being through recognition by, and bond to, a surrounding community of persons.
Each person holds inalienable rights from birth; community is a contract that adds nothing real.
The self is illusion; liberation is dissolving the ego into an impersonal cosmic order beyond ties.
Moral worth lies in autonomous rational willing; others matter only because reason commands respect.
context: Ubuntu, developed philosophically by Desmond Tutu and Mogobe Ramose among others, frames personhood relationally rather than individually. The distractors map onto Locke's individualist rights, Advaita Vedanta's dissolution of self, and Kant's autonomy — three real rival accounts of what makes a self.

question: Vine Deloria Jr. titled his 1973 book God Is Red and argued Western and tribal religions answer different opening questions. What did he say the difference was?
answer: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
choices: Western religion organizes meaning around time and events; tribal religion around place and land.
All religions express the same perennial truths in different wrappers; the wrappers vary, not the core.
Religion is the alienated form of social production; both Western and tribal religions cloak relations.
Genuine religion arises only from private mystical experience; ritual and community are later add-ons.
context: Deloria, a Standing Rock Sioux scholar, contrasted sacred time (Sinai, Easter) with sacred place (Bear Butte, Blue Lake). The distractors map onto Huxley's perennialism, Marx's religion-as-alienation, and James's experiential individualism — three real rival framings of what religion is.

question: Stoics and Buddhists, separated by centuries and continents, both diagnosed human suffering as rooted in a wrong relation with desire. Where did they agree on the root cause?
answer: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
choices: Both blamed attachment to fleeting goods — clinging to what cannot last produces the suffering.
Both denied desire any role at all — the sage simply ceases to want, and cessation is wisdom.
Both treated suffering as illusion — the awakened person sees the pain as empty and unreal.
Both prescribed withdrawal from public life — only the monk or hermit attains the inward peace.
context: Epictetus held suffering comes from judgments about events, not events themselves. The Buddha named tanha — craving — as the second noble truth. They differ on technique: Stoics retrain judgment; Buddhists follow the eightfold path. The distractors are caricatures both schools would reject.

question: A politician's tax plan is criticized only by noting he once cheated on his own taxes. The plan itself goes unaddressed. This move has a Latin name. What is it?
answer: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
choices: Ad hominem — attacking the arguer rather than the argument they made.
Tu quoque — replying that you also fail rather than answering the point.
Red herring — dragging in something unrelated to distract from the issue.
Straw man — attacking a weakened version of the opponent's real claim.
context: Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. A flawed person can still be right; a saint can still be wrong. The argument's truth is independent of who makes it.

question: Someone says trade should be expanded gradually. Their opponent shouts back: 'so you want to ship every job overseas.' The opponent has replaced the real claim with a wilder one. What is this move?
answer: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
choices: Straw man — attacking a distorted version of the opponent's claim.
Red herring — pulling discussion onto a different unrelated topic.
Slippery slope — claiming one step must lead to a disastrous result.
Loaded question — asking something that presupposes a disputed point.
context: A straw man is easier to knock down because you built it. The fix is the steel man: state the opponent's view in its strongest form, then engage that.

question: Socrates fought in three campaigns and once saved Alcibiades in battle. At his trial he insisted philosophy itself was military service. What had he been doing?
answer: Acting as a gadfly stinging a noble horse — keeping Athens awake to its confusions.
choices: Acting as a gadfly stinging a noble horse — keeping Athens awake to its confusions.
Serving as physician of the soul — diagnosing the city's moral sicknesses like Hippocrates.
Working as midwife of ideas — helping citizens deliver truths he himself did not possess.
Standing watchman at the gates — guarding against new gods that would corrupt the virtues.
context: The gadfly image is in the Apology. The horse — Athens — is too big and lazy without its gadfly. The metaphor takes weight knowing Athens killed its gadfly.

question: Plato founded a school outside Athens around 387 BC, on land that had been a grove sacred to a local hero. The grove gave the school its name — now used for every learning institution. What was it?
answer: The Academy — its inscription warned the geometrically untrained not to enter.
choices: The Academy — its inscription warned the geometrically untrained not to enter.
The Lyceum — Aristotle's rival walking-school in the grove of Apollo Lyceus.
The Garden — Epicurus's community, men and women and slaves studying together.
The Stoa — the Painted Porch where Zeno's school took the name Stoicism.
context: Plato's Academy ran in various forms for nearly 900 years before Justinian closed it in 529 AD. Aristotle studied there for twenty years before founding his own rival school nearby.

question: Aristotle was tutor to a 13-year-old prince at the Macedonian court for three years. The boy would later conquer the known world from Greece to the Punjab. Who was the student?
answer: Alexander the Great — who carried Greek language and philosophy from Persia to India.
choices: Alexander the Great — who carried Greek language and philosophy from Persia to India.
Pyrrho of Elis — the skeptic who marched with Alexander and met the Indian sages.
Antisthenes the Cynic — older student of Socrates and ancestor of the Cynic tradition.
Speusippus the Academic — Plato's nephew who took over the Academy after his uncle.
context: Alexander reportedly slept with a copy of the Iliad annotated by Aristotle under his pillow. The young king sent biological specimens back from his campaigns for his old teacher's research.

question: Epictetus had been born a slave in Rome and lived with a permanent limp from his master's cruelty. After manumission, he taught Stoic philosophy in Greece. What did he say his philosophy was for?
answer: Sorting what is in our power from what is not — wanting only what is in our power.
choices: Sorting what is in our power from what is not — wanting only what is in our power.
Rising above attachments of family, city, and reputation — each binds the soul to fortune.
Cultivating the soul's natural impulse toward pleasure — nature shows us what is good.
Sharpening the mind by suspending judgement — tranquility replaces the restless arguing.
context: Epictetus's whole philosophy comes from the moment-by-moment practice of his sorting rule: this — is it up to me, or not? The slave's limp had taught him the rule on his body.

question: Zeno of Citium had been a Phoenician merchant whose ship sank off Greece around 300 BC. Stranded in Athens, he read a book on Socrates and became a philosopher. He founded a school named for where it met. What was it?
answer: The Stoa — the Painted Porch in Athens, source of the name Stoicism.
choices: The Stoa — the Painted Porch in Athens, source of the name Stoicism.
The Garden — Epicurus's suburban plot for cultivating untroubled calm.
The Lyceum — Aristotle's grove of Apollo where students walked while learning.
The Cynics' Tub — Diogenes' wine-jar dwelling in the Athenian marketplace.
context: Zeno's biography became part of his philosophy: a shipwreck turned out to be the best business decision he ever made. Loss had revealed what was actually his — his judgements, and nothing else.

question: Heraclitus called fire the basic stuff of the world, but he meant something stranger than burning logs. What did he say fire was a figure for?
answer: The endless transformation that is reality itself — one unified process behind every visible change.
choices: The endless transformation that is reality itself — one unified process behind every visible change.
An eternal substance that, unlike water or air, can never itself be transformed or destroyed.
The divine spark hidden inside each soul that returns to its source when the body dies.
A physical element more refined than air, condensing downward into all other forms of matter.
context: For Heraclitus, fire is reality's master metaphor: it is never the same flame twice, yet it remains itself. The world burns continuously — what we call 'things' are just the shapes the burning takes for a moment.

question: Heraclitus said the road up the mountain and the road down it are one and the same road. What philosophical claim was this image meant to support?
