answer: Opposites are two aspects of one thing, and the tension between them is what holds the world together.
choices: Opposites are two aspects of one thing, and the tension between them is what holds the world together.
Every path eventually returns the traveler to where they began, since space curves back on itself.
Words like 'up' and 'down' are mere convention; the world itself contains no real directions at all.
Motion is impossible — what looks like a journey is only a string of unconnected stationary moments.
context: Heraclitus called this the 'unity of opposites.' Hot and cold, sleeping and waking, life and death — each pair names one continuous process. Strip away the tension and you would not get peace; you would get nothing at all.

question: Parmenides argued that 'nothing' cannot exist, because the moment you speak of it you have made it into a something. What strange conclusion did he then draw?
answer: Change cannot be real, since change would require a thing to pass into what-is-not, and what-is-not cannot be.
choices: Change cannot be real, since change would require a thing to pass into what-is-not, and what-is-not cannot be.
Matter is made of tiny indivisible particles, and their rearrangement only appears to us as change.
All things are fire transforming endlessly; what looks like stasis is just slow, invisible burning.
Time is something the mind lays over a world that in itself stands wholly outside any sequence.
context: Parmenides bequeathed Western philosophy its first proof — and a baffling one. If 'is not' is unsayable, then nothing can come into being or pass away. The river we see flowing must, behind appearance, be a single unchanging block.

question: Zeno of Elea imagined an arrow in flight. At any single instant, the arrow is not moving — it occupies a space equal to its own length. What was Zeno trying to prove?
answer: If motion is made of motionless instants, then motion itself is impossible — defending Parmenides on change.
choices: If motion is made of motionless instants, then motion itself is impossible — defending Parmenides on change.
Any physical object can be cut in half without limit, so matter has no smallest indivisible building block.
The arrow's path must be determined in advance, so human freedom is an illusion in a fated universe.
Sense-perception fails for fast objects, so we should not trust the eyes about anything in motion at all.
context: Zeno was Parmenides' student, and his paradoxes were arguments by reductio: if you accept that motion is real, you end up with contradictions. The arrow paradox would wait for calculus, 2,200 years later, to be properly dissolved.

question: Pythagoras heard hammers of different weights strike a forge and noticed the sounds formed harmonies. From this he built a sweeping claim about reality itself. What did he conclude?
answer: The deepest structure of reality is mathematical — numbers and ratios, not water or fire, are what things are.
choices: The deepest structure of reality is mathematical — numbers and ratios, not water or fire, are what things are.
The natural world is alive throughout, and even stones carry a faint share of the same soul we have.
Music has a moral effect on the listener, so cities should regulate which scales their citizens hear.
Craft skill arises only by long imitation, so the smith and the philosopher learn in the same way.
context: The hammer story is likely legend, but the insight was real: pluck a string at half its length and you get the octave; at two-thirds, the fifth. Pythagoras took this as proof that whole-number ratios run beneath everything — even the planets, he thought, made music.

question: Pythagoras forbade his followers from eating beans and ordered five years of silence before they could speak in his school. These rules pointed toward what core doctrine?
answer: Souls move from body to body after death, so the body must be purified to ready the soul for its journey.
choices: Souls move from body to body after death, so the body must be purified to ready the soul for its journey.
Knowledge is recovered only by careful logical proof, so disciples must master geometry before speaking.
The gods envy mortal speech, so silence and abstinence are needed to avoid drawing their dangerous notice.
All living beings share one single soul, so eating any plant or animal does harm to the eater's own self.
context: Pythagoras taught metempsychosis — the soul moves from body to body, possibly across species. Diet and silence were spiritual training. He once reportedly stopped a man beating a dog, claiming to recognize the voice of a dead friend in its yelps.

question: Bastiat in 1845 wrote a mock petition from candle-makers begging parliament to block out the sun, whose free light undercut their trade. What was the joke's target?
answer: Any protectionist case that treats a cheaper source of supply as an injury rather than a gain to consumers.
choices: Any protectionist case that treats a cheaper source of supply as an injury rather than a gain to consumers.
Any subsidy from the state to a producer who has not first proven the social usefulness of the trade.
Any law against a private monopoly when the same privilege is freely granted to a politically favored guild.
Any tax on imports that fails to fall in proportion to the buyer's wealth rather than the good's price.
context: The candle-makers complained of a rival who 'floods our market with light at a price ridiculously low.' By demanding parliament shutter every window, Bastiat showed that every tariff argument has the same shape as a war on the sun.

question: Socrates asks Euthyphro: are holy things holy because the gods love them, or do the gods love them because they are holy? Why is the fork uncomfortable?
answer: If divine love makes a thing holy, morality is arbitrary; if the gods see prior holiness, good stands above them.
choices: If divine love makes a thing holy, morality is arbitrary; if the gods see prior holiness, good stands above them.
If gods agreed on holiness, the matter would close; their endless quarrels make every human verdict guesswork.
If holiness is a single thing, every act is wholly holy or not; with degrees, no act is ever fully pious.
If piety is taught at home, each city has its own gods; if known by reason, the gods of all peoples are one.
context: The dilemma is staged outside the courthouse before Socrates' own trial. Either horn costs believers something: divine authorship of morality, or moral standards more fundamental than divinity. Aquinas and later theologians have spent centuries trying to slip between the horns.

question: Friends came to Socrates' cell with a bribed guard and an escape route. He refused. In the Crito, his reason was not courage — something else he owed Athens. What was it?
answer: He had benefited from Athens' laws all his life; breaking them now would undermine the rule he had agreed to.
choices: He had benefited from Athens' laws all his life; breaking them now would undermine the rule he had agreed to.
The gods had arranged the verdict from the start, and a wise man bends to fate rather than fighting its course.
Fleeing would only delay worse punishment from above, since the gods cared more for impiety than for sentencing.
His friends would face certain reprisal once he was gone; no philosopher buys his life with others' suffering.
context: The Crito gives Western political philosophy one of its earliest social-contract arguments. Socrates personifies the Laws of Athens: you ate our bread, raised children under us, stayed when you could have left. To break us is to be the kind of person you've argued against.

question: Socrates compared himself not to a teacher but to a midwife — his mother's trade. He insisted he had no wisdom of his own to deliver. What did the comparison capture about how his questioning worked?
answer: He produced no ideas himself; he drew out what others already believed, then tested whether the belief survived.
choices: He produced no ideas himself; he drew out what others already believed, then tested whether the belief survived.
He worked alongside the one reasoning, sharing the labor of thought as a midwife shared a mother's labor.
He took no payment, just as a midwife served poor women who could not afford a doctor's fees themselves.
He waited for the right moment, as a midwife waited for the body's readiness, never forcing things early.
context: The midwife image runs through the Theaetetus. The Socratic 'I know nothing' is not false modesty: it is the working condition of the method. A midwife who herself gives birth on the labor-room floor cannot help anyone else.

question: The Delphic oracle said no one in Athens was wiser than Socrates. He felt he knew nothing, so he tried to refute the oracle. His conclusion was darker than flattering.
answer: Others reputed wise were as ignorant as he, but did not know it; his only edge was knowing the size of his ignorance.
choices: Others reputed wise were as ignorant as he, but did not know it; his only edge was knowing the size of his ignorance.
Others reputed wise hid real knowledge from the public, fearing what Athens would do if their doctrines became known.
Others reputed wise knew their crafts but not the gods; he knew the gods but had never mastered any craft at all.
Others reputed wise had bought their reputations with money; he, owning nothing, had never sold truth for standing.
context: From the Apology. Socrates kept questioning poets, politicians, craftsmen — each supposed expert collapsed under three follow-up questions. The oracle's verdict, he decided, was not praise of him but a backhanded indictment of everyone else.

question: In Plato's Meno, Socrates walks an uneducated slave boy through doubling a square's area — asking only questions. Plato uses this for a startling conclusion. What is it?
answer: The boy was not learning but remembering; the soul knew the truth before birth, and education recovers what is there.
choices: The boy was not learning but remembering; the soul knew the truth before birth, and education recovers what is there.
The boy was not reasoning but copying; the mind imitates patterns shown to it, so good and bad examples both stick.
The boy was not equal in capacity to a free citizen; what looked like grasp was a trained reflex, not real insight.
The boy was not solving anything himself; Socrates fed every step, and the dialogue made teaching only look real.
context: This is Plato's doctrine of anamnesis — recollection. The soul, having existed before incarnation, has glimpsed the eternal Forms; what we call learning is the slow reawakening of those buried memories. Innate knowledge, two and a half millennia before the modern debate.

question: In Plato's Symposium, Diotima describes love as a ladder. You start with one beautiful body, but the climb forces an unexpected destination. Where does it lead?
answer: Beyond bodies and minds, to Beauty itself — the form everything else has been a partial reflection of all along.
choices: Beyond bodies and minds, to Beauty itself — the form everything else has been a partial reflection of all along.
Beyond mortal attraction altogether, to one god whose perfection makes every human beloved look pale by comparison.
Beyond lover and beloved, to a union of two souls into one — the shared life the highest aim of erotic desire.
Beyond passion into friendship, since steady affection between equals satisfies more than first infatuation can.
context: Diotima's ladder reverses the modern picture of love. Instead of romance as the deepest thing, particular romance is the first rung — the form of Beauty itself is what one is really moving toward, often without knowing it. Plato will not let eros stay small.

question: In Plato's Republic, the soul has three parts — reason, spirit, appetite — and so must the just city. He was not arguing for balance among them. What was his actual claim?
answer: Reason rules, spirit enforces, appetite obeys; injustice is any of the three doing another's work.
choices: Reason rules, spirit enforces, appetite obeys; injustice is any of the three doing another's work.
Reason and appetite negotiate as equals while spirit settles deadlocks between them as needed.
Reason yields to spirit when honor demands and to appetite when the body insists; balance is wisdom.
All three vote as equal partners on every action with mandatory unanimity required before doing it.
context: The Republic argues that 'justice' is the same word for two scales: a person whose reason commands and whose passions obey is just, and so is a city in which philosopher-rulers command and producers obey. A radical claim — political and psychological order are literally the same problem.

question: Plato's ideal city depends on what he calls a 'noble lie' told to every citizen from childhood. What was this lie meant to do?
answer: Convince each class that the gods mixed different metals into their souls at birth, so the social order felt natural.
choices: Convince each class that the gods mixed different metals into their souls at birth, so the social order felt natural.
Convince the rulers that an oracle had chosen them rather than a committee, so power felt granted rather than seized.
Convince the soldiers that the gods watched every battle in person, so they fought from divine fear, not love of city.
Convince the people that an old prophecy promised the city's rise, so hardships felt like the cost of shared destiny.
context: Plato calls it a 'noble' lie (gennaion pseudos), but a lie all the same. The myth of the metals — gold, silver, bronze — sorts citizens into rulers, soldiers, and producers. Karl Popper would later read this as a founding document of authoritarian politics. Plato thought he was preventing tyranny.

question: In Plato's Phaedo, Socrates spends his last hours arguing that his friends should not weep — because death is good. What was his central argument?
answer: The soul is immortal and the body has blocked its view of truth; death frees the soul to know the eternal Forms.
choices: The soul is immortal and the body has blocked its view of truth; death frees the soul to know the eternal Forms.
The soul is fine atoms that escape the body at death and enter a new being shaped by the previous life.
The soul does not survive, but a life of wisdom is already complete; nothing is owed to one who reasoned well.
The soul belongs to the gods, who recall it at the appointed hour; resisting that summons would be impiety.
context: The Phaedo's dying-day setting is part of the argument. Socrates is calm because his philosophy commits him to be — fear of death, on this view, betrays an attachment to embodiment the lover of wisdom should have outgrown long ago. Whether his actual friends were consoled is another question.

question: Aristotle's doctrine of the mean places virtue between two vices — courage between rashness and cowardice. What did he warn was the most common mistake?
answer: Reading the mean as an exact midpoint between extremes, when it is the right amount for this person now — a moving target.
choices: Reading the mean as an exact midpoint between extremes, when it is the right amount for this person now — a moving target.
Reading the mean as the moderate option always, when in real emergencies it is better to overshoot than err on caution.
Reading the mean as something anyone can find, when only the rare wise statesman has standing to identify it for others.
Reading the mean as a rule for actions, when Aristotle meant it for the feelings beneath — emotions must be moderate.
context: Aristotle is explicit: the mean is not 'the same for everyone.' A wrestler eats more than a clerk; the courage of a soldier is not the courage of a child. Mistaking the mean for an arithmetic average has produced centuries of cardboard Aristotelianism.

question: Aristotle said a full explanation needs four causes: material (bronze), formal (shape), efficient (sculptor), final. What did he mean by the fourth?
answer: The end or purpose a thing is for — the goal explaining why it came to be; nature, he held, has goals as well as causes.
choices: The end or purpose a thing is for — the goal explaining why it came to be; nature, he held, has goals as well as causes.
The last event in the chain — the final push that finished the work, set apart from earlier pushes that only partly mattered.
The eternal pattern the thing imitates — the perfect form it strives to match, which alone determines a true example.
The hidden underlying agent — the unseen force behind the others, which philosophy and not observation can reveal.
context: Final causes — telos — are what later science threw out. A stone falls, for Aristotle, because earth seeks its place; for Newton, because of gravity, full stop. Aristotle's purposive universe died slowly, and biology is still arguing about whether it should ever have left.

question: Aristotle called humans the 'political animal' — zoon politikon. This was not about caring for politics. It was a metaphysical claim. What did he mean?
answer: A human apart from the polis is not yet fully human; we complete our nature only in a community of laws and speech.
choices: A human apart from the polis is not yet fully human; we complete our nature only in a community of laws and speech.
A human is factional by instinct; we form parties and rivalries as wolves form packs — politics is unavoidable.
A human is ruled by ambition over other appetites; honor-seeking in public is the single deepest motive we have.
A human only flourishes under good rulers; we are dependent creatures whose virtue rises with the city's leaders.
context: Aristotle's point is steeper than 'humans are social.' Bees are social. He means that without polis — law, deliberation, the back-and-forth of public reason — a human being is not yet what a human being is. A man outside the city, he says, is either a beast or a god.

question: Aristotle's Poetics asks why people pay to watch terrible things on stage. Tragedy, he said, works by katharsis. What was his actual claim about how this works?
answer: The audience feels real pity and fear at safe distance; the experience purges those emotions, leaving viewers calmer.
choices: The audience feels real pity and fear at safe distance; the experience purges those emotions, leaving viewers calmer.
The audience identifies with the hero's choices; learning from his ruin, they leave the theater wiser about pride.
The audience watches the gods enforce moral law; seeing wickedness punished, they grow committed to the city's justice.
The audience sees a craft they cannot do; admiring the artistry, they leave with refined taste rather than feeling.
context: Katharsis is one of the most contested words in ancient philosophy. Aristotle's metaphor is medical — purgation, clearing — not moral. Watching Oedipus tear out his eyes is supposed to drain the audience of an excess they carried in, not to teach a lesson about humility. Theory has been arguing with him ever since.

question: Epicurus wrote out a 'four-part cure' that his followers were told to memorize like a basic medicine. What four fears did he say it dissolves?
answer: Fear of the gods, fear of death, fear that good is unreachable, and fear that pain cannot be borne.
choices: Fear of the gods, fear of death, fear that good is unreachable, and fear that pain cannot be borne.
Fear of poverty, fear of illness, fear that friendship is fragile, and fear that pleasure must be earned.
Fear of error, fear of shame, fear that the world is hostile, and fear that the soul will be punished.
Fear of tyrants, fear of exile, fear that virtue brings danger, and fear that the city cannot be trusted.
context: Epicureans called it the tetrapharmakos — gods are not to be feared, death is not to be felt, the good is easy to get, the terrible is easy to endure. A medicine cabinet for the mind, recited until it became reflex.

question: Lucretius taught that atoms fall through the void. But if every atom fell in perfectly parallel lines, nothing could ever happen. What rescue did he propose?
answer: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
choices: An unpredictable swerve — atoms now and then deviate slightly, so collisions, worlds, and choice become possible.
A guiding intellect — some divine mind nudges atoms into the patterns the visible cosmos requires for order.
A primal vortex — the original whirling motion of matter explains why parallel paths could never have held.
A web of attractions — atoms pull on one another so parallel falling is broken by their natural affinities.
context: The clinamen, or swerve, was Lucretius and Epicurus's most controversial physics. Cicero mocked it as causeless motion. Defenders said it was what saved the universe from a frozen, pointless rain.

question: Epictetus opened his Handbook with a single sorting rule any student had to master first. What were the two boxes he sorted everything into?
answer: Things up to us — judgment, desire, action — and things not up to us, like body, wealth, reputation.
choices: Things up to us — judgment, desire, action — and things not up to us, like body, wealth, reputation.
Things the gods govern — fate, fortune, weather — and things mortals govern, like household, trade, oath.
Things the body suffers — hunger, cold, pain — and things the soul suffers, like envy, grief, longing.
Things one ought to do — duty, oath, care — and things one only might do, like leisure, art, friendly visits.
context: The Stoic dichotomy of control. Epictetus said almost all human misery comes from confusing the two — trying to control what we cannot, neglecting what we can. The slave-born teacher built his whole ethics on this distinction.

question: Marcus Aurelius told himself to picture Rome from far above — rooftops, markets, armies, parties — until everything looked small. What did the Stoics say this was for?
answer: To shrink your private quarrels and ambitions back to their real size against the scale of the whole cosmos.
choices: To shrink your private quarrels and ambitions back to their real size against the scale of the whole cosmos.
To learn the city's geography so that, in a crisis of office, the statesman can move armies without delay.
To prepare the soul for its release at death, when it will look down on the body it has finally left behind.
To detach from politics entirely, since the Stoic sage withdraws from civic life to tend the inner citadel.
context: The Stoics called it the view from above — a deliberate widening of perspective. The trick is that nothing visible from that height stays as urgent as it felt from inside. Modern astronauts have reported the same effect from orbit.

question: Seneca told his friend Lucilius to spend a few minutes each morning rehearsing the day's disasters — shipwreck, exile, a child's death. What was the point?
answer: To rob the worst events of their shock — a misfortune already imagined cuts shallower when it arrives.
choices: To rob the worst events of their shock — a misfortune already imagined cuts shallower when it arrives.
To inspire urgent action — the man who pictures ruin clearly will work harder to keep his household secure.
To purify desire by exposure — naming each loss strips its hold on the mind until none of it pulls anymore.
To appease the unseen powers — by speaking the worst aloud, the wise turn the gods' attention elsewhere.
context: Premeditatio malorum — premeditation of evils. The Stoics thought sudden grief came from unprepared minds, not from the events themselves. A father who has already pictured his child's death does not love the child less; he is just no longer ambushed.

question: The Stoics held that the wise person aims at apatheia. Translators warn this is NOT what English speakers hear in the word. What did Stoics actually mean?
answer: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
choices: Freedom from the destructive passions — fear, greed, rage — not the absence of love, joy, or rational concern.
Withdrawal from civic life — the sage retires from politics entirely to attend solely to the inner citadel.
Total indifference to others — the wise person feels neither pity nor delight at what happens to anyone else.
Calm acceptance of ignorance — the sage suspends judgment on every question that reason cannot fully settle.
context: Modern 'apathy' is a Stoic word with the meaning sandblasted off. The Stoic sage felt friendship, civic duty, and 'good feelings' like rational joy; what they refused were the disordered passions that warp judgment.

question: Crates the Cynic gave away his fortune to live in rags. The aristocrat Hipparchia married him, then joined him sleeping and eating in the open agora. The marriage was a deliberate demonstration. Of what?
answer: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
choices: That a virtuous life and a real marriage need no property, status, or privacy at all.
That a woman could match any man in argument — Hipparchia debating philosophers as proof.
That romantic love is the highest of human goods, exceeding every other claim on a life.
That children belong to all — Cynic adults would raise any offspring as a shared ward.
context: Crates and Hipparchia were ancient Athens's most scandalous philosophical marriage. They lived, ate, and conducted married life openly in the agora — putting Cynic shamelessness (anaideia) on display as a kind of moral demonstration.

question: Diogenes called his routine askesis — training, like an athlete's. He walked barefoot in winter, hugged bronze statues in summer, begged from people he knew would refuse. Why?
answer: To harden the soul against fortune — one who practices loss in small doses cannot be ruined by larger.
choices: To harden the soul against fortune — one who practices loss in small doses cannot be ruined by larger.
To shame the wealthy — public displays of want were calculated insults to the comfortable men of Athens.
To purge the body's gross humors — Cynics held that physical hardship rebalances the soul's physiology.
To gather followers by spectacle — Diogenes was building a school, and theatrical poverty drew the pupil.
context: Cynicism took its name from the Greek for 'dog' — the Cynic lived plainly, like an animal that knows what it really needs. Askesis is the same root the word 'ascetic' grew from, but for the Cynics it was muscle-training for freedom, not piety.

question: Pyrrho went with Alexander's army to India, met local sages, came home with a strange practice: never affirming or denying anything firmly. What followed, he said?
answer: A deep calm settled over him — when no opinion is gripped tightly, no opinion can disturb its holder.
choices: A deep calm settled over him — when no opinion is gripped tightly, no opinion can disturb its holder.
A keen new sight opened — when opinion was set aside, the world appeared as it truly is for the first time.
A close bond with the gods — for Pyrrho, suspending judgment was the only honest worship of beings beyond.
A clear sense of duty — once private opinion fell silent, the voice of common custom alone showed the way.
context: Pyrrho's Skepticism was a therapy, not just an epistemology. Epoche — suspension of judgment — produced ataraxia, untroubled calm. His followers called it the discovery of the Hellenistic age: peace of mind through letting go of all your firm convictions.

question: Epicureans called wealth, fame, and political office 'natural but unnecessary' — or vain and dangerous. One good they treated as essential and worth the trouble. What was it?
answer: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
choices: Friendship — a small circle of close, trusted companions who would stand by you when fortune turned bad.
Family — the household into which one is born sets the lifelong limits of duty, affection, and honor.
Citizenship — the engaged civic life remains the highest training the city offers a soul that wants joy.
Solitude — only the philosopher who withdraws from human company can master the discipline fortune demands.
context: Epicurus's Garden was a community. He wrote that of all the goods wisdom provides for the happy life, by far the greatest is friendship. The garden welcomed women and slaves at a time when neither was welcome in most schools — a fact Romans found suspicious for centuries.

question: Laozi argued that a clay pot, a wheel hub, and an empty room share one feature that makes each one useful. What did he say it was?
answer: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it
choices: The empty space inside — usefulness comes from absence, not from the material surrounding it
The skilled craft of the maker who shapes raw material into a precise and functional form
The natural function of clay, wood, and stone, which determines the purpose each can serve
The harmony between maker and material, achieved when neither dominates the creative act
context: Daodejing Chapter 11. Thirty spokes share one hub: the empty space at the center is what makes the wheel turn. Clay is molded into a vessel: the empty space inside is what holds the water. Doors and windows are cut in a wall: the empty space is what makes the room livable. Laozi was making a general philosophical point — what is absent is often what does the work, and a culture that fixates on what is there will miss what is not there.

question: Laozi wrote that the best ruler is one whose people barely know exists — yet at the end of his reign they look around and say 'we did this ourselves.' He called it wu wei. What kind of rule is it?
answer: Wu wei — accomplishing without forcing; the ruler removes obstacles, the people do the doing.
choices: Wu wei — accomplishing without forcing; the ruler removes obstacles, the people do the doing.
Ren — leading by visible moral example, so subjects watching the ruler are inspired to imitate.
Li — performing each role in the social order with care, sincerity, and the proper deference.
Fa — strict laws applied identically to everyone, holding the state together by force of rule.
context: Daodejing Chapter 17. Laozi's political claim is sharper than it first sounds — he is not endorsing weak government but criticizing the activist ruler who believes constant intervention improves things. Compare the three classical rivals: Confucian li (ritual roles), Confucian ren (moral example), and Legalist fa (strict law). Hayek made a structurally similar argument 2,400 years later.

question: Among the Confucians, the admirable person was the polished scholar — schooled, ritually trained, ornamented by years of study. Laozi pointed to the opposite: pu, the uncarved block of wood. Why was that the higher ideal?
answer: The uncarved block still holds every possibility; the polished scholar has been locked into one shape.
choices: The uncarved block still holds every possibility; the polished scholar has been locked into one shape.
The uncarved block has memorized every text and ritual the tradition has ever produced over time.
The uncarved block has trained each latent talent to its fullest through long, disciplined effort.
The uncarved block has renounced ordinary life and withdrawn entirely from all social attachment.
context: Pu (樸) recurs across the Daodejing (Ch. 15, 19, 28, 32, 37, 57). The block is wood that still holds every possibility because the carver has not yet locked it into one shape. The contrast with the Confucian junzi (cultivated gentleman) is direct. Pu is not anti-skill; it is anti-overshaping.

question: Picture two woodworkers. One fights the grain to force the wood into a court-approved design. The other studies the grain first and lets the shape follow it. Laozi called this second way ziran — not wild instinct, not laissez-faire, but the natural pattern each thing carries within. What does ziran point at?
answer: Each thing has its own pattern of unfolding; wisdom is letting that pattern emerge in yourself.
choices: Each thing has its own pattern of unfolding; wisdom is letting that pattern emerge in yourself.
Each generation should follow inherited custom exactly as the ancestors handed it down.
Each person should return to primitive village life — the small farming community is best.
Each thoughtful person derives conduct from universal principles their reason verifies alone.
context: Daodejing Chapter 25: Dao follows ziran. The term resists clean translation — it does not mean wild nature, nor laissez-faire, nor instinct. Laozi's claim is that each thing has its own pattern of unfolding, and the wise person allows that pattern in themselves rather than overriding it with externally imposed structures.

question: Zhuangzi told of a huge tree whose wood was knotty, twisted, and useless to carpenters — and which therefore lived for centuries while straight trees were cut down. What was his point?
answer: Being useful by other peoples standards can be the surest path to an early destruction
choices: Being useful by other peoples standards can be the surest path to an early destruction
Trees and people both flourish only when shaped to serve a clear and external purpose
Nature gives every creature the form it needs, so worrying about ones own form is foolish
A long life is the highest good, and any conduct that secures it is therefore justified
context: Zhuangzi Chapters 1, 4, and 20 all feature the useless-tree story. The carpenter passes it because the wood is no good for buildings, coffins, or tools — and so the tree survives. Zhuangzi extends the point to people: the talented and ambitious are conscripted, exiled, executed, or worn out, while the apparently useless live out their lives. This is not a counsel of laziness — it is a sharp critique of letting other peoples definitions of value determine your shape. The distractors include the Confucian role-fulfillment view and a Stoic-style natural-form view, both real rivals.

question: Zhuangzi watched fish darting in a stream and said, See how the fish are enjoying themselves. His friend Huizi replied, You are not a fish — how do you know? What was Zhuangzis comeback?
answer: You are not me, so how do you know that I do not know what the fish are enjoying down there
choices: You are not me, so how do you know that I do not know what the fish are enjoying down there
I observed them closely, and the patterns of their movements indicate clear states of pleasure
All conscious beings share the same basic feelings, so inferring fish joy from my own is valid
The Dao flows through fish and humans alike, so what one feels the other must also feel too
context: Zhuangzi Chapter 17, the bridge over the Hao River. Huizi was a logician — the leading representative of the Mingjia, or School of Names — and the two were lifelong sparring partners. Zhuangzi's reply turns Huizi's own skeptical move back on him: if you cannot know what a fish feels because you are not a fish, then you cannot know what I know because you are not me. The exchange is a serious epistemic argument about the limits of skepticism from the outside, and it is also Zhuangzi enjoying himself.

question: Augustine in Confessions recalls stealing pears as a boy. No hunger, no want of the pears, fed them to pigs. What troubled him about the memory?
answer: That he had loved the wrongness of the act for its own sake — proof the will could turn to evil with no good in view.
choices: That he had loved the wrongness of the act for its own sake — proof the will could turn to evil with no good in view.
That bad company had drawn him in, suggesting virtue holds only while the friends a young man keeps prefer it.
That he had judged the orchard's owner unworthy, masking an injustice behind a borrowed principle of justice.
That his appetites had outrun his reason, the lower parts of the soul overturning the higher unless trained.
context: Most thieves want the thing stolen. Augustine kept asking why he, with nothing to gain, had wanted only the offense itself. Not the pears, not the company, not appetite, but love of the deed because it was forbidden. Evil, he concluded, was not always a misguided pursuit of some good.

question: Pressed on how a good God could permit evil, Augustine answered not with God's reasons but with a claim about what evil is. What was his move?
answer: Evil is not a thing but a privation — the absence of a good that ought to be there, as blindness is the absence of sight.
choices: Evil is not a thing but a privation — the absence of a good that ought to be there, as blindness is the absence of sight.
Evil is a force coeternal with the good, the visible world a running battle between two equally real powers.
Evil is a stage in cosmic development, friction by which the good in the long run refines itself toward maturity.
Evil is the soul's punishment for a fall in a prior life, the suffering each meets matching an earlier offense.
context: Augustine had been a Manichaean before his conversion and had taken evil to be a substance, a dark counter-stuff at war with the light. Privation theory was the alternative he settled on: rot is not a thing added to wood but the failing of what wood ought to be. The good is real; evil is the hole in it.

question: Twelve centuries before Descartes, Augustine answered the skeptics who said nothing can be known. He had one fact they could not touch. What was it?
answer: Si fallor, sum — if I am deceived, then I am: the act of doubting requires someone existing to do the doubting.
choices: Si fallor, sum — if I am deceived, then I am: the act of doubting requires someone existing to do the doubting.
That memory cannot lie about its contents, since the act of recalling is itself evidence the recalled occurred.
That moral truths are known by an inner light prior to teaching, a child grasping justice before instruction.
That mathematics holds whether the world exists or not, its truths certain even if every other claim turned false.
context: The Academy in Cicero's day had argued every claim should be suspended. Augustine, in De Civitate Dei XI and earlier in the Soliloquies, pointed out that doubt itself is an act and an act needs an actor. Descartes, who knew his Augustine well, walked the same path 1,200 years later — and the move everyone remembers is the older one's.

question: Kierkegaard described a man at the edge of a cliff. He is not afraid of falling. He is afraid of jumping — of what he could do. Kierkegaard called this anxiety. What did he say it reveals?
answer: Freedom itself — the dizziness of seeing that nothing outside you decides the next step, and you must.
choices: Freedom itself — the dizziness of seeing that nothing outside you decides the next step, and you must.
Original sin inherited — the soul recognizes a primal guilt it carries before any deed it has done itself.
The death drive working — a hidden wish for self-destruction surfaces wherever lethal options lie open.
Mortality at last met — the body knows, before reason does, that one slip would end the life it holds.
context: The Concept of Anxiety (1844) distinguishes anxiety (angst) from fear. Fear has an object: the wolf, the cliff edge. Anxiety has no object — it is the vertigo of facing one's own possibility. Kierkegaard's line: 'Anxiety is the dizziness of freedom.' Later existentialists picked it up: Heidegger's Angst, Sartre's nausea — all descendants of this Danish original.

question: Kierkegaard read Genesis 22 — Abraham with the knife over Isaac. Abraham is not, he insisted, a moral hero. What was his claim?
answer: Faith can suspend the ethical for a higher duty — Abraham obeys God against moral law, and only faith names him innocent.
choices: Faith can suspend the ethical for a higher duty — Abraham obeys God against moral law, and only faith names him innocent.
Abraham was tested by his own conscience — the voice he heard as God was moral law speaking, and obedience was simply reason.
The story dramatizes a stage of Spirit — Abraham figures humanity moving from blood-religion to ethical universality.
Abraham knew the order would be revoked — his trust rested on prior promise, so the act was prudence and no leap at all.
context: Fear and Trembling (1843), under the pseudonym Johannes de Silentio. If Abraham is judged by Kant's universal moral law, he is a would-be murderer. Kierkegaard names what he does the 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — faith places a single individual above the universal in relation to the Absolute. Either Abraham is a knight of faith or he is lost; there is no third option, and the silence of Genesis is the silence of that risk.

question: Dostoevsky's Underground Man rejects the 'crystal palace' — the reformers' idea that a society arranged by reason would make us happy. What does he insist on instead?
answer: The right to act against his own interest — to prove, by spiteful choice, that he is a man and not a piano key.
choices: The right to act against his own interest — to prove, by spiteful choice, that he is a man and not a piano key.
The right to private property — a sphere the rational planners cannot enter, where conscience remains his own affair.
The right to traditional faith — only the inherited ritual of the village church can shield man from the engineer.
The right to revolution — only seizing the palace and remaking it on workers' terms answers the engineer on his ground.
context: Notes from Underground (1864) opens Dostoevsky's mature work. The target is Chernyshevsky's What Is to Be Done? and the broader Russian rational-egoist current, which held that man, properly enlightened about his real interest, will choose it. The Underground Man's reply: even if you proved my interest was X, I would choose not-X, simply to show I am free. The novel inaugurates a century of philosophical fiction.

question: The Grand Inquisitor confronts a silent Christ in 16th-century Seville. The Church, he says, has fixed Jesus's mistake. What was the mistake?
answer: Christ gave humans freedom of conscience — a burden most cannot bear, when bread, miracle, and authority would content them.
choices: Christ gave humans freedom of conscience — a burden most cannot bear, when bread, miracle, and authority would content them.
Christ refused to found an institution — leaving only sayings, when a hierarchy with sacraments was needed to preserve faith.
Christ taught nonviolence — disarming a faith that had to win territory if its message was to outlast a generation.
Christ idealized poverty — embarrassing a Church that needed wealth to feed the poor and build the schools to teach them.
context: Ivan Karamazov's poem within The Brothers Karamazov (1880). The Inquisitor accuses Christ of overestimating humanity. The three temptations in the wilderness — bread, miracle, authority — were the three things Christ refused, and the three things the Inquisitor says the Church has restored, mercifully, against him. Dostoevsky lets the case land at full force; the rebuttal is not argument but the silent kiss Christ leaves on the old man's lips.

question: Plato in the Republic and Confucius in the Analects each tied political order to the ruler's virtue. What did they share?
answer: A polity is shaped by the moral character of those who govern; the inner cultivation of the few orders the many.
choices: A polity is shaped by the moral character of those who govern; the inner cultivation of the few orders the many.
Written law alone, strictly enforced, suffices for order; virtue in the ruler is a private matter without civic effect.
Popular consent alone is the source of legitimacy; the ruler's character matters only insofar as the people approve.
Commerce and contract bind a stable polity; the virtues of rulers matter less than the institutions that constrain.
context: Plato's philosopher-king is just because the soul is rightly ordered; the city mirrors the soul. Confucius held that if the ruler is upright (zheng), the people follow without command. Both make governance an extension of personal cultivation.

question: In Capital I Marx said a wooden table, the moment it became a commodity, 'stands on its head' and seemed to take on a life of its own. What did he name this trick by which objects appear to act?
answer: Commodity fetishism: social relations between people come to take the form of relations between things.
choices: Commodity fetishism: social relations between people come to take the form of relations between things.
Reified abstraction: concrete goods are reduced to a single number, the price, that hides their real qualities.
Productive idolatry: workers come to worship the great machines that produce wealth far in excess of wages.
False consciousness: workers misread their own class interests through the moral concepts of the ruling class.
context: A table is wood and labor. As a commodity it becomes a value comparable, exchangeable, weighed against shoes or hours. Marx's claim was not that commodities are illusions but that the social labor congealed in them comes to look like a power belonging to the things themselves — and the market appears as the rule of objects, not of people.

question: The Buddha asked his monks to look hard for the self. He told them to check five places: body, feeling, perception, mental habits, awareness. What did he claim they would find?
answer: Five shifting processes and nothing else holding them together — no unified self standing behind the five.
choices: Five shifting processes and nothing else holding them together — no unified self standing behind the five.
An eternal soul (atman) shining through each process — the witness whose presence the Vedas had described.
A subtle thinking-stuff (jiva) coloured by karma — the substance the Jains held survived between rebirths.
A ruling faculty (hegemonikon) governing the rest — the inner sovereign the later Stoics would name.
context: The five skandhas (aggregates) analysis appears in the Anattalakkhana Sutta, preached at Sarnath shortly after the Deer Park sermon. The Buddha walks the monks through each aggregate and asks: is this permanent? Under your control? Could a self be this? The argument is close to what Hume would make 2,300 years later — a bundle of perceptions, no perceiver underneath. The Brahmanical, Jain, and Stoic distractors are real rival views actually held by neighbouring traditions.

question: The Buddha taught a twelve-link chain: ignorance to mental shaping, to awareness, to body and mind, on through craving and rebirth. What was the chain meant to show?
answer: Suffering arises from prior conditions, not from a creator or a self — break any link and the chain unwinds.
choices: Suffering arises from prior conditions, not from a creator or a self — break any link and the chain unwinds.
A soul travels intact through twelve stages of purification before its final release from the cycle of rebirth.
Twelve cosmic powers govern human fate, and a sage learns the rituals that appease each in its proper turn.
All events repeat in a fixed twelve-stage cycle, and no human action can alter what is already written down.
context: Pratityasamutpada — dependent origination — is the Buddha's account of how suffering keeps reproducing itself. Each link conditions the next: ignorance > mental formations > consciousness > name-and-form > the six senses > contact > feeling > craving > clinging > becoming > birth > aging-and-death. No first cause, no creator, no continuous self riding the chain — just conditions giving rise to conditions. The transmigrating-soul, twelve-deities, and fatalism distractors are positions Indian traditions actually held; the Buddha is rejecting each.

question: Asked whether the self exists forever after death, the Buddha would not say yes. Asked whether it is destroyed at death, he would not say no. Why did he decline both?
answer: Both questions assume a fixed self in the first place — once that assumption goes, both answers go with it.
choices: Both questions assume a fixed self in the first place — once that assumption goes, both answers go with it.
Both answers could be known only by the gods; a wise teacher does not speculate past direct human experience.
Both views had been argued for centuries without resolution; continuing the dispute only deepened the suffering.
Both claims required mystical insight not yet open to the monks, who needed practice before metaphysics.
context: The Buddha called eternalism (sassatavada) and annihilationism (ucchedavada) the two extreme views, and rejected both as built on the same mistake — assuming a self that could either persist or be destroyed. The move is structural, not evasive: if the entity in the question is fictional, both yes and no smuggle the fiction in. The agnostic, weary, and elitist distractors are common misreadings of the Buddha's silence — each treats the refusal as practical rather than logical.

question: The Buddha framed his teaching as four claims in a specific order. He likened them to a doctor's procedure. What is the structural shape of the four noble truths?
answer: There is a disease, the disease has a cause, the disease admits a cure, and a definite treatment exists.
choices: There is a disease, the disease has a cause, the disease admits a cure, and a definite treatment exists.
There is a god, the god has acted, the god demands response, and a sacred ritual completes the relation.
There is a duty, the duty is universal, the duty admits no exceptions, and reason discovers it on its own.
There is a soul, the soul has fallen, the soul seeks return, and disciplined meditation completes the way.
context: The Buddha's framing in the Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta is medical, not metaphysical: dukkha (symptom), samudaya (cause), nirodha (cessation), magga (prescribed path). Each truth is a claim a doctor might make. The theological, Kantian, and Vedantic distractors are all four-step structures real traditions held — none is the Buddha's. Asking the shape rather than the content (already the §4 exemplar) keeps the question fresh.

question: At Deer Park the Buddha began with a warning. He told the five ascetics that two paths he had himself tried both led nowhere. Which two had he ruled out?
answer: Indulgence in sense pleasure and the harsh self-mortification he had practised with the forest ascetics.
choices: Indulgence in sense pleasure and the harsh self-mortification he had practised with the forest ascetics.
Solitary withdrawal from the world and the busy life of householder duty the Brahmins had recommended.
The path of book-learning prized by the priests and the devotional surrender offered by the bhakti poets.
Speculation about origins and the strict ritual rule-following the early Jains were demanding of devotees.
context: Siddhartha had lived as a prince in pleasure, then for six years had nearly starved himself with five fellow ascetics until his body could barely sit. The Deer Park sermon opens by ruling out both extremes — not as a compromise but because each had failed by its own measure. The middle path (majjhima patipada) names what is left once both fail. The hermit-vs-householder, Brahmin-vs-bhakti, and metaphysics-vs-Jainism distractors are real contemporary disputes — none is the dichotomy the Buddha actually addressed.

question: Nagarjuna used the word emptiness (sunyata) for the central claim of his school. Western readers often hear it as nothingness. What did he actually mean?
answer: Nothing exists with its own independent nature; each thing is what it is only in relation to conditioned others.
choices: Nothing exists with its own independent nature; each thing is what it is only in relation to conditioned others.
Nothing exists in any sense at all; the world that appears to us is a void on which the mind paints illusions.
Nothing physical truly exists; only consciousness is real and matter is a projection it generates from within.
Nothing matters in the long run; since all things pass, attachment to anything is the irrational mistake to undo.
context: Sunyata is Nagarjuna's negation of svabhava — own-being or inherent existence. A chariot has no chariot-nature apart from its parts; a self has no self-nature apart from the aggregates; even emptiness has no inherent emptiness-nature. The point is relational, not nihilistic — Nagarjuna spends much of the Mulamadhyamakakarika defending himself against exactly the nothingness reading the distractor names. The nihilist, idealist, and pessimist distractors are the three misreadings Buddhist and non-Buddhist critics have actually made for eighteen centuries.

question: Berkeley said a tree exists only when perceived. Critics asked what becomes of it unseen. His answer kept idealism from solipsism. What sustains the world?
answer: God perceives the tree continuously — an infinite mind upholds the public world finite minds drop in and out of.
choices: God perceives the tree continuously — an infinite mind upholds the public world finite minds drop in and out of.
Trees persist as permanent possibilities of sensation — patterns yielding experience to anyone correctly placed.
Lesser finite spirits perceive in turn; the cosmos is a federation of many minds, not a single divine one.
Trees are causal powers that keep producing perceptions whether or not any mind currently registers them.
context: Berkeley's God is not a deus ex machina; he is the metaphysical guarantor of an orderly public world. Ronald Knox's limerick captures the move: a tree continues 'since observed by yours faithfully, God.' Mill later proposed 'permanent possibilities of sensation' to do the same job without theism.

question: Nietzsche took a textbook value — pity, guilt, 'good' — and traced it backward to the people who first needed it and what naming it that way bought them. Shabby origins, he warned, do not refute. What did the method show?
answer: That values have a history — descended from particular motives, not justified by reason alone.
choices: That values have a history — descended from particular motives, not justified by reason alone.
That values converge on a single rational law any honest mind will reach by careful argument.
That values are slow refinements of revealed commands, purified by reflection across the ages.
That values arise from a moral sense planted in each human heart at birth by nature or by God.
context: Genealogy was Nietzsche's substitute for the older question 'is this moral claim true?' He asked instead: who first needed this idea, and what did naming it that way accomplish for them? Descent is not refutation — a concept can have shabby origins and still be useful — but the move undoes the air of self-evident rationality that values like 'good,' 'guilt,' and 'pity' carried in the textbooks of his day.

question: In the Genealogy Nietzsche traced 'good' and 'evil' to an event he called the 'slave revolt in morality.' What did he say happened in that revolt?
answer: The powerless inverted the noble vocabulary — calling weakness 'good' and the strong's vitality 'evil.'
choices: The powerless inverted the noble vocabulary — calling weakness 'good' and the strong's vitality 'evil.'
Medieval peasants overthrew aristocratic codes through gradual literacy and the spread of printed books.
The poor united in Christ's name and seized political power from the Roman patricians by force of arms.
Late-antique merchants replaced warrior virtues with bourgeois ones — thrift, prudence, sober dealing.
context: Nietzsche's claim was not biographical about any one priest. He argued that within the world of the Roman empire and the Jewish prophets, a long inversion took place: the values of the strong (noble, beautiful, powerful, fortunate) were re-described from below as marks of evil, and their opposites (meek, suffering, poor) as marks of goodness. Christianity, in his reading, completed and globalized the re-valuation. Whether his history is right is a separate question from what the thesis says.

question: The phrase 'will to power' is regularly read as a license for raw domination. In Beyond Good and Evil §13 Nietzsche stated it as a thesis about life itself. What did he actually claim?
answer: That every living thing seeks first to discharge its strength — and only secondarily to survive.
choices: That every living thing seeks first to discharge its strength — and only secondarily to survive.
That every human carries a hidden drive to dominate weaker people around them, by any means at hand.
That every state, given the chance, expands by force until it is checked by the equal force of a rival.
That every organism is a survival machine — reproduction is the master drive that all else finally serves.
context: Nietzsche wrote against Schopenhauer's 'will to live' and against the Darwinism of his day. Life, he said, is not first the urge to persist but the urge to spend itself — to grow, to overcome resistance, to interpret and shape. Power here is closer to capacity discharged than to domination achieved; a poem and a tyranny can both be its expressions. The Nazi reading, canonized by his sister's edits to the unpublished notes, took the slogan and stripped the philosophy.

question: Nietzsche introduced the eternal recurrence in Gay Science §341 as a demon whispering you will live this life again, infinitely. He did not offer it as cosmology. What was it?
answer: A test of life-affirmation — could you meet the thought with joy, or only with despair at your own life?
choices: A test of life-affirmation — could you meet the thought with joy, or only with despair at your own life?
A proof from physics — that energy is finite and time is endless, so every configuration must return.
A doctrine of fate — that recurrence is real, and human freedom is therefore an illusion we cannot escape.
A claim about memory — that the deepest moments leave traces that recur involuntarily across one lifetime.
context: The demon arrives in solitude. He tells you the spider in the corner, the moonlight, every joy and every pain, will return in the same sequence forever. Would you fall to your knees and curse him, or call him a god? Nietzsche used the thought as a weight — a way to ask whether your present life is one you could will again, in full. The notebooks contain stray attempts at a physical proof; the published philosophy uses recurrence as ethics, not physics.

question: In Gay Science §125 a madman runs into the marketplace at noon with a lit lantern, seeking God. Bystanders laugh — they no longer believe. What was Nietzsche's claim?
answer: The framework grounding modern values was collapsing, but those living within it had not noticed.
choices: The framework grounding modern values was collapsing, but those living within it had not noticed.
Atheists arguing publicly against religion had now successfully refuted the old philosophical proofs.
Secular institutions of Europe had grown strong enough to take over the moral functions of Christianity.
Metaphysics was finished as a discipline — only natural science could yield real knowledge of the world.
context: The bystanders are not believers Nietzsche is mocking. They are the comfortable post-Christians of his own century — keeping the moral furniture (compassion, equality, human dignity) while quietly losing the foundation that held it up. The madman's terror is that no one has yet drawn the long consequence: that severing the root will, in time, reach the branches. 'I come too early,' he says. 'This deed is still on its way.' The diagnosis is of a delay, not a triumph.

question: Twentieth-century regimes seized on the word Übermensch and gave it a racial meaning. What did Nietzsche himself, in Thus Spoke Zarathustra, present the Übermensch as?
answer: A future kind of human who creates new values rather than inheriting them from a dying tradition.
choices: A future kind of human who creates new values rather than inheriting them from a dying tradition.
A biologically superior breed, descended by eugenic selection from the strongest European stock.
A spiritual elite recognized only by other elites, set apart from the corrupting modern crowd.
A philosopher-king after Plato — the wise ruler whose grasp of the Good entitles him to direct the polity.
context: Zarathustra speaks of the Übermensch as a goal that lies ahead of present humanity, the way humanity lies ahead of the ape. The figure is not a race already extant but a possibility for human beings willing to create rather than inherit. The Nazi appropriation — driven heavily by his sister Elisabeth, who edited his Nachlass after his collapse — converted a philosophical aspiration into a racial typology Nietzsche himself, on the textual record, despised. The misreading is not fringe; it shaped the word for a century.

question: Sartre watched a Paris cafe waiter — too precise, too solicitous, performing the role with theatrical exactness. He called this 'bad faith.' What was the man fleeing?
answer: His own freedom — pretending the role chose him, rather than that he chose, each moment, to be a waiter.
choices: His own freedom — pretending the role chose him, rather than that he chose, each moment, to be a waiter.
A dialectical recognition — playing so others would confirm his identity within a master-servant order.
His alienation under capital — he had sold his labor and his bearing, leaving no self that was his own.
His own mortality — busying himself with public chatter to avoid the anxiety that solitude would compel.
context: Being and Nothingness (1943) uses the waiter as the textbook case of 'mauvaise foi.' The man tries to be a waiter the way an inkwell is an inkwell — fixed, with no inner reservation. But Sartre's claim is that consciousness can never coincide with a role; the performance itself proves a free chooser stands behind it, denying his own freedom in the act of denying it.

question: Sartre describes spying through a keyhole, absorbed — then footsteps. Suddenly seen. Shame floods him. What did the footsteps reveal?
answer: That another consciousness was looking — fixing him as object, eavesdropper, in a world he no longer owned alone.
choices: That another consciousness was looking — fixing him as object, eavesdropper, in a world he no longer owned alone.
That his curiosity had broken a Kantian duty — using the watched person as means rather than as end in herself.
That guilt before God had returned — a watcher above renaming his act sin, calling his conscience to a higher court.
That society's reputation game had caught him — his standing in others' eyes would suffer if the tale spread.
context: The keyhole passage in Being and Nothingness sets up 'the look.' Before the footsteps, the spy is wholly absorbed in the scene beyond the door — pure subject. The footsteps install a second consciousness in the world, one that sees him as a thing among things. Shame, for Sartre, is the lived registration of being made an object by another's freedom. Hell, the play would later say, is other people.

question: De Beauvoir agreed with Sartre that freedom is the human condition. Yet she said a woman in 1949 France was not free as a man was. Why?
answer: Freedom is always situated — institutions, custom, and a body marked 'second' set the field on which choice is made.
choices: Freedom is always situated — institutions, custom, and a body marked 'second' set the field on which choice is made.
Freedom is illusion in society — only the solitary mystic, withdrawn from history, escapes the chains others forge.
Freedom is granted by the state — a woman's vote arrived late in France, so the formal freedom itself was missing.
Freedom is a male invention — women possess a different, intuitive faculty for choice that liberal theory misses.
context: The Second Sex (1949) reads existentialism through a feminist lens. Beauvoir kept Sartre's claim that we are condemned to be free; she added that this freedom is always exercised inside a situation that men, on the whole, had spent centuries shaping. 'One is not born, but rather becomes, a woman' is the famous line. Situated freedom is real freedom, with real obstacles — neither nothing nor everything.

question: Once Camus identified the absurd, three exits offered: suicide, the religious leap, and a third. Which did he name the right response?
answer: Revolt — keep both the demand for meaning and the world's silence alive in tension, refusing to dissolve either.
choices: Revolt — keep both the demand for meaning and the world's silence alive in tension, refusing to dissolve either.
Acceptance — school the will, after the Stoics, until it ceases to demand what the indifferent cosmos cannot give.
Resignation — admit reason has failed, withdraw from public striving, and live quietly within the open question.
Faith — recognize, with Kierkegaard, that reason has reached its limit and the leap to God is the only honest move.
context: Camus rejected Kierkegaard's leap as 'philosophical suicide' — answering the absurd by erasing one of its terms. He also rejected literal suicide for the same reason in reverse. Revolt, by contrast, is living in the contradiction. Sisyphus rolls the stone, sees the stone roll back, and rolls it again — conscious, unreconciled, and (Camus insists) we must imagine him happy.

question: Anselm defined God as that than which no greater can be conceived. A monk named Gaunilo replied with a perfect island. What was Gaunilo trying to show?
answer: The same move would conjure a perfect island into being; so the recipe overproduces and must be wrong.
choices: The same move would conjure a perfect island into being; so the recipe overproduces and must be wrong.
The mind cannot truly conceive a maximal being; the words name nothing the intellect actually holds in view.
Existence is not a real predicate; saying a thing exists adds no greatness to the concept of that thing.
Faith comes before reason; arguments cannot reach what only prayer and grace disclose to a finite mind.
context: Gaunilo's reply (in 'On Behalf of the Fool') ran the ontological argument against itself: if greatness implies existence for a being, the parallel argument should yield a perfect island. Anselm answered that islands have no maximum greatness; only a maximally perfect being does. The dispute is alive a thousand years later.

question: Pascal's Wager is often caricatured. In the 'Pensées' he in fact argues from a specific decision-theoretic structure. What is the actual shape of his argument?
answer: Reason cannot settle the question; under genuine uncertainty, the expected payoff of believing dominates.
choices: Reason cannot settle the question; under genuine uncertainty, the expected payoff of believing dominates.
Reason can prove a first cause; from there, ordinary inference yields the God of revelation by short steps.
Reason discloses moral law; only a divine lawgiver can ground it, so belief is the price of taking ethics seriously.
Reason confirms revelation; the historical evidence for miracles is strong enough to make belief more probable.
context: Pascal grants that proofs of God's existence are inconclusive — that is his premise, not a weakness. The move is then decision-theoretic: finite cost on one side, possibly infinite gain on the other, the expected-value calculation tilts. The 'many gods' objection (which God to wager on?) is the most serious modern reply, alongside worries about whether belief can be willed at all.

question: A child drowns in a shallow pond. Wading in would ruin your shoes. Singer's 1972 argument runs through that scene to a startling global conclusion. What is the load-bearing premise?
answer: If we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we are obligated to.
choices: If we can prevent something bad without sacrificing anything of comparable moral importance, we are obligated to.
Inaction in the face of preventable harm makes us causally responsible; failing to act equates morally with causing.
Each person's obligation scales with their resources, talents, and prior contribution to the harm at hand.
Suffering at any distance imposes the same duty as suffering in front of us, provided we know and can act on it.
context: 'Famine, Affluence, and Morality' rested on a deceptively modest principle: if we can prevent a bad thing at no comparable moral cost, we ought to. The shallow-pond scene was an intuition pump to win assent to the premise; once accepted, the demanding global conclusion followed. Distractor B is the act/omission collapse some critics charge Singer with; C is a desert-based rival; D restates the conclusion as if it were the premise (a common student confusion).

question: Avicenna asked his reader to imagine a man created fully grown, floating in empty air, blindfolded, limbs apart. What did he claim such a man would still know?
answer: That he himself exists — self-awareness needs no body, no sensation, no memory to ground it.
choices: That he himself exists — self-awareness needs no body, no sensation, no memory to ground it.
That a creator must exist — the gift of consciousness so plainly given points beyond him to its source.
That nothing at all exists — without input from the senses, every claim about an outside world collapses.
That space and time exist — even cut off from body, the floating man still finds himself extended in both.
context: Six centuries before Descartes ran a similar argument, Ibn Sina used the Floating Man to argue the soul knows itself directly, without help from senses or body. The thought experiment appears in the Kitab al-Shifa and remains one of medieval philosophy's most striking arguments for an immaterial self.

question: The sentence 'This sentence is false' looks innocent. If it is true, then it is false; if false, then true. What does the liar paradox specifically break?
answer: The classical assumption that every meaningful sentence has exactly one stable truth-value, true or false.
choices: The classical assumption that every meaningful sentence has exactly one stable truth-value, true or false.
The grammatical rule that a sentence cannot use the word 'sentence' to talk about its own internal structure.
The empirical principle that any claim worth examining must be checkable against some observation of the world.
The psychological habit of supposing that a careful reader will reach the same conclusion as any other reader.
context: The liar puts pressure on bivalence — the principle that every proposition is true or false. Tarski responded by banning self-reference: truth must live in a higher language than the sentences it judges. Dialetheists like Graham Priest answer instead that the liar is genuinely both, and logic must learn to live with it.

question: A village barber shaves every man who does not shave himself, and only those men. Does the barber shave himself? Russell's puzzle of this form destroyed what?
answer: Naive set theory — the assumption that any property at all defines a set of the things having it.
choices: Naive set theory — the assumption that any property at all defines a set of the things having it.
Aristotle's syllogistic logic, which could not represent statements involving more than one quantifier at a time.
Hilbert's formalism — the program of proving every mathematical truth from a finite list of stated axioms.
Boolean algebra, by showing that 'and' and 'or' cannot be defined without already presupposing each other.
context: Frege had nearly finished his life's work deriving arithmetic from logic when Russell's letter arrived in 1902. The set of all sets that do not contain themselves both contains itself and does not. Naive set theory died that day. Zermelo, Fraenkel, and others rebuilt the foundations with stricter rules about which collections count as sets at all.

question: One grain is not a heap. Adding a grain to a non-heap cannot make one. So no number of grains is a heap. What does sorites expose?
answer: That many ordinary concepts have vague borders, and tiny changes cannot be ruled out where the borders fall.
choices: That many ordinary concepts have vague borders, and tiny changes cannot be ruled out where the borders fall.
That arithmetic itself is unreliable, because adding small numbers eventually fails to produce a large number.
That the senses are illusions, since a pile we can clearly see may turn out not to fit any concept we hold.
That language is purely a private code, so any two speakers may simply mean different things by 'heap.'
context: Sorites means 'heap' in Greek. Wang's paradox sharpens the move: if a number is small, its successor is small too — so every number is small. Some philosophers respond with epistemicism (there is a precise boundary, hidden from us), others with degree-theoretic logics where 'heap' admits values between 0 and 1.

question: A teacher promises a surprise exam next week — surprise meaning the day cannot be predicted. The students reason that no day works. What does this show?
answer: Self-referential predictions can undermine themselves: a claim about being unpredictable becomes predictable.
choices: Self-referential predictions can undermine themselves: a claim about being unpredictable becomes predictable.
Backward induction is invalid in any setting where future agents hold private information about each other's plans.
Promises about future actions never bind, because circumstances may always change before they come due in fact.
Teachers and students apply incompatible probability rules, so no shared expectation can ever form between them.
context: Rule out Friday — by Thursday night the students would know. So rule out Thursday — same reason. The chain rolls back to Monday, and no day is possible. Yet the exam happens on Wednesday and surprises everyone. The paradox sits at the joint of knowledge, prediction, and self-reference; Quine and Kripke both wrote on it.

question: Achilles races a tortoise given a head start. When he reaches where it was, it has crept on; reaching that spot, it has crept again. What does Zeno argue?
answer: Motion through continuous space is incoherent: reaching any point requires completing infinite sub-distances.
choices: Motion through continuous space is incoherent: reaching any point requires completing infinite sub-distances.
Faster runners hold an unfair natural advantage, so any 'fair' race should give the slower runner a head start.
Observation deceives us: the eye smooths over a world that is actually composed of separate static jump-frames.
Space and time are only mental constructs, and the apparent footrace happens entirely inside the observer's mind.
context: Zeno was Parmenides' student, and his paradoxes were weapons. If the world really is many and moving, you can decompose any journey into infinitely many sub-journeys and never finish. Calculus, much later, showed that infinite sums can converge to a finite total — but the philosophical puzzle about continuity and completion is still discussed.

question: Hobbes described life outside a sovereign authority with a famous list of five adjectives. Which set did he use?
answer: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short — a life of constant fear in the war of all against all.
choices: Solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short — a life of constant fear in the war of all against all.
Equal, free, peaceful, simple, and pious — a state Rousseau later thought modern men had ruined.
Cruel, lawless, hungry, fierce, and proud — a savagery only a wise lawgiver could ever discipline.
Open, equal, hardy, plain, and just — Locke's picture of natural reason guiding men before kings.
context: Hobbes's Leviathan (1651) imagined people roughly equal in strength and ambition, with no common power above them. The result was perpetual war, not because men were monsters, but because rational fear of being attacked first made attack itself rational. Only an absolute sovereign could break the spiral.

question: Shankara used the image of a rope mistaken for a snake at dusk. The lamp arrives, the snake vanishes, the rope was there all along. What was his argument?
answer: Plural appearance is misperception of a single underlying reality — what dissolves under analysis was never quite real.
choices: Plural appearance is misperception of a single underlying reality — what dissolves under analysis was never quite real.
Perception is reliable but partial; the sage's task is to assemble partial views into the picture none alone gives.
The world flickers in and out of being moment by moment, sustained only by divine attention re-creating it.
Sense and object share the same stuff, so things are real, but only for whoever happens to perceive them.
context: Shankara, Brahma-Sutra-Bhashya, adhyasa-bhashya. The rope-snake (rajju-sarpa) is the central Advaita analogy. The snake is real enough to make you jump — Shankara calls this vyavaharika reality — but it is not what is there. Distractors are perspectivism, Ash'arite occasionalism, and Berkeleyan idealism.

question: Mencius asked readers to imagine seeing a child about to fall into a well. Any person, he said, would feel a sudden pang. What did this prove?
answer: Human nature carries innate moral sprouts; the pang shows compassion is original to us, not calculated from interest.
choices: Human nature carries innate moral sprouts; the pang shows compassion is original to us, not calculated from interest.
Human nature is shaped by upbringing alone; the pang is residue of training the parents and village impressed.
Human nature is at root self-interested; the pang is reputation-seeking, dressed in the costume of sudden feeling.
Human nature mirrors the Dao's spontaneous patterning; the pang is unforced response of the unconditioned mind.
context: Mencius's thought experiment (2A6) cuts off escape routes. The witness has no time to court the parents' praise, no neighbors to win, no acquaintance with the child. Yet the pang comes. From it, Mencius read off something about what we are.

question: From the well-child pang, Mencius generalized to four 'sprouts' (siduan) every person shares. What did he claim these sprouts were?
answer: Beginnings of four virtues — humaneness, rightness, ritual sense, and wisdom — innate but needing cultivation to mature.
choices: Beginnings of four virtues — humaneness, rightness, ritual sense, and wisdom — innate but needing cultivation to mature.
Stages each soul moves through toward enlightenment, like the four meditative absorptions taught by the Buddha.
Four roles within the family — father, son, elder brother, younger brother — from which wider bonds are drawn.
Four temperaments fixed by one's balance of qi at birth, determining which virtues each person can ever attain.
context: The siduan (2A6) are seeds, not finished plants. Compassion is the sprout of ren; shame of yi; deference of li; the sense of right and wrong of zhi. A seed needs soil, water, time. Nature gives the start; cultivation completes it.

question: A monk asked Zhaozhou whether a dog has buddha-nature. Zhaozhou replied, "Mu." Generations sat with this syllable. What were they meant to do with it?
answer: Press the question until conceptual thinking exhausts itself — the answer sought is the collapse of the yes-no frame.
choices: Press the question until conceptual thinking exhausts itself — the answer sought is the collapse of the yes-no frame.
Defend a measured no with scriptural citation — the trainee who could marshal sutras best had passed the test.
