Settle the metaphysical fact about dogs — the student had to rule that buddha-nature was present or absent.
Recite the syllable as a protective formula — the chanted sound itself purifies karma over time.
context: Gateless Gate, Case 1. Mahayana doctrine says all beings have buddha-nature, so a flat yes would be correct and useless. Mu refuses the yes-no slot itself. The koan is not a riddle with a hidden answer; it is a wedge driven into the habit that questions like this admit clean propositional answers. The scholastic, metaphysical, and mantric distractors are real Buddhist uses of language Chan is pushing against.

question: The Japanese Zen master Dogen coined the word uji — usually rendered 'being-time.' He insisted the dash mattered: being and time are not two separate things that meet, like a pine standing still while a clock ticks past. What did Dogen claim instead?
answer: The pine is not a being inside time; the pine's standing IS its piney-timing — no still being underneath on which time falls.
choices: The pine is not a being inside time; the pine's standing IS its piney-timing — no still being underneath on which time falls.
Time is the moving image of an unmoving eternity — beings rise and fall in it but eternity itself does not enter time.
Time is a form the mind imposes on experience — beings in themselves stand outside it and we have only filtered access.
Time is the measure of motion against the heavens — beings have their own substance and time is the count we keep.
context: Shobogenzo, Uji fascicle (1240). Dogen pushes against the picture where beings stand on one side, a time-line on the other, and the beings pass through. He claims the picture is wrong: the spring is its springing-time. Distractors are real rival theories of time — Platonic-Plotinian eternity, Kantian form of intuition, Aristotelian measure of motion. Each is held seriously; none is Dogen's.

question: Spinoza's Ethics drives at one shocking phrase: Deus sive Natura — God or Nature. What does the identification claim?
answer: God and the universe are one substance; nature is not made by a creator but is itself the divine, viewed in all aspects.
choices: God and the universe are one substance; nature is not made by a creator but is itself the divine, viewed in all aspects.
God made the universe but stands distinct from it; nature shows his mind without being his being, as art shows an artist.
God is the soul that pervades nature; matter is his outward garment, hiding the divine person dwelling within all things.
God hides behind nature as its first cause; the world is a screen, and what lies behind it cannot be reached by reason.
context: Spinoza was excommunicated from the Amsterdam synagogue in 1656 for views the elders found scandalous, and Christian neighbors thought no better. Deus sive Natura — "God or Nature" — said God is not a person beyond the world but the single substance of which the world is the modes. Pantheism, his critics called it; one substance, he called it.

question: Kant said one rule tests any moral choice: could you will the maxim of your act to be a universal law? What does it do?
answer: Asks if all could act on the rule without contradiction — lying promises fail because none would trust promises if all lied.
choices: Asks if all could act on the rule without contradiction — lying promises fail because none would trust promises if all lied.
Asks if the act produces good consequences — the right rule is whichever brings the greatest happiness across the world.
Asks if one's peers would approve the act — the moral law rests on the customs of a nation and the judgment of citizens.
Asks if the act fits God's revealed will — the moral law is divine command, known through scripture and conscience.
context: Kant's first formulation of the Categorical Imperative is a test of self-consistency, not of outcomes. If everyone tried to make a lying promise, the practice of promising would collapse — so the rule undoes itself when universalized. The moral law, Kant said, is what reason alone, stripped of inclination, demands of any rational being.

question: James told of campers fighting over a squirrel: a man circles a tree, the squirrel scurries opposite. Does he go around the squirrel?
answer: No answer until you fix what "around" means; with one sense yes, with the other no — pragmatism dissolves the dispute.
choices: No answer until you fix what "around" means; with one sense yes, with the other no — pragmatism dissolves the dispute.
A real answer in nature exists; only study of how the squirrel rotates tells which side faces the man in each moment.
No real answer is possible; the dispute shows ordinary language fails to track real motion — wiser to stay silent.
A clear yes; geometry guarantees that walking a full circle round any object means encircling it, whatever it does.
context: From Pragmatism, Lecture 2 (1907). James returned from a hike to find his friends quarreling — the squirrel always kept the trunk between itself and the man, so was the man going around it? James said: depends what you mean. "Around" can mean "reaching each compass-point in turn" (yes) or "facing each side of the squirrel in turn" (no). The dispute evaporates once you ask what difference each meaning makes.

question: Pascal said since reason cannot prove whether God exists, we must wager — one side is plainly the smarter play. Why?
answer: Bet on God: if right, you gain infinite reward; if wrong, you lose finite pleasures only — the expected payoff is infinite.
choices: Bet on God: if right, you gain infinite reward; if wrong, you lose finite pleasures only — the expected payoff is infinite.
Bet against God: belief costs the honesty of accepting what reason cannot prove, and honest doubt is itself a moral good.
Bet on neutrality: stay open, since taking either side without evidence stains the mind and closes off honest inquiry.
Bet on tradition: side with the church of one's fathers, since habit and culture supply reasons that pure logic cannot.
context: Pascal — a founding figure of probability theory — applied expected-value reasoning to belief in the Pensées (published 1670, after his death). Finite cost, possible infinite gain: the math, he argued, makes the wager one-sided. Critics from Voltaire onward replied that one cannot make oneself believe by calculation, and that an infinite-stakes argument works for any god one cares to invent.

question: Someone says: 'If we lower the drinking age to 18, next it'll be 16, then 14, then toddlers ordering beer.' Each step is treated as inevitable, with no reason given. What is this fallacy?
answer: Slippery slope — asserting one step must trigger a cascade without showing why each step must follow the previous one.
choices: Slippery slope — asserting one step must trigger a cascade without showing why each step must follow the previous one.
False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions available is in fact substantially wider.
Hasty generalization — drawing a sweeping conclusion from a single case or a sample too thin to support the claim.
Appeal to consequences — claiming a position must be false because its truth would lead to unwelcome outcomes.
context: Slippery-slope arguments can be valid if you give reasons each step really does cause the next. The fallacy is asserting the chain without showing it.

question: A talk-show host says: 'Either you back our entire foreign policy or you hate this country.' Two options where the real range is much wider. What is this move?
answer: False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions is broader and includes serious alternatives.
choices: False dichotomy — framing only two options when the real range of positions is broader and includes serious alternatives.
Loaded question — asking something whose form presupposes a controversial claim the listener has not yet agreed to.
Equivocation — using one word in two senses inside one argument, so the inference depends on a hidden shift in meaning.
Begging the question — assuming the conclusion in one of the premises, so the argument moves in a small circle.
context: Also called the black-and-white fallacy. The cure: ask whether a third (or fourth) option has been hidden.

question: After a vaccine campaign expands, autism diagnoses rise. Headlines conclude the vaccine caused the rise. The two events did happen in sequence. What is this error?
answer: Post hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding B was caused by A just because B followed A, without ruling out other causes.
choices: Post hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding B was caused by A just because B followed A, without ruling out other causes.
Cum hoc ergo propter hoc — concluding one thing caused another because both happen together, when both share a third cause.
Texas sharpshooter — drawing the target around the bullet holes after firing, finding chance patterns and calling them real.
Hasty generalization — leaping to a sweeping conclusion from a single anecdote or sample too thin to support the claim.
context: Diagnostic criteria for autism widened in the same window vaccine programs expanded — the rise is real, but the cause is largely better identification. Correlation is not causation.

question: Someone argues God exists because the Bible says so, and the Bible is reliable because it is the word of God. The reasoning loops. The conclusion is buried inside the premise. What is this called?
answer: Begging the question — assuming what you are supposed to prove inside one of your premises, so the argument moves in a circle.
choices: Begging the question — assuming what you are supposed to prove inside one of your premises, so the argument moves in a circle.
Appeal to authority — backing a claim by citing an expert's say-so instead of the reasons the expert would give for it.
Equivocation — using one key term in two senses inside one argument, so a step that looks valid trades on shifting meaning.
False dichotomy — framing options as a forced choice between two when the actual range of positions is much broader.
context: Also called petitio principii. The phrase 'begs the question' in everyday speech now usually means 'raises the question' — but in logic it remains this circular move.

question: An opponent points out a cereal claiming to be healthy contains massive sugar. The reply: 'no true Scotsman cares about sugar.' The reply redefines the group. What is this?
answer: No true Scotsman — narrowing a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample, saving the claim by definition.
choices: No true Scotsman — narrowing a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample, saving the claim by definition.
Equivocation — sliding between two senses of one key word inside one argument, so a step that looks valid rests on a hidden shift.
Special pleading — exempting a favored case from a general rule without giving a principled reason why this case is different.
Tu quoque — replying to a criticism by pointing out the critic also fails, rather than engaging whether the criticism is correct.
context: Antony Flew named the move from an imagined Scotsman who insists no true Scot puts sugar in his porridge — then, faced with one who does, says no TRUE Scot would.

question: An argument runs: 'Feathers are light. What is light cannot be dark. So feathers cannot be dark.' The form looks tight, but one word shifts meaning between lines. What is this fallacy?
answer: Equivocation — using one key word in two senses across premises, so an argument looks valid only because the meaning quietly shifted.
choices: Equivocation — using one key word in two senses across premises, so an argument looks valid only because the meaning quietly shifted.
Composition — assuming what is true of each part of a whole must also be true of the whole, when wholes and parts can differ.
Amphiboly — exploiting a sentence's grammatical ambiguity, where one reading supports the conclusion and the other does not.
Division — assuming what is true of a whole must also hold of every part, when whole-properties need not transfer to pieces.
context: 'Light' shifts from 'low in weight' to 'bright.' Equivocation is the engine of most word-puzzle paradoxes and a surprising number of bad political arguments.

question: Plato's Republic ends with the Myth of Er — souls between lives choose their next existence from a heap of lots. The souls who chose worst had been the most virtuous in the life just past. Why?
answer: Virtue gained by habit alone is fragile — a soul that has not understood why goodness matters will grab a tyrant's life from greed.
choices: Virtue gained by habit alone is fragile — a soul that has not understood why goodness matters will grab a tyrant's life from greed.
Virtue practiced in one life carries no weight in the next — every soul restarts from scratch, so moral progress across lives is impossible.
Virtue is rewarded with privileged choice — souls who lived best get first pick, while the wicked must draw last from what is left.
Virtue chooses for itself — a soul that has lived well finds the next life already determined by the character it has formed.
context: The Republic argues philosophy is the only education that holds across lives. The previously virtuous in the myth had been GOOD without UNDERSTANDING good — and so could not recognize the trap.

question: Aristotle thought the cosmos contained a peculiar entity needed to explain why anything moves at all — yet which itself never moved. What did he call this, and why required?
answer: The Unmoved Mover — pure activity drawing all motion toward itself the way a beloved draws the lover.
choices: The Unmoved Mover — pure activity drawing all motion toward itself the way a beloved draws the lover.
The Demiurge — a divine craftsman who shaped chaotic matter, working from the Forms as from a model.
The Active Intellect — a cosmic mind thinking all universal truths, letting human minds abstract forms.
The World Soul — a living principle pervading the cosmos, animating heavens and individual organisms.
context: Aristotle's Unmoved Mover is famously thought-thinking-itself — pure self-contemplation. The medievals inherited the idea and identified it with the God of Genesis, with consequences for theology that lasted centuries.

question: Plato pictured the world we see as a shadow of a deeper reality. Just acts only imperfectly imitate Justice itself; beautiful things only imitate Beauty itself. What did he call these higher realities the visible world copies?
answer: The Forms — eternal, perfect, unchanging archetypes apart from the physical world, the real objects of knowledge.
choices: The Forms — eternal, perfect, unchanging archetypes apart from the physical world, the real objects of knowledge.
The Numbers — eternal mathematical principles structuring the physical world from outside, the source of harmony.
The Atoms — eternal, indivisible, unchanging bits of matter moving through void, the smallest constituents.
The Categories — fundamental, irreducible kinds of being into which any existing thing must fall.
context: The Forms are Plato's solution to the one-over-many problem: why do many different beautiful things all count as beautiful? Because they all participate in the one Form of the Beautiful.

question: Bastiat told of a shopkeeper whose son broke a window. Neighbors said it was good news — the glazier got work. Bastiat said the argument missed a step. What did he say we should also count?
answer: The shoes the shopkeeper would have bought instead — the seen gain hides an unseen loss of equal weight.
choices: The shoes the shopkeeper would have bought instead — the seen gain hides an unseen loss of equal weight.
The glazier's profit was already promised by the shopkeeper's plan to commission new shelves the next month.
The boy's discipline, since unpunished destruction trains the rising generation in the habits of casual mischief.
The glazier's customers downstream, since his new earnings travel through the village in a series of small gains.
context: Bastiat called this the seen and the unseen — the first lesson of economics. Every public sum requires adding what was *not* done because resources went elsewhere. Stimulus by breakage is no stimulus; it is a transfer with a smashed window thrown in.

question: Jefferson wrote, 'I tremble for my country when I reflect that God is just.' What was the danger he had in mind?
answer: That the moral arithmetic of slavery would catch up with the nation that practiced it, and the bill would come due in blood.
choices: That the moral arithmetic of slavery would catch up with the nation that practiced it, and the bill would come due in blood.
That without strict religious establishment the people would lose the virtue any free republic needs to keep itself standing.
That European powers would punish the colonies for taking liberties their own subjects were forbidden from claiming at home.
That commercial wealth would dissolve the simple habits of the citizen-farmer the new constitution had presupposed.
context: The line is from Notes on the State of Virginia, in a passage about slavery. Jefferson owned slaves; the contradiction between his words and his life is a famous American wound. The line endures because he saw the wound, said so in writing, and could not bring himself to act on what he had seen.

question: Hume in 1748 examined reports of miracles. He did not argue they cannot happen. He argued something subtler about when a witness should be believed.
answer: No testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event the witness reports.
choices: No testimony suffices unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event the witness reports.
No testimony suffices unless several independent witnesses have agreed on the same observation without prior contact.
No testimony suffices unless the witness has nothing to gain from the report being widely believed by others.
No testimony suffices unless the reported event is corroborated by a written record made at the moment it happened.
context: Enquiry §10. Hume weighs the prior improbability of any miracle against the likelihood that humans deceive or are deceived; the second is almost always greater.

question: Kant divided judgments into analytic ('bachelors are unmarried' — true by meaning) and synthetic (true by how the world is). He then announced a strange new class. What was it?
answer: Synthetic a priori — judgments that add real content yet hold necessarily, like the mathematical truth that 7 plus 5 is 12.
choices: Synthetic a priori — judgments that add real content yet hold necessarily, like the mathematical truth that 7 plus 5 is 12.
Analytic a posteriori — judgments true by meaning yet learned through experience, like discovering that water turns out to be H2O.
Empirical a priori — judgments confirmed by observation yet known in advance, like the geometric facts about visible circles drawn on paper.
Synthetic a posteriori — judgments that add real content learned from the world, like the historical fact that Napoleon lost at Waterloo.
context: Critique of Pure Reason, Introduction. The synthetic a priori was Kant's great innovation — and Quine's main target in 'Two Dogmas of Empiricism' (1951).

question: Heraclitus wrote: 'character is destiny.' The slogan is famous but the philosophical claim is sharper than it sounds. What was he asserting against older Greek views?
answer: Your fate flows from the inner stamp of your own settled disposition — not from gods or fortune, but from the soul you have shaped.
choices: Your fate flows from the inner stamp of your own settled disposition — not from gods or fortune, but from the soul you have shaped.
Your fate is locked in by divine decree before birth — the gods assign a life-pattern no human effort can ever change in any case.
Your fate is set by social standing — birth into family, city, or trade decides outcomes; character only adjusts how the fate is borne.
Your fate is fixed by the cosmic stars — heavenly bodies at the moment of birth imprint a destiny astrology learns to read.
context: Fragment B119, ethos anthropoi daimon. Heraclitus turned daimon — usually 'guiding spirit' — inward. The line shaped Aristotle's character ethics and Stoic moral psychology.

question: Parmenides' poem has two parts. The Way of Truth — reality is one and unchanging. The Way of Opinion follows. What odd role did Parmenides give the second part?
answer: A best-possible map of the appearances mortals must navigate — false at root, yet ordered, so the philosopher would not be tricked by folk talk.
choices: A best-possible map of the appearances mortals must navigate — false at root, yet ordered, so the philosopher would not be tricked by folk talk.
A genuine second domain of reality alongside the unchanging one — the changing world of opinion was as real, just known by another faculty.
A polemical attack on rival cosmologies of his predecessors — Parmenides walked through Milesian and Pythagorean accounts to expose them.
A series of religious revelations from the goddess narrating the poem — the second part conveyed mysteries reserved for Eleatic initiates.
context: Fragments B8–B19. The Way of Opinion gave detailed cosmology — light, night, heavenly bodies. The plausible reading: useful fiction for the world we inhabit anyway.

question: Seneca wrote to his friend Lucilius about the one resource humans waste most freely. Money is hoarded; time is not. He pressed a particular point about everyday delays.
answer: Postponing real living until a more convenient moment — 'we shall live tomorrow,' Seneca wrote, while the only hour we ever own slips past.
choices: Postponing real living until a more convenient moment — 'we shall live tomorrow,' Seneca wrote, while the only hour we ever own slips past.
Spending the best years on building up wealth — Seneca counseled early retirement from business so vigorous decades could go to study.
Wasting attention on news from distant cities — Seneca urged friends to ignore the constant chatter of gossip that consumed hours uselessly.
Letting the rich eat our days with duty visits — Seneca complained the Roman patron-client system stole the best hours in morning calls.
context: Letters to Lucilius, especially Letter 1 (On Saving Time). Time is the one possession even the powerful cannot recover. Montaigne, Pascal, and modern self-help all drew on the book.

question: Anaximander rejected his teacher Thales' claim that everything is made of water. He argued the basic stuff could not be any familiar substance at all. What was his reasoning?
answer: If one element were basic, it would have already overwhelmed the others; so it must be something boundless.
choices: If one element were basic, it would have already overwhelmed the others; so it must be something boundless.
Water, fire, earth, and air are made of atoms, so none of them can itself be the simplest building block.
Familiar substances are real only when perceived, so basic stuff must be something a mind cannot witness.
All four elements transform into one another, so each is only a passing phase of a single hidden element.
context: Anaximander called it the apeiron — the 'boundless.' If water were primary, the world would already be drowned in it; if fire, burned up. Something with no specific qualities must lie beneath the qualities we see. He had reasoned his way to a placeholder for what no eye could see — and he was the first to try.

question: Tocqueville called the New England township the school of American self-government. A citizen who had only voted for a president, he warned, would be helpless. Why?
answer: Liberty as a skill is learned by handling concrete matters close by; distant choices teach almost none of it.
choices: Liberty as a skill is learned by handling concrete matters close by; distant choices teach almost none of it.
Federal elections turn on questions no ordinary voter has the time or specialist knowledge to judge well.
National politics inflames the passions; local matters cool them and let reason take its proper place.
Voting for a president grants symbolic dignity; real freedom requires owning the productive land one farms.
context: For Tocqueville the township was a schoolroom. Citizens argued about the road, the schoolhouse, the constable, and so learned the unglamorous arts of compromise that make a free people. A republic without local life would still have ballots — but no living liberty behind them.

question: Mises insisted value never lies in an object — not in its weight, not in its labor cost, not even in its usefulness in itself. Where did he say value resides?
answer: In the ranking a particular person makes at a particular moment between concrete alternatives they could pursue.
choices: In the ranking a particular person makes at a particular moment between concrete alternatives they could pursue.
In the average preference revealed by the population once individual eccentricities cancel one another out.
In the labor time socially necessary to bring the good to the market under prevailing conditions of trade.
In a fixed natural order of goods, with the staffs of life above luxuries and necessities above embellishment.
context: Mises called this methodological subjectivism: economics begins with the acting person choosing, not with the object chosen. A diamond and a glass of water have no value in themselves; they get whatever value they have only when some person, at some moment, must pick between them.

question: Oakeshott set the engineer who scraps the inherited machine and starts again against a different figure who refuses. What did he say that second figure prizes?
answer: The familiar, the workable, and the small adjustment over a perfect design that has never been tried in life.
choices: The familiar, the workable, and the small adjustment over a perfect design that has never been tried in life.
The authority of legitimate hierarchy and the duty of each rank to defer to the wisdom of the rank above it.
The unchanging moral law revealed in scripture and tradition over the shifting opinions of any human council.
The hard-won settlement of past struggles, which no living generation has any standing to revisit or to undo.
context: Oakeshott called this the conservative disposition — not a doctrine but a temperament. To be conservative was to prefer 'the tried to the untried, the actual to the possible, the convenient to the perfect.' Not because the present is good, but because it is ours.

question: Scruton argued the love of one's own place — a village, a neighborhood, a hillside — was not sentimental but a precondition for something larger. What did he say it founded?
answer: The willingness to be bound by laws made with strangers, since you trust the soil they share with you.
choices: The willingness to be bound by laws made with strangers, since you trust the soil they share with you.
The capacity to perceive beauty in the wider world, first cultivated in landscapes one knows by heart.
The religious sense of the sacred, which can only later be extended from particular shrines to the cosmos.
The economic productivity of a settled people, which exceeds that of a population willing to move for work.
context: Scruton called it oikophilia — love of the home. He thought modern politics had grown ashamed of it, mistaking it for hostility to outsiders. His answer: only people who love a particular place develop the loyalty that lets a free society of millions of strangers hold together.

question: A million fans each pay Wilt Chamberlain 25 cents, voluntarily, to watch him play. Whatever patterned distribution you started with — equal shares, need-based — is upset. What did Nozick argue this shows?
answer: Justice turns on the history of voluntary steps producing a holding, not on the resulting pattern.
choices: Justice turns on the history of voluntary steps producing a holding, not on the resulting pattern.
Justice requires inequalities to raise the least advantaged group’s absolute share above any rival.
Justice rewards merit, measured by a person’s contribution to the common good across a lifetime.
Justice demands strictly equal shares, with any deviation needing the explicit consent of all parties.
context: Nozick called his theory historical and unpatterned. Two photographs of incomes might look identical, yet one be just and the other not — depending entirely on how they came about. Liberty upsets patterns, as the Chamberlain crowd shows. Justice tracks what people did, not what the resulting graph looks like.

question: Aristotle named akrasia — weakness of will. You know the cake is bad, judge you should refuse, eat it anyway. Socrates had denied this. What was the older view?
answer: No one knowingly does wrong; whoever chose badly must, in that moment, have stopped really believing the act was bad.
choices: No one knowingly does wrong; whoever chose badly must, in that moment, have stopped really believing the act was bad.
Knowing the good is hard but acting on it is easy; if our actions miss, the reasoning, not resolve, has gone astray.
Desire is a force apart from reason; we choose badly when desire wins, and the cure is to harden reason against it.
Habit runs deeper than thought; one reasoning well still falls into bad action if the body has not first been trained.
context: Aristotle's correction is one of philosophy's great empirical victories. Yes, he says, people do see clearly and choose badly — and the explanation needs more than Socrates' single faculty of knowledge. Appetite has its own pull, and a moral psychology that ignores it will not survive a single Saturday night.

question: Sextus Empiricus catalogued ten 'modes' for suspending judgment. One observed that the same honey tastes sweet to the healthy and bitter to a person with jaundice. From this fact, what did the Skeptic say followed?
answer: Opposing reports from different perceivers leave no neutral standpoint — so suspend judgment.
choices: Opposing reports from different perceivers leave no neutral standpoint — so suspend judgment.
Perception co-creates its object; sweetness is partly produced by the tasting, not just received.
The contrast is a divine sign — providence sends bitterness to the sick, sweetness to the well.
Only the healthy organ reports truth about its proper kind of thing; the jaundiced report is invalid.
context: The Pyrrhonian modes are gymnasium exercises in argument: for every claim, find the equal and opposite report. If experience does not settle which observer is right, the Skeptic says, the honest move is to withhold the verdict. The mode of disagreement is the engine — once internalized, the urge to pronounce loosens its grip.

question: Constant pressed Kant: a murderer asks where your friend hides. Kant said lying is still forbidden. Why is a lie wrong here, despite the cost?
answer: A lie wrongs truthfulness itself, the ground of all right; consequences of a true word are not the speaker's.
choices: A lie wrongs truthfulness itself, the ground of all right; consequences of a true word are not the speaker's.
A lie only delays the murderer; a determined killer will find the victim by another route anyway.
A lie corrupts the liar's own character; habitual deception ruins the disposition for virtuous action.
A lie violates the friend's autonomy; the friend, not the speaker, should choose to face the threat.
context: Kant's 1797 reply to Constant has shocked readers ever since. The point was not callousness about the friend. Truthfulness, he held, is the condition of all contracts and law; once a speaker takes the future into his own hands by lying, no one else can rely on language at all.

question: Augustine asked in Confessions XI how we measure time when the past is gone, the future not yet, and the present a vanishing instant. Where did he locate it?
answer: In the mind — as memory of the past, attention to the present, and expectation of the future, held together at once.
choices: In the mind — as memory of the past, attention to the present, and expectation of the future, held together at once.
In the steady motion of the heavens, against which every shorter duration takes its measure and its name.
In an invisible river of moments flowing past the soul, whose current the careful observer learns to feel.
In the relations between bodies that change — without motion or alteration, no time for the word to pick out.
context: Augustine's puzzle: how can a length of time be long if no part of it presently exists? He relocates the extension from the world into the soul. We measure not the moments themselves but the trace of past moments and the reach of expected ones — the mind, paying attention, stretches between them.

question: Augustine split history into the City of God and the City of Man. The line, he insisted, was not believer vs pagan, ruler vs ruled. What was it?
answer: The line between two loves — love of God carried to contempt of self, and love of self carried to contempt of God.
choices: The line between two loves — love of God carried to contempt of self, and love of self carried to contempt of God.
The line between those who held office under the cross and those who held office under pagan Rome's eagle.
The line between contemplatives withdrawn from the world and active citizens who carried its burdens daily.
The line between those born inside the visible church and those whose forebears remained outside its rites.
context: City of God was written after Rome fell in 410, when pagans were blaming the Christians. Augustine's reply cut differently: the two cities run through every age, every empire, every parish. A bishop could belong to the earthly city; a soldier could belong to the heavenly one. What sorted them was the love that ordered the heart.

question: Boethius in his cell asked how freedom survives if God knew every choice he would make. Lady Philosophy answered with a distinction. What was it?
answer: God does not foresee in advance — God sees from eternity, where every moment is present at once: knowing, not predicting.
choices: God does not foresee in advance — God sees from eternity, where every moment is present at once: knowing, not predicting.
God knows only what the divine will causes, leaving the contingent acts of creatures outside any divine knowing.
God's foreknowledge fixes the broad sweep of providence; the particular choice a soul makes is undetermined.
God permits humans to make their choices first, then matches divine knowing to what they have already settled.
context: Boethius's worry: if God knew yesterday I would do X today, then I cannot now do otherwise — freedom becomes a polite fiction. His resolution, drawing on Plotinus, lifts God out of the temporal sequence. Foreknowledge is the wrong word; eternal knowledge is. A spectator on a hilltop watches a road from above, but the travelers walk it freely.

question: Origen drew controversy in his century and after it for a doctrine called apokatastasis. What did the word claim?
answer: That every rational creature — every soul, even the devil — would in the end be restored to God; nothing made would be lost forever.
choices: That every rational creature — every soul, even the devil — would in the end be restored to God; nothing made would be lost forever.
That every soul existed before its body, its station in this world decided by choices already made in a prior state.
That the visible cosmos would be consumed by fire and re-created identically, the same souls repeating the same acts.
That scripture could be read on three levels at once, the literal yielding to the moral and the moral to the spiritual.
context: Apokatastasis means restoration of all things. Origen took New Testament passages on God being all in all and read them universally — no rational being, however fallen, was finally beyond return. The doctrine was condemned at the Second Council of Constantinople in 553. It still has serious defenders today; the debate has never closed.

question: Plotinus refused to call the first principle Being. To say it is would already be to say what kind of thing it is. What did he call it instead?
answer: The One — beyond being and beyond intellect, the source from which all being flows but itself no thing among things.
choices: The One — beyond being and beyond intellect, the source from which all being flows but itself no thing among things.
The Demiurge — a divine craftsman who shapes pre-existing matter into the cosmos by gazing at the eternal Forms.
The Unmoved Mover — pure act and thought thinking itself, drawing all things toward itself as their final end.
The Logos — the rational word and pattern of the world, in whom each created thing finds its measure and order.
context: Plotinus pressed the apophatic move: any predicate would limit the principle. Even 'exists' would group it with existing things. The One is what every being depends on without belonging among them — known by what we must deny of it, not by what we can say.

question: Plotinus arranged reality in three levels — One, Nous, Soul. Each overflows into the next. What did he insist this overflow is not?
answer: Not a choice or creation — the One does not decide to produce; lower levels stream out as light streams from the sun.
choices: Not a choice or creation — the One does not decide to produce; lower levels stream out as light streams from the sun.
Not a downward fall — the cosmos is the willed work of a personal god, made deliberately and pronounced good.
Not an eternal pair — matter and spirit are coeternal forces, neither prior to the other, locked in long contest.
Not a play of forms — the visible world is the gods sporting with appearances, with no real ground beneath.
context: Emanation is involuntary plenitude. The One is too full not to overflow; what flows is less than its source but real. This is why Christian readers would later distinguish their doctrine of creation ex nihilo — God chooses, freely — from emanation, which is necessary and continuous.

question: Plotinus split the soul. A lower part attends the body and its world; a higher part remains above, never wholly descended. What is the higher part always doing?
answer: Contemplating the Forms in Nous — even when we attend to nothing of it, the higher soul has not turned away.
choices: Contemplating the Forms in Nous — even when we attend to nothing of it, the higher soul has not turned away.
Acting in the world for its neighbors — virtue is practical and shared, not a withdrawal from a city's affairs.
Suffering imprisonment in matter — its task is endurance until release by a saving knowledge given from above.
Sleeping a forgetful sleep — only ritual, gift, and right invocation of the gods can wake what sleeps in us.
context: Most of us live mostly in the lower soul. But the higher soul never fully comes down, and contemplation is not an achievement we initiate so much as an attention we recover. Action is not despised — it is contemplation's overflow, weaker than its source.

question: Porphyry's short Isagoge introduced Aristotle's Categories with five terms for defining anything. For a thousand years they shaped how Europe argued. What were they?
answer: Genus, species, difference, property, accident — predicables by which any subject was to be analyzed.
choices: Genus, species, difference, property, accident — predicables by which any subject was to be analyzed.
Substance, quality, quantity, relation, place — principal categories Aristotle laid down for predication.
Affirmation, denial, conversion, opposition, contradiction — basic operations a proposition undergoes.
Being, unity, truth, goodness, beauty — convertible transcendentals every thing possesses by existing.
context: Translated by Boethius and read in every medieval school, the Isagoge framed the universals debate that would set realists against nominalists for centuries. Porphyry meant a modest preface to logic; it became one of the most consequential textbooks in Western history.

question: Hypatia taught Platonism and mathematics in Alexandria in the late fourth century. Her own writings are lost. What survives points to her teaching?
answer: Commentaries on mathematical works — Apollonius on conics, Diophantus on number — and the Platonism she built on them.
choices: Commentaries on mathematical works — Apollonius on conics, Diophantus on number — and the Platonism she built on them.
A treatise on the One, long fragments quoted in later Byzantine writers who admired her dialectical method.
A school manual on theurgic rites that Iamblichus had ordered, preserved by her father among Alexandrian papyri.
Letters between her and an Athenian rival on the soul's descent, the only known copies of which she signed.
context: Synesius of Cyrene's letters and references in the Suda preserve what we know. Hypatia headed the Neoplatonic school at Alexandria, drew Christian as well as pagan students, and was murdered by a mob in 415. Her teaching ran through mathematics — the discipline Plato had set at the threshold of philosophy.

question: Kant called the thing-in-itself unknowable. Schopenhauer agreed it lay beyond perception, but claimed each of us already knows it from one inside angle. What did he say it was?
answer: Will, the blind striving we feel inside as the body bracing, reaching, suffering, recognized everywhere.
choices: Will, the blind striving we feel inside as the body bracing, reaching, suffering, recognized everywhere.
Spirit unfolding in history, knowing itself through human thought and completing its rational journey.
Pure mathematical order, the same structure that physics describes from outside in measurable laws.
A divine intellect whose ideas are archetypes; finite minds glimpse them by abstraction from sensed things.
context: Schopenhauer's move in The World as Will and Representation: from the outside the body is one more object in the world of appearance, but from the inside its hungers, gestures, and pains are felt directly. That inside acquaintance, he said, gives the name of the noumenon Kant left blank: will. The rest of nature, then, is the same striving wearing other shapes.

question: Schopenhauer argued that ordinary life is structurally unhappy, not by accident but by design. What was the structure of his case for pessimism?
answer: Will is endless wanting; each satisfaction breeds new lack, while contentment quickly slides into boredom.
choices: Will is endless wanting; each satisfaction breeds new lack, while contentment quickly slides into boredom.
Sin entered through one act; every later misery flows from a free will turned away from its true good.
History repeats the same cycle; ages of vigor decay into corruption, then collapse, then begin again.
Pleasure and pain balance on the ledger; lives feel poor only because losses weigh heavier than gains.
context: The argument is not a mood. Striving without an object is suffering, since wanting is a felt lack. Striving that reaches its object dissolves the wanting and leaves boredom, which is just the will hunting for a new lack. Between the two there is no third state where the will simply rests. Pessimism for Schopenhauer is the honest report of that swing, not a temperament that good fortune could cure.

question: Schopenhauer ranked the arts by how completely they let us forget our own striving. Music sat above the rest. What did he claim music alone does?
answer: It copies the will itself, not the world that wears its shape, sounding the same urge we feel from inside.
choices: It copies the will itself, not the world that wears its shape, sounding the same urge we feel from inside.
It tunes the soul to mathematical ratios the cosmos already obeys, restoring the heavens inside the listener.
It rouses the noblest passions and channels them toward virtue, the role Plato gave the disciplined modes.
It speaks in a universal language requiring no concepts, so listeners of any nation share one direct feeling.
context: Painting and poetry, on Schopenhauer's hierarchy, show the will at one remove, dressed in the world's particular forms. Music skips the costume. A slow theme sounds like longing because it is longing, the same striving heard in another medium. The listener's own willing relaxes for the length of the piece, not by being silenced but by being absorbed into a copy that wants nothing back. Wagner read these pages and never recovered.

question: Schopenhauer rejected both Kantian duty and Christian command as the root of ethics. He named one motive as the only authentic moral basis. What was it, and why?
answer: Compassion (Mitleid): the helper sees through the illusion that you and the other are different beings at root.
choices: Compassion (Mitleid): the helper sees through the illusion that you and the other are different beings at root.
Sympathy: lively imagination of another pain stirs feelings that incline us to relieve them by acting.
Reverence for law: a maxim chosen for its own sake escapes the sway of self-interested impulse.
Enlightened self-love: durable cooperation rewards each agent who learns to weigh long gain over near.
context: Other moralities, Schopenhauer said, smuggle reward back in: heaven, duty's self-approval, future cooperation. Mitleid is the one motive where the helper's own striving falls away. The metaphysical claim under it: the boundary between self and other is part of the world of appearance, and compassion is the moment the boundary dissolves. He treated the Upanishadic tat tvam asi, you are that, as the same insight stated in another vocabulary.

question: Young Nietzsche read Schopenhauer with reverence, then spent his maturity turning against him. What position did the eternal recurrence answer?
answer: Schopenhauer pessimism: where the older man said life is best refused, Nietzsche dared the willing of it again.
choices: Schopenhauer pessimism: where the older man said life is best refused, Nietzsche dared the willing of it again.
Hegel optimism: where Hegel said history climbs toward reason, Nietzsche pictured the same hour returning unchanged.
Christian afterlife: where the church promised heaven beyond, Nietzsche turned eyes back to the present world.
Stoic indifference: where the Stoic met fate with calm acceptance, Nietzsche demanded fierce embrace of all.
context: Schopenhauer's verdict on life was that the will should be quieted; the saint and the ascetic were his heroes. The recurrence, in Gay Science 341, is the demon's question put to the same data: every joy and every pain, exactly as they were, again and forever. To meet that thought without horror is to have valued one's life on terms the older pessimism could not allow. Nietzsche kept the diagnosis of striving and refused the cure.

question: Sickness Unto Death calls despair more universal than illness. Most despairing people, Kierkegaard said, do not even know they despair. What is despair, for him?
answer: A misrelation in the self — the self that refuses, or fails, to become what before God it is, whether knowingly or not.
choices: A misrelation in the self — the self that refuses, or fails, to become what before God it is, whether knowingly or not.
A passing failure of mood — sadness deep enough to color belief but not deep enough to alter who one truly is.
An error of the intellect — false judgment about goods, correctable when one is shown reasons one had not weighed.
A symptom of alienated labor — under modern conditions the worker is severed from product, peer, and own activity.
context: Sickness Unto Death (1849), under Anti-Climacus. Kierkegaard names four forms: not knowing one has a self, not willing to be oneself, willing to be a self one is not, and defiantly willing to be one's own self apart from God. Despair is structural, not emotional — you can be cheerful and in despair. The cure is to relate the self transparently to the power that established it.

question: Bacon named four 'idols' that warp the mind before evidence even arrives. His Idols of the Marketplace targeted a source most thinkers had ignored. What did he blame?
answer: Words themselves; loose names force confused thoughts on minds that traffic in them.
choices: Words themselves; loose names force confused thoughts on minds that traffic in them.
Crowd opinion; the common run of people prefer easy stories to careful inquiry.
Greedy patrons; merchants funding study bend findings toward their own pockets.
Native superstition; folk beliefs about omens quietly shape what scholars accept.
context: Bacon's Idola Fori (Novum Organum, 1620) target language itself. Tribe = shared human biases; Cave = personal quirks; Theater = inherited dogmas; Marketplace = the slippage of words in common exchange. He thought bad terminology was the deepest of the four.

question: Aristotelian science leaped from a few observations to the broadest axioms, then deduced particulars back down. Bacon's Novum Organum demanded a different climb. What did he insist on?
answer: A graded ladder of axioms; ascend through middle generalizations, pruned by negative instances.
choices: A graded ladder of axioms; ascend through middle generalizations, pruned by negative instances.
A purely mathematical deduction; from the right starting principle, the rest of nature follows.
A skeptical suspense of judgment; observation supports no general claim, so the wise stay silent.
A reliance on ancient authority; the findings of Aristotle still outrank any modern experimenter.
context: Bacon attacked the syllogistic leap from a few cases to a sweeping principle. He wanted slow ascent through 'middle axioms,' with crucial instances and negative cases pruning the tree. Newton's hypotheses-then-test method later resembled this in spirit, though not in detail.

question: Galileo argued that tastes, smells, and colors live in the perceiver, while shape, number, and motion live in the body itself. What did he say about a feather drawn across skin?
answer: The feather has shape and motion; the tickle exists only in the tickled animal, not in the feather.
choices: The feather has shape and motion; the tickle exists only in the tickled animal, not in the feather.
The feather and the tickle are equally real; both belong to the joint event, not to either party alone.
The feather has a hidden tickling power; sensitive bodies merely register a quality the feather carries.
The feather and the tickle alike are mental; matter is an inference, never appearing to any mind directly.
context: In Il Saggiatore (1623), Galileo used the feather-tickle to argue that secondary qualities are not in objects. Locke later named the primary/secondary distinction; Berkeley pushed further and denied primary qualities a mind-independent home too.

question: Aristotelian physics treated falling bodies as seeking their natural place, heavier ones falling faster. Galileo replaced this with a new method. What was his central move?
answer: Abstract from real surfaces; reason about frictionless planes, then confirm by timing inclined rolls.
choices: Abstract from real surfaces; reason about frictionless planes, then confirm by timing inclined rolls.
Catalog every observed fall; only the patient gathering of cases without theory can ground a science.
Begin from divine geometry; the heavens reveal mathematical laws and earthly motion must mirror them.
Trust the senses directly; what eyes plainly report about heavy and light must outweigh artificial setups.
context: Galileo's inclined-plane work combined idealization (no air, no friction) with quantitative measurement (time as the ratio of distances). It broke with Aristotelian observation, which read appearances at face value, and with pure geometric deduction from first principles.

question: Newton's Principia gave a law of universal gravitation but no mechanism for how bodies pulled across empty space. To critics demanding a cause, he wrote 'hypotheses non fingo.' What was he refusing?
answer: Speculative causes; he stated the law the phenomena demanded, declining to invent a hidden ether.
choices: Speculative causes; he stated the law the phenomena demanded, declining to invent a hidden ether.
Mathematical idealization; he described bodies as observed, not abstracted into dimensionless points.
Theological language; he treated gravitation as pure mechanism, keeping the Creator out of physics.
Empirical generalization; he derived gravity from rational axioms, not from observed planetary motion.
context: In the General Scholium (1713), Newton — himself a serious theist who wrote more on biblical chronology than on physics — distinguished the law of gravitation, which the phenomena demanded, from any underlying cause, which they did not. Leibniz attacked the move; Newton held firm.

question: Descartes held that space is just extended matter, so motion is purely relative to neighboring bodies. Newton's bucket argument cut against this. What did the spinning bucket show?
answer: Water climbs the sides while at rest relative to the bucket; rotation is real against absolute space.
choices: Water climbs the sides while at rest relative to the bucket; rotation is real against absolute space.
Water stays flat with the rope twisted but bucket still; motion is only change against neighboring bodies.
Water stays level whatever the bucket does; rotation is a sensory illusion from the observer's own motion.
Water mirrors the curve of the heavens; terrestrial motion borrows its measure from the celestial sphere.
context: In the Principia's scholium on space and time, Newton argued the concave surface of spinning water cannot be explained by Cartesian relative motion alone. Leibniz and later Mach pushed back; the dispute over substantival vs. relational space runs straight into modern physics.

question: John Mbiti wrote that African religions treat time as deepening backward: past events crowd a vast region (Zamani); the present forms a short zone (Sasa). What followed about being?
answer: A person grows more real by passing into Zamani through ancestral memory; existence deepens by accumulation.
choices: A person grows more real by passing into Zamani through ancestral memory; existence deepens by accumulation.
Reality reduces to the present instant; remembered past and imagined future are fictions with no real standing.
Each soul climbs through cycles of rebirth toward release; the future holds the only real goal worth pursuing.
History unfolds by a providential plan ending in judgment; the present gains meaning only by orienting to that end.
context: Mbiti's African Religions and Philosophy (1969) contrasts a backward-deepening ontology with Heidegger's being-toward-future. Distractors are presentism, samsara, and Augustinian eschatology. The reading is contested by Wiredu.

question: Kwasi Wiredu noted that Akan councils did not vote — they deliberated until everyone agreed. He made this a critique of modern democracy. What did he argue?
answer: Majority voting permanently splits a polity into winners and losers; consensus lets dissent reshape the decision.
choices: Majority voting permanently splits a polity into winners and losers; consensus lets dissent reshape the decision.
Procedure does not produce legitimacy; only a leader embodying the people's spirit can transcend faction and unify.
Universal suffrage presumes equal political competence; rule should pass to those whose education qualifies them to judge.
Democracies necessarily breed alienation; only abolishing private property removes the conditions creating division.
context: Wiredu's Cultural Universals and Particulars (1996) defends consensus democracy as a no-party model. Distractors are populist authoritarianism, Platonic guardianship, and Marxist critique.

question: Iamblichus broke with Plotinus on the soul's ascent. He argued contemplation alone cannot reach the gods, since the soul is too descended. What did he add?
answer: Theurgy — sacred acts and symbols by which the gods themselves draw the soul up; the work is divine, not ours.
choices: Theurgy — sacred acts and symbols by which the gods themselves draw the soul up; the work is divine, not ours.
Asceticism — long withdrawal from food, sleep, and company, until the body no longer drags attention earthward.
Dialectic — disciplined questioning of a partner, by which the soul reasons its own way out of false opinions.
Faith — assent to a saving teaching delivered from above, trusted before it is understood and understood within.
context: Plotinus had treated rites as crutches; the philosopher ascended by thought. Iamblichus answered that no thought, however pure, can cross the gap between our fallen soul and the divine. The gods left tokens in things and rites — symbola — and the operator who uses them rightly is moved by the gods, not by his own effort.

question: Nishida Kitaro opened his 1911 Inquiry into the Good with junsui keiken, pure experience. He placed it below something most philosophy starts from. Below what?
answer: The split between the one experiencing and what is experienced — the seeing of red prior to a self and a red.
choices: The split between the one experiencing and what is experienced — the seeing of red prior to a self and a red.
The split between reason and sensation in the soul — raw sense data shaped by later judgment into knowing.
The split between waking life and dreaming — an inner stream that ran on whether one was awake or asleep.
The split between private feeling and public report — felt quality prior to the words that fixed it for others.
context: Nishida read William James and pushed harder. James let subject and object be late constructions on a prior stream; Nishida built the Kyoto School on the move. The Kantian, dream-versus-waking, and private-language distractors are real rival pictures of pre-reflective awareness — none Nishida's.

question: Watsuji Tetsuro noted ningen, the word for human, held nin (person) and gen (between). Ethics, he said, lived in the gen. What did he mean?
answer: A person is made by relations — child, neighbor, citizen — and ethics is the practice of those betweens, not of one will.
choices: A person is made by relations — child, neighbor, citizen — and ethics is the practice of those betweens, not of one will.
A person owes duties up a hierarchy — ruler over subject, father over son — ethics keeps each station faithfully.
A person aggregates the preferences of a group — ethics is the calculus by which a community sums its welfare.
A person realizes universal reason alone — ethics is the maxim each rational will legislates, bonds secondary.
context: Rinrigaku (1937). Watsuji read Heidegger and thought Sein und Zeit had stranded the human as a solitary Dasein. The aidagara, the between, is prior: I become a son in being one, a teacher in teaching. Distractors are real rivals — Neo-Confucian station-ethics, utilitarian aggregation, Kantian autonomy.

question: Motoori Norinaga drew mono no aware from the Tale of Genji. Western readers gloss it as melancholy. What did the 18th-century scholar say it was?
answer: A trained sensitivity to things as they pass — knowing the cherry falls is what makes seeing it bloom matter so.
choices: A trained sensitivity to things as they pass — knowing the cherry falls is what makes seeing it bloom matter so.
A sorrow at impermanence the Buddhist path teaches one to overcome — aware the affliction, detachment the cure.
A romantic melancholy at the gap between ideal and real — what German Sehnsucht and Portuguese saudade name.
A samurai composure in the face of death — readiness to die at any hour, hardened by training and tested in war.
context: Motoori spent decades on Genji and rejected the standing Confucian and Buddhist readings. Aware is the moved response of one who notices. Buddhist sorrow-to-be-cured, Sehnsucht and saudade as supposed equivalents, and the bushido reading are real positions on similar terrain — none is Motoori's. The claim is not uniqueness; it is what Motoori meant.

question: Vine Deloria Jr.'s God Is Red (1973) argued Western and tribal religions answer different opening questions. What was his core claim?
answer: Western religion orders meaning around time and events; tribal religion orders meaning around place and the land itself.
choices: Western religion orders meaning around time and events; tribal religion orders meaning around place and the land itself.
All religions encode the same perennial truths beneath surface symbols; only the cultural wrapping really varies between them.
Religion is the alienated form of social production; both Western and tribal forms mask the material relations beneath them.
Genuine religion arises from individual mystical experience; communal ritual is later scaffolding added on top of that core.
context: Deloria argued sacred history (Sinai, Calvary) frames Christianity as temporal, while sacred places (Bear Butte, Blue Lake) frame tribal religion as spatial. Distractors map onto Huxley, Marx, and James.

question: Hegel's master-slave story: the master sets the terms, the slave must seek the master's recognition just to count as a person. Glen Coulthard, a Yellowknives Dene theorist, applied this to indigenous peoples seeking recognition from colonial states. In Red Skin, White Masks (2014), what did he argue?
answer: Recognition by a colonial state reproduces the asymmetry it claims to fix; the colonized learn to want what the master grants.
choices: Recognition by a colonial state reproduces the asymmetry it claims to fix; the colonized learn to want what the master grants.
Recognition grows durable when minority rights gain constitutional protection; charter entrenchment supplies the remedy.
Recognition fails because identity is a fiction; emancipation begins by replacing group categories with personal rights.
Recognition belongs to civil society, not the state; public life concerns property and contract, not acknowledgment.
context: Coulthard, drawing on Fanon, argues Hegelian recognition becomes a colonial mechanism when one side controls the terms. Distractors are Kymlicka-flavored liberalism, post-identity liberalism, and Hegel's civil-society reading.

question: Carl Mika argues that in te ao Maori (the Maori world), a stone, river, or ancestor is not an object sitting out there waiting to be examined by a knower standing apart. Knower and known are tangled from the start. What is the claim?
answer: Things and the persons who know them arise together in one web of relations; isolating a 'thing in itself' already distorts it.
choices: Things and the persons who know them arise together in one web of relations; isolating a 'thing in itself' already distorts it.
The mind builds phenomena from sense data; talk of standalone objects is shorthand for stable bundles of perception.
Reality splits into mind and extended matter; knowing succeeds when an inner representation mirrors the outer object.
Concepts carve nature at its joints; thought reaches reality when our language tracks the genuine kinds the world has.
context: Mika and Mike Ross argue matauranga Maori treats knowing as participation, not spectatorship. Distractors are Berkeleyan idealism, Cartesian dualism, and natural-kind realism.

question: Adam Smith, seventeen years before The Wealth of Nations, asked how strangers come to judge their own conduct. The answer anchors his Theory of Moral Sentiments. What device did he propose?
answer: An impartial spectator within — we picture how a fair stranger would view the act and adjust accordingly.
choices: An impartial spectator within — we picture how a fair stranger would view the act and adjust accordingly.
A built-in moral sense from the Creator — conscience reports on conduct as the eye reports on light.
A calculation of pleasure and pain — right acts are those that produce the greatest balance of happiness.
A rational test of the act's maxim — what cannot be willed as a universal law cannot be done at all.
context: Smith argued in 1759 that sympathy with a hypothetical impartial observer is how the moral judgment of strangers is internalized. The device made morality social without making it merely conventional, and later shaped Darwin, Sen, and contemporary virtue ethics.

question: Nineteenth-century critics named the Adam Smith Problem: the sympathy of 1759 seemed to contradict the self-interest of 1776. How did Smith himself unify the two books?
answer: Both books assume the same agent — the spectator already trims the self-interest the market then channels.
choices: Both books assume the same agent — the spectator already trims the self-interest the market then channels.
Wealth was a youthful error he disowned — late edits to Sentiments quietly retract its economic appendices.
Each book covers one sphere — public commerce runs on interest, private life on sympathy, never the two mixed.
Self-interest replaces sympathy as society matures — markets succeed when older moral bonds finally dissolve.
context: Smith revised Moral Sentiments throughout his life, including after Wealth of Nations. The butcher serves us from self-love, but he is also the spectator-formed neighbor ashamed to cheat. The two-Smith reading is a nineteenth-century projection his texts resist.

question: Voltaire wrote his Treatise on Tolerance in 1763 after Jean Calas was tortured to death on a false charge. What was the core philosophical argument?
answer: No human judge is certain enough about another's soul to inflict irreversible harm for a doctrine.
choices: No human judge is certain enough about another's soul to inflict irreversible harm for a doctrine.
All religions are equally false; toleration follows because no doctrine deserves the state's backing.
Truth is whatever a free society agrees upon; persecution is wrong because consensus alone legitimates.
Conscience is a private taste, like a love of music — the magistrate has no business in such feelings.
context: Voltaire's argument turned on epistemic humility, not on indifference to truth. Calas, a Huguenot, was broken on the wheel in Toulouse on suspicion of killing his son to prevent a Catholic conversion. Voltaire kept the family alive while overturning the verdict.

question: Voltaire's Candide mocks a tutor named Pangloss who, after every disaster, insists this is the best of all possible worlds. Whose system was the parody aimed at, and what was the actual objection?
answer: Leibniz's theodicy — no armchair proof of divine optimization survives the dead of the 1755 Lisbon quake.
choices: Leibniz's theodicy — no armchair proof of divine optimization survives the dead of the 1755 Lisbon quake.
Spinoza's necessitarianism — a wholly determined world leaves no room for the moral agent's striving.
Rousseau's natural goodness — civilization cannot be the corruption of an originally innocent human.
Berkeley's idealism — the reality of material suffering refutes the claim that only minds exist.
context: Leibniz argued that an omnipotent, benevolent God necessarily chose the optimal possible world; apparent evils are local costs of a globally best plan. The Lisbon quake of All Saints' Day 1755 killed tens of thousands at prayer. Voltaire's satire was not against theism but against the move from armchair proof to consolation.

question: Condorcet, hiding from the Jacobins who would soon kill him, proved a theorem about juries voting independently on a yes-or-no question. What did the result show?
answer: If each voter is more than half likely right, the majority's accuracy rises toward certainty as the jury grows.
choices: If each voter is more than half likely right, the majority's accuracy rises toward certainty as the jury grows.
If voters reason independently, cycles among three options make no stable collective ranking possible at all.
If voters share information, larger assemblies converge on the median voter's view regardless of any truth.
If voters are evenly split, the lottery of a tiebreaker yields outcomes no worse than further debate would.
context: Condorcet's 1785 jury theorem is one of the first mathematical defenses of democracy: many fallible judges, voting independently, outperform any one expert. He wrote it while drafting a constitution. The Terror caught him in 1794; he died in a cell, having argued to the end for indefinite human progress through reason.

question: Aldo Leopold's *A Sand County Almanac* (1949) closes with the 'land ethic.' Ethics had governed person-to-person, then person-to-society. What was his next extension?
answer: The moral community widens to include soils, waters, plants, animals — the land as fellow member
choices: The moral community widens to include soils, waters, plants, animals — the land as fellow member
Wildlife policy must rest on scientific data alone, since aesthetic responses cannot ground real duties
Private ownership of wild land is the only safeguard, since shared resources collapse under common use
Conservation succeeds only when nature is shown to serve the long-run welfare of future human beings
context: Leopold's move was structural: ethics had widened twice — kin, then citizens — and the next widening was to the biotic community. 'A thing is right when it tends to preserve the integrity, stability, and beauty of the biotic community.' Land becomes member, not commodity.

question: Holmes Rolston III argued nature has 'intrinsic value' — but he meant something stronger than 'humans find it beautiful.' What was his actual claim?
answer: Living things pursue their own good objectively; that achievement carries value with or without a valuer
choices: Living things pursue their own good objectively; that achievement carries value with or without a valuer
Wild places trigger spiritual responses in humans that no manufactured environment can ever replicate
Ecosystems aggregate the preferences of sentient creatures, and that sum grounds the value we ascribe
Biodiversity is irreplaceable insurance for future humans, so present generations owe its preservation
context: Rolston's claim is metaphysical, not psychological. A wild plant pursues its own telos — water, light, reproduction — and that 'good of its own' exists prior to any observer. Value is *discovered* in nature, not *projected* onto it. The strongest realist position in environmental ethics.

question: Madison in Federalist 10 argued the cure for the dangers of faction was counterintuitive — not to suppress factions, but the opposite. What did he propose?
answer: Extend the republic over a large territory so many rival interests check each other and none can dominate.
choices: Extend the republic over a large territory so many rival interests check each other and none can dominate.
Empower an upper chamber of long-tenured statesmen who can rise above any single popular faction.
Hold elections often enough that a faction which captures office is turned out before it entrenches.
Cultivate civic virtue in the schools so citizens learn to set narrow interest aside in the assembly.
context: Madison inverted the classical worry that only small republics could be stable. A large republic multiplies the interests so much that no faction can become a permanent majority — the cure for faction is more of it, channeled through institutions.

question: Lincoln at Cooper Union (1860) argued the founders held a specific view on slavery's spread into federal territory. What did he claim the record showed?
answer: A majority of the framers had voted, in Congress or conventions, to restrict slavery's spread in federal territory.
choices: A majority of the framers had voted, in Congress or conventions, to restrict slavery's spread in federal territory.
The founders treated slavery as a moral evil and intended its full abolition within one generation of the Union.
Most signers were anti-slavery but lacked the votes at Philadelphia to write abolition into the new charter.
The Constitution's silence on slavery in the territories left the matter wholly to the settlers, as Douglas held.
context: Lincoln spent weeks in a New York library reading every recorded vote of the 39 framers. His finding — that 21 of them had at some point voted to restrict slavery in federal territory — was meant to show the Republicans, not the Democrats, were faithful to the founders' practice.

question: Lincoln's Second Inaugural (1865) refused to call the war a simple righteous cause. Both sides, he said, 'read the same Bible.' Where did he locate moral judgment?
answer: With a providence whose purposes neither side fully grasps; the war may be God's woe for the offense of slavery.
choices: With a providence whose purposes neither side fully grasps; the war may be God's woe for the offense of slavery.
With Northern moral conviction against slavery, vindicated by the weight of Union victory on the battlefield.
With the verdict of future historians, who will weigh both sides once the war's passions have finally cooled.
With the conscience of each citizen alone, since no national judgment can settle so deep a moral quarrel.
context: The address is remarkable for refusing the rhetoric of triumph six weeks before Appomattox. Lincoln framed the war as a divine reckoning on the whole nation — North and South — for the offense of slavery, and called for charity rather than recrimination.

question: Douglass broke with Garrison over the U.S. Constitution. Garrison called it 'a covenant with death.' What did Douglass come to argue?
answer: Read by its plain words, the Constitution is a liberty document; slavery survives only by extra-textual compromise.
choices: Read by its plain words, the Constitution is a liberty document; slavery survives only by extra-textual compromise.
The Constitution was a pro-slavery bargain; the abolitionist's duty is to break the Union itself to be free of it.
The Constitution is neither pro- nor anti-slavery; the matter was left wholly to states and to private conscience.
The Constitution's natural-rights language was rhetoric for foreigners; its working clauses settled little of substance.
context: Garrison burned a copy of the Constitution on July 4, 1854, calling it a pact with slaveholders. Douglass, after long study of figures like Lysander Spooner, came to the opposite view: the document's plain language nowhere named slavery, and the Preamble's purposes were freedom's.

question: Calhoun rejected 'all men are created equal' as a dangerous Lockean abstraction. What did he say was true of human beings instead?
answer: No state of nature ever existed; humans are born into ranked societies, and liberty is a reward earned by advanced peoples.
choices: No state of nature ever existed; humans are born into ranked societies, and liberty is a reward earned by advanced peoples.
Natural rights are real, but only the states, not the federal Union, may translate those rights into binding civil law.
Equality is moral, never political; the framers wrote the Declaration as inspiration, not as binding civil doctrine.
Men begin equal in some natural sense, but the social compact trades that equality for the order any society needs.
context: Calhoun's Disquisition on Government (1851) argued the founders had imported a false abstraction from Locke. Men, he said, are never found in any 'state of nature' — only in societies, ranked. The bank holds the natural-rights tradition Calhoun rejected; his position is presented here in his own terms.

question: King wrote from Birmingham jail to clergy urging patience with the law. Drawing on Aquinas, he distinguished just from unjust laws how?
answer: A just law is a human code that squares with the moral law; an unjust law degrades personality and may be defied.
choices: A just law is a human code that squares with the moral law; an unjust law degrades personality and may be defied.
A just law commands the same conduct of every citizen; an unjust law binds a minority to terms the majority refuses.
A just law arises from procedures of constitutional consent; an unjust law comes from a regime no consent legitimized.
A just law serves the long-term welfare of the community; an unjust law sacrifices that good to a momentary passion.
context: King's April 1963 letter answered eight white clergymen who had called his protests 'unwise and untimely.' He invoked Aquinas's distinction between lex humana and lex aeterna: a statute that conflicts with the moral law is no law at all, and breaking it openly, accepting the penalty, is itself a witness.

question: Kirk in The Conservative Mind (1953) listed six canons of conservative thought, and said one was the keystone the other five rested on. Which canon did he name as foundational?
answer: A transcendent moral order to which custom, convention, and the laws of any people are finally answerable.
choices: A transcendent moral order to which custom, convention, and the laws of any people are finally answerable.
A natural hierarchy of classes and orders; trying to flatten society always produces a worse tyranny in its place.
A jealous defense of private property as the one shield that keeps a citizen from the reach of arbitrary power.
An English common-law inheritance whose precedents bind any reform that would invent rights from theory alone.
context: Kirk drew the canons from Burke and the English-American conservative line through Adams. The transcendent-order canon was the keystone: without it, he thought, the others collapsed into mere prudence. The book gave American conservatism a self-conscious philosophical genealogy.

question: Sowell in A Conflict of Visions (1987) argued political quarrels trace to two opposing pictures of human nature. How did he label them?
answer: Constrained — humans are limited and self-interested; and unconstrained — they are perfectible by reason.
choices: Constrained — humans are limited and self-interested; and unconstrained — they are perfectible by reason.
Tragic — history records recurring evils to endure; and progressive — history bends toward justice if rightly steered.
Empiricist — knowledge grows by trial; and rationalist — knowledge comes by deduction from the first principles of reason.
Communal — the person is constituted by tradition; and individualist — the person stands prior to and judges the group.
context: Sowell argued that Burke and Hamilton work from one picture, Rousseau and Godwin from the other, and the same split runs through every later debate. Each side's policies look obviously right from inside its own vision and obviously dangerous from the other.

question: Solzhenitsyn argued that Western readers got the Soviet camps wrong by treating them as a Stalin aberration. What did he claim instead?
answer: They were built into the regime from 1918, designed by Lenin from the start, not bolted on by Stalin later.
choices: They were built into the regime from 1918, designed by Lenin from the start, not bolted on by Stalin later.
They were a wartime improvisation of the 1940s that hardened into permanence once peace gave the police room.
They were the Tsarist katorga the Bolsheviks merely scaled, retaining the prior juridical theory more or less.
They were the work of Beria personally and would have dissolved within a decade under a different police chief.
context: The Gulag Archipelago tracks the camps to a Lenin decree of 1918, years before Stalin held power. The Western fellow-traveler line — that a humane revolution had been hijacked by one cruel man — could not survive the dates Solzhenitsyn put on the page.
