answer: Death as my ownmost possibility — the one no one can take over for me; owning rather than fleeing it lets me live my own life, not the anonymous one.
choices: Death as the gateway to the soul's true homeland — the religious horizon against which earthly attachments shrink and the order of goods is at last restored.
Death as the great equalizer — the biological fact that rich and poor alike must die, which dissolves the vanities of rank and grounds the demand to be just.
Death as a natural process to be accepted — the Stoic discipline of consenting to what nature requires, freeing the mind from futile fear of a sure terminus.
Death as my ownmost possibility — the one no one can take over for me; owning rather than fleeing it lets me live my own life, not the anonymous one.
context: Being and Time §§46–53. The point is not 'we all die, so be serious.' Death is the one possibility no one can take over for me. Recognizing this strips away the everyday flight into how 'one' lives, what 'one' does. Authentic existence is not gloomy heroism — it is owning the finitude that makes any particular life mine.

question: Duns Scotus asked what makes Socrates *this* Socrates rather than merely an instance of humanity. His answer added a new metaphysical layer. What did he call it?
answer: Haecceitas — a thing's individual 'thisness,' a positive principle distinguishing each from every other.
choices: Haecceitas — a thing's individual 'thisness,' a positive principle distinguishing each from every other.
Quidditas — a thing's 'whatness,' the shared essence that makes it the kind of thing it ultimately is.
Materia signata — matter marked by quantity, the Thomist principle that one human differs from another.
Hypokeimenon — Aristotle's underlying substrate, the bare particular bearing all properties of a thing.
context: Scotus rejected Aquinas's view that individuation comes from 'signate matter' (matter with specific dimensions) — that would make pure spirits like angels indistinguishable. His alternative: each individual has a haecceity, a primitive principle of thisness, irreducible to any form, matter, or accident. Gerard Manley Hopkins, the Victorian poet, called it 'inscape' and credited Scotus with showing him how to see particulars as unrepeatable.

question: Aquinas treated intellect as ruling will; the intellect sees the good and the will follows. Duns Scotus reversed the order. What did he claim about the relation?
answer: The will is free to choose against what intellect judges best; freedom is the will's primacy, not its servitude.
choices: The will is free to choose against what intellect judges best; freedom is the will's primacy, not its servitude.
The will is the executor only; if intellect judges rightly, the will must follow what reason has clearly seen.
The will is moved by passion alone; reason is the slave of the passions, as Hume would later restate it.
The will is determined entirely by grace; without supernatural aid, the will cannot move toward the good.
context: Scotus's voluntarism: the will is the noblest faculty because it alone is genuinely free. Intellect cannot but assent to what is clearly true (you cannot decide 2+2=5); only the will can choose between alternatives both presented as good. The position pushes back against Aquinas's intellectualism and prepares the ground for modern accounts of liberty. Critics worry it threatens to make God's will arbitrary; defenders say it grounds real moral responsibility.

question: What is a number? Frege's 1884 Grundlagen answered logically. Take five: fingers on a hand, points on a star, the Great Lakes. What such collections share, he said, is being 'equinumerous' — same size. So 5 is the set of concepts equinumerous with 'finger on a hand.' The hidden claim?
answer: Numbers are objects of pure logic — not of the mind, not of physical groups. If number is defined by equinumerosity (a logical relation), arithmetic is logic in disguise.
choices: Numbers are objects of pure logic — not of the mind, not of physical groups. If number is defined by equinumerosity (a logical relation), arithmetic is logic in disguise.
Numbers are mental constructions the mind forms by abstracting away the differences between groups and retaining only their bare quantitative likeness (the psychologist's view).
Numbers are linguistic conventions — convenient labels for tracking collections, with no existence outside the social practices of speakers using the labels in everyday counting.
Numbers are properties of physical aggregates of objects, so 'three' picks out a feature shared by every real-world collection containing exactly three items (Mill's empiricist proposal).
context: Frege's logicist program. He attacked Mill (numbers as features of physical aggregates), Kant (numbers as synthetic a priori intuitions of time), and the psychologists (numbers as mental images). His alternative: number-statements are claims about *concepts*, and concepts plus equinumerosity belong to logic alone. The program collapsed when Russell sent his paradox in 1902 — but the question of what numbers are has never recovered.

question: Principia Mathematica ran three volumes; it took until page 379 of volume 1 to prove 1+1=2. Russell and Whitehead weren't being slow. What were they trying to do that required such patience?
answer: Derive every arithmetical truth from purely logical axioms with no mathematical assumption smuggled in — every move had to be justified before arithmetic could appear
choices: Derive every arithmetical truth from purely logical axioms with no mathematical assumption smuggled in — every move had to be justified before arithmetic could appear
Build a notation general enough to express every theorem ever proven, so the early volumes were spent designing the symbolic apparatus itself
Catalogue every known proof of basic arithmetic into one system, exposing redundancies in mathematical practice that nineteenth-century rigor missed
Replace ordinary mathematics with a constructive alternative in which only objects explicitly buildable from prior objects would be allowed in proofs
context: Principia Mathematica (1910–1913). The logicist project: arithmetic is logic in disguise. They never finished — volume 4, on geometry, was abandoned. The famous page-379 proof of "1+1=2" carries a wry footnote: "The above proposition is occasionally useful." Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems would later show the larger project couldn't succeed in principle, but the technical apparatus reshaped logic permanently.

question: Hegel never wrote the formula thesis-antithesis-synthesis in his major works; the triad came from a Fichte summary. What is his real move?
answer: A concept pressed strictly contains its own opposite; the contradiction is lifted into a richer concept holding both.
choices: A concept pressed strictly contains its own opposite; the contradiction is lifted into a richer concept holding both.
A thesis is set against an antithesis; reason picks whichever side has the stronger empirical evidence behind it.
A claim is tested by deducing consequences; if they fail, the claim is replaced by a wholly new claim built fresh.
A position is asserted as truth; opposing claims are refuted by common sense and the tradition's broad consensus.
context: The textbook triad is a Chalybaus summary of Fichte that stuck to Hegel by accident. Hegel's actual move is immanent: follow a concept far enough and it turns into its opposite. The new concept (Aufhebung) cancels, preserves, and lifts the prior pair.

question: Hegel's word Geist gets translated as Spirit or Mind, but neither quite fits. What does Geist actually name in his use?
answer: A shared life of self-aware reason carried by persons and institutions, growing toward fuller self-knowledge.
choices: A shared life of self-aware reason carried by persons and institutions, growing toward fuller self-knowledge.
A divine personal substance distinct from the world, acting on history from outside as providence directs it.
A psychological faculty inside each individual; the private inner stream of thought conscious beings share.
A material force underlying nature; the productive energy that completed physics will eventually describe.
context: Geist is not a ghost, not a private psyche, not a force of nature. It is reason as a shared, public life carried in laws, art, religion, and philosophy. History, for Hegel, is Geist coming to recognize itself in what it has built.

question: Kojeve and Fukuyama drew the end of history thesis from Hegel. What did Hegel himself mean by saying history reaches an end?
answer: Not that events stop, but that the principle of freedom is achieved in principle, leaving only its working-out.
choices: Not that events stop, but that the principle of freedom is achieved in principle, leaving only its working-out.
That a final empire will unify all peoples under one rational state, ending political diversity for good.
That events become cyclical once reason matures; civilizations rise and fall on a pattern with no progress.
That philosophy itself ends with his system; later thinkers can only repeat what he has already shown them.
context: Kojeve read Hegel as predicting a final universal state; Fukuyama applied the line to 1989. Hegel's own claim was about a principle, not a date: once it is grasped that every person is free, the basic logic of history is complete. The working-out continues.

question: Schelling around 1801 offered a striking image: a single root beneath both the tree of thought and the tree of nature — one reality showing itself in two ways. He called this root the absolute, and the position identity philosophy. What was his core claim about that root?
answer: The root is not a finished thing but a productive activity — the same self-grounding power that produces nature also produces mind, and only its products show up as the two-sided world.
choices: The root is not a finished thing but a productive activity — the same self-grounding power that produces nature also produces mind, and only its products show up as the two-sided world.
The absolute is a perfect God beyond all finite things; mind and nature are created products that lie outside it and depend entirely on it for their being and order.
The absolute is the moral law within rational wills; mind and nature only matter as the field on which that commanding moral form takes effect in the world of action.
The absolute is bare matter in motion; mind is a late surface effect produced by the deeper physical processes that nature has quietly been running all along.
context: Around 1801 Schelling argued the absolute is not a static stuff but a producing activity — the Spinozist natura naturans (producing nature) standing prior to natura naturata (produced nature). The two-sided world of mind and nature is what gets produced; the unity sits at the level of the production itself. Hegel later complained this absolute was 'the night in which all cows are black' — too undifferentiated to do philosophical work — but the move was foundational.

question: Schelling thought earlier philosophy treated nature as a finished product to analyze. What did his Naturphilosophie put in its place?
answer: Nature is a living productivity; products are temporary forms, like waves, in an ongoing creative process.
choices: Nature is a living productivity; products are temporary forms, like waves, in an ongoing creative process.
Nature is a closed mechanical system; every event follows fixed laws from prior states, nothing more.
Nature is the mind's unconscious projection; rivers and stars are categories imposed on raw sensation.
Nature is morally indifferent stuff; only human freedom matters, and nature is the stage for action.
context: Schelling distinguished natura naturans (nature naturing — the productive activity) from natura naturata (nature natured — the finished products). Stones, rivers, organisms are crests on a deeper generative current. The image shaped later philosophies of organism.

question: Hegel's Philosophy of Right places civil society between family and state. What did he argue civil society alone could not achieve?
answer: A common life oriented to the good of all; markets coordinate private interests but cannot form citizens.
choices: A common life oriented to the good of all; markets coordinate private interests but cannot form citizens.
An efficient allocation of resources; without planning, price signals cannot guide economic activity at all.
The protection of property rights; without a sovereign above the market, contracts collapse into conflict.
A class of skilled workers; without compulsory schooling, the trades will not reproduce over generations.
context: Hegel saw civil society as the realm of self-interested exchange — vital, but not enough. It produces wealth and a 'rabble' alongside it. The state, for Hegel, is the institution that lifts private agents into a shared ethical life oriented to common purposes.

question: Carnap's 1932 essay analyzed Heidegger's line "the nothing itself noths" (*das Nichts selbst nichtet*). He didn't call it false. He didn't call it wrong. He made a sharper move. What was it?
answer: The sentence is grammatical but logically empty — "nothing" is a quantifier, not a name, so the line says nothing and is not a candidate for truth
choices: The sentence is grammatical but logically empty — "nothing" is a quantifier, not a name, so the line says nothing and is not a candidate for truth
The sentence expresses existential anxiety the speaker undergoes, functioning as poetry but masquerading as a metaphysical thesis about reality
The sentence commits a category mistake confusing the realm of beings with the realm of Being, which only phenomenological reduction could disentangle
The sentence is a synthetic claim awaiting confirmation by future neuroscience, since talk of nothingness concerns absences in our conscious experience
context: Carnap's "Überwindung der Metaphysik durch logische Analyse der Sprache" (1932). His diagnosis: traditional metaphysics consists of pseudo-statements — strings that violate the logical syntax of language. Heidegger replied that logic itself rests on a prior metaphysical decision about Being. The exchange defined the analytic-continental split for decades.

question: Ayer's *Language, Truth and Logic* (1936) brought logical positivism to England. He distinguished two versions of the verification principle. What was the distinction — and why was it needed?
answer: Strong demands conclusive proof; weak asks only that observation count for or against — needed because no universal law admits conclusive finite proof
choices: Strong demands conclusive proof; weak asks only that observation count for or against — needed because no universal law admits conclusive finite proof
Direct covers reports the speaker checks personally; indirect covers reports relayed by others, with translation rules linking indirect back to direct
Linguistic handles statements about word meaning; empirical handles statements about fact — splitting the criterion across the two domains of inquiry
Synthetic applies to claims about the world; analytic applies to claims of pure logic — making the principle a pair of separate parallel standards
context: Ayer wrote *Language, Truth and Logic* at 24 after staying with the Vienna Circle. The strong-weak distinction was meant to rescue scientific laws. But weak verification proved too generous — Isaiah Berlin and others showed almost any sentence could be weakly verified given enough auxiliary hypotheses. Ayer's 1946 preface conceded the criterion still hadn't been satisfactorily stated.

question: Habermas in 1962 traced what he called the bourgeois public sphere: 18th-century coffeehouses and journals where private citizens debated common concerns. He argued this sphere had declined. What was his thesis?
answer: Mass media and the welfare state turned reasoned public debate into staged spectacle and managed opinion, eroding the space for rational consensus.
choices: Mass media and the welfare state turned reasoned public debate into staged spectacle and managed opinion, eroding the space for rational consensus.
The bourgeois public sphere was always a fiction concealing exclusion; its 'decline' is just previously silenced voices entering the wider discourse.
The public sphere has only flourished as commercial media expand; the wider the audience reach, the more vigorous and inclusive deliberation becomes.
The public sphere was destroyed mainly by state censorship and totalitarian propaganda; once those are lifted, free deliberation returns intact.
context: Habermas saw a narrow historical window where private people gathered as a reasoning public — neither subjects of the state nor consumers in a market. He thought modern conditions had largely closed that window, though he believed reopening it remained possible.

question: Gettier, 1963. Smith justifiedly believes "the man who gets the job has ten coins" — Jones, he thinks, will get it, and Jones has ten. Smith gets it instead, and happens to have ten coins. Why did three pages overturn two millennia?
answer: The belief is justified and true, but only luckily — JTB is not enough for knowledge
choices: The belief is justified and true, but only luckily — JTB is not enough for knowledge
The belief rests on a false middle step, so knowledge must rule out any false lemma
The belief is underdetermined by evidence, so justification has to be probabilistic
The belief is valid but unsound, so logical form alone cannot license knowledge
context: "Is Justified True Belief Knowledge?" broke the Plato-derived analysis by separating justification from the truth-maker: the route from one to the other passes through a false step. The fourth-condition repairs — no-false-lemmas (Clark), defeasibility, sensitivity, safety — have never converged.

question: Goldman, 1979. A working thermometer's reading is knowledge; a broken one's lucky correct reading is not. He said the difference lies not in the believer's reasons but in the process behind the belief. What was the move?
answer: A belief is justified when produced by a process that reliably yields truths, regardless of access
choices: A belief is justified when produced by a process that reliably yields truths, regardless of access
A belief is justified when the believer holds evidence open to introspection and defense
A belief is justified when it coheres with the rest of the believer's web of beliefs
A belief is justified when it traces by inference to self-supporting foundational beliefs
context: Process reliabilism. The move is externalist: justification depends on world-facts (the process's track record) the believer need not access. A child or an animal can know without articulating why. Distractors map onto access-internalism, coherentism, foundationalism, and social-practice views.

question: Gadamer described the hermeneutic circle: you cannot understand the parts of a text without a sense of the whole, yet the whole is built from the parts. What did he say a reader must keep doing?
answer: Revising the pre-understanding the reader brought in — projecting a sense of the whole, then letting the parts force that projection to be rewritten.
choices: Revising the pre-understanding the reader brought in — projecting a sense of the whole, then letting the parts force that projection to be rewritten.
Suspending every prior belief before reading — only a fully blank mind lets the text speak in its own voice rather than in the reader's familiar voice.
Decoding the underlying structural pattern of opposed terms — every text rests on binary codes that reveal what the surface narrative quietly conceals.
Distrusting the manifest meaning as a screen for hidden interest — only tracing the text to power, class, or drive saves the reader from being deceived.
context: Truth and Method (1960). The circle is older than Gadamer (Schleiermacher, Heidegger), but Gadamer made the productive point: it is not a flaw to escape. We arrive with anticipations of meaning; honest reading is the back-and-forth that lets the text correct them.

question: Gadamer used 'fusion of horizons' for what happens when a modern reader meets an ancient text. What did he say the encounter produces?
answer: A new horizon larger than either alone — the reader's questions and the text's answers meet, and each shifts in light of the other rather than one swallowing it.
choices: A reconstruction of the author's original horizon — the reader sets aside present concerns and reenters the past as the author lived it, recovering an intended meaning.
A new horizon larger than either alone — the reader's questions and the text's answers meet, and each shifts in light of the other rather than one swallowing it.
A demonstration of an underlying universal structure — ancient text and modern reader share invariant codes of mind, and contact across time reveals what was always there.
A controlled procedure of reconstructive reasoning — the reader applies ideal-speech rules to discount distorted communication and recover what a rational author meant.
context: Truth and Method (1960). Gadamer rejects Schleiermacher's goal of recovering the author's mind. Understanding is not psychological reentry; it is the meeting of two situated horizons whose joint movement makes a third. Habermas pressed him: do not all traditions need a critical check?

question: Parfit posed a puzzle: a woman is told conceiving now will produce a child with a mild disability, while waiting two months produces a different, healthier child. She conceives now. The child grows up with a life worth living. Who has she wronged?
answer: No one — the disabled child cannot complain, since the alternative was not their healthy life but their own non-existence
choices: No one — the disabled child cannot complain, since the alternative was not their healthy life but their own non-existence
The disabled child, since deliberately choosing worse conditions for a future person counts as harm in the usual sense
The healthier child she might have conceived, who has been denied existence through a foreseeably reckless choice
The wider community, since the avoidable disability raises social costs the mother foresaw but chose to impose anyway
context: Parfit's *Reasons and Persons* (1984) called this the non-identity problem. The standard account of harm — making someone worse off than they would have been — cannot reach this case, because the alternative for *this* child is not health but non-existence. Yet the choice still seems wrong. Parfit argued our intuitions outrun person-affecting principles; future-people ethics may need an impersonal foundation, which is exactly what makes it philosophically explosive.

question: McMahan asked a sharper version of the abortion/euthanasia question. Most bioethics asks whether the being is a person — yes/no — and lets that settle the case. McMahan said no: what matters is how strongly your current self is psychologically tied to your future. He called these its time-relative interests. What follows?
answer: Wrongness of ending a life scales with the present psychological link to the future. Embryos and the deeply demented lose far less by dying than middle-aged adults.
choices: Wrongness of ending a life scales with the present psychological link to the future. Embryos and the deeply demented lose far less by dying than middle-aged adults.
Killing any sentient being is the same wrong, since loss of subjective experience cannot be ranked by quantity without slipping into arbitrary speciesism.
Ending a life is wrong only when the being can presently form a verbal preference to continue existing — the preference-utilitarian line McMahan rejects.
Wrongness depends only on the future experiences a being is deprived of, with no extra weight given to whether a present self is psychologically tied to it.
context: In *The Ethics of Killing* (2002), McMahan rejected the all-or-nothing personhood framework that drives most bioethics debates. His time-relative interests account asks how strongly the present subject is psychologically bound to its own future. A late-term fetus has weak ties; a demented adult has lost them. Death takes less from beings whose grip on their own future is thin. The view delivers unusually graded verdicts on abortion, euthanasia, and animal killing alike.

question: Warhol's 'Brillo Box' looked identical to the cardboard boxes in any supermarket. The supermarket boxes were not art; Warhol's were. Arthur Danto built a theory around the puzzle. What did he conclude?
answer: What makes something art is not its visible properties but its place in a theory and history — the 'artworld' of practices that lets an object count as art
choices: What makes something art is the artist's sincere expression of an inner emotion in the object, which the indifferent factory worker never gives to ordinary goods
What makes something art is the arrangement of formal qualities — line, color, mass — that produces aesthetic emotion regardless of subject matter or origin
What makes something art is not its visible properties but its place in a theory and history — the 'artworld' of practices that lets an object count as art
What makes something art is craft excellence relative to a tradition — fine joinery makes a chair art, and a printed carton fails by showing no comparable skill
context: Danto's 1964 essay 'The Artworld' asked the obvious question: if two things look identical and one is art, the difference cannot be perceptual. He argued artworks live inside an 'atmosphere of theory' without which the category does not apply. George Dickie later formalized this as the 'institutional theory': art is whatever the relevant institutions confer that status on. Critics from Scruton onward argue this collapses art into power.

question: Saadia Gaon, in tenth-century Baghdad, opened his *Book of Beliefs and Opinions* by listing the roads to certain knowledge. He named four. What were they?
answer: Sense perception, self-evident truths of intellect, logical inference, and reliable transmitted tradition.
choices: Sense perception, self-evident truths of intellect, logical inference, and reliable transmitted tradition.
Direct revelation, prophetic vision, ecstatic contemplation, and assent of the gathered community of Israel.
Mystical union, contemplative ascent, scriptural exegesis, and inner illumination of the rational soul.
Mathematical demonstration, scientific induction, lawyerly cross-examination, consensus of authorities.
context: Saadia (882–942), Gaon of Sura, wrote the *Kitab al-Amanat* in Arabic to defend rabbinic Judaism against Karaites, Muslims, Christians, and skeptics. The four roads — sense, reason, inference, and *naql* (reliable report) — let him put revelation on the same epistemic shelf as everyday knowing. The move is structurally parallel to the Mu'tazila kalam he learned from, and prepared the ground Maimonides would later till.

question: Gersonides faced a dilemma: if God foreknows every free choice, choice is not free; if not, omniscience cracks. He chose. What did he conclude God does not know?
answer: Future contingents — not-yet-settled choices of free agents — though He knows all general orders.
choices: Future contingents — not-yet-settled choices of free agents — though He knows all general orders.
Particular material things — only their universal forms, since matter is the principle of imperfection.
The acts of evil agents — for God turns away from sin and does not behold the deeds of the wicked.
Anything outside Himself — God knows only Himself, and the world follows as a side effect of that.
context: Levi ben Gershon (1288–1344), in *The Wars of the Lord* III, argued that genuine contingency is built into the world; God knows the order of things as ordered, but the not-yet-actualized branch of a free choice is not yet a fact for anyone, including God. Crescas attacked this fiercely, defending full foreknowledge with compatibilist freedom. Aquinas had taken a third route: God sees all time at once eternally. Gersonides' move was the boldest of medieval theism.

question: Dogen described awakening as shinjin datsuraku — "body and mind dropped off." He meant the phrase precisely. What was being dropped?
answer: The habit of holding body and mind as things one owns — what falls away is the owning, not the breathing or the thinking.
choices: The habit of holding body and mind as things one owns — what falls away is the owning, not the breathing or the thinking.
The body's claims on the mind through hunger and pain — ascetic discipline weakens the flesh until the soul rises free.
The mind's attachment to one material form between lives — the released consciousness then takes a new subtler vehicle.
The illusion that any mind exists at all behind the senses — only momentary impressions remain, and these too scatter.
context: Dogen recorded the phrase as the moment his teacher Rujing's words broke through. The point is not annihilation of body or mind, and not Cartesian separation either. The dualism that drops is the grasping that takes body-as-mine and mind-as-mine; zazen teaches the dropping. Distractors: classical Indian asceticism, transmigration of a subtle body, Humean bundle — real positions, none Dogen's.

question: A ship has every plank replaced over years. The discarded planks are then reassembled into a second ship. Which is the original Theseus sailed? Plutarch's puzzle drives at what philosophical question?
answer: Whether an object's identity through time tracks its matter, its form and continuity, or some other criterion — and whether identity can ever be sharply settled.
choices: Whether an object's identity through time tracks its matter, its form and continuity, or some other criterion — and whether identity can ever be sharply settled.
Whether a single object can occupy two places at once, given that the rebuilt ship and the repaired ship sit in different harbors yet share one origin.
Whether craftsmanship is preserved through gradual replacement, given that no carpenter's original plank now remains and the labor itself has been lost.
Whether an object outlives its function, given that neither vessel still sails as a working warship though both are physically preserved as relics.
context: Modern responses range from Locke's continuity-based theory of identity, to Lewis's four-dimensionalism (objects as time-extended worms), to van Inwagen's view that there are no composite objects at all.

question: Marx's 1844 Manuscripts named four kinds of alienation under industrial wage labor. The worker is cut off from the product (someone else owns it), from the work (it is forced), and from other workers (competition replaces cooperation). What is the fourth — the one Marx thought cut deepest?
answer: Alienation from species-being — from the human capacity to plan, shape, and recognize oneself in freely chosen creative work.
choices: Alienation from species-being — from the human capacity to plan, shape, and recognize oneself in freely chosen creative work.
Alienation from political life — workers without time or education cannot meaningfully take part in the public debates of the day.
Alienation from religion — the older village faith dissolves in the factory town, leaving the worker without the consolation it offered.
Alienation from the soil — peasants pulled into cities lose contact with the rural rhythms that gave their forebears a settled identity.
context: Gattungswesen — 'species-being' — is Marx's most humanistic move, the early Marx rediscovered by 20th-century existentialists.

question: The Communist Manifesto (1848) opens: 'The history of all hitherto existing society is the history of class struggles.' Engels added a footnote in 1888 conceding the line needed qualification. What had it failed to take into account?
answer: Pre-class societies — early communal forms studied by 19th-century anthropologists, where Engels thought no class structure had yet appeared.
choices: Pre-class societies — early communal forms studied by 19th-century anthropologists, where Engels thought no class structure had yet appeared.
Slave societies — Engels worried the line conflated ancient slavery and modern wage labor under one word, blurring real differences.
Religious wars — the great conflicts of the 17th century were as much about theology as class, and the formula erased that side.
Colonial conquest — the line implicitly treated European history as world history, ignoring societies built on different axes.
context: Engels's 1888 footnote to the English edition. Morgan's Ancient Society (1877) had convinced him of older communal forms.

question: In the Genealogy of Morals (1887), Nietzsche traced the words 'good' and 'evil' to a historical event he called the slave revolt in values. The earlier aristocratic vocabulary — 'good' meant noble, strong — was overturned. Who, on his account, were the agents of that revolt?
answer: Resentful priestly cultures — above all the prophets of ancient Israel and early Christianity — who recoded weakness as virtue and mastery as sin.
choices: Resentful priestly cultures — above all the prophets of ancient Israel and early Christianity — who recoded weakness as virtue and mastery as sin.
Cosmopolitan merchants of the late Roman empire whose commercial interests required peaceful trading partners rather than warrior aristocrats.
Enlightenment philosophers in 17th-century France whose new science of nature demanded a parallel new science of equality between humans.
Industrial workers in 19th-century trade unions whose collective bargaining replaced the old aristocratic code of personal honor and rank.
context: Genealogy of Morals, First Essay. Nietzsche names the diagnosis explicitly; whether one accepts it is another matter.

question: Nietzsche in Twilight of the Idols listed four 'great errors.' One was confusing cause and effect; another was projecting human reason onto nature. The error he attacked most directly attacks the moralist's basic move. What was it?
answer: Mistaking effects for causes — treating a person's habits and physiology as freely chosen acts the person could be praised or blamed for.
choices: Mistaking effects for causes — treating a person's habits and physiology as freely chosen acts the person could be praised or blamed for.
Mistaking words for things — the grammatical subject 'I' makes us posit a soul behind every action that is doing the choosing.
Mistaking the rare for the typical — moral theories generalize from heroic cases that almost no real person ever actually faces.
Mistaking the future for the present — promises bind the will of a later self who never consented to what an earlier self pledged.
context: Twilight of the Idols, 'The Four Great Errors.' Part of a broader campaign against the picture of a free agent standing behind action.

question: Kierkegaard's three spheres — aesthetic, ethical, religious — are ways a life can be organized. The aesthete lives for the interesting; the ethical person lives for duty. The religious life breaks with the ethical at one point. What does Abraham raising the knife over Isaac illustrate?
answer: A 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — a moment when faith requires acting beyond universal moral rules toward a wholly individual command.
choices: A 'teleological suspension of the ethical' — a moment when faith requires acting beyond universal moral rules toward a wholly individual command.
A failure of ordinary parental love that a healthier religion would have prevented by reading the Genesis passage strictly as allegory.
An aesthetic high point — the kind of intense and irreversible moment the aesthete lives for, dressed up in the costume of religion.
A primitive survival from human sacrifice that the later Hebrew tradition rejected; Kierkegaard reads it as a cautionary tale.
context: Fear and Trembling (1843). Abraham is not a moral hero on the universal account — and that he is more than a murderer is the puzzle of faith.

question: Søren Kierkegaard spent his short life walking the streets of Copenhagen in the 1840s, watching ordinary people and writing pseudonymous books. He attacked one institution sharply near the end of his life. Whom did he attack?
answer: The official Danish Lutheran Church — for having made Christianity comfortable and respectable, and so emptying it of its actual demand.
choices: The official Danish Lutheran Church — for having made Christianity comfortable and respectable, and so emptying it of its actual demand.
The University of Copenhagen — which he believed had become a factory of Hegelian dogma that crushed independent thought in his generation.
The Danish royal family — whose absolutist rule he opposed in pamphlets calling for a constitutional regime closer to the Norwegian model.
The Copenhagen newspapers — which he accused of personal libel after a public quarrel with the satirical paper The Corsair in 1846.
context: His late pamphlets, collected as Attack Upon Christendom (1855), savaged the comfortable state Lutheranism of his day. He died at 42.

question: Hegel's master-slave passage imagines two self-consciousnesses meeting and fighting for recognition. One risks death and wins; the other yields and becomes the slave. Hegel argues the next stage is paradoxical. Who develops more fully?
answer: The slave — by working on the world, the slave shapes objects and comes to recognize his own activity, while the idle master stagnates.
choices: The slave — by working on the world, the slave shapes objects and comes to recognize his own activity, while the idle master stagnates.
The master — by winning the recognition stakes, the master gains the freedom to develop the higher capacities of mind without distraction.
Neither — the encounter is a dead end, and Hegel uses it to argue that real self-knowledge requires withdrawing from any social conflict.
Both equally — through their conflict, master and slave together develop the political institutions of the modern constitutional state.
context: Phenomenology of Spirit (1807). Marx read this as the kernel of his theory of labor; Kojève's 1930s Paris lectures shaped a generation of French thought.

question: Sartre describes peering through a keyhole, absorbed in what he sees — then he hears footsteps in the hall. Suddenly he feels seen. Shame floods him. Sartre used the scene in Being and Nothingness to make a philosophical point about other people. What was it?
answer: Another person's gaze reveals me to myself as an object in their world — I encounter my own being-for-others, and shame is its mark.
choices: Another person's gaze reveals me to myself as an object in their world — I encounter my own being-for-others, and shame is its mark.
Privacy is a basic moral right grounded in human dignity, and political theory must build its institutions to defend that right above all.
Bodies are governed by social conventions about respectable conduct, and most behaviors a person calls private are quietly regulated by class.
Conscience is the internalized voice of the parents and society, and its judgments simply repeat what the larger group has already decided.
context: Being and Nothingness, Part III. Sartre's account of the Look is one of the most cited passages in 20th-century philosophy.

question: Albert Camus opened The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) with one startling sentence: 'There is but one truly serious philosophical problem, and that is suicide.' He spent the book working out his answer — neither suicide nor what he called the 'philosophical suicide' of religion. What is the third option?
answer: Revolt — to keep facing the absurd contradiction between human longing for meaning and the world's silence, without giving up on either side.
choices: Revolt — to keep facing the absurd contradiction between human longing for meaning and the world's silence, without giving up on either side.
Surrender — to abandon the demand for meaning, accept that the question itself is malformed, and live as untroubled animals seem to live.
Distraction — to fill every waking hour with work, family, and small pleasures so that the larger question never has the room to surface.
Faith — to commit to a religious tradition despite knowing it cannot be rationally established, on the grounds that some commitment is better than none.
context: The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) ends: 'One must imagine Sisyphus happy.' The boulder always rolls back; he keeps pushing.

question: Russell's 1902 letter to Frege described a single set. Consider the set of all sets that are not members of themselves. Is that set a member of itself? Either answer breaks. Frege was finishing Volume II of Grundgesetze. What did the paradox show about his project?
answer: His basic law allowing any property to define a set led directly to contradiction — set theory needed a restriction Frege had not seen.
choices: His basic law allowing any property to define a set led directly to contradiction — set theory needed a restriction Frege had not seen.
His treatment of natural numbers as objects was incoherent because numbers really name properties of concepts, not things in their own right.
His distinction between sense and reference applied only to proper names and not to predicates, so the whole semantic theory needed redoing.
His system was sound but used a notation so awkward that mathematicians never adopted it and his results passed unnoticed for decades.
context: Frege added a hasty appendix and abandoned the project's logicist ambitions. Russell's later theory of types tried to patch the gap.

question: The early Wittgenstein claimed sentences 'picture' facts — they share a logical form with what they depict. By the 1930s he had broken with this entirely. Philosophical Investigations rejects the picture theory. What does Wittgenstein now say words get their meaning from?
answer: The rule-governed practices of using them — the 'language games' built into ordinary life, where meaning is use rather than picture.
choices: The rule-governed practices of using them — the 'language games' built into ordinary life, where meaning is use rather than picture.
Mental images that accompany them — to understand a word is to call up the right inner picture and check the world against it.
Definitions found in dictionaries — every word has a precise meaning given by an explicit rule fixed by linguistic experts.
The intentions of the speaker — what a word means in a sentence is whatever the speaker had in mind when using it at that moment.
context: Philosophical Investigations §§1–43. Chess pieces, building blocks, slabs — all examples of meaning grounded in use.

question: Carnap in a famous 1932 essay analyzed Heidegger's line 'the nothing itself noths' (das Nichts selbst nichtet). He did not call it false. He used it to illustrate a sharper charge against a class of metaphysical sentences. What was Carnap's charge?
answer: Such sentences are not false but cognitively meaningless — they violate the rules of logical syntax and so say nothing that could in principle be true or false.
choices: Such sentences are not false but cognitively meaningless — they violate the rules of logical syntax and so say nothing that could in principle be true or false.
Such sentences are politically dangerous because they prepare the ground for irrationalism — the same line of attack that would have stopped fascism in time.
Such sentences are merely poetic and belong in a separate domain — Heidegger had simply confused poetry with science by writing in apparent assertions.
Such sentences are correct but unprovable — they describe genuine features of being that lie outside what the verification principle is able to capture.
context: 'The Elimination of Metaphysics through Logical Analysis of Language' (1932). Carnap's reading helped harden the split between analytic and continental philosophy for decades.

question: Peirce gave a rule in 1878 for clearing up philosophical disputes. Ask, he said, what practical difference would follow if the idea were true. Two beliefs predicting exactly the same experience under every test are not really in dispute. What did he call the rule?
answer: The pragmatic maxim — the meaning of an idea is the sum of its conceivable practical consequences for action and experience.
choices: The pragmatic maxim — the meaning of an idea is the sum of its conceivable practical consequences for action and experience.
The principle of sufficient reason — every fact has an explanation, and any belief without one should be set aside until reasons appear.
The verification rule — a sentence is meaningful only if it can be empirically tested by observation under controlled experimental conditions.
The principle of charity — interpret an opponent's view as the strongest possible version, then test that version against your own commitments.
context: 'How to Make Our Ideas Clear' (1878). Peirce later renamed his view 'pragmaticism' to distance himself from what James did with it.

question: Rousseau opens The Social Contract (1762) with one of the most famous lines in political philosophy: 'Man is born free, and everywhere he is in chains.' Many take the line as complaint. Rousseau immediately complicates it. What does he ask in the very next sentences?
answer: Not how the chains arose, but how they can be made legitimate — what conditions would turn obedience into something rationally acceptable.
choices: Not how the chains arose, but how they can be made legitimate — what conditions would turn obedience into something rationally acceptable.
Whether the chains can be broken at all, and whether revolution is the only available means to do so given the strength of established regimes.
Who first placed the chains on humanity, and whether a specific historical event — the founding of agriculture — can be located as the moment.
How children should be educated to resist the chains, with the rest of the book treating political theory as an extension of pedagogy.
context: The Social Contract, Book I, ch. 1. Rousseau's general will is his answer: only laws each citizen could rationally will for all could legitimately bind.

question: Montesquieu in The Spirit of the Laws (1748) is remembered today as the source of 'separation of powers' — the doctrine America borrowed in 1787. The bigger argument of the book is less famous. Why, on his account, do the same laws work in one country and fail in another?
answer: Laws live inside a whole 'spirit' — climate, terrain, customs, religion, commerce — and any law that ignores its setting will not actually function there.
choices: Laws live inside a whole 'spirit' — climate, terrain, customs, religion, commerce — and any law that ignores its setting will not actually function there.
Some peoples are biologically suited to liberty and others to despotism, with national character being inherited rather than culturally formed by history.
Laws follow economic interest entirely; the underlying mode of production determines which legal arrangements will survive in any society.
Divine providence assigns each nation its government, and human reformers cannot alter what God has appointed for a particular people.
context: The Spirit of the Laws (1748). The argument is empirical and comparative — twenty years of work — and shaped Madison's Federalist 51.

question: Francis Bacon in the Novum Organum (1620) listed four 'idols' that warp the human mind before evidence reaches it. Idols of the Tribe come from being human; Idols of the Cave from personal history. What was Bacon naming with the Idols of the Marketplace?
answer: Misleading effects of common language — vague words exchanged in conversation make muddled ideas look sharper than they really are.
choices: Misleading effects of common language — vague words exchanged in conversation make muddled ideas look sharper than they really are.
Distortions from political loyalty — what one's faction holds becomes harder to question, and group attachment overrides honest inquiry.
Greed and self-interest — the merchant's calculations bleed into intellectual life and bias the verdicts a free mind would reach unaided.
Sensory illusions — the eyes and ears mislead the mind in everyday perception in ways only careful instruments can finally correct.
context: Novum Organum, Book I. Bacon meant the marketplace literally — the spot where people exchange words as well as goods.

question: Simone de Beauvoir agreed with Sartre that freedom is the human condition. Yet in The Second Sex (1949) she argued a French woman in 1949 was not free in the way an Algerian colonial subject was not free. What did she say women experience that complicates the simple Sartrean picture?
answer: Women are made — through upbringing, custom, law, and language — into a 'second sex' whose freedom is constrained before any individual woman wakes up to it.
choices: Women are made — through upbringing, custom, law, and language — into a 'second sex' whose freedom is constrained before any individual woman wakes up to it.
Women are biologically determined by reproductive function — their lives must accommodate facts of childbearing that no political reform can eliminate entirely.
Women are entirely free in modern France — Beauvoir wrote to show that no further legal change was needed to bring women's freedom into being.
Women are oppressed only economically — Beauvoir argued the situation would resolve itself once industrial employment had become widely available to them.
context: The Second Sex (1949). Beauvoir's 'one is not born, but becomes, a woman' was a direct application of existentialist freedom to the situation she actually inhabited.

question: Hakuin Ekaku revived Rinzai Zen in eighteenth-century Japan by systematizing koan study. He gave students an opening koan he had devised himself. What does 'the sound of one hand clapping' aim to do?
answer: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
choices: Defeat the discursive mind's attempt to find a referent — there is no answer to fetch, and exhausting the search is where the practice begins.
Test the student's familiarity with classical Chinese — the koan only makes sense in its original Tang-dynasty context, which Hakuin used as an entry exam for serious study.
Train the imagination to visualize impossible objects vividly — the meditative skill that Hakuin held was required for the more advanced visualizations later in the curriculum.
Convey the inseparability of action and inaction — the right hand cannot clap alone, just as conventional life cannot proceed without the support of monastic discipline.
context: Hakuin's 'sekishu no onjo' (the sound of one hand) was constructed to replace the older Mu koan as a fresh barrier for beginners. The point is not that there exists some hidden right answer that a clever student can deduce — koan practice in Rinzai uses such barriers to bring the discursive intellect to a halt, opening a different mode of seeing. The Soto school under Dogen emphasized shikantaza (just sitting) over koan work, marking a real intra-Zen split.

question: Zhiyi, founder of the Tiantai school in sixth-century China, taught the threefold truth — emptiness, provisionality, and the middle. He claimed this resolved a tension in Nagarjuna. What did he hold the middle truth was?
answer: The simultaneous holding of emptiness and provisionality at once — neither truth left behind in favor of the other, but each seen through the other in a single integrated view.
choices: The simultaneous holding of emptiness and provisionality at once — neither truth left behind in favor of the other, but each seen through the other in a single integrated view.
A compromise position somewhere between the extremes of emptiness and provisionality, calibrated case by case depending on which side of the doctrinal dispute appears stronger.
A higher third truth above the other two that absorbs them into itself — emptiness and provisionality are mere stepping-stones the advanced practitioner finally discards.
A pragmatic adjustment to the audience's level of understanding — the threefold truth is a pedagogical device with no ontological standing of its own beyond classroom utility.
context: Zhiyi's threefold truth (san-di) was an interpretation of Nagarjuna's Mulamadhyamakakarika 24.18 — 'emptiness, provisional designation, and the middle way.' Where Indian Madhyamaka generally took these as roughly synonymous, Zhiyi developed them as distinct but mutually entailing truths grasped together. The doctrine became foundational for the entire East Asian Buddhist synthesis, including Pure Land and Chan.

question: Xunzi opposed Mencius and argued that human nature is bad. But he did not mean humans are evil in a moral sense the way some later readers heard him. What did he actually claim?
answer: Human nature is the bundle of raw desires we are born with — good must be made through ritual training, not awaited as something innate that already lies sleeping inside us.
choices: Human nature is the bundle of raw desires we are born with — good must be made through ritual training, not awaited as something innate that already lies sleeping inside us.
Human beings inherit guilt from earlier lives that ritual practice gradually wears down — until the karmic burden is cleared, the original goodness of the heart cannot emerge.
Human beings are radically corrupted by an original transgression from which only divine intervention can deliver them — Xunzi anticipated the later Christian doctrine here.
Human nature combines good and bad tendencies in equal measure and rests on the deliberate cultivation of one or the other through one's chosen company throughout life.
context: Xunzi's chapter Xing'e ('Human nature is bad'). His claim is closer to Hobbes than to Augustine: humans are not depraved, just unfinished. The raw nature must be transformed by li (ritual) and learning — and the master image is the carpenter who steams crooked wood straight, the potter who shapes clay. Mencius said the sprouts grow if watered; Xunzi said straightness must be imposed. The dispute defined classical Confucianism.

question: Wang Yangming broke with Zhu Xi on a famous case. Zhu had instructed him to investigate bamboo in his garden to discover its principle — Wang stared at it for a week, fell ill, and concluded the method was wrong. What did Wang come to teach instead?
answer: Liangzhi — the innate moral knowing already in the mind — needs only to be extended into action, not supplemented by outside investigation of patterns in distant objects.
choices: Liangzhi — the innate moral knowing already in the mind — needs only to be extended into action, not supplemented by outside investigation of patterns in distant objects.
The investigation of things in Zhu's sense should be replaced by chanting classical texts daily — knowing principle directly was beyond ordinary minds and required the scriptures.
Investigating outer things does work, but only for natural objects; the moral principles within human relationships required a separate empirical method drawn from the histories.
Both the inside-out and the outside-in routes are valid in their own spheres, and the sage uses each as the occasion demands without committing in advance to either pathway.
context: Wang Yangming's Chuanxilu records the bamboo episode and the doctrine of liangzhi (often rendered 'pure knowing' or 'innate moral knowledge'). The dispute with Zhu's school turns on whether moral cultivation is a project of outward investigation (Zhu) or inward extension (Wang). Both schools cited the Great Learning's 'investigation of things' as their key text — and read it in opposite directions. Wang's school dominated late Ming Confucianism.

question: The Daodejing opens with one of philosophy's strangest sentences: 'The Dao that can be spoken is not the constant Dao; the name that can be named is not the constant name.' What argument is Laozi making about language?
answer: Naming carves a fluid reality into bounded items; the more precisely you name, the more you lose the unbroken whole the name was trying to point toward.
choices: Naming carves a fluid reality into bounded items; the more precisely you name, the more you lose the unbroken whole the name was trying to point toward.
Names are conventional and arbitrary signs and the wise person uses any naming system without believing in it — Laozi shares the Mohist functional view of language here.
Names refer to ideas in the speaker's mind rather than to anything in the world outside it — Laozi anticipated the British empiricists' representational theory by two thousand years.
Names work well for everyday objects but fail for sacred matters that only privileged ritual specialists are entitled to discuss in their proper hereditary technical vocabulary.
context: Daodejing, Chapter 1. The Chinese verb 'dao' is itself a near-pun: dao means both the Way and to speak. So the line literally reads: 'The way that can be wayed is not the constant way.' Speaking the way already departs from it, since speaking requires fixed concepts and the way is just what cannot be fixed. The point is not mysticism — it is a careful observation about what naming inherently does to its objects.

question: Daoism shares with Confucianism the term de — usually rendered 'virtue' or 'power.' But Daoist de means something different from Confucian de. What is the contrast that the Daodejing presses?
answer: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
choices: Confucian de is cultivated character that earns moral standing; Daoist de is the inherent power a thing has when it is fully itself, without effort to be anything other than what it is.
Confucian de belongs to humans only and to humans only after deliberate training; Daoist de is the property of any natural object whatsoever and lacks any specifically moral content at all.
Confucian de is taught through ritual practice in the village school; Daoist de is acquired through ascetic discipline practiced in the mountains far from the corrupting influence of cities.
Confucian de is a public reputation built across many years; Daoist de is the inner felt sense of one's own goodness that requires no outside witness or acknowledgement in any form.
context: Daodejing chapters 38, 51, and 65 develop Daoist de. The line in chapter 38 — 'The highest de is not de, and so it has de; the lowest de does not lose de, and so it has no de' — pokes directly at the Confucian project of self-conscious cultivation. Daoist de is more like what a sharp knife or a clear stream has: it is the way that thing works when nothing obstructs its functioning. Confucian de is a moral inheritance accumulated through effort; the two readings of the same word run on different rails.

question: J.L. Schellenberg argues that the existence of nonresistant nonbelievers — people open to God but unconvinced — counts as evidence against God. What is the structure of his argument?
answer: A perfectly loving God would ensure that nonresistant seekers find Him, since love wants relationship — nonresistant nonbelievers exist, so a perfectly loving God of that kind does not.
choices: A perfectly loving God would ensure that nonresistant seekers find Him, since love wants relationship — nonresistant nonbelievers exist, so a perfectly loving God of that kind does not.
A perfectly just God would punish unbelief — but billions live and die without ever hearing the message, so divine punishment of unbelief would be unfair to most of the human race in history.
A perfectly powerful God would compel belief — but belief remains free across the human population, so divine power must be limited in ways traditional theism cannot easily accommodate.
A perfectly truthful God would speak clearly — but religious traditions contradict each other on key claims, so divine communication has failed at the most basic standards of clarity.
context: Schellenberg's Divine Hiddenness and Human Reason (1993) and later Wisdom to Doubt (2007) developed the hiddenness argument. The key premise is that perfect love seeks relationship, and relationship requires belief in the other's existence, so a loving God would not let nonresistant nonbelief occur. Theists have responded by questioning whether loving openness requires belief now (perhaps belief can come later), or whether divine reasons for some hiddenness might be inscrutable, or whether the actual instances of nonresistant nonbelief are as widespread as Schellenberg claims.

question: Vine Deloria Jr. in God Is Red (1973) argued that Christian thought treats history as the primary stage of revelation while Indigenous American thought treats place as the primary stage. What does the contrast generate?
answer: Sacred history happens to a people across time and travels with them; sacred place happens to a particular landscape and cannot be transplanted — uprooting a people severs them from revelation itself.
choices: Sacred history happens to a people across time and travels with them; sacred place happens to a particular landscape and cannot be transplanted — uprooting a people severs them from revelation itself.
Sacred history is a linear sequence with a beginning and end; sacred place is cyclical and renews itself in spring — the contrast is between progressive and recurrent visions of time alone.
Sacred history is recorded in scriptures that travel; sacred place is recorded in oral traditions that fade — the contrast is methodological rather than reflecting any deeper metaphysical commitment.
Sacred history concerns events that did happen; sacred place concerns events that could happen — the contrast is between actual and possible, with each tradition prioritizing one of them.
context: Deloria (Standing Rock Sioux, 1933-2005) wrote God Is Red as a sustained comparison of Christian and Indigenous religious thought. His core claim — that the sacred geography of Indigenous traditions is not a primitive prefiguring of universalist religion but a genuine philosophical alternative — has shaped subsequent Indigenous philosophy. The implication for federal land policy is direct: removing a people from their landscape destroys what cannot be moved with them, in a way unintelligible to a religion that travels through history rather than dwelling in place.

question: Leopold Senghor, poet and first president of Senegal, argued that 'emotion is African as reason is Hellenic.' Hountondji read this as racial essentialism. What did Senghor's defenders say he meant?
answer: Not that Africans cannot reason, but that African knowing engages the world through participation rather than detached analysis — a different mode of knowing, not a lesser one.
choices: Not that Africans cannot reason, but that African knowing engages the world through participation rather than detached analysis — a different mode of knowing, not a lesser one.
Not that Africans have no reason, but that emotion was the politically more useful capacity for anti-colonial mobilization at the time — Senghor was making strategy, not philosophy.
Not that all Africans are emotional, but that the leadership class trained in French schools had lost the African mode and needed to recover it through deliberate cultural work.
Not that Africans differ from Europeans, but that all humans combine emotion and reason in different proportions — Senghor was making a universal claim with African examples.
context: Senghor's negritude movement, developed with Aime Cesaire and Leon Damas in 1930s Paris, asserted distinctively African modes of being against colonial dismissal. The 'emotion is African' line, taken in isolation, sounds like the very stereotype it meant to reclaim. Defenders point out Senghor was not denying African reason but redescribing the participatory engagement he saw as the African contribution to world philosophy. Hountondji and others have rejected the framing as still operating within colonial categories of comparison.

question: Mises argued in 1920 that a socialist economy could not even in principle calculate what to produce. The issue, he said, was not effort or honesty but information of a specific kind. What was missing?
answer: Market prices for capital goods — without those, no planner can compare alternative uses of steel, labor, or land.
choices: Market prices for capital goods — without those, no planner can compare alternative uses of steel, labor, or land.
Reliable surveys of consumer demand — without those, no planner can match output to the public's actual preferences.
Detailed inventories of physical stocks — without those, no planner can know which inputs the economy currently holds.
Skilled production engineers — without those, no planner can translate aggregate targets into specific factory schedules.
context: Mises's 1920 essay set the terms every Marxist economist of the next sixty years had to answer. Without prices for the inputs themselves, the question 'is this steel better used for tractors or for rails?' has no rational answer. Lange and others tried to simulate prices administratively; Hayek extended the critique to the knowledge problem.

question: Calhoun's 1837 'Positive Good' speech rejected the Founders' embarrassment about slavery and defended it on its own terms. What was his central philosophical claim?
answer: Liberty is a privilege earned by a capable race, not a natural right of every human being — so the Declaration's premise is itself false.
choices: Liberty is a privilege earned by a capable race, not a natural right of every human being — so the Declaration's premise is itself false.
Slavery is a transitional institution suited to a stage of development, to be replaced by free labor as economies grow more complex.
Slavery is a private matter for the states; federal philosophy has no standing to evaluate the moral worth of any local arrangement.
Slavery is unfortunate but unavoidable, since the cost of immediate emancipation would impose suffering greater than the institution itself.
context: Calhoun's break with the Founders' apologetic stance shaped the Confederate philosophical position. The Declaration's claim that all men are created equal, he held, was 'the most dangerous of all political errors.' Lincoln and Douglass each replied by refusing to surrender the premise.

question: Hobbes argued that even an absolute sovereign cannot demand one specific thing of a subject. Where did he draw the limit?
answer: A subject is never bound to submit to his own immediate killing — the contract was for self-preservation, and that limit holds.
choices: A subject is never bound to submit to his own immediate killing — the contract was for self-preservation, and that limit holds.
A subject is never bound to confess a religious belief he does not hold — Hobbes treated conscience as outside the sovereign's reach.
A subject is never bound to surrender his property — Hobbes anticipated Locke in giving property a foundation prior to the state.
A subject is never bound to obey an unjust law — the sovereign loses authority over any command demonstrably contrary to reason.
context: Hobbes was surprisingly clear on this. Even the absolute sovereign cannot demand that a man cooperate in his own death. The contract was rational only because it secured self-preservation; a command to die ran against the very reason for entering the contract. Religion, property, and justice — all could be regulated. Life itself could not be required.

question: Sidgwick saw a 'dualism of practical reason' that he never resolved. What was the deep tension he diagnosed?
answer: Rational egoism and rational universalism each seem self-evident, yet neither can be reduced to the other on any defensible footing.
choices: Rational egoism and rational universalism each seem self-evident, yet neither can be reduced to the other on any defensible footing.
Pleasure and pain are commensurable in the agent but not across persons, so no aggregate calculation can ever be coherent.
Common-sense morality and utilitarian calculation diverge at the margins, so utilitarianism must absorb common-sense rules wholesale.
Higher and lower pleasures are incommensurable, so Mill's qualitative move collapses the calculus into incomparable rankings.
context: Sidgwick's Methods of Ethics (1874) is the most rigorous utilitarian work in English. He could find no rational refutation of someone who said 'why should I care about others?' yet also found the impartial standpoint self-evident. The two axioms together generate no contradiction in any particular case — yet neither is a theorem of the other.

question: Bernard Williams pressed a particular objection against impartialist ethics. What did he say its demand on the agent missed?
answer: That a person has projects and commitments that make them who they are — and a theory that asks them to set those aside has asked too much.
choices: That a person has projects and commitments that make them who they are — and a theory that asks them to set those aside has asked too much.
That impartial reasoning is inherently impossible — every standpoint is partial in some respect, and the pretense of impartiality is fraud.
That impartial conclusions cannot motivate action — only desire can move an agent, and impartiality has no purchase on desire.
That impartiality is psychologically impossible — humans evolved to favor kin and group, and theory cannot override evolved nature.
context: Williams's 'integrity' objection ran against both Kantian and utilitarian universalisms. Each demanded that the agent step outside their own life and judge as anyone might judge. But the self that does the judging, Williams said, is built from particular commitments; strip those away and there is no agent left to do the judging.

question: Michael Sandel argued against germline gene editing on grounds independent of safety or fairness. What did he say it threatened?
answer: The 'giftedness' of the child — the parent's openness to what arrives, without which love bends toward inspection and design.
choices: The 'giftedness' of the child — the parent's openness to what arrives, without which love bends toward inspection and design.
The species-level genetic diversity — the variety on which evolution depends, which uniform editing would slowly erode away.
The natural-law foundation of human dignity — which Sandel grounded in the unmodified body as a token of divine creation.
The principle of consent of future persons — who cannot, by the temporal structure of the case, ever agree to their own design.
context: Sandel's The Case Against Perfection turned the question away from safety and equity, where most policy debates lived. The deeper change, he argued, was in the parent — between welcoming what comes and ordering what you wanted. The latter, he thought, was a kind of love that cannot survive the practice it shapes.

question: Descartes built his dualism on a famous test of conceivability. What did he claim to discover by trying to doubt his own existence?
answer: He could doubt that he had a body, but not that he was thinking — so the two could not be the same thing.
choices: He could doubt that he had a body, but not that he was thinking — so the two could not be the same thing.
He could doubt every memory of his life, but not the experience of doubt itself — so memory required a separate faculty.
He could doubt the testimony of the senses, but not mathematical truths — so reason and sensation had different sources.
He could doubt the existence of others, but not his own existence — so the social world was less certain than the private one.
context: Descartes's argument in the Sixth Meditation moves from a difference in what can be conceived to a difference in what the things are. Critics from Arnauld to Kripke have pressed the inference. Even if you can conceive your body and your thought separately, it does not follow that they actually are separate things in the world.

question: Functionalists argued that mental states are not identical to brain states. They proposed a different identity claim. What did they say a mental state was?
answer: Whatever role plays the right causal part — taking inputs, producing outputs, and connecting to other mental states in characteristic ways.
choices: Whatever role plays the right causal part — taking inputs, producing outputs, and connecting to other mental states in characteristic ways.
Whatever neural substrate the human brain uses — pain is a kind of brain firing, even if some other creature realizes pain otherwise.
Whatever pattern of behavior the agent reliably exhibits — pain just is wincing, withdrawal, complaint, and the rest of pain-behavior.
Whatever feels a certain way from inside — the felt quality of pain is itself what pain is, with brain talk being incidental to the matter.
context: Functionalism's appeal was that it cut across substrates. Silicon, neurons, ancient slime molds — if the causal pattern matched, the mental state was there. The view dominated philosophy of mind for decades and lies behind much of contemporary cognitive science. Searle and Chalmers attacked it from opposite directions.

question: Searle's 1980 Chinese Room argument denied that running the right program could ever amount to understanding. What was his core distinction?
answer: Syntax is not sufficient for semantics — manipulating symbols by rule never amounts to grasping what the symbols mean.
choices: Syntax is not sufficient for semantics — manipulating symbols by rule never amounts to grasping what the symbols mean.
Speed is not sufficient for thought — even a very fast symbol-shuffler is still only a shuffler, and pace does not add comprehension.
Computation is not sufficient for biology — without the right organic substrate, no amount of processing can produce a mind.
Behavior is not sufficient for inner life — fluent outputs prove only that the test was passed, not that any experience occurred.
context: Searle's 1980 paper claimed program-running by itself is the wrong kind of activity to produce understanding. The man in the room shuffles symbols by rule and answers questions in fluent Chinese — yet understands no word. Whatever role he plays, the program he runs cannot bridge the gap to meaning.

question: Imre Lakatos thought Popper and Kuhn each got something wrong. He proposed a unit larger than the theory and smaller than the paradigm. What did he name it?
answer: A research program — a hard core of protected assumptions surrounded by an auxiliary belt that takes on the refutations.
choices: A research program — a hard core of protected assumptions surrounded by an auxiliary belt that takes on the refutations.
A conceptual scheme — a shared vocabulary of basic terms within which every legitimate scientific question must be posed.
A model — a simplified mathematical structure tested independently of the broader theory whose features it represents.
A community of inquirers — a self-policing body of trained specialists whose consensus alone establishes what counts as a fact.
context: Lakatos's research programs progress when their auxiliary modifications anticipate novel facts; they degenerate when modifications only protect against known refutations. The unit was meant to be testable in Popper's sense without collapsing to the strict either/or of falsification or the looser Kuhnian paradigm shift.

question: Feyerabend called his own position 'anything goes.' Critics took this as nihilism. What was the more careful claim?
answer: No single method has done the historical work; great science has often progressed by breaking rules current methodologies declared sacred.
choices: No single method has done the historical work; great science has often progressed by breaking rules current methodologies declared sacred.
No method can ever fail; whatever a scientist does is automatically justified by the fact that they are a credentialed scientist doing it.
All worldviews are equally valid; astrology, voodoo, and physics have the same epistemic standing on close inspection.
Knowledge is socially constructed without remainder; what counts as truth is whatever the relevant community currently agrees to.
context: Against Method (1975) argued from historical cases — Galileo, Copernicus, Aristarchus — that progress had repeatedly required violating the methodological canon of its day. The slogan was rhetorical; the underlying claim was that methodology must be empirically humble about how science has actually worked.

question: Mary Midgley reviewed Dawkins's The Selfish Gene and made an objection she returned to for decades. What did she charge his metaphors had done?
answer: They smuggled moral character into descriptions of genes — 'selfish' is a verdict on agents, and genes are not agents at all.
choices: They smuggled moral character into descriptions of genes — 'selfish' is a verdict on agents, and genes are not agents at all.
They smuggled empirical mechanisms into philosophical claims — genes do many things, but 'replication strategy' is a story, not data.
They smuggled species into individuals — what 'the gene' does is what populations do, and the singular usage obscures the level.
They smuggled physics into biology — talk of 'forces' shaping selection borrows authority from a discipline that did not vouch for it.
context: Midgley argued that Dawkins's poetic vocabulary kept slipping from useful description into evaluative pretension. Beasts and Man, Wickedness, and later works pressed this against scientism more broadly. Calling a gene 'selfish' was not innocent shorthand; it imported the language of moral persons onto bits of DNA that had no morals at all.

question: Nussbaum developed a 'capabilities approach' to social justice. She agreed with Rawls that resources matter, but pressed a different question. What did she ask we measure?
answer: What people are actually able to do and be — not income alone, but health, education, voice, love, and other concrete capabilities.
choices: What people are actually able to do and be — not income alone, but health, education, voice, love, and other concrete capabilities.
What people prefer at the moment of measurement — adaptive preferences track what citizens want from policy in any given period.
What people receive from formal institutions — only state-provided goods can be measured fairly across populations and over time.
What people report on surveys — self-reported flourishing remains the only direct measure of well-being available to policymakers.
context: Nussbaum and Sen built the capabilities approach against narrowly economic measures. A society with the same per-capita income might do well or badly depending on whether its citizens were healthy enough to use it, free enough to choose with it, and connected enough to share it. The framework reshaped development economics from the 1990s on.

question: Sakharov's 1968 essay 'Reflections on Progress, Peaceful Coexistence, and Intellectual Freedom' surprised both sides of the Cold War. What did he argue?
answer: The capitalist and socialist systems were each better than the other in some respects, and their convergence — not their war — was the rational future.
choices: The capitalist and socialist systems were each better than the other in some respects, and their convergence — not their war — was the rational future.
