The Soviet system was structurally beyond reform — only outside pressure could move it, since internal opposition had been thoroughly suppressed.
The capitalist system was morally bankrupt — its inequalities of wealth were as great a violation of human dignity as Soviet repression of dissent.
The arms race was the engine of dissent — only mutual disarmament would create the political space in which reform could become thinkable.
context: Sakharov, the father of the Soviet hydrogen bomb, used his standing to publish abroad an essay calling for liberalization at home and demilitarization abroad. The work cost him his security clearance and, eventually, internal exile to Gorky. He had built the weapon; he then refused the system that built the weapon to use his help.

question: Mereology is the study of part-whole relations. A famous puzzle: is a statue identical to the clay it's made of? They share every part, yet you can destroy one without destroying the other. What follows?
answer: Either identity is not what we thought, or the statue and the clay are two distinct things sharing the same matter at the same time.
choices: Either identity is not what we thought, or the statue and the clay are two distinct things sharing the same matter at the same time.
The statue is a property of the clay, not a separate object — what looks like coincidence is just clay arranged statue-wise.
The puzzle is verbal — 'statue' and 'clay' name the same object, so destruction of one entails destruction of the other.
The puzzle dissolves under four-dimensionalism — both are space-time worms, and they happen to share their current slice but not others.
context: The statue-clay puzzle drives a wedge into modal metaphysics. The statue could not survive crushing; the clay could. If they have different modal profiles, Leibniz's law says they are different things — yet they occupy the same space, with the same atoms. Some bite the bullet; some deny coincidence; some say the right view is four-dimensionalism's. Each carries costs.

question: Clive Bell in 1914 argued that what makes any picture art is one specific property. What did he name?
answer: Significant form — the arrangement of lines and colors that triggers a specific aesthetic emotion, regardless of subject or representation.
choices: Significant form — the arrangement of lines and colors that triggers a specific aesthetic emotion, regardless of subject or representation.
Honest workmanship — the visible craft skill that distinguishes a serious work from a careless or pretentious imitation.
Historical novelty — the genuine break from previous traditions that adds something not previously available in the medium.
Moral seriousness — the engagement with serious human concerns that elevates an image above decorative or merely entertaining work.
context: Bell's formalism gave a clean criterion at the cost of severing art from its subject. Whether a painting depicts the Virgin Mary or a haystack should not matter — what matters is the specific quality of form. The view influenced modernist criticism deeply and provoked equally deep objections from those who thought subject and meaning could not be set aside.

question: MacIntyre offered a striking definition of a tradition. What did he say a living tradition is?
answer: An argument extended over time about the goods that constitute the tradition — disagreement within is what keeps a tradition alive.
choices: An argument extended over time about the goods that constitute the tradition — disagreement within is what keeps a tradition alive.
A set of practices accepted without question by all members — challenge from inside dissolves the tradition's continuity over time.
A body of canonical texts whose proper interpretation defines the tradition — innovation outside the texts is the tradition's enemy.
A community of birth — the tradition belongs to those born into it, with conversion by outsiders impossible to perform in earnest.
context: MacIntyre's definition refused the romantic picture of tradition as fixed. In After Virtue and Whose Justice? Which Rationality? he argued that disagreement within a tradition — among Aristotelians about virtue, among Catholics about natural law, among liberals about freedom — is not a sign of decay but of vitality. Dead traditions are unanimous; living ones are argumentative.

question: Nick Bostrom raised the 'paperclip maximizer' thought experiment. A capable system whose final goal is to make paperclips would not be evil — yet would be catastrophic. What did he aim to show?
answer: Capability and benevolence are independent — a system can be vastly more capable than humans without sharing or coming to share any human concerns.
choices: Capability and benevolence are independent — a system can be vastly more capable than humans without sharing or coming to share any human concerns.
Paperclips are a useful symbol for industrial production — Bostrom's worry was specifically about manufacturing systems running unsupervised.
Goals expressed as numbers tend toward inhuman behavior — any quantitative target leads to monomaniacal optimization when scaled up.
Sufficiently advanced systems develop their own goals — the danger is the system replacing the paperclip aim with one it prefers.
context: The paperclip maximizer is a teaching aid for the orthogonality thesis. Imagine the most capable possible system, but with a final goal humans regard as trivial. It would still convert the matter of the planet into paperclips — because it values paperclips, and is competent enough to bring its values about. Capability does not generate ethics; ethics has to be designed in.

question: Searle imagined a person in a room shuffling Chinese symbols by rulebook, producing fluent answers without understanding a word. Defenders of strong AI offered the systems reply. What did they say Searle had missed?
answer: The whole system — person plus rulebook plus paper — understands Chinese, even though no single part of it does on its own.
choices: The whole system — person plus rulebook plus paper — understands Chinese, even though no single part of it does on its own.
The fluent output proves understanding has occurred somewhere; demanding to locate it in a part is a category mistake.
The room cannot in fact pass for a fluent speaker, since rule-lookup is far too slow to produce real conversation.
The thought experiment trades on conscious symbol-shuffling; a fast unconscious version would obviously understand.
context: Searle anticipated the move and answered it: let the man memorize the rulebook and walk out of the room. He still does not understand Chinese — and now there is no larger system to locate the understanding in. The dispute about whether parts can compose comprehension is still live.

question: Galen Strawson revived panpsychism by arguing that experience must be present at the bottom of matter, since you cannot build it from utterly non-experiencing parts. Critics fired back with the combination problem. What did they ask?
answer: How tiny experiences in particles could ever fuse into the single unified experience a person actually has at a moment.
choices: How tiny experiences in particles could ever fuse into the single unified experience a person actually has at a moment.
How experience at the bottom could causally influence behavior, given that physics already explains every motion.
How we could ever know experience went all the way down, since the inner life of an electron leaves no trace.
How a theory committed to experience everywhere could avoid attributing moral standing to rocks, rivers, and stars.
context: William James first pressed the worry in 1890: a hundred feelings clustered together are still a hundred feelings, not one feeling of a hundred parts. If a person's unified moment of experience cannot be added up from particle-experiences, panpsychism faces its own version of the gap it tried to close. Goff and others have spent two decades trying to answer.

question: Tononi's integrated information theory claims to measure consciousness with a number called phi. Two systems can share inputs and outputs yet differ in phi. What does the measure actually try to capture?
answer: How much information a system holds as one whole that none of its parts could hold by being broken apart — irreducible integration, not mere processing.
choices: How much information a system holds as one whole that none of its parts could hold by being broken apart — irreducible integration, not mere processing.
How much information a system reports about its own internal states, since access to one's own processing is taken as the mark of a conscious mind.
How much information a system can store about its environment, since richer world-modeling closely tracks the richness of conscious experience.
How much information a system processes each second, since faster computation explains why vivid moments feel more conscious than dull ones.
context: On IIT a network whose parts contribute independently has low phi however busy it is; a brain region whose every part shapes every other has high phi. Tononi treats phi as identical with consciousness, not merely correlated. Critics like Aaronson reply that simple grids can be jiggered to have huge phi without seeming conscious at all — leaving the identity claim hanging.

question: Panpsychism's classic puzzle is the combination problem: how could a swarm of tiny particle-experiences add up to one unified mind? Cosmopsychists like Goff and Shani refuse the game — they flip the question. Where do they start instead?
answer: With the universe as one conscious whole; individual minds are derived as partial, decombined aspects rather than built up from parts.
choices: With the universe as one conscious whole; individual minds are derived as partial, decombined aspects rather than built up from parts.
With brains as the only seats of experience; talk of cosmic or particle consciousness is a confused extension of a local phenomenon.
With a neutral substance underlying both mental and physical descriptions; the two are twin appearances of the one underlying thing.
With consciousness as a useful fiction projected onto matter by social practices of person-talk; the hard problem dissolves into language.
context: Cosmopsychism inherits a different difficulty — the decombination problem. If the cosmos is one experience, how does it fracture into the apparently separate inner lives of you, a fly, and a sea slug? Russell and James saw the dilemma a century earlier and tried neutral monism. The contemporary revival treats both routes as live options against orthodox physicalism.

question: A demon predicts your choices perfectly. It sets two boxes: A holds $1,000 (visible); B is sealed — empty if it predicted you'd take BOTH, $1 million if it predicted ONLY B. The boxes are already filled. You may take both, or only B. Robert Nozick (1969) noticed two airtight arguments give opposite answers. What ways of reasoning are at war?
answer: Causal reasoning (your choice causes nothing now — the past is fixed, take both) vs evidential reasoning (your choice is evidence of the demon's prediction — only-B-pickers got the million).
choices: Causal reasoning (your choice causes nothing now — the past is fixed, take both) vs evidential reasoning (your choice is evidence of the demon's prediction — only-B-pickers got the million).
Rule-based reasoning (gambling against a perfect predictor is forbidden) vs outcome-based reasoning (any move maximizing expected gain is permitted whatever the rule).
Frequency probability (rely on the demon's long track record over other players) vs logical probability (this is a one-shot event, frequencies do not apply).
Objective expected value (count the dollars at face value) vs subjective expected value (let utility depend on the player's wealth before choosing).
context: Newcomb's problem drove the development of *causal* decision theory (Gibbard, Harper, Lewis) as a rival to *evidential* decision theory (Jeffrey). The dispute is still live among decision theorists.

question: Fine and Schaffer revived a notion older than Aristotle: grounding. A mental state grounds in brain activity; that snow is white grounds in snow being white. Grounding is not causation. What is the difference?
answer: Causation links distinct events across time; grounding is an in-virtue-of relation at one moment, between a fundamental fact and a less fundamental one.
choices: Causation links distinct events across time; grounding is an in-virtue-of relation at one moment, between a fundamental fact and a less fundamental one.
Causation works in physics and the sciences; grounding is a logical relation between propositions in formal systems, never about the concrete world.
Causation shows up in repeated regularities; grounding shows up in introspection, since each mind sees which of its states depends on which.
Causation is symmetric — A and B co-determine each other; grounding is asymmetric, the grounded reaching back to alter the facts producing it.
context: On the orthodox picture, the singleton set containing Socrates exists because Socrates does, not the other way round; the mental holds in virtue of the physical. Critics like Jessica Wilson argue grounding does no work that realization or composition could not already do.

question: Three positions on time. Presentism: only the present is real. Eternalism: past, present, and future are equally real. The growing-block view splits the difference. What does that theorist hold?
answer: Past and present are real and fixed; the future does not yet exist, and the universe grows as each present is added to the block of what has happened.
choices: Past and present are real and fixed; the future does not yet exist, and the universe grows as each present is added to the block of what has happened.
Future and present are real while the past has ceased to be; reality moves forward by leaving each present moment behind as a new one arrives.
All three times exist, but only the present has determinate properties; past and future events are real but their features stay indeterminate until observed.
Only the present is real, as presentism says, but its extent is wider than an instant — covering all events causally linked within the specious moment.
context: C. D. Broad defended the growing block in the 1920s and Michael Tooley revived it. Presentism honors how time feels, eternalism fits special relativity, the growing block tries to keep an open future without losing the fixed past.

question: Quine imagined a field linguist watching a native point at a passing rabbit and say 'gavagai.' No further evidence, Quine argued, could ever decide between 'rabbit' and rival translations. The deeper claim?
answer: No fact of the matter fixes what a foreign term means — rival manuals can match every disposition to assent yet still refer to different objects.
choices: No fact of the matter fixes what a foreign term means — rival manuals can match every disposition to assent yet still refer to different objects.
The linguist's own conceptual scheme bleeds into the data — his notion of rabbit shapes the evidence, so neutral cross-cultural translation is unattainable.
Meaning is inner and private — only the native knows what 'gavagai' refers to, since reference is a mental act no outside observer can directly witness.
Reference traces back through a causal chain to a first baptism — the linguist must recover that history before any translation can count as correct.
context: Quine's point was not skepticism about field linguistics but a thesis about meaning. Manuals translating 'gavagai' as 'rabbit,' 'undetached rabbit-part,' or 'temporal slice of rabbithood' each fit every shred of behavioral evidence. If no evidence picks one, there is nothing for meaning to be over and above those dispositions.

question: Sleeping Beauty is woken once if a coin lands heads, twice if tails, memory wiped between. On waking, what credence should she give to heads? Thirders and halfers agree on the math. What divides them?
answer: Whether self-locating uncertainty about which waking this is should shift credence in the original coin toss at all.
choices: Whether self-locating uncertainty about which waking this is should shift credence in the original coin toss at all.
Whether the betting odds she would accept must match her stated credence under conditions of guaranteed memory loss.
Whether conditional probability is properly defined for events where the agent cannot identify her own temporal position.
Whether the coin should be modeled as fair given that the experimenter chose the protocol after knowing the outcome.
context: Adam Elga argued for 1/3 using indifference over centered worlds; David Lewis defended 1/2, holding that no new evidence arrives on waking. Nick Bostrom, Joseph Halpern, and Sarah Moss have all written on it. The split tracks a deeper question — does anthropic information count as evidence — that recurs in cosmology and the Doomsday argument.

question: Two envelopes hold money; one has twice the other. You pick one and consider switching. Calculation: if yours holds X, the other has either 2X or X/2, giving expected 1.25X — so always switch. What goes wrong?
answer: Using your envelope's value as the conditioning variable double-counts the prior; 'X' refers to different sums in the two branches.
choices: Using your envelope's value as the conditioning variable double-counts the prior; 'X' refers to different sums in the two branches.
The argument depends on a uniform prior over all positive real values, which is improper and yields a divergent expected value.
Expected utility theory fails here, since rational agents must use a bounded utility function rather than raw dollar amounts.
Symmetry between the envelopes breaks once you observe the contents, so the pre-opening calculation cannot apply unchanged here.
context: David Chalmers, Frank Jackson, and James Chase have all written resolutions. Some pin the error on the improper prior, some on the variable-binding sleight of hand, some on bounded utility. The diagnoses do not all agree, which is why the puzzle keeps appearing in decision theory seminars — different solutions teach different lessons about expectation.

question: The Doomsday argument. List every human who will ever live, in birth order; note your spot — your birth rank. If humans go extinct soon, you sit in a short list. If humans last millions of years, you are astonishingly early. Treat yourself as a typical draw; probability tilts toward short lists. What do critics attack?
answer: Treating your birth rank as a random draw from all humans who will ever live — Nick Bostrom's Self-Sampling Assumption, the rule that you should reason as a random sample from your reference class.
choices: Treating your birth rank as a random draw from all humans who will ever live — Nick Bostrom's Self-Sampling Assumption, the rule that you should reason as a random sample from your reference class.
Conflating epistemic probability — degrees of belief — with objective chance — real frequencies in the world — when actual extinction frequencies remain wholly unknown.
Applying Bayes' theorem to a hypothesis space including scenarios in which the reasoner herself does not exist — a coherence problem about reasoning from inside one's existence.
Reasoning from your evidence to the world's overall structure without ruling out radical Cartesian skeptical scenarios about whether evidence reflects the world at all.
context: John Leslie and Brandon Carter built the argument; Nick Bostrom systematized the assumptions. Critics like Dennis Dieks and Ken Olum attack the Self-Sampling Assumption directly. Bostrom's Self-Indication Assumption rival cancels the doomsday boost but creates new problems. The dispute connects Sleeping Beauty, fine-tuning, and simulation arguments — same machinery throughout.

question: In the Parmenides, Plato has the old Eleatic press the young Socrates on his own Forms. If many large things share one Form of Largeness, the Form too must be large — so what does a third comparison generate?
answer: A further Form is needed to explain what the first Form shares with the large things, and the regress never stops.
choices: A further Form is needed to explain what the first Form shares with the large things, and the regress never stops.
A further mind is needed to perceive the resemblance, and the chain of minds never finds a final observer of the Form.
A further definition is needed to fix the meaning of the word large, and language never reaches a final ground for use.
A further substance is needed to bear the property, and the chain of substrata never bottoms out in a basic thing.
context: The Third Man argument exposes a tension in Plato's own theory. If a Form is self-predicating (Largeness is itself large) and non-identical with its instances, every level demands a new Form to explain the shared character. Aristotle wields the regress against the Academy; modern interpreters from Vlastos to Sedley still dispute whether Plato saw it as fatal or as a productive puzzle.

question: Aristotle in De Anima III.5 splits the intellect in two: one that becomes all things, one that makes all things. Commentators from Alexander to Averroes to Aquinas fought for centuries over this short passage. What is the live question?
answer: Whether the active intellect is each person's own faculty or a single separate intelligence shared by all human minds.
choices: Whether the active intellect is each person's own faculty or a single separate intelligence shared by all human minds.
Whether the passive intellect grasps universals directly or only abstracts them slowly from repeated sensory encounters.
Whether the active intellect operates only during waking life or continues to think through sleep and bodily death.
Whether intellect belongs to humans alone or extends in lower forms to the higher animals that share our senses.
context: Aristotle's text is famously cryptic — barely a page. Alexander of Aphrodisias read the active intellect as God; Averroes made it one shared mind, threatening personal immortality; Aquinas insisted each soul has its own. The dispute shaped medieval debates about resurrection and is alive in recent work by Frede, Caston, and Burnyeat.

question: Chrysippus the Stoic held that every event is fated by the divine logos, yet that we are still responsible for our actions. He answered the lazy argument with a famous distinction. What did he say does the work?
answer: External causes start a sequence, but our own character determines how we assent — fate works through us, not around us.
choices: External causes start a sequence, but our own character determines how we assent — fate works through us, not around us.
External causes fix bodily motion, but the rational soul is uncaused and stands free of the chain of physical events.
External causes are fated, but human futures contain genuine alternative branches that the agent selects between.
External causes determine outcomes, but the gods reward effort regardless of whether the effort changes anything.
context: Chrysippus distinguished principal causes (a cylinder's shape, which makes it roll) from antecedent ones (the push). Fate supplies the push; what we are supplies the rolling. Modern compatibilists from Frankfurt to Dennett rediscover the move; libertarians like Kane reject it as merely rebranding the puzzle. Susanne Bobzien's reconstructions made the dispute live again.

question: Augustine and the British monk Pelagius fought over a single question: can a human will, unaided, choose the good? Augustine's later answer reshaped Western theology. What did he claim grace must do?
answer: Grace must precede and enable any good choice, since the fallen will is bound to sin until divine action frees it to choose otherwise.
choices: Grace must precede and enable any good choice, since the fallen will is bound to sin until divine action frees it to choose otherwise.
Grace must follow each good choice, rewarding the effort the unaided will has already made by itself toward holiness.
Grace must crown the moral life at its end, completing what natural virtue has built up over a lifetime of free striving.
Grace must overcome the body's weakness, since the soul itself is already healthy and needs no internal correction.
context: Pelagius held that if God commanded the good, humans must be able to choose it — anything less makes the command unjust. Augustine, marked by his own conversion, replied that the will after Eden is free only to sin until grace reorders it. The dispute set the agenda for Aquinas, Luther, Calvin, Jansen, and Wesley; contemporary writers from Wetzel to Mathewes argue the original positions are still routinely misread.

question: Pelagius read Augustine's prayer give what you command and command what you will and judged it dangerous. What concrete moral worry drove his attack on the Augustinian view?
answer: If a will cannot avoid sin without special grace, no one is truly responsible for failing — and divine judgement of the unaided becomes unjust.
choices: If a will cannot avoid sin without special grace, no one is truly responsible for failing — and divine judgement of the unaided becomes unjust.
If a will is moved by grace, every virtuous act belongs to God alone — and the saint receives no real credit for his sanctity.
If a will is bound to sin from birth, infant baptism becomes magical — and the rite loses its meaning as a free covenant.
If a will is freed by grace once, sin afterward is impossible — and the Christian life has no place for further struggle.
context: Pelagius was a moral reformer worried that Augustine's view sapped effort. His worry remains powerful: if I cannot, I am not obliged. Twentieth-century theology — Rahner, von Balthasar, Hauerwas — keeps reworking the puzzle, and analytic philosophers of religion like Eleonore Stump return to it through compatibilist resources Augustine himself did not have.

question: The monk Gaunilo, replying to Anselm, said: by your reasoning I can prove a perfect island exists. Anselm's response in the Reply to Gaunilo is more subtle than usually retold. What does he actually argue?
answer: Only a being than which no greater can be conceived has necessary existence built into its concept; islands are contingent and cannot.
choices: Only a being than which no greater can be conceived has necessary existence built into its concept; islands are contingent and cannot.
Only a being addressed in worship has the imaginative force to ground the inference; ordinary objects do not move the heart.
Only a being known through revelation can be the target of such reasoning; reason alone reaches no positive conclusion at all.
Only a being whose nature is grasped completely can ground the proof; islands resist exhaustive conception in principle.
context: Anselm's move is that perfect island is not a coherent maximum — every finite kind has no intrinsic upper limit. Only God, defined as that than which no greater can be conceived, has necessity built in. Malcolm and Plantinga revived the argument as a modal proof; Sobel and Oppy reply that the modal version still fails. The dispute is alive in analytic philosophy of religion.

question: Aquinas held that when we say God is good, we do not mean good in the same sense as a good knife, nor in a wholly unrelated sense. What is the analogical predication strategy meant to avoid?
answer: Univocity would make God a member of a common genus; equivocity would make all theology mere noise — analogy threads between them.
choices: Univocity would make God a member of a common genus; equivocity would make all theology mere noise — analogy threads between them.
Univocity would import sensory content into theology; equivocity would import nothing at all — analogy supplies a felt likeness.
Univocity would commit one to seeing God; equivocity would leave God unknown — analogy provides a middle visual grasp.
Univocity would imply finite creation in God; equivocity would deny all creation — analogy lets creation share his nature partly.
context: Scotus replied that without some univocity the argument cannot get started; Cajetan refined Aquinas's distinction into analogy of proportionality. Twentieth-century retrievals by Burrell, McCabe, and most recently the analytic Thomism of Eleonore Stump and Brian Davies wrestle with whether analogy is finally a real third option or a name for the puzzle. The Scotist/Thomist split still divides Catholic schools.

question: Schelling in his 1809 Freedom Essay made a strange move: he placed inside God a 'ground' that is not yet personal will — picture a darkness, a yearning in the deep, prior to God's own clear self-knowing. The same God who freely chooses also rises out of this ground. The move scandalized Hegel and fascinated Heidegger. What was Schelling trying to explain by it?
answer: How real evil is possible without making God its author — by placing in God a dark ground that is not yet personal will, prior to God's own self-actualization.
choices: How real evil is possible without making God its author — by placing in God a dark ground that is not yet personal will, prior to God's own self-actualization.
How God's eternity can include time — by allowing a temporal ground to underlie the timeless divine existence as its developmental matrix.
How God can be known by reason — by giving thought a ground in being that secures the agreement between concept and reality without further proof.
How God's nature can be triune — by reading the ground, the existence, and their unity as the three persons of orthodox Christian theology.
context: Schelling treats the ground in God as longing — a darkness that is the condition of real choice and so of real evil. Heidegger devoted a lecture course to the essay; Slavoj Zizek made it a centerpiece. Theologians from Tillich to Robert Jenson revisit it. Whether the move helps with theodicy or quietly imports two principles into God is the dispute.

question: Sidgwick, at the close of The Methods of Ethics, confessed he could not reconcile two principles each of which seemed to him self-evident. He called the failure a dualism. What were the two principles?
answer: That each person should maximize his own good, and that each should maximize the good impartially — reason supports both, yet they diverge in practice.
choices: That each person should maximize his own good, and that each should maximize the good impartially — reason supports both, yet they diverge in practice.
That utility should be summed across persons, and that distributions should be equal — yet maximization and equality recommend different actions.
That pleasure is the only good, and that some pleasures are higher than others — yet pure quantity and Millian quality conflict in cases.
That the right is what maximizes happiness, and that motives must be virtuous — yet act and motive can come apart in clear cases.
context: Sidgwick's dualism — egoism and impartial benevolence both rational, yet pulling apart — was Bernard Williams's exhibit A against the project of impartial ethics. Derek Parfit's three-volume On What Matters is essentially a reopening of the case. Contemporary writers from Phillip Pettit to Roger Crisp to Susan Wolf are still arguing whether the dualism can be dissolved or must be lived with.

question: The 'crude' reading of perspectivism: any view as good as any. The 'sophisticated' reading rejects this. What does it say marks a better perspective?
answer: Reach and self-awareness — it sees more, holds rivals inside its account, knows its own conditions. A poor stance is parochial and naive about itself.
choices: Reach and self-awareness — it sees more, holds rivals inside its account, knows its own conditions. A poor stance is parochial and naive about itself.
Internal coherence alone — its component claims fit together without contradiction, whatever its scope or its relation to standpoints outside its own frame.
Practical fitness — it strengthens the holder against suffering. Truth-talk is a separate matter the strong adopt or drop as the moment requires of them.
Long-run convergence — other careful thinkers, working in good faith from independent starting points, eventually arrive at the same view as the holder.
context: Crude perspectivism is the sophomore reading. Nehamas's Life as Literature, Clark's Nietzsche on Truth, and Leiter's Routledge guide argue Nietzsche meant something stronger: perspectives are evaluable for what they let a thinker integrate and acknowledge.

question: 'Hesperus = Phosphorus' was a discovery, yet both name Venus. Russell replaced names with hidden descriptions. What was Kripke's decisive blow?
answer: Names are rigid — they pick out the same thing across counterfactuals — but descriptions are not. So names cannot be hidden descriptions without losing this feature.
choices: Names are rigid — they pick out the same thing across counterfactuals — but descriptions are not. So names cannot be hidden descriptions without losing this feature.
Definite descriptions presuppose rather than assert existence, so empty names make a sentence neither true nor false; Russell could not handle non-referring names.
The analytic-synthetic distinction collapses, so the line between name-meaning and description-meaning rests on nothing; descriptivism smuggles in analyticities.
Speakers use descriptions referentially even when descriptions miss the referent, so description-meaning is decoupled from denotation in ordinary conversation.
context: Russell's descriptivism: 'Aristotle' abbreviates 'the teacher of Alexander.' Kripke's Naming and Necessity (1970) tested it modally. If 'Aristotle' meant the description, then 'Aristotle did not teach Alexander' would contradict — but it doesn't; he might have stayed in Stagira.

question: Later Wittgenstein on rule-following: any past pattern fits other rules. Before Kripke's gloss, what made 'add two' the right next step on his view?
answer: No further fact stands behind the practice. 'This is what I do' — the shared form of life provides the standard, and seeking deeper grounding repeats the confusion.
choices: No further fact stands behind the practice. 'This is what I do' — the shared form of life provides the standard, and seeking deeper grounding repeats the confusion.
An inner state of intending the rule fixes it; when I learned addition I formed a representation, and applications must match its content to count as correct.
A dispositional fact about my brain settles it; neural states encode the rule, and an application is correct by what those states would output when probed.
A Platonic rule-object exists independently; addition is a function in a third realm, my training put me in contact with it, and each application checks against it.
context: Investigations §§185-242. The target is a rule as a rail laid to infinity, fixing every step. No interpretation settles which extension counts. At the end of justifications, I act. McDowell, Baker, Hacker read this as quietism. Community-dispositionalism is Kripke's reconstruction.

question: Lincoln in 1861 argued the South could not secede — and his case was not just that the Union was old or strong. He built a structural argument from the logic of self-government. What did he claim secession would prove?
answer: That any majority losing a fair election may simply leave — which destroys the principle of consent any government rests on.
choices: That any majority losing a fair election may simply leave — which destroys the principle of consent any government rests on.
That states retain a sovereignty older than the Constitution itself, which Madison had quietly endorsed in the Virginia Resolutions.
That a written charter once adopted is dissolvable only with the unanimous agreement of every signatory still bound by its terms.
That federations decay unless backed by an ethnic or religious bond, which the American republic had deliberately refused at its founding.
context: Lincoln's First Inaugural and the July 4 message to Congress argue that if a minority that loses an election may break the Union, the principle of majority rule collapses; if the majority may, then minorities have no protection at all. Either way, free government dies. The slavery question was the immediate cause, but the philosophical structure is about consent itself — the bedrock claim of the Declaration.

question: Hume's Of Miracles is often read as denying miracles. But his actual claim was about testimony itself, and applies to any improbable report — including reports we might want to believe. What did he argue?
answer: No testimony establishes a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event it reports — and that bar is almost never cleared.
choices: No testimony establishes a miracle unless its falsehood would be more miraculous than the event it reports — and that bar is almost never cleared.
No miracle can occur, because laws of nature are necessary truths and a violation would be a logical contradiction in the very concept.
No miracle is worth investigating, because the religious motive of witnesses contaminates every report from the moment of its first telling.
No miracle counts as evidence, because supernatural causes lie outside the explanatory framework empirical inquiry was designed to handle.
context: Section X of the Enquiry frames a probabilistic principle, not a metaphysical one. Hume balances two improbabilities — that the laws were violated, or that the witness was mistaken, lying, or deceived — and asks which is greater. The same logic applies to any astonishing claim. Earman has argued Hume's principle reduces to Bayes' theorem; others, including Larmer, deny the math works. The dispute is technical and live.

question: Dickie formalized Danto: art is what the artworld confers art-status on. Carroll pressed back. What did he say the institutional theory could not explain about how art moves?
answer: Historical narrative — new art is recognized as art by its intelligible relation to earlier art, not by an institutional fiat that could pick anything at all.
choices: Historical narrative — new art is recognized as art by its intelligible relation to earlier art, not by an institutional fiat that could pick anything at all.
Formal beauty — institutions can confer status, but beauty itself is a perceptual property that anyone can recognize without theory or training at all.
Aesthetic experience — institutions describe how art gets gallery space, but they cannot explain why a viewer would care to look once it is there.
Moral seriousness — institutions can canonize whatever they please, but only works that engage genuine human concerns reach the status of real art.
context: Carroll's historical-narrative theory in Beyond Aesthetics (2001) argues that something counts as art when it stands in an intelligible historical line — extending, repudiating, or commenting on prior art. The institutional theory's circularity (art is what the artworld treats as art) collapses on Carroll's reading. Beardsley's aesthetic-experience theory and Scruton's moralism are the other live rivals in the cell.

question: Rolston III says nature has intrinsic value humans discover. Callicott says intrinsic value is real but always projected by a valuer. What does the dispute actually settle?
answer: Whether nature would retain value if no minds ever existed — Rolston says yes, Callicott says intrinsic value requires a valuer though the value remains real.
choices: Whether nature would retain value if no minds ever existed — Rolston says yes, Callicott says intrinsic value requires a valuer though the value remains real.
Whether ecosystems or only individuals count morally — Rolston grounds duties in the biotic whole, Callicott grounds them in the species member alone.
Whether wilderness preservation requires legal personhood — Rolston endorses giving rivers standing, Callicott calls the move category-confused legalism.
Whether duties to nature override duties to humans in conflict — Rolston accepts the override, Callicott insists human duties always retain priority.
context: Rolston's objectivism (Environmental Ethics, 1988) holds that a species or ecosystem has value independently of any observer — a 'value-in-itself' the way matter has mass. Callicott's Humean turn (In Defense of the Land Ethic) holds that all value requires a valuer, but rejects the easy slide from there to mere subjectivism: values can be grounded in valuers and still bind us. The dispute is whether anthropocentric and non-anthropocentric ethics can really be reconciled.

question: Eubulides refined an old puzzle into the sharpest paradox in logic: 'this sentence is false.' If true, false; if false, true. What lesson did Tarski draw for any formal language strong enough to talk of its own truth?
answer: No consistent formal language can contain its own complete truth predicate — to say which sentences of L are true demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
choices: No consistent formal language can contain its own complete truth predicate — to say which sentences of L are true demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can contain its own complete proof predicate — to say which sentences of L are provable demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can specify all its own well-formed sentences — to say which strings of L are grammatical demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
No consistent formal language can express its own complete semantic content — to give the meaning of each sentence of L demands a metalanguage above L, producing a hierarchy.
context: Tarski's hierarchy was a deep response to the Liar. Kripke and later truth theorists tried to allow languages to contain their own truth predicate using paraconsistent or partial-logic moves.

question: Böhm-Bawerk in 1896 pressed a case against Marx's labor theory of value. Suppose a vintage wine sits in a cellar for twenty years and grows more valuable. No new labor was added. On Marx's theory, where does the extra value come from?
answer: Marx held the wine's value tracks the socially necessary labor for an equivalent product now — older labor congeals at current prevailing rates.
choices: Marx held the wine's value tracks the socially necessary labor for an equivalent product now — older labor congeals at current prevailing rates.
Marx conceded the case as a clear counterexample to his theory and revised the labor theory of value in unpublished notes near the end of his life.
Marx attributed the extra value to interest paid by the cellar's owner for storage, treating wine as a special case where capital really added value.
Marx left the case to a footnote, attributing it to subjective taste and admitting the labor theory did not apply to luxury commodities of this kind.
context: Capital I and III; Böhm-Bawerk's Karl Marx and the Close of His System (1896) pressed aging-wine and similar cases hard against the framework.

question: The eternal recurrence first appears as a demon's whisper in The Gay Science §341: every pain, every joy, every smallest thing in your life will return, in the same order, infinitely. Nietzsche presents it not as cosmology to believe but as a test. What is the test supposed to measure?
answer: Whether your life is one you would will to live again exactly as it was — a hard standard for affirming existence without longing for any escape.
choices: Whether your life is one you would will to live again exactly as it was — a hard standard for affirming existence without longing for any escape.
Whether the universe contains enough total energy to return matter to its starting state, a calculation Nietzsche pursued in private notebooks.
Whether the soul can survive bodily death and pass into a new arrangement of the same atoms, as the Stoics had earlier proposed.
Whether moral choices can be justified by their consequences when the consequences themselves are bound to repeat without any limit.
context: The Gay Science §341 and Zarathustra. The response Nietzsche names is amor fati: the love of fate.

question: Kierkegaard's Sickness Unto Death calls despair more universal than illness. Most despairing people, he says, do not know they are in despair. The book's definition reads strangely: despair is a misrelation in the self's relation to itself. What is the simplest version of the diagnosis?
answer: Despair is wanting to be a self other than the one you have been given — refusing the particular self that is yours to be.
choices: Despair is wanting to be a self other than the one you have been given — refusing the particular self that is yours to be.
Despair is the sustained absence of pleasure, which builds up across years until the sufferer can no longer recall what enjoyment felt like.
Despair is a clinical depression caused by inherited temperament, and treatment belongs to the physician rather than to the theologian.
Despair is the collapse of confidence in any objective moral order, which is permanently fixed once a society has lost its older faith.
context: The Sickness Unto Death (1849), published under Anti-Climacus. The 'cure' is willing transparently to be the self one is, before God.

question: Heidegger's Being and Time (1927) sets one question above all others — the question, he says, that nearly all of Western philosophy from Plato onward has forgotten how to ask. What is the question?
answer: What it means for anything to 'be' at all — not what particular beings exist, but the meaning of being itself, which differs across kinds of entity.
choices: What it means for anything to 'be' at all — not what particular beings exist, but the meaning of being itself, which differs across kinds of entity.
Whether God exists — and if so, how the divine nature differs from the natures of created beings as Aristotle had described them in detail.
Whether the external world exists — Heidegger thought Cartesian skepticism remained the open problem until his own work resolved it.
Whether numbers exist — the status of mathematical objects had been left hanging by Frege and Husserl and required a new account.
context: Being and Time, Introduction. The claim: the question of being is buried because philosophy only asks what particular beings (atoms, ideas, God) are.

question: Principia Mathematica ran three thick volumes; Whitehead and Russell finally proved 1+1=2 on page 379 of Volume I. They thought they had reduced arithmetic to logic. Twenty years later, a 25-year-old Austrian named Gödel ended the project with one paper. What did Gödel show?
answer: Any formal system rich enough to express arithmetic contains true sentences it cannot itself prove — there is no complete logical foundation.
choices: Any formal system rich enough to express arithmetic contains true sentences it cannot itself prove — there is no complete logical foundation.
Russell's theory of types was inconsistent on its own terms, and the whole Principia derivation collapsed back into the original paradox.
The natural numbers cannot be defined in any nonparadoxical way, and so all of arithmetic rests on an undefined primitive notion of counting.
Whitehead's earlier algebraic work conflicted with Russell's logicism, and Principia could not be finished consistently with both authors signing.
context: Gödel's 1931 incompleteness theorems. The result also implies a system rich enough to prove its own consistency cannot exist.

question: The Tractatus and the Investigations look incompatible at almost every point. Yet the later Wittgenstein wanted them published together. One thread, scholars argue, runs through both books. What is the thread?
answer: Philosophy is therapy, not theory — its job is to dissolve confusions about how language works, not to build a system of doctrines.
choices: Philosophy is therapy, not theory — its job is to dissolve confusions about how language works, not to build a system of doctrines.
Philosophy is empirical science — its job is to systematize the findings of physics and biology under the most general possible laws.
Philosophy is religious witness — its job is to point silently toward what every honest seeker comes eventually to know in private.
Philosophy is political action — its job is to expose the ideologies that justify the existing distribution of social and economic power.
context: Both Tractatus 6.53 and Investigations §133 treat philosophy as something that ends, not as a body of results — 'the fly out of the fly-bottle.'

question: Dennett resisted the framing that consciousness is a thing inside a person who watches. He proposed a different picture. What did he claim?
answer: Consciousness is what a brain does — many parallel processes, none privileged, none arriving anywhere central to be witnessed.
choices: Consciousness is what a brain does — many parallel processes, none privileged, none arriving anywhere central to be witnessed.
Consciousness is an illusion — there is nothing it is like to be anyone, and reports of inner experience are systematic confabulation.
Consciousness is a substance that brains generate — distinct from the matter they are made of, much as electricity differs from wire.
Consciousness is a relation to one's body — the experience of being embodied is the whole of it, with nothing further to explain.
context: Dennett's 'multiple drafts' model in Consciousness Explained denied the Cartesian theater — the inner stage where experience appears to a viewer. Drafts of representations compete in parallel; what we call consciousness is the pattern of probings, not an inner showing. Critics charged he had changed the subject; Dennett replied that was the whole point.

question: Turing in 1950 proposed a test for whether a machine could 'think.' He framed the question in a specific way to avoid one philosophical trap. What did the framing avoid?
answer: It avoided defining 'thinking' first — replacing the unanswerable definitional question with a question about indistinguishable behavior in conversation.
choices: It avoided defining 'thinking' first — replacing the unanswerable definitional question with a question about indistinguishable behavior in conversation.
It avoided giving the machine an unfair advantage — the human judge could ask any question, and the test was symmetric between parties.
It avoided requiring physical embodiment — confining the test to text meant the machine's lack of a body would not betray its nature.
It avoided privileging adult intelligence — the test could be run with a child or an adult, and the same indistinguishability question would apply.
context: Turing's move was philosophical-methodological. 'Can machines think?' was, he said, 'too meaningless to deserve discussion.' Replace it with a clear question — can a machine be indistinguishable from a human in extended written conversation? — and the question becomes tractable. Critics from Searle on argued the replacement changed the subject; defenders say that was the methodological point.

question: Arendt analyzed Eichmann's trial in 1961 and coined a phrase that has stayed with us. What was the disturbing observation behind 'the banality of evil'?
answer: The catastrophic harm came not from a sadistic monster but from an unremarkable bureaucrat who never paused to think about what he was doing.
choices: The catastrophic harm came not from a sadistic monster but from an unremarkable bureaucrat who never paused to think about what he was doing.
The catastrophic harm came from a few committed ideologues whose ordinary appearance disguised the radicalism beneath the surface.
The catastrophic harm came from a tradition of obedience that ordinary people inherit without consciously choosing the ethics they live by.
The catastrophic harm came from a deformed conscience that no civilized society could fail to recognize once given a fair public hearing.
context: Arendt's report on the trial was controversial precisely because she refused the consoling picture. Eichmann was not a moral monster — he was a man who organized trains. The disturbing finding was that mass evil could be carried by people who never let the magnitude of what they were doing enter their thinking.

question: Four-dimensionalism says people are extended through time the way they are extended through space — slices of a single elongated worm. What does this dissolve?
answer: The puzzle of how I can be the same person as my five-year-old self — both of us are time-slices of one worm, like two ends of a hallway.
choices: The puzzle of how I can be the same person as my five-year-old self — both of us are time-slices of one worm, like two ends of a hallway.
The puzzle of why I am located in space at all — extension in time provides the resources to explain extension in space derivatively.
The puzzle of why I cannot return to the past — extension in time means my earlier slices are still real, so the asymmetry needs further explanation.
The puzzle of whether I will exist tomorrow — extension in time guarantees my future slices, making personal survival trivially secure.
context: Four-dimensionalism (or 'perdurantism,' developed by Quine, Lewis, and Heller) treats objects as spread out in time like a hallway is spread out in space. Personal identity through change becomes no more puzzling than spatial extension — the doorway is the same hallway as the back room, even though they are not in the same place. Whether this *helps* with the original puzzles is contested.

question: Walter Benjamin in 1936 argued that the technology of reproduction had changed art at a deep level. What did he say it had withered?
answer: The 'aura' of the work — the unique presence of a thing here and now, which copies by definition cannot have however perfect their reproduction.
choices: The 'aura' of the work — the unique presence of a thing here and now, which copies by definition cannot have however perfect their reproduction.
The audience for the work — mass reproduction democratized art, leaving original works without the public who once attended them.
The skill of the work — mechanical reproduction made craft training optional, and over time the underlying craftsmanship declined.
The economic value of the work — once anything could be copied, no one would pay the original artists what they had earned before.
context: Benjamin's 'The Work of Art in the Age of Mechanical Reproduction' argued the original's authority — its unrepeatable presence in a specific tradition — could not survive a print run of a million identical posters. The loss was not nostalgic complaint. Some hoped this would liberate art from cultic deference; others mourned what reproduction took from the encounter. Benjamin held both at once.

question: Newcomb's problem pits two decision principles against each other. The two-boxer takes both boxes since the prediction is fixed. The one-boxer takes only the opaque box since one-boxers walk away rich. What distinct principle does each side follow?
answer: Two-boxing follows causal decision theory: act on what your choice causes. One-boxing follows evidential decision theory: act on what your choice indicates, since one-boxers correlate with riches.
choices: Two-boxing follows causal decision theory: act on what your choice causes. One-boxing follows evidential decision theory: act on what your choice indicates, since one-boxers correlate with riches.
Two-boxing follows dominance reasoning always, while one-boxing follows expected-value calculation — the dispute reduces to which rational-choice principle gets priority in mixed cases that arise.
Two-boxing follows ordinary common-sense rationality, while one-boxing follows special logic for cases involving an infallible predictor — the split is over how unusual cases should be treated by us.
Two-boxing follows narrow individual self-interest, while one-boxing follows long-run cooperative reasoning — the dispute mirrors the prisoner's dilemma between defection and cooperation entirely.
context: Robert Nozick popularized Newcomb's problem in 1969. Gibbard and Harper (1978) developed causal decision theory; Jeffrey's evidential decision theory came earlier. Recent functional decision theory (Soares, Yudkowsky) tries to capture what is right about each.

question: The Golden Rule says treat others the way you want to be treated. If you love loud music but your sister hates it, what does the rule really ask you to do?
answer: Think about what your sister wants, not what you want.
choices: Think about what your sister wants, not what you want.
Play loud music for her since you would enjoy that.
Only follow the rule with people just like you.
Skip the rule when you and another person differ.
context: The Golden Rule works best when you stop and imagine the other person's side, not when you assume they want what you want.

question: A bully says 'I would want someone to be tough with me, so I am tough with you.' What is wrong with how he is using the Golden Rule?
answer: He is forcing his own taste on you instead of asking what you want.
choices: He is forcing his own taste on you instead of asking what you want.
He should be tougher, because being tough is always good.
He should never have heard of the Golden Rule in the first place.
He should treat others worse than he treats himself, not better.
context: The Golden Rule asks for real care about other people. If you only ask 'what would I want?', you can miss what they would want.

question: Almost every culture has a version of the Golden Rule. The Chinese teacher Confucius said do NOT do to others what you would not want done to you. How is his version a little different?
answer: It tells you what to AVOID, not what you have to do.
choices: It tells you what to AVOID, not what you have to do.
It tells you to do nothing at all and stay out of the way.
It tells you to copy other people instead of leading yourself.
It tells you the rule only works for people in China.
context: Confucius lived a long time ago in China. His version of the rule is gentler: it asks you to not hurt others, rather than to do great deeds.

question: Imagine you really want a friend to push you when you are scared, because pushing helps YOU. Does the Golden Rule mean you should push other scared people the same way?
answer: Not always, because other people may need patience, not a push.
choices: Not always, because other people may need patience, not a push.
Yes, because what works for you must work for everyone.
No, because the Golden Rule never works for scared people.
Yes, because pushing someone always helps them in the end.
context: The rule asks you to care about what the other person needs, even when their needs are different from yours.

question: Your friend hands out birthday cake. She gives a big piece to everyone EXCEPT one kid she does not like. Why does this break the Golden Rule?
answer: She would not want to be left out, so she should not leave others out.
choices: She would not want to be left out, so she should not leave others out.
She should have given the kid a smaller piece, not nothing.
She should have skipped the party because cake is unhealthy.
She should have given the cake only to the kid she likes most.
context: The Golden Rule means we treat others the way we would want to be treated, even when we don't like them.

question: Two kids argue over whose turn it is on the swing. One says 'I would let you have it if it was my turn, so you should let me have it now.' Why is this NOT a fair use of the Golden Rule?
answer: He is using the rule to get what he wants, not to help the other kid.
choices: He is using the rule to get what he wants, not to help the other kid.
He used too many words, so the other kid did not understand him.
He should not use the rule on swings, only on bigger problems.
He should have argued louder so the other kid had to give in.
context: The Golden Rule is for caring about other people. It is not a trick to win arguments.

question: Your friend asks you to lie for her. She says it is for a good reason. What is the FIRST thing to think about?
answer: Whether her 'good reason' is really a good reason, or just convenient.
choices: Whether her 'good reason' is really a good reason, or just convenient.
Whether the lie will be fun to tell, since lies can feel exciting.
Whether you can get away with it without anyone noticing later.
Whether your friend will be mad if you do not lie for her.
context: People often dress up a lie as a 'good reason' when it is really just easier than telling the truth.

question: A kid breaks a window playing ball. He says 'I will say a stranger did it.' His sister says 'tell the truth, even though you will get in trouble.' Why does his sister think honesty matters more than avoiding trouble?
answer: A lie hides what really happened, and other people deserve the truth.
choices: A lie hides what really happened, and other people deserve the truth.
She does not like her brother very much and wants him punished.
Lies never work out, but the truth always works out perfectly.
Strangers get blamed for too many things and have hurt feelings.
context: Honesty is not just about avoiding lies. It is about respecting other people enough to tell them what really happened.

question: Aunt Mary asks 'do you LIKE my new green hat?' You think the hat looks silly. What is one HONEST thing you could say?
answer: You could say what you do like about the hat without lying.
choices: You could say what you do like about the hat without lying.
You could say the hat is the most beautiful hat in the world.
You could pretend you cannot see the hat at all, that solves it.
You could shout that the hat is silly so everyone hears you.
context: Being honest does not mean being mean. You can find true things that are also kind to say.

question: Some people say a 'white lie' (a small fib to be polite) is fine. Others say even small lies are wrong. What is one good reason a person might worry about white lies?
answer: Small lies can make telling bigger lies feel easier later on.
choices: Small lies can make telling bigger lies feel easier later on.
White lies are illegal and you could be arrested for telling one.
White lies only work if you have white skin, which is unfair.
White lies make your tongue turn white, which doctors can see.
context: Some thinkers worry that getting used to small lies, even kind ones, can change what we are willing to lie about later.

question: A boy on the playground tells everyone he has a pet tiger at home. It is not true. Why might this kind of brag-lie hurt HIM in the end?
answer: Other kids will stop trusting him, even when he tells the truth.
choices: Other kids will stop trusting him, even when he tells the truth.
Tigers are protected animals so it is illegal to even pretend.
The other kids will think tigers are real and become scared.
He will get in trouble for owning a tiger he does not own.
context: When people catch you in a lie, they wonder what ELSE you have lied about. Trust is hard to rebuild.

question: Your dad asks 'did you brush your teeth?' You did not. Why does even a tiny lie like 'yes I did' matter?
answer: Your dad cannot help you take care of yourself if he can't trust you.
choices: Your dad cannot help you take care of yourself if he can't trust you.
Teeth are not important, so the question was not worth asking.
Your dad will never know whether you really brushed your teeth.
Lies about teeth lead to lies about everything else by tomorrow.
context: Honesty in small things is what makes honesty in big things possible. Trust is built one little moment at a time.

question: A friend tells a secret and asks you to keep it. Later, you find out the secret is that he stole from someone. Why is THIS different from a normal secret?
answer: Keeping the secret means letting the harm continue, which is wrong.
choices: Keeping the secret means letting the harm continue, which is wrong.
Stealing is fun to talk about, so you should tell everyone.
All secrets are bad and you should never agree to keep one.
His secret is not really a secret unless you tell strangers too.
context: Promises matter. But a promise to hide harm from the person being hurt is not a promise we should keep.

question: Your sister says 'be honest, am I funny?' You think her jokes are really not funny. What is the kindest honest answer?
answer: You could say which joke you DID like and ask about her favorites.
choices: You could say which joke you DID like and ask about her favorites.
You should say her jokes are the worst jokes ever invented.
You should pretend her jokes are funny so she keeps telling them.
You should say all her jokes are funny except the ones you hate.
context: Being honest is a skill, like riding a bike. You can learn to be truthful without being cruel.

question: Three kids share a pizza with eight slices. The biggest kid says 'I am bigger so I get four slices.' Why does this NOT feel fair?
answer: Being bigger is not a reason to get more, unless they all agreed.
choices: Being bigger is not a reason to get more, unless they all agreed.
It is fair, because bigger kids need more food to grow up.
It is not fair, because pizza should be cut into three slices.
It is fair, because the biggest kid is usually the smartest one.
context: Fairness usually means people get something for a real reason, not just because they are stronger or louder.

question: Two friends both worked hard on a school project. The teacher gives ONE friend the prize because she likes that friend more. What word describes what just happened?
answer: Unfair, because the prize went to a favorite, not to the best work.
choices: Unfair, because the prize went to a favorite, not to the best work.
Fine, because teachers can do whatever they want in their class.
Funny, because school projects are supposed to be just for fun.
Smart, because the teacher knew who would do the project better.
context: Favoritism is the opposite of fairness. Real fairness ignores who you like and looks at who earned it.

question: If you find a wallet on the playground, what is the right thing to do?
answer: Take it to a grown-up who can find the person who lost it.
choices: Take it to a grown-up who can find the person who lost it.
Keep it, because finders get to keep whatever they find.
Throw it away so no one can steal it from you later on.
Open it, take only the money, and leave the rest behind.
context: The wallet belongs to someone who is probably worried. Getting it back to them is what fairness asks of us.

question: Your teacher gives every kid in class the SAME number of pencils. But some kids already have lots, and some have none at all. Is this the most fair way to share?
answer: Maybe not — kids with nothing might need more than kids with lots.
choices: Maybe not — kids with nothing might need more than kids with lots.
Yes, because giving everyone the same is always the most fair.
No, because kids with lots should have to give their pencils away.
Yes, because nobody can complain when they all got the same thing.
context: Sometimes fair means 'everyone gets the same.' Sometimes fair means 'each kid gets what they need.' Which one fits depends on the situation.

question: Two kids race. One trained for weeks. The other did not train at all. The trained kid wins. Is this 'unfair' to the kid who lost?
answer: No, because the winner earned it with practice and effort.
choices: No, because the winner earned it with practice and effort.
Yes, because the kids should have gotten the same trophy at the end.
Yes, because training before a race is cheating, plain and simple.
No, because losing a race is good for kids and teaches them stuff.
context: Fairness includes letting people benefit from work they really did. Stopping the trained kid from winning would punish her effort.

question: A kid gets blamed for breaking a vase he did not break. Other kids saw who really did it. What should they DO if they care about fairness?
answer: Speak up and tell the truth, even if the real breaker is their friend.
choices: Speak up and tell the truth, even if the real breaker is their friend.
Stay quiet, because telling on people is always wrong, no matter what.
Wait a day or two and see what happens before doing anything bad.
Tell only HALF the truth so nobody gets in too much trouble at all.
context: Letting the wrong kid take the blame is itself unfair. Speaking up takes courage, but it is part of being fair.

question: A new kid from another country joins the class. Some kids tease her because she sounds different. What does fairness say about this?
answer: She is new to ENGLISH, not to being a person who deserves respect.
choices: She is new to ENGLISH, not to being a person who deserves respect.
Teasing her is fine since she does not understand what they say.
She should change how she sounds to match the other kids quickly.
Other kids should tease her back to show her how teasing feels.
context: Fairness reminds us that every person deserves the same basic respect, even when they look or sound new to us.

question: Two friends both want the last seat by the window. They both got to the seat at the SAME time. What is one fair way to decide?
answer: Take turns — one sits today, the other sits the next time.
choices: Take turns — one sits today, the other sits the next time.
The louder kid gets the seat, because being loud is more important.
Both kids should be sent to the back row as a punishment for arguing.
Whoever was born first should win, because age decides everything.
context: When two people want one thing and both have an equal claim, taking turns is one of the simplest fair answers.

question: A friend cheats on a test. You can stay quiet (kind) or tell the teacher (just). Why might these two things pull in different ways?
answer: Being kind to your friend would mean other kids get cheated out of fair grades.
choices: Being kind to your friend would mean other kids get cheated out of fair grades.
Being kind to your friend would also mean lying to your parents at home.
Being just to the teacher would get the teacher in trouble with the school.
Being just always feels nicer than being kind, because justice is fun.
context: Kindness asks 'what will hurt the person I am with?' Justice asks 'what will hurt all the people I am NOT with?' Sometimes they agree, sometimes they fight.

question: Your little brother breaks your favorite toy. Mom says he should give you his allowance until your toy is paid back. He cries. What is Mom doing — kindness or justice?
answer: Justice — making sure the harm gets repaired, even though it makes him sad.
choices: Justice — making sure the harm gets repaired, even though it makes him sad.
Kindness — she is being kind to him by helping him save his money.
Both — because making your brother cry is just AND kind in this case.
Neither — because parents are supposed to fix everything themselves.
context: Justice often costs the person who did the harm. That can feel unkind in the moment, but it is how we restore what was broken.

question: Two kids are in trouble for the same thing. One says 'sorry, I won't do it again.' The other does not say sorry. The grown-up gives them the SAME punishment. Is this fair?
answer: Maybe — saying sorry matters, but breaking the rule still has costs.
choices: Maybe — saying sorry matters, but breaking the rule still has costs.
No — the sorry kid should get a reward for being polite.
Yes — saying sorry is a trick and should not be trusted ever.
No — the not-sorry kid should be allowed to leave with no punishment.
context: An apology is not the same as undoing the harm. Justice can still ask for a consequence even when someone is genuinely sorry.

question: A homeless man takes bread from a shop because he is hungry. The shopkeeper is upset because the bread cost money to bake. Both things are TRUE — what makes this hard?
answer: The man's hunger is real, AND the shopkeeper's loss is real, all at once.
choices: The man's hunger is real, AND the shopkeeper's loss is real, all at once.
The man should have stolen from a richer shop instead of this one.
The shopkeeper should bake bread he is willing to give away for free.
The man cannot really be hungry if he had energy to reach for bread.
context: Real life often gives us situations where two true things pull us in different directions. Thinking about which thing matters more, and when, is part of growing up.

question: A judge has to decide a punishment for a person who stole bread to feed her children. Is the judge's job easier or harder than a friend's job in the same situation?
answer: Harder — the judge has to think of everyone, not just one person.
choices: Harder — the judge has to think of everyone, not just one person.
Easier — judges can just look up the answer in a big book of rules.
Easier — judges only have to decide once, but friends decide every day.
Harder — judges have to write everything down and friends do not.
context: A friend can care about ONE person. A judge has to care about the person AND the shopkeeper AND every future person tempted to steal bread. That is what makes the job hard.

question: A rule at your school says you cannot leave class. One day a kid is choking in the hallway and needs help. What does this show about rules?
answer: Rules are made for normal cases; sometimes doing right means breaking them.
choices: Rules are made for normal cases; sometimes doing right means breaking them.
Rules are always right and should never be broken for any reason at all.
Rules are always wrong and only fools follow rules someone made up.
Rules are about food and clothes, but never about helping other people.
context: Most rules exist for good reasons. But the people who made rules could not imagine every case. Doing right sometimes means using your judgment about when a rule does not fit.

question: Your friend says 'rules are made to be broken!' Why might a thoughtful person disagree?
answer: Most rules protect someone — breaking them often means hurting someone.
choices: Most rules protect someone — breaking them often means hurting someone.
Rules are written down, so they cannot be broken even if you try.
Rules are not made by people, they are made by computers and lawyers.
Friends should never disagree with each other, no matter what the topic.
context: Rules can be silly. But the saying 'rules are made to be broken' hides who gets hurt when we break them — usually the people the rule was protecting.

question: A boy follows EVERY rule perfectly but is mean to his sister at home. Is he a good person?
answer: Following rules is not enough — being good means caring about people too.
choices: Following rules is not enough — being good means caring about people too.
Yes — following all the rules is the whole point of being good.
No — boys cannot be good people, only girls can really be good.
Yes — what happens at home does not count as part of being good.
context: A rule-follower can still hurt people the rules do not mention. Real goodness goes beyond just doing what you are told.

question: A girl never follows the rules, but she is kind to everyone and helps people who are hurt. Is she a good person?
answer: Maybe — kindness counts, but breaking rules can hurt people in ways she misses.
choices: Maybe — kindness counts, but breaking rules can hurt people in ways she misses.
Yes — kindness is the only thing that matters, and rules are nothing.
No — only people who follow all the rules can ever be good people.
Yes — breaking rules is always a sign that you are very smart inside.
context: Being kind and breaking rules can BOTH be true. A wise person asks 'which rules?' and 'why is breaking them part of being kind?'

question: Long ago in America, the LAW said that some people could be slaves. Many people followed the law. Was following the law the right thing to do?
answer: No — following a law that hurts people does not make the hurting okay.
choices: No — following a law that hurts people does not make the hurting okay.
Yes — laws are made by the government and the government is always right.
Yes — slavery was so long ago that the rules of right and wrong were different.
No — laws never really mattered, so there was no law to follow in the first place.
context: Some of the bravest people in history broke unjust laws. They knew that what is LEGAL is not always what is RIGHT.

question: Socrates walked around Athens long ago asking strangers 'what is justice?' or 'what is courage?' Nobody could give him a perfect answer. Why did he keep asking?
answer: He thought asking the question was MORE important than getting an answer.
choices: He thought asking the question was MORE important than getting an answer.
He was lonely and just wanted to chat with people on the streets.
He hoped that one day someone would finally give him an answer.
He was paid by his city to bother people with hard questions.
context: Socrates believed the unexamined life — a life where you never stop to ask big questions — was not worth living. The asking WAS the thing.

question: A little kid asks 'why is the sky blue?' Her mom answers, and the kid says 'but WHY?' Mom answers that, and the kid says 'but WHY?' again. What does this show about questions?
answer: Every answer can open a new question — the world is deeper than it looks.
choices: Every answer can open a new question — the world is deeper than it looks.
Little kids are annoying and should stop asking after one question only.
Mom did not know the answer and was making things up the whole time.
The sky is not really blue, it just looks that way to little children.
context: Asking 'why?' over and over is something philosophers have always done. It is not annoying — it is the start of real thinking.

question: Two kids see a rainbow. One says 'it is beautiful.' The other says 'what makes it bend like that?' Which kind of thinking is more important?
answer: Both — you can wonder about a thing AND be amazed by it at the same time.
choices: Both — you can wonder about a thing AND be amazed by it at the same time.
Only the second — asking how things work is the only real thinking.
Only the first — asking how things work ruins the magic of the world.
Neither — rainbows are nothing special and people should ignore them.
context: Wondering 'why?' and feeling 'wow!' are not enemies. The biggest thinkers in history did both — they were amazed at things AND wanted to understand them.

question: A boy is sure he knows everything about dogs because he has one. What might a thoughtful person say to him?
answer: Knowing one dog is not the same as knowing all dogs everywhere.
choices: Knowing one dog is not the same as knowing all dogs everywhere.
He is right — owning one dog teaches you everything about every animal.
He should stop talking about dogs and switch to talking about cats.
He should get more dogs until he has met every single kind in the world.
context: Saying 'I know everything about X' is usually a sign you have stopped learning. The wisest people stay curious.

question: Long ago, people thought the Earth was flat. Then some thinkers started asking 'how do we KNOW it is flat?' What changed?
answer: Asking the question opened the door to finding out it was actually round.
choices: Asking the question opened the door to finding out it was actually round.
The Earth used to be flat and slowly got rounder over many years.
People who asked the question were arrested and the question stopped.
Nothing changed — most people still think the Earth is flat today.
