context: Questions can sound dangerous because they shake up what everyone 'just knows.' But that is how we ever find out anything new.

question: A grown-up says 'because I said so.' Is this a good answer to the question 'why?'
answer: Sometimes — but it does not actually answer the question itself.
choices: Sometimes — but it does not actually answer the question itself.
Always — grown-ups know everything and should not have to explain.
Never — grown-ups should always explain every choice they ever make.
Always — children should not be allowed to ask 'why?' to begin with.
context: 'Because I said so' is sometimes what a grown-up says when they are tired or in a hurry. It is not a real answer, but it can be okay when time is short.

question: Two kids see the same dog. One says 'he is friendly.' The other says 'he is scary.' Both are looking at the same dog. What is going on?
answer: They have different past experiences with dogs, so they see different things.
choices: They have different past experiences with dogs, so they see different things.
One of the kids is lying, because a dog can only really be one way.
Dogs change their friendliness depending on who is looking at them.
The dog is actually both friendly and scary on different days of the week.
context: We do not just SEE the world — we see it through what has happened to us before. Two people can look at the same thing and notice different parts.

question: Your friend believes ghosts are real. You think they are not. Neither of you is being silly. What might be a good way to talk about this?
answer: Listen to her reasons, and share yours — try to learn from each other.
choices: Listen to her reasons, and share yours — try to learn from each other.
Tell her she is wrong and stupid until she changes her mind quickly.
Agree with her so she does not feel bad, even if you do not really agree.
Stop talking to her, because friends should believe the same things.
context: Disagreeing well is a skill. You can say 'I do not see it that way' without saying 'you are dumb.' Real friends can disagree.

question: Different families have different rules. Some kids have a bedtime at 8, some at 10. One family eats meat, another does not. What does this show?
answer: There can be many right ways to live, even when families do things differently.
choices: There can be many right ways to live, even when families do things differently.
Whichever family has the latest bedtime is the smartest family of all.
Families with different rules are all wrong except for one family.
Families should all do the exact same thing or nothing will work.
context: Many small life-choices are not 'right' or 'wrong' — they are just different. Knowing the difference between 'different' and 'wrong' is important.

question: Long ago, almost everyone in one part of the world thought the Sun moved around the Earth. They were wrong. What does this teach us?
answer: Even when MANY people believe a thing, they can still all be mistaken.
choices: Even when MANY people believe a thing, they can still all be mistaken.
We should trust whatever most people believe, because the crowd is wise.
The Sun used to move around the Earth and only stopped doing it recently.
Old people are always wrong and young people are always right about science.
context: 'Everyone thinks so' is not the same as 'it is true.' History has many stories of crowds being wrong and a few thinkers being right.

question: A kid is sure his favorite movie is the best movie ever. Why might other kids think a DIFFERENT movie is the best?
answer: We all bring our own taste, our own family, and our own friends to what we like.
choices: We all bring our own taste, our own family, and our own friends to what we like.
They are all wrong, because his favorite movie really is the best one.
They are lying about which movie they like to make him feel bad.
They have not watched his favorite movie yet, but they will agree later.
context: Taste is not the same as truth. Two people can like different things and BOTH be right, because they are not making a claim about the world.

question: Two kids disagree about whether a game is fair. They are about to fight. What is one good way to find common ground?
answer: Ask each kid to say what would make the game more fair, and listen.
choices: Ask each kid to say what would make the game more fair, and listen.
Tell the louder kid he wins the argument and the game both at once.
Stop playing forever, because two kids cannot ever agree on games.
Pretend nothing is wrong and play the game even though they hate it.
context: Common ground is what both people can agree on, even when they disagree about a lot. Finding it usually starts with listening.

question: A kid says all olives are gross. Another kid loves olives. Is there ANY common ground here?
answer: Yes — they can both agree that taste differs from person to person.
choices: Yes — they can both agree that taste differs from person to person.
No — they should fight about olives until one of them gives up.
Yes — only kids who hate olives can be right, so the lover should give in.
No — common ground is impossible when two people disagree about food.
context: Even on small things like food, people who disagree can usually agree on SOMETHING. The art is finding that thing.

question: Your friend and you both want to play, but you want kickball and she wants tag. You are stuck. What is one way to handle this?
answer: Play kickball first, then tag — or look for a third game you both like.
choices: Play kickball first, then tag — or look for a third game you both like.
Play whatever YOU want and tell your friend to deal with it.
Give up and play nothing, since you cannot both have your way.
Decide whoever cries loudest gets to pick the game today.
context: Stuck moments are normal between friends. Looking for a 'we both win' answer is usually better than 'one of us wins, one loses.'

question: Two countries disagree about where their border should be. Their leaders sit down to talk. What does common ground LOOK LIKE here?
answer: Finding a deal both sides can live with, even if neither gets everything.
choices: Finding a deal both sides can live with, even if neither gets everything.
One country admits the other was right about EVERYTHING all along.
Both countries refuse to talk and just keep arguing for many years.
Both countries shrink to nothing so the border problem goes away.
context: Real-world disagreements rarely end with one side admitting it was completely wrong. Common ground usually means each side gives a little.

question: Two friends argue about a movie. One yells 'you are stupid!' The other yells 'no, YOU are stupid!' What has gone wrong?
answer: They stopped talking about the movie and started attacking each other.
choices: They stopped talking about the movie and started attacking each other.
Nothing — yelling 'stupid' is how grown-ups settle most disagreements.
The first kid was right, because the second kid called names first.
They should switch what they are arguing about to something different.
context: Attacking the person instead of the idea is a kind of giving up. It feels like you are arguing, but you have actually stopped.

question: Aristotle was Plato's student. He liked to look at REAL things in the world — animals, plants, governments — and figure out how they worked. How was this different from Plato?
answer: Plato looked up at perfect forms; Aristotle looked at the world around him.
choices: Plato looked up at perfect forms; Aristotle looked at the world around him.
Aristotle did not like Plato and never read any of his books at all.
Aristotle thought there was no world to look at, only perfect forms.
Aristotle and Plato were exactly the same on every single subject.
context: Plato wanted to look beyond the world to perfect forms. Aristotle thought you could find truth by carefully looking AT the world. Both moves shaped Western thought.

question: Confucius said a 'gentleman' (junzi in Chinese) is someone who is kind, honest, and respectful — not someone born rich. What was new about that?
answer: Anyone could become a gentleman by acting well, not just by being born rich.
choices: Anyone could become a gentleman by acting well, not just by being born rich.
Only rich kids could become gentlemen, no matter what they did or learned.
Gentlemen were a kind of fancy food eaten at parties by Chinese rulers.
Women could never be gentlemen, even if they tried their hardest to be.
context: Long ago, most people thought you were born into your place. Confucius said your CHARACTER mattered more than your family. That was a big idea in his time.

question: Long ago a man named Diogenes lived in a barrel and made fun of rich people in the streets. He had almost nothing. Why did he live this way on purpose?
answer: He wanted to show that you do not need much stuff to live a good life.
choices: He wanted to show that you do not need much stuff to live a good life.
He could not afford a house, so he made it look like a choice on purpose.
He hated rich people and broke into their houses every single night.
He thought living in a barrel would help him grow up to be a big king.
context: Diogenes was a 'Cynic' philosopher. He thought we are tricked into thinking we need money, fancy clothes, and high titles to be happy. He lived in a barrel to prove the point.

question: A philosopher named Epictetus was born a SLAVE. He later wrote that what hurts us is not what HAPPENS to us — it is what we THINK about what happens. What is one example of his idea?
answer: Two kids in a rainstorm: one is upset, one is happy — same rain, different thinking.
choices: Two kids in a rainstorm: one is upset, one is happy — same rain, different thinking.
Two kids in a rainstorm: one gets wet, one stays dry, because of the rain.
Two kids in a rainstorm: only one gets a rainbow, because life is unfair.
Two kids in a rainstorm: both kids think the same exact thing about the rain.
context: Epictetus taught Stoic philosophy. He said we cannot always control what happens — but we can usually control how we answer it inside ourselves.

question: You see an ant crawling on the sidewalk. Should you avoid stepping on it? What kind of reasons might say YES?
answer: The ant is alive and wants to live, just like you want to live.
choices: The ant is alive and wants to live, just like you want to live.
Stepping on ants is illegal in most countries around the world.
Ants will bite back if you step on them, so you should not try.
Ants are made of glass and will shatter under your heavy shoe.
context: How we treat small creatures says something about what KIND of person we are. There are no rules saying you have to avoid the ant — but it is the kind of question worth asking.

question: Your dog wags her tail when you come home. She seems happy. But can we REALLY know what she is feeling, since she cannot tell us in words?
answer: We can guess from her body, but we cannot be totally sure what she feels.
choices: We can guess from her body, but we cannot be totally sure what she feels.
We can know exactly, because dogs feel the same things people feel.
Dogs do not feel anything, so the wagging tail does not mean a thing.
We can know because the wag of a tail is described in every dog book.
context: Other minds are mysterious — even other PEOPLE's minds. We guess based on their bodies, words, and history. We rarely know for sure.

question: A river flows down a hill. Nobody told the river to do that. The river just DOES it. Does this mean the river has a mind?
answer: Probably not — the river follows gravity, not a choice it makes itself.
choices: Probably not — the river follows gravity, not a choice it makes itself.
Yes — anything that moves on its own must have a mind inside of it.
No — minds only exist in cats and dogs, never in any other things.
Yes — rivers have small minds, while oceans have very big minds.
context: Just because something MOVES does not mean it CHOOSES. A river does what gravity asks. Choice is something different.

question: You promise your sister you will play her game later. But then your favorite show comes on. What did your PROMISE actually mean?
answer: You agreed to do something even when you might not feel like it later.
choices: You agreed to do something even when you might not feel like it later.
You agreed to play only if your favorite show was not on at the time.
Promises are not real, so it does not matter what you said earlier.
Promises are real, but only if the other person remembers them clearly.
context: A promise made only when convenient is barely a promise. Real promises matter most exactly when they are HARD to keep.

question: A toddler hits another kid and says 'sorry.' Five minutes later, she does it again. Why might her 'sorry' have not been enough?
answer: Saying sorry without changing what you do does not really fix the harm.
choices: Saying sorry without changing what you do does not really fix the harm.
Toddlers are not allowed to say sorry — only big kids can do it.
She should have said 'I apologize' instead of using shorter words.
Saying sorry twice would have fixed it, so she only needed to repeat.
context: 'Sorry' is a small word that gets bigger when it changes your behavior. A real apology comes WITH a change.

question: Your brother does something nice for you. Later, he expects you to do something nice for him. Is this fair, or is he ruining the niceness?
answer: It is fair to expect kindness back, but a real gift does not come with a bill.
choices: It is fair to expect kindness back, but a real gift does not come with a bill.
It is always ruined — kindness should never go in both directions ever.
It is always fair — kindness MUST come with a bill or it is not real.
It is fair — your brother should charge you money for every nice thing.
context: Helping others usually feels best when it is freely given. But real friendships and families ALSO depend on give-and-take over time.

question: Two kids both think they are the smartest kid in the class. What might a wise person tell them?
answer: Knowing how much you do NOT know is a sign of being truly smart.
choices: Knowing how much you do NOT know is a sign of being truly smart.
Have a fight, and whoever wins gets to be the smartest one in class.
They are both wrong, because the teacher is the smartest one of them all.
Whoever has the loudest voice during arguments must be the smartest of them.
context: Socrates said something like 'I am wise because I know how little I know.' Real wisdom usually comes with humble curiosity, not loud bragging.

question: A boy says 'I am SO unlucky.' But he has food, a home, friends, and a family. What is one good question to ask him?
answer: Compared to WHO are you unlucky — and what would lucky even look like?
choices: Compared to WHO are you unlucky — and what would lucky even look like?
Why do you not just buy more luck at the store like everyone else?
How dare you say that when other people have less than you do?
Should you stop trying altogether since you are unlucky already?
context: Lucky and unlucky depend on what we compare ourselves to. Slowing down to ask 'compared to what?' often changes how a thing looks.

question: A girl says 'I cannot help it — that is just how I am.' Is this a good reason for everything she does?
answer: Not always — some of who we are can change with effort over time.
choices: Not always — some of who we are can change with effort over time.
Yes — once you say 'that is how I am,' nothing can ever change you.
No — kids must not be allowed to talk about themselves in this way.
Yes — saying it makes the words come true automatically, like magic.
context: 'Just who I am' can be honest — some things really are hard to change. But it can also be an excuse. The wise person knows the difference.

question: Two kids are at the playground. One wants to play, one wants to swing alone. Are both kids RIGHT, or is one of them being weird?
answer: Both are fine — people have different ways of liking the same place.
choices: Both are fine — people have different ways of liking the same place.
The one who wants to play is right, because being alone is always weird.
The one who swings alone is right, because playing with others is bad.
Neither is right — kids should all want to do exactly the same thing.
context: Wanting to be alone is not weird. Wanting to play together is not weird either. People are different — and a wise place for kids has room for both.

question: Your friend made a mistake and feels really bad. You can say 'it is okay, forget it' or 'you messed up, but I still like you.' Which is more honest AND more kind?
answer: The second — because it tells the truth AND keeps loving him.
choices: The second — because it tells the truth AND keeps loving him.
The first — because forgetting is the only way to fix mistakes.
The second — because it makes him feel worse, which is a good lesson.
The first — because honesty hurts and kindness should never hurt.
context: Real kindness does not need lies. You can name the mistake and STILL love the person. Pretending nothing happened is not the same as forgiving.

question: A kid feels bad about losing his big game. His coach says 'you still played really well.' That is true — but the kid wanted to WIN. What might his coach also need to say?
answer: That losing hurts AND it is okay to feel sad about it for a while.
choices: That losing hurts AND it is okay to feel sad about it for a while.
That winning is the only thing that matters in any kind of game.
That losing means he should never play games like this ever again.
That his sadness is silly and he should just smile and forget about it.
context: Cheering up is good. But sometimes a person needs their hard feelings named first, before they can hear the cheerful part.

question: A boy says 'I would never steal — but only because I would get caught.' Is this REALLY being a good person?
answer: Not quite — a good person also chooses not to steal when no one is looking.
choices: Not quite — a good person also chooses not to steal when no one is looking.
Yes — what matters is the outcome, and he is not stealing right now anyway.
Yes — getting caught is the only reason anyone ever chooses to be good.
No — he should steal to find out what it really feels like to be caught.
context: Plato told a story called 'Ring of Gyges' about a magic ring that made you invisible. He asked: would you still be good if nobody could see you? That is the test of real goodness.

question: Your friend wants to copy your homework. You know she will get in trouble if you tell, but you also know she will not learn if you say yes. What is the LOVING thing to do?
answer: Say no, and offer to help her learn the answers herself instead.
choices: Say no, and offer to help her learn the answers herself instead.
Say yes, because friends help each other no matter what is asked.
Say nothing and run away from your friend so she cannot ask you again.
Say yes to her face, but later tell the teacher about everything.
context: Real friends help each other GROW. Sometimes the loving answer is the harder one — not the easier one.

question: A grown-up says 'when I was your age...' before telling a story. Why might it be worth listening, even if the story sounds old?
answer: Grown-ups remember problems you have not faced yet, and what worked.
choices: Grown-ups remember problems you have not faced yet, and what worked.
Old stories are always more interesting than anything kids say.
Kids should listen to every word from grown-ups without thinking.
Listening to a story means you have to agree with all of it later.
context: You do not have to AGREE with everything an older person says. But they have lived through things you have not yet. Listening costs nothing and sometimes pays a lot.

question: A girl finds out her best friend has been talking behind her back. She wants to do something MEAN back. Her grandmother says 'wait one night, then decide.' Why this advice?
answer: Anger is hot, and big choices made in anger are usually ones we regret.
choices: Anger is hot, and big choices made in anger are usually ones we regret.
Anger always goes away after one night, and there is no need to act later.
Grandmothers always say wait one night, no matter what the trouble is.
Doing mean things back is only allowed after waiting one full week first.
context: Many traditions teach 'cool down before you act.' The Stoics, Buddhists, and Christians all noticed that hot anger makes us say and do things we did not really mean.

question: Your little cousin asks 'why are people sometimes mean to each other?' What is one honest answer a thoughtful kid could give?
answer: People can be scared, hurting, or tired — and meanness sometimes leaks out.
choices: People can be scared, hurting, or tired — and meanness sometimes leaks out.
People are mean because they are simply born that way and cannot change.
Only kids are mean — grown-ups have grown out of it for the most part.
People are mean because the moon was full on the day they were born.
context: Mean behavior usually comes FROM something — fear, hurt, tiredness, jealousy. Naming that does not excuse meanness, but it helps us understand it.

question: Long ago a sailor was lost at sea and used the stars to find his way home. What does this story show about KNOWING things?
answer: Knowing something true can keep you safe when nothing else around you helps.
choices: Knowing something true can keep you safe when nothing else around you helps.
Sailors should never trust stars and should ask passing fish for help.
Stars move too much to be useful for anything besides being pretty.
Sailing should be avoided since the sea will always trick anyone on it.
context: Knowledge is not just for school. The stars guided sailors home for thousands of years. Real knowledge can save lives.

question: A boy thinks 'I will be HAPPY when I am rich.' His grandfather says 'I have been rich and I have been poor.' What might Grandpa say next?
answer: That being happy comes from inside, not from how much money you have.
choices: That being happy comes from inside, not from how much money you have.
That being rich is the only way to actually be happy in any life.
That being poor is fun and everyone should try it for many years.
That happiness depends on the kind of car you can afford to buy.
context: Many thinkers across history have pointed out that money buys comfort, but not joy. Joy comes from inside — from your habits, people, and choices.

question: Two friends play a board game. One wins by following the rules. The other wins by cheating when nobody is looking. Did both kids actually WIN?
answer: Only one of them — winning by cheating is not really winning at all.
choices: Only one of them — winning by cheating is not really winning at all.
Yes — winning is winning, no matter how it happens in any game.
Yes — if the cheating kid does not get caught, the cheating was fair.
No — neither of them won, because games never have real winners.
context: A win you got by cheating only LOOKS like a win. You did not really do the thing you say you did. Some thinkers call this an empty win.

question: Utilitarians say we should pick the choice that creates the most happiness for the MOST people. What is one problem with this rule?
answer: It can excuse hurting a few people if it makes more people happy.
choices: It can excuse hurting a few people if it makes more people happy.
It only works for groups of less than five people at any one time.
It says happiness does not actually matter and pain matters more.
It is too easy to follow, so philosophers usually pick harder rules.
context: Utilitarianism asks one simple question — what creates the most good? But the simplicity can hide tough cases. Five people's happiness should not always outweigh one person's real harm.

question: Jeremy Bentham, who started utilitarian thinking, said we should add up pleasures and pains like a kind of math. Why did some thinkers later push back on this 'pleasure math'?
answer: Not all pleasures and pains can really be measured or added up.
choices: Not all pleasures and pains can really be measured or added up.
Math is bad for thinking, since it confuses people about everything.
Bentham was a very mean man, so nobody wanted to use his rules.
Pleasures and pains do not really happen at all, since they are not real.
context: Bentham hoped to make ethics scientific by adding up happiness. Critics asked: how do we compare a kid's joy at ice cream with an adult's joy at a job well done? Not all pleasures are the same kind of thing.

question: John Stuart Mill, who came after Bentham, said some pleasures were 'higher' than others. What kind of pleasure did he call higher?
answer: Pleasures of the mind — reading, music, conversation — over just bodily ones.
choices: Pleasures of the mind — reading, music, conversation — over just bodily ones.
Pleasures of the body — eating, sleeping, swimming — over thinking ones.
Pleasures that lasted exactly one hour, not more and not less, anywhere.
Pleasures that came only from being rich enough to pay for them today.
context: Mill said it is 'better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a pig satisfied.' He thought a person who has tried both bodily and mental pleasures would say the mental ones run deeper.

question: Socrates said 'the unexamined life is not worth living.' What did he mean?
answer: A life without asking real questions about it is barely a life at all.
choices: A life without asking real questions about it is barely a life at all.
Doctors should not examine you because all checkups are a waste of time.
Only philosophers should be allowed to live, and everyone else must stop.
Examining other people is more important than examining your own life.
context: Socrates believed thinking carefully about your own life — what you want, what you believe, how you treat others — was the work of being human. Skipping that work was, for him, skipping life itself.

question: Socrates often said 'I know that I know nothing.' What did he gain by saying this?
answer: He could keep learning, because he had not closed off any question yet.
choices: He could keep learning, because he had not closed off any question yet.
He could pretend to be smarter than people who knew real facts.
He could avoid being asked questions, since he claimed to know nothing.
He could avoid paying taxes by saying he knew nothing of money matters.
context: Socrates noticed that 'experts' often confidently held wrong ideas. He thought admitting your own ignorance was the first step toward actually learning anything.

question: Socrates and his friends would argue back and forth, building an idea by testing it. This is called the SOCRATIC METHOD. What is its main trick?
answer: Use careful questions to find weak spots in an idea, then fix them.
choices: Use careful questions to find weak spots in an idea, then fix them.
Use loud shouting to make the other person give up the argument.
Use the same question over and over until people stop answering at all.
Use complicated words so people get confused and give in to your side.
context: The Socratic method is not about winning — it is about TESTING. Good teachers, lawyers, and scientists still use it: ask questions until you find what doesn't quite fit.

question: Plato told a story called the 'Allegory of the Cave.' People are chained in a cave watching shadows on a wall. They think the shadows ARE the world. What is the cave a picture of?
answer: Our normal life — taking things at face value without really thinking.
choices: Our normal life — taking things at face value without really thinking.
A real cave that Plato actually visited near the city of Athens.
The future, where all of us will live in shadowy caves underground.
A puzzle for children to solve as part of their schoolwork in class.
context: Plato's Cave is one of the most famous pictures in philosophy. He thought most people live looking at 'shadows' — appearances — without ever turning around to see what casts them.

question: Plato said 'philosopher-kings' should rule — people who love wisdom more than power. Why did he think this would work better than just letting anyone be king?
answer: A ruler who loves wisdom would govern for the good of the people, not himself.
choices: A ruler who loves wisdom would govern for the good of the people, not himself.
Philosophers are stronger fighters than other people, so they could win wars.
Philosopher-kings would all happen to be born in the city he loved most.
Only philosophers know how to wear crowns and sit in royal chairs properly.
context: Plato had watched Athens go through wars, plagues, and bad leaders. He thought democracy let popular but unwise people lead. He hoped a ruler trained in philosophy would chase what was good, not what felt good.

question: Aristotle said being a good person means having good HABITS, not just having good ideas. Why did he focus on habits?
answer: You become good by doing good things over and over until they feel natural.
choices: You become good by doing good things over and over until they feel natural.
Habits are easier to talk about than ideas, so they are more popular.
Habits never change, so once you have one you cannot mess up your life.
Habits are the only things grown-ups can do, since kids do not have any.
context: Aristotle's idea is called 'virtue ethics.' He thought you cannot just READ about courage or kindness — you have to PRACTICE them, the same way you practice a sport.

question: Aristotle taught about the 'Golden Mean' — being good means finding the right balance between TWO extremes. For courage, what are the two extremes he warned about?
answer: Cowardice (too scared) and recklessness (jumping into danger for no reason).
choices: Cowardice (too scared) and recklessness (jumping into danger for no reason).
Anger (too mad) and kindness (too nice), one on each side of courage.
Cowardice (too scared) and patience (too calm), one on each side of courage.
Recklessness (too brave) and bravery (just brave), one on each side of courage.
context: The Golden Mean is not a boring middle. It is the right amount, which is often hard to find. Brave is good — but diving into a fire to grab a sandwich is foolish, not brave.

question: The Stoic philosopher Epictetus said some things are IN our control, and some things are NOT. What did he say we should focus on?
answer: Only what is in our control — our own thoughts, choices, and actions.
choices: Only what is in our control — our own thoughts, choices, and actions.
Only what is NOT in our control, since we cannot waste time on the rest.
Both, equally, since you cannot tell the difference between them.
Things that are halfway in our control, like the weather and how friends act.
context: Epictetus's idea is that worrying about traffic, weather, or what others think is wasted effort. Worrying about your own honesty, courage, and effort actually helps.

question: A young Stoic complains 'my friend insulted me!' His Stoic teacher would say something like: 'is the insult IN you, or is it just in the air?' What does this teach?
answer: Words only hurt as much as we let them — the choice to be hurt is partly ours.
choices: Words only hurt as much as we let them — the choice to be hurt is partly ours.
Insults are made of magical material that can really physically wound you.
Insults are illegal under Roman law, so they should be reported to police.
Insults can only hurt people who are weak, so toughen up and ignore them.
context: The Stoics did not say insults felt nice. They said the STING comes partly from how we respond. Two people can hear the same insult; one shakes it off, the other carries it for a week.

question: Marcus Aurelius, the Stoic emperor, wrote 'you have power over your mind, not outside events. Realize this, and you will find strength.' What does he mean by 'strength'?
answer: The ability to stay calm and act well, even when bad things happen around you.
choices: The ability to stay calm and act well, even when bad things happen around you.
Lifting heavy things, which he learned to do as part of his Roman army.
Becoming so rich and powerful that nothing bad ever happens to you again.
Hiding from the world so that no events can ever reach you in any way.
context: Stoic 'strength' is inner, not outer. Bad things still happen — the emperor lost children, fought wars, faced plagues. The strength was in HOW he answered them, not in stopping them from coming.

question: Immanuel Kant said we should ask before each action: 'what if EVERYONE did this?' If the answer is bad, the action is wrong. What is this rule called?
answer: The categorical imperative — a universal test for any action.
choices: The categorical imperative — a universal test for any action.
The popular vote rule — most people decide what is right and wrong.
The personal rule — whatever feels right to YOU is right for you.
The friend rule — whatever your best friend approves of must be allowed.
context: Kant's test asks: could I want this action to become a general rule? Lying to get out of trouble fails: if EVERYONE lied, nobody could trust anyone, including liars.

question: Existentialist philosophers like Sartre said 'existence comes before essence.' A simpler way: you EXIST first, and THEN you decide who you are. What is one big claim hidden in this?
answer: There is no pre-set 'right' way to be human — we choose who we become.
choices: There is no pre-set 'right' way to be human — we choose who we become.
There is a strict pre-set 'right' way that everyone must follow exactly.
Babies decide their identity at age zero and can never change it later.
Only French philosophers know what humans should be like, no one else.
context: Existentialism rejects the idea that you were born to be a certain kind of person. You wake up each day and pick again, by your choices, who you actually are. Some find this scary; others find it freeing.

question: Sartre wrote that humans are 'condemned to be free.' Why is freedom a 'condemnation' — sounds like a bad thing?
answer: Because freedom means everything is YOUR choice, with no excuses left.
choices: Because freedom means everything is YOUR choice, with no excuses left.
Because being free in Sartre's France was actually illegal, so it hurt.
Because freedom causes a kind of disease that affects only philosophers.
Because Sartre hated being free and wanted someone to choose for him.
context: If nothing is pre-set, then YOU chose your job, your friends, your habits. You cannot say 'I had to.' Sartre thought this was a heavy load — but also the only honest way to see ourselves.

question: Confucius taught that to be a 'gentleman' (junzi), you must work on five virtues. One was REN — sometimes translated as 'humaneness' or 'true caring.' What kind of thing was it?
answer: Caring about other people in a deep way that shows up in everything you do.
choices: Caring about other people in a deep way that shows up in everything you do.
A kind of food eaten only at very fancy Chinese banquets long ago.
A musical instrument played only by emperors during religious ceremonies.
A magic word that, when spoken, would protect you from any kind of harm.
context: Ren is the heart of Confucius's teaching. It is not just being nice — it is a steady, deep care for others that shapes how you eat, work, speak, and rule.

question: Buddhism teaches the 'Four Noble Truths.' The first is that life involves SUFFERING — including aging, loss, and disappointment. Why start there?
answer: Honesty about pain is the first step toward dealing with it well.
choices: Honesty about pain is the first step toward dealing with it well.
If life is suffering, then nothing else matters and you should give up.
Buddhists love being sad and want everyone to feel sad along with them.
Buddhists are forced by law to start with the saddest part of the lesson.
context: Many traditions try to skip past pain or pretend it is not there. Buddhism starts by NAMING it — not because it loves suffering, but because pretending pain is not real never actually fixes anything.

question: The second Noble Truth says the CAUSE of much suffering is 'tanha' — a kind of clinging or craving. What is one way tanha shows up in everyday life?
answer: Wanting a thing so badly you cannot enjoy what you already have.
choices: Wanting a thing so badly you cannot enjoy what you already have.
Drinking lots of water during the day to stay healthy and hydrated.
Studying very hard for a test even when you do not feel like it.
Letting other people have things you do not need yourself anymore.
context: Tanha is not just 'wanting' — it is the white-knuckle grip on a want. A kid can want a toy AND enjoy his other toys. Tanha is when the wanting blocks out the having.

question: The Buddhist 'Middle Way' was the Buddha's answer to two extremes he had tried himself. What were the two extremes?
answer: Total comfort in the palace, and total self-denial of even basic needs.
choices: Total comfort in the palace, and total self-denial of even basic needs.
Total comfort in the palace, and total power as a Roman emperor.
Total self-denial, and total commitment to never speaking to anyone.
Total agreement with everyone, and total disagreement with everyone.
context: The Buddha grew up in a palace with every comfort. Then he tried strict fasting and pain. He found both extremes missed the point. The 'Middle Way' is the balanced path between them.

question: Rene Descartes wanted to know what he could be ABSOLUTELY sure of. He started by doubting everything — even his own eyes. Then he hit one thing he could not doubt. What?
answer: That something was doing the thinking — even if everything else was a trick.
choices: That something was doing the thinking — even if everything else was a trick.
That the floor was real, because he could feel it under his Roman shoes.
That his books were real, because he could read the words inside them.
That his clothes were real, because the cold air would have shown otherwise.
context: Descartes' famous line 'I think, therefore I am' was the ONE thing he found impossible to doubt. To doubt you have to be doing the doubting — and the doing proves a doer.

question: Descartes split everything into TWO basic kinds of stuff: minds (which think) and bodies (which take up space). This is called DUALISM. What is one problem this raises?
answer: How do something with no body (mind) and a body (brain) talk to each other?
choices: How do something with no body (mind) and a body (brain) talk to each other?
Why do French philosophers always start with the letter D in their names?
How can a mind be inside a body if minds are bigger than human bodies?
Why did Descartes pick two kinds of stuff, and not five or six instead?
context: Descartes' dualism feels intuitive: your thoughts feel different from your foot. But how does an immaterial mind MOVE the material foot? Descartes guessed the pineal gland — most modern thinkers reject the picture.

question: David Hume noticed something strange: just because the sun rose every day so far, can we be SURE it will rise tomorrow? What was Hume's answer?
answer: No — we expect it from habit, not because we proved it would happen.
choices: No — we expect it from habit, not because we proved it would happen.
Yes, because the sun has a contract with Earth that it cannot break.
Yes, because Hume personally checked the sun every morning of his life.
No, because the sun is just a kind of cosmic joke played on humans.
context: Hume's puzzle is called 'the problem of induction.' We act as if past patterns will continue, but the proof is shakier than it feels. Every scientist still wrestles with this.

question: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote that humans are 'born free' but are 'everywhere in chains.' He did not mean iron chains. What did he mean?
answer: Society and habits limit us in ways we barely notice from the inside.
choices: Society and habits limit us in ways we barely notice from the inside.
Most people are kept in iron chains by their bosses every day of their lives.
The French king put real chains on Rousseau personally, which he hated.
Babies are born already wearing tiny chains that we cannot see clearly.
context: Rousseau saw people boxed in by jobs, expectations, rules, and customs — and acting as if those were just nature. He thought a better society would set people freer than the one he lived in.

question: Friedrich Nietzsche imagined a 'demon' that whispers: 'you will live this exact life over again, every detail, forever.' He asked: would the news make you cheer or despair? Why?
answer: It tests whether you actually love the life you are living right now.
choices: It tests whether you actually love the life you are living right now.
It tests whether you know enough math to count to forever or higher.
It tests whether you have ever heard the word 'demon' in your life before.
It tests whether you can write down a 'yes' or 'no' answer fast enough.
context: Nietzsche called this 'eternal recurrence.' He did not claim it was real — he used it as a thought experiment. If you would cheer, you are living rightly. If you would despair, ask yourself what to change.

question: Nietzsche talked about a 'will to power.' This is OFTEN misunderstood as wanting power over other people. What did he actually mean?
answer: The drive in each person to grow stronger and become more themselves.
choices: The drive in each person to grow stronger and become more themselves.
The drive to grab as much money as possible from anyone within reach.
The drive to win every kind of board game that a person ever plays.
The drive to fly an airplane, which Nietzsche thought he could really do.
context: Nietzsche's 'will to power' is closer to a plant pushing toward the sun than to a bully grabbing lunch money. He thought every living thing wants to expand and grow into what it could be.

question: John Stuart Mill argued for a HARM PRINCIPLE: the only reason to use power over a free adult is to prevent harm to OTHERS. What does this rule NOT count as a reason?
answer: That the person is hurting only themselves, with no harm to others.
choices: That the person is hurting only themselves, with no harm to others.
That the person is hurting many other people in many different ways at once.
That the person is robbing someone else and refusing to stop after warnings.
That the person is yelling 'fire' in a theater that is full of crowded people.
context: Mill's principle is the heart of modern free-society thinking. You can disagree with what an adult does to himself — but if no one else is being harmed, you do not get to force him to stop.

question: Mill defended free speech, even for ideas you HATE. He had a clever reason: even a WRONG opinion is useful in a debate. Why?
answer: Defending the truth against a wrong claim makes you understand the truth better.
choices: Defending the truth against a wrong claim makes you understand the truth better.
Wrong opinions become correct opinions after about ten years of being wrong.
Mill enjoyed reading wrong things, so he wanted them protected by the law.
Wrong opinions are illegal in most places, so it was Mill being naughty.
context: Mill's argument cuts deep: if no one challenges the truth, even believers will hold it as 'just because.' Letting a wrong opinion speak forces the right side to really know its own reasons.

question: John Rawls invented a thought experiment: imagine you must pick the rules of a society, but you do NOT yet know whether you will be rich or poor, healthy or sick. What does he call this?
answer: The veil of ignorance — picking rules without knowing where you will end up.
choices: The veil of ignorance — picking rules without knowing where you will end up.
The mirror test — checking if you would still pick the rules in a mirror.
The clock principle — deciding all the rules in less than one hour total.
The blank slate — starting with no rules at all and adding one at a time.
context: Rawls's veil is a famous test. If you do not know whether you will be born rich or poor, you have a strong reason to pick rules that protect even the WORST-off — because that could end up being you.

question: Rawls said behind the veil, you would pick rules that MAXIMIZE the situation of the WORST-OFF in society. What does this rule push against?
answer: Letting the rich get very rich while the poor get very poor.
choices: Letting the rich get very rich while the poor get very poor.
Letting people work hard and earn money for the work that they really do.
Letting any people at all be born into any kind of family they want to.
Letting people have hobbies, friends, or any kind of free time at all.
context: Rawls's 'difference principle' says inequalities are okay only if they HELP the worst-off (e.g., paying doctors more leads to more doctors for poor patients). The principle is hotly debated.

question: Robert Nozick offered a famous reply to Rawls. He said: if I bake a pie in my own kitchen, the question of how to share it is NOT the same as the question of who BAKED it. What is his point?
answer: Justice is partly about who created the thing in the first place.
choices: Justice is partly about who created the thing in the first place.
Pies are too small to share, so they should not be shared at any time.
Baking is harder than philosophy, so philosophers should not weigh in.
Kitchens are private spaces, so pies in them are invisible to everyone.
context: Nozick said redistribution can sound fair when you look at the slices already on the table. But asking 'where did the slices COME FROM?' changes the question. He thought what people created with their own work belonged to them.

question: Philosophers argue about FREE WILL — whether your choices are really YOURS, or whether your brain was always going to pick what it picked. What is one reason this matters?
answer: If choices are never really free, blame and praise lose their meaning.
choices: If choices are never really free, blame and praise lose their meaning.
If choices are never really free, then nobody can ever go to school again.
If choices are never really free, then ice cream will stop tasting good.
If choices are never really free, then nobody can read books any more.
context: If your brain made you do it, can we really PUNISH you for doing it? Can we PRAISE you for being kind, if you had no real choice? The question is older than philosophy itself and still matters today.

question: Some thinkers say free will is COMPATIBLE with everything in the brain being caused. They are called 'compatibilists.' What do they say a 'free' choice is?
answer: A choice that flows from YOUR own thinking — not one forced from outside.
choices: A choice that flows from YOUR own thinking — not one forced from outside.
A choice that comes from nowhere at all and surprises even yourself.
A choice that is made without any thought, just a quick guess off the cuff.
A choice that follows a strict set of rules written down at your birth.
context: Compatibilists redefine 'free' to mean 'not coerced.' If your choice came from your own reasons (even reasons that came from genes and upbringing), that is free enough. Many disagree, but it is one of the main answers.

question: Carol Gilligan studied how PEOPLE think about moral problems. She noticed many WOMEN focused on relationships and care, while many MEN focused on abstract rules. What did she think this showed?
answer: Both approaches matter — care for people and respect for rules are both real ethics.
choices: Both approaches matter — care for people and respect for rules are both real ethics.
Women are usually wrong about ethics, while men are usually right about it.
Men should not be allowed to study ethics, since they only focus on rules.
Moral problems only have one correct answer, no matter who is thinking about them.
context: Gilligan pushed back against psychologists who said one moral style was more 'mature' than the other. She argued that an ethics of care — paying close attention to who gets hurt, and how — is just as serious as an ethics of rules.

question: American philosopher William James said the test of an idea is whether it WORKS — whether using it makes a real difference in life. This view is called PRAGMATISM. What does it push back against?
answer: Treating ideas as true or false in a way that does not connect to real life.
choices: Treating ideas as true or false in a way that does not connect to real life.
Treating ideas as worth thinking about when they help us live better.
Treating ideas about science as important to test against the world.
Treating ideas with curiosity rather than treating them as boring facts.
context: James was tired of philosophers arguing forever about things that made no difference to how anyone lived. Pragmatism asks: if I held idea A versus idea B, would my behavior be different? If not, why are we fighting?

question: The ancient Chinese book the Daodejing (Tao Te Ching) says 'the way that can be told is not the eternal way.' Why would a BOOK start with the line that the truth cannot really be put into words?
answer: To warn the reader at the start: words are pointers, not the whole truth.
choices: To warn the reader at the start: words are pointers, not the whole truth.
Because the writer had run out of ink and could not finish the introduction.
Because the book was supposed to be a riddle and not be read by anyone.
Because Chinese books always start with a line saying not to read them at all.
context: Daoism warns against thinking you have captured truth in a clever sentence. The 'Dao' (the way) is something you have to live, not just say. Other traditions — Zen Buddhism, mystical Christianity — share this caution.

question: Daoists talk about 'wu-wei' — usually translated 'effortless action' or 'non-doing.' It does NOT mean laziness. What does it actually mean?
answer: Acting in tune with how things naturally flow, instead of forcing things.
choices: Acting in tune with how things naturally flow, instead of forcing things.
Doing absolutely nothing on purpose, all day, every day, for your whole life.
Doing the opposite of whatever Chinese rulers told you to do every day.
Doing many things at once until you wear yourself out and have to stop.
context: Wu-wei is like a good swimmer who works with the river instead of fighting it. You are still ACTING — but the action does not feel like a battle, because you are not pushing against what is.

question: Philosophers ask: what IS a thought? Is it just brain cells firing, or something more? People who say a thought is JUST brain activity are called 'physicalists.' What is one argument FOR their view?
answer: Damage to the brain changes thoughts — pointing to a strong brain-mind link.
choices: Damage to the brain changes thoughts — pointing to a strong brain-mind link.
Thoughts can be photographed by a camera if you hold the camera close enough.
Thoughts cost money to make, so they must be small machines in the brain.
Thoughts are visible during medical X-rays, so they must be in the bones.
context: Strokes, drugs, and head injuries change what people think and feel. That seems like strong evidence the mind depends on the brain. Critics push back: 'depends on' is not the same as 'is.'

question: If thoughts are just brain cells, what about FEELINGS — the actual experience of seeing the color red, or tasting chocolate? Some thinkers say this 'feel' is something extra. What word do they use for it?
answer: Qualia — the 'felt quality' of what an experience is like from inside.
choices: Qualia — the 'felt quality' of what an experience is like from inside.
Quotas — the strict limits a brain places on how many feelings it can have.
Quibbles — small arguments about how feelings actually work inside your head.
Quizzes — the tests a brain runs to check that its feelings are working well.
context: Two people can both see red, but their inner experience of 'red' might be totally different. The fact that science has not explained these qualia is one of the biggest puzzles in philosophy of mind.

question: If a powerful, all-knowing, all-good God exists, why is there evil and suffering in the world? This puzzle is called the 'problem of evil.' What is ONE attempted answer?
answer: A world with free choice must allow that people sometimes choose evil.
choices: A world with free choice must allow that people sometimes choose evil.
Evil does not really exist; people only imagine it during nightmares at night.
God does exist but does not actually know what is going on most of the time.
Evil happens because nobody asked God to stop it nicely in their daily prayers.
context: This is called the 'free will defense.' Critics ask: what about natural evils — earthquakes, diseases — that no one chose? The problem of evil has many proposed answers, none of them quick.

question: Other thinkers say evil is part of how SOULS GROW — without challenges, courage and kindness would never develop. This is called a 'soul-making' theodicy. What is one criticism of this view?
answer: Some suffering is so extreme it destroys, rather than builds, a person.
choices: Some suffering is so extreme it destroys, rather than builds, a person.
Souls do not grow at all; they are just balloons inside our bodies somewhere.
Soul-making is a kind of cheese, so the theory is about food, not evil.
Souls cannot be made by humans, so a theory of soul-making is impossible.
context: If suffering builds character, what about a child who dies in pain, with no chance to grow? Or a survivor whose trauma destroys him? The soul-making view answers part of the problem but not all of it.

question: Philosophers often define knowledge as 'justified true belief.' If you BELIEVE something, and it IS true, and you have REASONS, then you know it. What is one tricky case where this DEFINITION breaks down?
answer: You can believe something true for the wrong reason — and 'know it' by accident.
choices: You can believe something true for the wrong reason — and 'know it' by accident.
You can believe something only when you are watching a TV show about it.
You can only believe things that are true, since beliefs cannot be wrong.
You can never have reasons for any belief, so knowing is totally impossible.
context: Edmund Gettier wrote a famous short paper showing 'lucky' true beliefs that meet the definition but do not really feel like knowledge. Philosophers have been arguing about fixes ever since.

question: An ancient kind of philosopher called SKEPTICS asked: are you ever REALLY sure of anything? Maybe your senses lie. Maybe your memory tricks you. What did some skeptics recommend as a result?
answer: Suspend judgment — don't strongly believe OR disbelieve until you have to.
choices: Suspend judgment — don't strongly believe OR disbelieve until you have to.
Believe everything you hear from any speaker, no matter who is talking.
Believe nothing at all, so you can never be wrong about any single thing.
Stop using your senses, since they are dirty and full of tricks against you.
context: The ancient Greek skeptics thought certainty was usually impossible. Their answer was not despair — it was a kind of calm: hold your beliefs loosely, do not get worked up about every claim, live by what seems most reasonable.

question: Is BEAUTY a real property of things, or just in the eye of the beholder? Philosophers have argued about this for a long time. What is one good reason to think beauty is MORE than just personal taste?
answer: People across cultures often agree on what counts as beautiful — too often for pure taste.
choices: People across cultures often agree on what counts as beautiful — too often for pure taste.
Beauty causes physical pain, which is why nobody likes looking at it for long.
Beauty is illegal in most countries, so it cannot be just personal taste.
Beauty was invented by Aristotle, so before him nothing was beautiful at all.
context: Different cultures find similar things beautiful — symmetry, certain ratios, certain melodies. If beauty were pure taste, this overlap would be hard to explain. Critics reply: maybe humans just have similar brains.

question: Why should anyone OBEY the law? Some thinkers say it is because we agreed (a 'social contract'). What is one complication with that idea?
answer: Most of us never actually agreed to anything — we were born into our country.
choices: Most of us never actually agreed to anything — we were born into our country.
Most of us already obey every single law, so the question never comes up.
Most of us live in countries that do not have any laws to obey in the first place.
Most of us are born inside contracts, since babies are born holding contracts.
context: The 'social contract' idea is powerful but tricky. Locke, Rousseau, and others imagined people CHOOSING to leave a wild 'state of nature' for a society. But none of us were actually there for that choice.

question: Epicurus is often misremembered as teaching 'eat, drink, and party!' He actually taught something quieter. What did he say the goal of life was?
answer: A calm, simple pleasure — friendship, conversation, the absence of pain.
choices: A calm, simple pleasure — friendship, conversation, the absence of pain.
A wild, loud party every single day with as much food and drink as possible.
A long life of suffering, since suffering builds the strongest character of all.
A short, fast, exciting life full of risks, since slow lives are not worth it.
context: Epicurus ate plain bread and water. His 'pleasure' was the absence of pain and the presence of good friends. The wild-party version of his name came later, from people who never read him.

question: Jamie says we should eat less candy because sugar harms our teeth. Mike replies: 'Don't listen to Jamie — she's bad at math!' What's wrong with Mike's reply?
answer: Ad hominem — Mike attacked Jamie's character instead of answering whether sugar really harms teeth.
choices: Ad hominem — Mike attacked Jamie's character instead of answering whether sugar really harms teeth.
Straw man — Mike rewrote Jamie's claim into a wilder version that was easier to mock or dismiss.
Red herring — Mike brought up math, a topic mostly unrelated to the sugar argument at hand.
Slippery slope — Mike claimed one cavity would lead to many cavities without giving reasons.
context: Ad hominem attacks the person, not the argument. Even a person bad at math can be right about sugar.

question: Mom says: 'If we let the dog on the couch, soon he'll sleep in our beds, then eat off our plates, then run the house.' What's wrong with her reasoning?
answer: Slippery slope — she claimed a chain of disasters without giving any reason each step must follow the last one.
choices: Slippery slope — she claimed a chain of disasters without giving any reason each step must follow the last one.
Hasty generalization — she drew a sweeping rule about all dogs from a single case she saw with this dog.
Ad hominem reasoning — she attacked the dog's character instead of giving an actual reason about couch behavior.
Bandwagon move — she claimed most families let dogs on couches, so this family should follow the popular crowd.
context: A slippery-slope argument can be valid if each step's link is shown. The fallacy is asserting the chain without showing it.

question: Your friend says: 'Come on, EVERYONE is making fun of the new kid — you should too.' Why isn't 'everyone is doing it' a good reason?
answer: Bandwagon fallacy — popularity is not evidence; many people can be wrong, and joining cruelty doesn't make it right.
choices: Bandwagon fallacy — popularity is not evidence; many people can be wrong, and joining cruelty doesn't make it right.
Ad hominem fallacy — the friend has attacked the new kid's character instead of arguing about ideas they hold.
Red herring fallacy — the friend has dragged in a topic that has nothing to do with the original question.
Strawman fallacy — the friend has invented a wilder version of your view in order to knock it back down.
context: The bandwagon move treats popularity as proof. Counting heads doesn't replace giving a reason.

question: Tara met two unfriendly cats this week. She now says, 'All cats are mean.' What's wrong with her conclusion?
answer: Hasty generalization — she made a sweeping rule about all cats from a tiny sample of only two unfriendly ones.
choices: Hasty generalization — she made a sweeping rule about all cats from a tiny sample of only two unfriendly ones.
Slippery slope reasoning — she claimed one mean cat would lead to all cats becoming mean later on.
Begging the question — she assumed her conclusion in her premise so the argument circles back on itself.
Appeal to authority — she cited a famous cat-expert who agrees, instead of showing real evidence for it.
context: Two cases isn't enough to support a claim about every cat. Hasty generalization is leaping from a thin sample.

question: You say: 'We should clean up after lunch.' Sam replies: 'So you want us to spend ALL DAY cleaning?!' What's wrong with Sam's reply?
answer: Straw man — Sam replaced your modest claim with a wilder version that was easier to mock instead of engaging it.
choices: Straw man — Sam replaced your modest claim with a wilder version that was easier to mock instead of engaging it.
Ad hominem move — Sam attacked your character or motives instead of dealing with the actual cleanup proposal.
Red herring move — Sam dragged in an unrelated topic to pull the discussion away from the cleanup question.
Bandwagon move — Sam claimed most kids never clean up after lunch, so we should follow the popular crowd.
context: A straw man is easier to knock down because the attacker built it. The cure: state the real claim, then engage that.

question: A TV ad says: 'Doctors recommend Choco-Crunch candy bars.' Even if that's true, why might it still not be a good reason to eat them?
answer: Appeal to authority — doctors are experts in health, not candy ads; their say-so isn't evidence about nutrition here.
choices: Appeal to authority — doctors are experts in health, not candy ads; their say-so isn't evidence about nutrition here.
Begging the question — the ad assumes its conclusion in its premise, looping the argument back on itself in a circle.
Hasty generalization — the ad rests on too small a sample of doctors to support a claim about all candy bars.
Equivocation move — the ad uses the word 'recommend' in two different senses across the message, shifting meaning.
context: Authority counts when the authority's training fits the question. A doctor recommending candy is the same as a chef recommending surgery.

question: Mom says: 'Either you finish your homework right now, or you're a total failure.' What's another possibility she's leaving out?
answer: False dilemma — she has framed only two options when many real ones exist: finishing later, taking a break, getting help.
choices: False dilemma — she has framed only two options when many real ones exist: finishing later, taking a break, getting help.
Genetic fallacy — she has rejected the homework idea based on its origin or source rather than its actual content.
Tu quoque fallacy — she deflected criticism by claiming you do the same thing she was just being criticized for.
Composition fallacy — she has assumed something true of each part of homework must also be true of the whole task.
context: Also called the either/or or black-and-white fallacy. The cure: ask whether a third option has been hidden behind the choice.

question: 'Why is broccoli good for you?' 'Because it's healthy.' 'Why is it healthy?' 'Because it's good for you.' What's the problem here?
answer: Circular reasoning — the answer assumes the very claim it was supposed to prove, so the argument loops in a small circle.
choices: Circular reasoning — the answer assumes the very claim it was supposed to prove, so the argument loops in a small circle.
Equivocation reasoning — the word 'broccoli' is used in two senses across the answers, so a step looks valid by quiet shift.
Appeal to ignorance reasoning — the speaker argued from a lack of evidence against broccoli to a positive claim about it.
Hasty generalization reasoning — the speaker drew a wide conclusion about all vegetables from one tiny anecdotal example.
context: Also called begging the question. The premise and conclusion are really the same claim, just dressed up differently each time.

question: Liam says: 'I've never seen a ghost, and nobody can prove ghosts aren't real, so they must exist!' What's wrong with this reasoning?
answer: Appeal to ignorance — not having evidence against something is not evidence for it; an unanswered question stays unanswered.
choices: Appeal to ignorance — not having evidence against something is not evidence for it; an unanswered question stays unanswered.
Slippery slope reasoning — Liam claimed one unexplained event would lead to many supernatural events afterward.
Ad hominem reasoning — Liam attacked the character of ghost-doubters instead of giving real reasons for his own view.
Bandwagon reasoning — Liam relied on the popularity of ghost stories among other people as the basis for his own claim.
context: Sherlock Holmes had this right: absence of evidence isn't evidence of absence. The burden of proof falls on the one making the claim.

question: Coach replies to a player asking why she was benched: 'I'm the coach, that's why.' What kind of reasoning is this?
answer: Appeal to authority — the coach cited her role to end the argument instead of giving a real reason for the bench decision.
choices: Appeal to authority — the coach cited her role to end the argument instead of giving a real reason for the bench decision.
Appeal to popularity — the coach pointed to what most other coaches do, treating crowd-following as the basis for action.
Appeal to consequences — the coach claimed the bench decision must be right because its truth would lead to good results.
Appeal to ignorance — the coach argued that lacking evidence against the bench choice was proof it must have been right.
context: Authority can fit a question — but 'because I said so' is not a reason. A good coach can also give a reason.

question: Nina says: 'Have you stopped cheating on your tests?' Yes or no? Why is this question unfair, even if Nina just asked it?
answer: Loaded question — the question presupposes you were cheating; saying yes or no both seem to admit it, which is the trap.
choices: Loaded question — the question presupposes you were cheating; saying yes or no both seem to admit it, which is the trap.
Circular question — the question and its answer use the same exact words, so any reply you give just loops back to it.
Slippery question — the question claims one small admission will lead to a chain of further admissions you cannot stop.
Vague question — the question uses one key word in two senses, so an inference looks valid only by a hidden meaning shift.
context: A loaded question hides a disputed claim inside the wording. The cure: refuse the question and challenge the buried assumption.

question: Tom says: 'Owen wears glasses, and Owen is smart, so all glasses-wearers are smart.' What is Tom's mistake?
answer: Hasty generalization — Tom drew a broad rule about all glasses-wearers from a single example, far too thin a sample.
choices: Hasty generalization — Tom drew a broad rule about all glasses-wearers from a single example, far too thin a sample.
False dilemma — Tom framed only two options when many real positions on glasses-and-smartness exist between them.
Tu quoque fallacy — Tom deflected criticism by pointing out his critic does the same thing he was just accused of.
Bandwagon fallacy — Tom relied on the popularity of his view among classmates rather than giving any solid reasons.
context: One case can't carry a claim about all. A stronger argument needs many cases drawn from a wide and fair sample.

question: Riley says: 'It's been raining for three days, so it'll definitely rain forever.' What's wrong with Riley's reasoning?
answer: Hasty generalization — Riley used a short pattern as evidence for a much larger sweeping claim the data cannot carry.
choices: Hasty generalization — Riley used a short pattern as evidence for a much larger sweeping claim the data cannot carry.
Ad hominem reasoning — Riley attacked weather forecasters' character rather than dealing with the actual rainfall data.
Strawman reasoning — Riley replaced the original claim about three days with a wilder version about the entire season.
Begging the question — Riley assumed forever-rain as a premise and then concluded forever-rain, so the loop is tight.
context: Three days is real evidence, but it's not enough for 'forever.' Inductive jumps need many cases and care.

question: Alex says: 'You can't tell me not to lie — you lied last week!' Even if Alex is right the critic lied, why is this a bad reply?
answer: Tu quoque — pointing out the critic's own fault doesn't show the original claim is false; the criticism still has to be answered.
choices: Tu quoque — pointing out the critic's own fault doesn't show the original claim is false; the criticism still has to be answered.
Slippery slope — Alex argued one small lie will lead to many bigger lies without giving any reason each step follows.
Appeal to ignorance — Alex used the lack of evidence against lying as positive proof that lying must be acceptable.
Hasty generalization — Alex drew a broad conclusion about all lying from a single small example his critic gave him.
context: Tu quoque means 'you too' in Latin. It feels like a clever comeback but doesn't actually address whether the original point was right.

question: Coach asks why Jordan missed practice. Jordan replies: 'Did you know Coach Wilson has the best record in the league?' What is Jordan doing?
answer: Red herring — Jordan dragged in an unrelated topic about Coach Wilson to pull attention from the question being asked.
choices: Red herring — Jordan dragged in an unrelated topic about Coach Wilson to pull attention from the question being asked.
Strawman tactic — Jordan replaced the question about missing practice with a wilder version that was easier to escape.
Slippery slope — Jordan claimed one missed practice would lead to many further misses without any reason given.
Loaded question — Jordan asked a question whose form presupposes a controversial claim the coach has not yet agreed.
context: A red herring is a smelly distraction. The name comes from dragging a fish across a trail to throw hounds off the real scent.

question: Ben hears one bad review of a restaurant. He declares: 'This place must be terrible — never go there!' What's wrong with Ben's reasoning?
answer: Hasty generalization — Ben drew a sweeping verdict about the whole restaurant from one review, far too thin a sample.
choices: Hasty generalization — Ben drew a sweeping verdict about the whole restaurant from one review, far too thin a sample.
Circular reasoning — Ben assumed the restaurant was bad in his premise and then concluded it was bad, looping back.
Equivocation reasoning — Ben used the word 'bad' in two different senses across the argument, shifting its meaning.
Appeal to fear reasoning — Ben argued the restaurant must be bad because its truth would lead to unpleasant results.
context: One review is a single data point. Many reviews from different people give a fairer picture of how the restaurant really is.

question: Greta says: 'My grandpa smoked his whole life and lived to 95, so smoking can't really be bad for you.' What's the flaw?
answer: Hasty generalization — one lucky case can't outweigh huge studies; rare survivors don't show smoking is safe for everyone else.
choices: Hasty generalization — one lucky case can't outweigh huge studies; rare survivors don't show smoking is safe for everyone else.
Loaded question fallacy — Greta's claim presupposes a disputed point that the listener has not yet agreed to accept on faith.
Appeal to ignorance — Greta argued from lack of evidence against smoking to a positive claim it must be perfectly safe to do.
Slippery slope fallacy — Greta claimed one smoker living long would lead to all smokers living a long time too in a chain.
context: One person's outcome is anecdote, not evidence. Large studies trump single stories when the question is about populations.

question: Mr. Lee says: 'Either we ban all phones at school, or learning will collapse completely.' What's wrong with this framing?
answer: False dilemma — he has framed only two extreme options when many fair middle paths exist: limits, classroom rules, certain hours.
choices: False dilemma — he has framed only two extreme options when many fair middle paths exist: limits, classroom rules, certain hours.
Hasty generalization — he has drawn a sweeping conclusion about all phones from a small sample of cases he saw in his class.
Ad hominem reasoning — he has attacked the character of phone-users instead of addressing whether phones really harm learning.
Begging the question — he assumes his conclusion inside his premise, so the entire argument just loops in a very small circle.
context: Forcing a choice between extremes hides every middle path. Ask: is there really no third option?

question: Tu quoque (Latin: 'you too') deflects criticism by accusing the critic of doing the same thing. Why is this a fallacy, even when the accusation is accurate?
answer: The critic's behavior doesn't change whether the original claim is true; even hypocrites can correctly identify wrong actions in others.
choices: The critic's behavior doesn't change whether the original claim is true; even hypocrites can correctly identify wrong actions in others.
The critic's behavior shows the original claim must be false; once a critic is hypocritical, nothing they say can be true at all.
The critic's behavior is the only evidence that counts; if a critic is hypocritical, the original criticism is fully cancelled out.
The critic's behavior switches the burden of proof; once accused, the critic must defend themselves before any claim can stand.
context: Tu quoque is the schoolyard 'I know you are but what am I.' It feels like a clever comeback but doesn't engage the actual claim being made.

question: A red herring introduces something off-topic to pull attention from the real argument. Which case below is the clearest example of this move?
answer: Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies by listing all the times the landlord refused to fix the broken heater last winter.
choices: Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies by listing all the times the landlord refused to fix the broken heater last winter.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that nobody has proven she lacked the funds, so she must have had them.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that her brother also pays late, so the criticism doesn't really apply to her.
Asked why she failed to pay rent, the tenant replies that the landlord has called her dishonest before, so he cannot judge her now.
context: Red herrings sound related but lead elsewhere. The cure: drag the conversation back to the original question and refuse to be diverted.

question: Post hoc ergo propter hoc (Latin: 'after this, therefore because of this') assumes that because B followed A, A caused B. Which of these cases makes this exact mistake?
answer: Every time the rooster crows, the sun rises right after; the farmer concludes the rooster's crowing is what causes the sun to rise.
choices: Every time the rooster crows, the sun rises right after; the farmer concludes the rooster's crowing is what causes the sun to rise.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer attacks the rooster's character instead of asking what really triggers the rooster's crow.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer claims one early-morning sound will lead to many disturbances throughout the rest of the day.
Every time the rooster crows, the farmer argues most farmers in the region also keep roosters, so keeping one must be a sound idea.
context: Sequence alone is not causation. Both events may share a third cause (here, the rotation of the Earth) that produces both at the same time.

question: Appeal to ignorance argues: 'Nobody has proven X is false, so X must be true' (or its mirror). What's the flaw at the heart of this move?
answer: Lack of evidence against a claim is not evidence for the claim; an open question remains open until positive evidence settles it.
choices: Lack of evidence against a claim is not evidence for the claim; an open question remains open until positive evidence settles it.
Lack of evidence against a claim makes the claim false by definition; without proof, no statement can ever count as true at all.
Lack of evidence against a claim shifts the burden onto the speaker; the listener must prove the claim true before doubting it.
Lack of evidence against a claim shows both sides are equally supported; truth and falsehood become a perfect tie in such cases.
context: The burden of proof falls on the one making a positive claim. 'You can't prove it isn't' doesn't replace 'here's why it is.'

question: Equivocation occurs when one key word shifts meaning across an argument. Which case below shows equivocation in action most clearly?
answer: 'A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So no feather can ever be dark in color.' The word 'light' shifts meaning between lines.
choices: 'A feather is light. What is light cannot be dark. So no feather can ever be dark in color.' The word 'light' shifts meaning between lines.
'A feather is light. So pillows full of feathers are light too.' The word 'feather' keeps one steady meaning across every premise.
'A feather floats in air. So all small objects must float in air.' The word 'float' keeps one steady meaning throughout the argument.
'A feather has a quill. Quills hold ink. So feathers hold ink.' The word 'quill' keeps one steady meaning throughout the argument.
context: Equivocation is the engine of word-puzzle paradoxes. 'Light' meaning low-weight and 'light' meaning bright are different concepts sharing one spelling.

question: No true Scotsman saves a general claim by redefining the category to exclude any counterexample. Which case shows this move most plainly?
answer: Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: well, no TRUE vegan would wear leather; those people aren't actually vegans at all.
choices: Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: well, no TRUE vegan would wear leather; those people aren't actually vegans at all.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: most vegans I know don't, so the criticism rests on too small a sample base.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: you've changed the original modest claim about food into a much wider one to mock.
Critic: many vegans wear leather shoes. Reply: that's just an attack on vegans' character, not a real argument about the diet itself.
context: Named by Antony Flew. The trick: face a counterexample, and rather than weaken the claim, redefine the term to expel the counterexample.

question: Composition fallacy assumes what is true of each part must be true of the whole. Which case below makes this mistake about parts and wholes?
answer: Every player on this team is highly skilled. So the team itself must therefore be one of the most skilled teams in the entire league.
choices: Every player on this team is highly skilled. So the team itself must therefore be one of the most skilled teams in the entire league.
