choices: Without rules, the strong can hurt the weak, and trust between people falls apart.
Without rules, the post office cannot deliver mail in any organized fashion.
Without rules, there is no way to print a calendar that everyone agrees on.
Without rules, the buildings will physically collapse from a lack of maintenance.
context: Hobbes called life with no rules 'nasty, brutish, and short.' Most thinkers since have agreed that the strong will dominate when nothing holds them back, even if they disagree on what the rules should be.

question: Socrates would ask people in the marketplace, 'What is courage?' When they tried to answer, he kept asking more questions until they weren't sure anymore. What was the point of this?
answer: To show that people often think they understand a word but really don't, so they should think harder.
choices: To show that people often think they understand a word but really don't, so they should think harder.
To prove that he was smarter than everyone else and could win any debate, they say.
To collect money from people who couldn't answer his hardest riddles right, they say.
To find someone willing to fight him, since he was secretly a great warrior, they say.
context: This is called the Socratic method: question by question, you find the shaky bits in what you believe. Socrates said it was the start of real wisdom, not the end of it.

question: Mill thought everyone's happiness should count the same in any choice. Why is this fairer than letting you put your own family first?
answer: Giving your own family extra weight is a rule you couldn't defend to the family you left out.
choices: Giving your own family extra weight is a rule you couldn't defend to the family you left out.
Families never argue with one another, so they don't need any fairness rule between them.
Strangers always pay more taxes than family members, and the tax law settles fairness.
Houses are small, and there is no real room in them for thinking about fairness deeply.
context: His standard of impartial counting is hard to live by. We do care more about people close to us. But if we had to justify the preference to a stranger, he said, we would be stuck.

question: Hume thought our judgments of right and wrong are powered by feelings of sympathy, not by pure thinking. Why does his view differ sharply from a view that treats right and wrong like math?
answer: Math rules don't need anyone to care; his view says right and wrong only make sense if real people feel for each other.
choices: Math rules don't need anyone to care; his view says right and wrong only make sense if real people feel for each other.
Math is hard, and he preferred easy subjects, so he picked feelings rather than equations to study.
Sympathy is a kind of hat, and his followers always wore one in their public talks at home, or so some say.
He disliked numbers, so he refused to study any subject that used them at any level, or so some say.
context: His stress on feeling makes him a sentimentalist in ethics. Critics worry this makes right and wrong too soft. Defenders ask: could math facts alone explain why we care about right and wrong?

question: A Stoic teacher tells his student: 'The rain will fall whether you shout at the sky or not.' What lesson is he trying to give about anger?
answer: Don't waste feeling on what you can't control; save your energy for what you can.
choices: Don't waste feeling on what you can't control; save your energy for what you can.
Anger at the sky always works if you shout loudly enough to be heard up there.
The student should buy an umbrella, since it solves every weather problem.
Shouting is good exercise, even when no one and nothing answers you back.
context: Stoics divide things into 'up to us' (our thoughts, our actions) and 'not up to us' (weather, other people's choices, illness). They train you to put your heart only in the first group.

question: An existentialist character is told, 'You are a baker. Just bake.' He answers, 'Maybe, but I have to decide whether to keep being a baker.' What is he refusing to accept?
answer: That his role is fixed for him; he insists that he, not his job, decides who he is.
choices: That his role is fixed for him; he insists that he, not his job, decides who he is.
That bakers should bake bread; he wants to bake only cakes from now on.
That his mother is his mother; he says he has decided to switch families.
That the sun is real; he claims he could make the sun disappear by choosing.
context: Existentialists reject the idea that you are 'just' whatever your job or label says. You are always free to step back and ask whether that's the life you mean to keep choosing.

question: A philosopher asks whether your senses could be deceiving you right now in some major way you couldn't possibly detect. What broad approach to knowledge does she belong to when she takes this question seriously?
answer: Skepticism, which questions whether we can be sure of much of what we ordinarily take for granted.
choices: Skepticism, which questions whether we can be sure of much of what we ordinarily take for granted.
Optimism, which assumes that all our beliefs are basically right by default.
Idealism, which holds that the world is made up entirely of solid matter, they say.
Realism, which simply trusts that things are as they appear in every case, they say.
context: Skeptics test the limits of knowledge by imagining how much could be wrong without our noticing. The point isn't always to give up on knowing, but to find out what really survives serious doubt.

question: A woman whose child had died brought the dead child to the Buddha and begged him to bring the boy back. He told her to fetch a mustard seed from any house where no one had ever died. What did she learn?
answer: That death visits every household; her loss is sharp but it is shared by all who love.
choices: That death visits every household; her loss is sharp but it is shared by all who love.
That mustard seeds were rare in her region and impossible to find that year.
That the Buddha didn't really know how to help her at all and was stalling for time.
That her child could be revived only if she brought seeds from one hundred homes.
context: She walked door to door and found no such house. Returning, she understood. The story teaches the Buddha's view of impermanence and the shared nature of grief: facing it is the start of healing it.

question: Hume said when he looked into himself, he never found a steady 'self' behind his thoughts — only a stream of changing feelings, ideas, and memories. What conclusion did he draw about personal identity?
answer: That the self is more like a bundle of changing experiences than a single unchanging thing.
choices: That the self is more like a bundle of changing experiences than a single unchanging thing.
That the self is a small object hidden inside the chest, near the heart.
That every person has exactly two selves, one for daytime and one for night.
That selves only exist in religious texts and have no place in serious philosophy.
context: Hume's bundle theory of the self is one of the more startling claims in modern philosophy. It denies that there is some 'I' that has experiences; the 'I' just is the flow of experiences, loosely held together.

question: An argument can be 'valid' yet still untrue. A valid argument is one where the conclusion follows from the premises by logical necessity. What further property does an argument need to be 'sound'?
answer: Its premises must actually be true, not just logically connected to the conclusion.
choices: Its premises must actually be true, not just logically connected to the conclusion.
Its conclusion must be famous in textbooks, since textbooks select sound arguments.
Its author must be respected by other philosophers in the same century at minimum.
Its premises must rhyme with each other, since rhyme is the standard test of soundness.
context: Validity is about the form of the argument. Soundness adds the demand that the premises be true. A valid argument from false premises is a warning sign: the logic is clean but the foundation is rotten.

question: John Rawls asked us to imagine designing a society from behind a 'veil of ignorance,' not knowing our own race, wealth, talents, or beliefs. Why did he think this thought experiment helped find fair rules?
answer: Because not knowing your own position pushes you to choose rules that are good even for the worst-off, in case that's you.
choices: Because not knowing your own position pushes you to choose rules that are good even for the worst-off, in case that's you.
Because the veil was made of magic cloth that gave wisdom to anyone who wore it, or so some say, they say.
Because rich people always wear veils anyway, so the picture would feel familiar, or so some say.
Because ignorance is wisdom, and the veil simply blocks the harmful light of truth, roughly speaking.
context: Rawls's veil tries to take selfishness out of political design. If you don't know where you'll land, you'll insist on a floor everyone could live on. The argument shaped much of 20th-century political theory.

question: In the Crito, Socrates is offered a chance to escape execution. He imagines the Laws of Athens speaking to him, asking how he could abandon them now after a lifetime of their protection. What kind of moral argument is he making against escape?
answer: An implicit-agreement argument: by accepting the benefits of the laws all his life, he had agreed not to break them when they turned against him.
choices: An implicit-agreement argument: by accepting the benefits of the laws all his life, he had agreed not to break them when they turned against him.
An economic argument: leaving Athens would cost him too much in lost property and trade, as the careless put it, or so some say.
A medical argument: travel after the hemlock would weaken him in a final unhealthy way, or so people guess, or so some say.
A romantic argument: his wife wanted him to stay even if her opinion did not matter, as the story goes, or so some say.
context: Socrates's argument in the Crito is an ancestor of the social-contract tradition. He saw himself as bound by his life-long acceptance of Athens's order, even though that very order had unjustly condemned him.

question: Aristotle distinguished four kinds of causes for any event: material, formal, efficient, and final. For a wooden table, what is the final cause?
answer: The purpose for which it exists, namely to be a surface where people work or eat or write.
choices: The purpose for which it exists, namely to be a surface where people work or eat or write.
The wood it is made of, since that is what gives it its weight and color.
The shape of its legs and top, which the carpenter cut and sanded into place.
The carpenter himself, whose hands and tools did the actual work on the wood.
context: Aristotle's four causes give a full picture: material (the wood), formal (the shape), efficient (the carpenter), and final (the purpose). Modern science quietly dropped the final cause for most things, but it is still useful for understanding made objects and living beings.

question: Sara wants a later bedtime. Her brother says: 'Sara has bad grades, so her idea is dumb.' What did the brother NOT do?
answer: Listen to Sara's reason for the later bedtime before judging her.
choices: Listen to Sara's reason for the later bedtime before judging her.
Bring up Sara's grades as the very important part of the talk.
Tell Sara to get better grades before she can ask for a change.
Help mom and dad make a fair bedtime rule that works for both.
context: Going after the person ('bad grades') instead of the actual idea is called ad hominem. Sara's grades have nothing to do with whether her idea is good or bad.

question: Tom says we should walk to school for exercise. His friend yells: 'so you want everyone to walk for HOURS each day?' What is wrong?
answer: Tom never said hours -- the friend made his idea sound much worse.
choices: Tom never said hours -- the friend made his idea sound much worse.
Tom forgot to say WHY walking would be good for kids at school.
The friend should say 'good idea' before he says any reason back.
Walking is fine but it should be only for kids who are healthy.
context: Twisting someone's small idea into a huge bad idea, then attacking THAT, is the straw man. Always check what the person ACTUALLY said.

question: Mom says: 'either you eat your spinach OR you do not love the family.' What is hidden in this choice?
answer: There are LOTS of ways to love your family -- spinach is one tiny thing.
choices: There are LOTS of ways to love your family -- spinach is one tiny thing.
Spinach is healthy and your family wants you to grow up strong, true?
Saying 'no' to spinach is the same as saying 'no' to mom for life.
Mom is right that loving family means eating what they cook for you.
context: When someone gives you ONLY two choices -- usually one good, one bad -- when more exist, it is called a false dilemma. Most real choices have many paths.

question: You say to mom: 'EVERYONE in fourth grade has these shoes, so I need them too!' Why is this a weak kind of reason for asking?
answer: Lots of kids wanting a thing does not make it a thing you need.
choices: Lots of kids wanting a thing does not make it a thing you need.
Fourth graders are too young to know what is right for any year.
Mom got HER shoes first, so you should wait until next school year.
Shoes are too costly for kids and mom should spend that on food.
context: The bandwagon fallacy says 'lots of people do it, so it must be good.' But lots of people can be wrong, and trends are not the same as needs.

question: Ben says: 'eating sugar all day is bad for kids.' Mia answers: 'but YOU eat candy at parties!' What did Mia NOT do?
answer: Answer whether Ben's point about sugar is true or false today.
choices: Answer whether Ben's point about sugar is true or false today.
Bring up that parties are special days when treats are normal.
Stop being mean to Ben and apologize for catching him eating it.
Tell her own parents that Ben thinks all sugar is bad for kids.
context: Tu quoque (you-too) flips the argument back at the speaker without answering it. Even if Ben breaks his own rule, his point about sugar can still be true.

question: Coach says: 'every great runner I know wakes up at five.' Lily wakes at five too, but she is slow. What went wrong here?
answer: Waking up early may happen with great runners -- but it does not MAKE them great.
choices: Waking up early may happen with great runners -- but it does not MAKE them great.
Lily should not be set against runners who are much older than she is.
Coach is right that morning is the best time for any kid to do a sport.
Lily should keep waking up at five and one day she will be a great runner.
context: Just because two things happen together does NOT mean one causes the other. Great runners may wake early for OTHER reasons than the wake-up.

question: Your friend says: 'pizza is YUMMY, so it must be HEALTHY too.' What did your friend mix up here?
answer: Tasting good and being good for you are two DIFFERENT things.
choices: Tasting good and being good for you are two DIFFERENT things.
Pizza is healthy if you add lots of veggies and skip the cheese.
Your friend probably had a bad health class at school this year.
Yummy food is bad for you because chefs trick your taste buds.
context: Mixing up two different ideas just because they sound similar -- yummy vs. healthy -- is a confusion of words. Always ask: are these REALLY the same?

question: Your friend says: 'this story is TRUE because the famous actor on TV said so.' What is the weak part of his reason?
answer: Famous people can be wrong too -- being on TV does not make it true.
choices: Famous people can be wrong too -- being on TV does not make it true.
Famous actors do not have time to learn about every story they share.
Stories on TV are mostly true, so the actor probably checked it first.
Your friend should ask the actor's name and see what he has said before.
context: Appeal to authority means 'a famous person said so, so it must be right.' Even smart famous people get things wrong. Always ask: what is the EVIDENCE?

question: Sam says: 'I read it on the internet, so it must be TRUE.' Why is this a weak kind of reason to fully believe it?
answer: Anyone can put anything on the internet -- writing it does not check it.
choices: Anyone can put anything on the internet -- writing it does not check it.
The internet is full of stories that are real but boring to read about.
Sam needs a faster computer to find the BEST sites in the country today.
Most teachers say to use books, not the internet, for getting any answers.
context: Just because words are written -- on TV, online, in a book -- does not mean they are true. Truth comes from CHECKING, not from being shown on a screen.

question: Mia says: 'no REAL Sox fan would skip a game tonight.' Dad is a Sox fan -- and he skipped. How is Mia cheating with words?
answer: She made up a fake rule for who counts as a 'real fan' to win the talk.
choices: She made up a fake rule for who counts as a 'real fan' to win the talk.
Mia is upset with Dad and is using harder words to show her feelings.
She is right that real fans go to games -- Dad is being lazy tonight.
Mia should ask Dad to take her to a future Sox game so she sees one.
context: The 'no true Scotsman' move re-names the group to shut out anyone who breaks the rule. A 'real fan' becomes whoever Mia wants -- that is not playing fair.

question: A new kid in your class has no snack today. You have two cookies. What is the GENEROUS thing to do that is not too much?
answer: Offer one cookie -- you give a real gift but you keep one for yourself.
choices: Offer one cookie -- you give a real gift but you keep one for yourself.
Eat both fast so the new kid does not see and feel bad about her snack.
Tell the new kid to ask her own mom to pack a snack for school tomorrow.
Take the cookies home so you can save them for a school day she has none.
context: Being generous does not mean giving up everything. It means choosing to share even when you do not HAVE to. One cookie of two is a real gift.

question: Your team wins because the other team had only six players. Coach says you were great. Do you DESERVE the praise all on your own?
answer: Some of it -- you DID play, but the win also came from the small other team.
choices: Some of it -- you DID play, but the win also came from the small other team.
All of it -- a win is a win in any game, and coach should keep on praising.
None of it -- a real player would say no to the praise and ask for a do-over.
Half of it -- you should always cut every kind of win in half to be quite fair.
context: Honesty about a win means seeing the whole picture. You did play. AND the other team was short. BOTH things are true at the same time.

question: Your friend tells you she is moving in a month and asks you to keep it quiet. Is this a secret you SHOULD keep for her?
answer: Yes -- her news is HER news to share, when and how she chooses to tell others.
choices: Yes -- her news is HER news to share, when and how she chooses to tell others.
No -- you should tell the teacher right away in case the move is somehow not safe.
Yes -- but only until other kids guess it and then you can say it out loud at school.
No -- big news like that should not be a secret because other kids will be very upset.
context: Some secrets keep people safe (good). Others hide harm (bad). News a friend has not yet told the world is HERS to share -- keeping it is a kind of trust.

question: You see a kid cheating on a small spelling quiz. Does it matter that the quiz does NOT count for the grade card?
answer: Yes -- cheating is about who you ARE, not just about whether the grade counts.
choices: Yes -- cheating is about who you ARE, not just about whether the grade counts.
No -- a quiz that does not count is just for fun, so the cheating cannot be real.
Yes -- but only because the teacher would be sad if a student lied to her again.
No -- cheating only counts when there are grades, awards, or prizes at the end.
context: What you do when 'it does not matter' shows your real character. A person who only stays honest for grades is not really honest yet.

question: Your sister keeps a promise to a friend even though it costs her a fun party. Why might this be a BRAVE thing for her to do?
answer: Doing what is right when you LOSE something for it is harder than easy bravery.
choices: Doing what is right when you LOSE something for it is harder than easy bravery.
She should have told her friend that the party is more important than a promise.
Being brave is for big choices like fighting fires, not small ones like a kid party.
The friend will probably let her go to the party anyway if she just asks one more time.
context: Bravery is not only about danger. Standing by your word when it costs you is one of the harder kinds of bravery in a kid's day.

question: Three friends plan a movie together. One gets sick. The other two go without her. Was this an UNKIND choice the two friends made?
answer: Maybe -- the right move is to ask the sick friend what SHE would like first.
choices: Maybe -- the right move is to ask the sick friend what SHE would like first.
No way -- one sick kid should not stop a movie plan for everyone else.
Yes always -- friends ALWAYS wait, no matter the day or the kind of sick.
Only if the friend who is sick told them to wait and the two did not listen.
context: Real kindness asks. Maybe she wants them to go. Maybe she wants a raincheck. The point is that she gets a voice in what happens next.

question: Augustine, a thinker long ago, stole pears from a tree -- not because he was hungry, but because it was BAD. Why did this puzzle him?
answer: He could not see why doing wrong on purpose, with no reward, felt fun at all.
choices: He could not see why doing wrong on purpose, with no reward, felt fun at all.
He had not stolen pears before, so he was not used to doing things like that.
The pears were old and small, so they were not worth the steps it took to take.
His parents had told him to share the pears with friends but he kept some back.
context: Augustine's famous 'pear theft' story in his Confessions asks a deep question: why do people sometimes want to do wrong, just because it is wrong?

question: Aquinas, a teacher long ago, said good kids FIRST learn right by SEEING others do right. What might this mean for your day at home?
answer: The grown-ups around you teach you good habits without even saying a single word.
choices: The grown-ups around you teach you good habits without even saying a single word.
You should read big old books on what is right before you do any tricky thing.
Doing right comes from being told the rules -- the more rules, the better you do.
Watching one good person is not enough -- you have to watch lots of them each day.
context: Aquinas thought we pick up good habits by watching kind, brave, fair people. What you SEE matters more than what you are TOLD.

question: Descartes, a thinker long ago, asked: 'how do I know I am not DREAMING right now?' Why was this a hard puzzle for him to crack?
answer: When you dream, things FEEL real -- so 'feels real' alone cannot prove you awake.
choices: When you dream, things FEEL real -- so 'feels real' alone cannot prove you awake.
He was tired and so it was hard for him to figure out the puzzle for many years.
He had eaten too much for dinner and the puzzle is one that comes after big meals.
Dreaming is rare so it took him a long time to find a single good way to test it.
context: Descartes pushed the dream puzzle hard to find out: what CAN I be sure of? His famous answer started 'I think, so I am' -- a thinker has to exist.

question: Locke, a thinker long ago, said the law should protect THREE big things for every person. What were the three things he listed?
answer: Your life, the things you own, and the right to make your own choices.
choices: Your life, the things you own, and the right to make your own choices.
Your house, your favorite toys, and your right to eat anything you wish to.
Your school, your family pet, and your friend who has been your best forever.
Your dog, the room where you sleep, and your right to do anything at school.
context: Locke's three: life, liberty, and property. Many later laws -- like in America -- were built on this same simple list of things to protect.

question: Mom's old car has had every part swapped over the years -- new tires, new seats, new engine. Is it STILL the very same car?
answer: Maybe -- it depends on if you mean the same parts, or the same role in her life.
choices: Maybe -- it depends on if you mean the same parts, or the same role in her life.
Yes for sure -- Mom calls it the same car, so the name makes it the same.
No way -- if every part is new, it is a totally new car that just looks old.
Yes always -- a car keeps its name forever, no matter how much you change.
context: This is the 'ship of Theseus' puzzle. There may not be ONE right answer -- but the question shows that 'same' is trickier than it sounds.

question: A photo from when you were two shows a tiny kid. Are you the SAME person as that tiny kid you see in the old family photo?
answer: Yes -- but a lot has changed: your body, your words, even what you can recall now.
choices: Yes -- but a lot has changed: your body, your words, even what you can recall now.
No way -- that kid was so small and so long ago that he counts as a new person.
Yes for sure -- being the same person is just the same body, even years later.
No -- you and the tiny kid in the photo share the same name but not the person.
context: What makes you YOU over time is one of the oldest puzzles. Most people say yes -- memory, body, story all link you to the tiny kid -- but it is not easy to PROVE.

question: Alex says: 'we should do less homework -- kids need rest.' Casey answers: 'Alex is just lazy.' What did Casey skip past in the talk?
answer: Whether kids really do need more rest, which is what Alex was talking about.
choices: Whether kids really do need more rest, which is what Alex was talking about.
Whether Alex's grades are good enough for her to make any rule for everyone.
Whether teachers can give the same homework to kids in lots of grade levels.
Whether the school day is too long and so kids cannot do homework at night.
context: Ad hominem skips the argument and goes for the person. The right move is to ANSWER Alex's point about rest -- not to label Alex.

question: Maya wants the school to add salad to lunch. Jake says: 'so Maya wants to BAN pizza forever!' How did Jake change Maya's idea?
answer: He took 'add salad' and stretched it into 'ban pizza' -- much bigger and worse.
choices: He took 'add salad' and stretched it into 'ban pizza' -- much bigger and worse.
Maya never said anything about pizza -- she only spoke about new salad bars.
Jake is right that adding salad will somehow lead to taking pizza away first.
Maya did not say HOW much salad she wants the school to add to lunch trays.
context: The straw man fallacy attacks a stretched, fake version of the other side. ALWAYS check: did the person actually SAY the thing you are arguing against?

question: Mom says: 'if I let you have your phone at dinner, soon you will want it at school, then in bed, then forever.' What is her fear?
answer: That ONE small allow will quickly snowball into many big bad allows.
choices: That ONE small allow will quickly snowball into many big bad allows.
That you are too young for a phone at all, even just for a quick text or two.
That dinner time is special and phones do not belong at the family table.
That you will forget to do homework if you keep your phone in your room.
context: Slippery slope says ONE allow leads to many disasters -- without showing each step. Maybe it WILL slide; maybe it will not. The arguer has to actually SHOW it.

question: Your friend says: 'either we get a DOG, or our family is no good.' What is hidden inside this kind of either-or choice?
answer: All the OTHER ways families can be good without picking up a single dog.
choices: All the OTHER ways families can be good without picking up a single dog.
The fact that dogs are messy and cost a lot of money to keep over their lives.
The truth that most families do not own a dog and they still seem fine.
The detail that cats are also good pets and would also make a family happy.
context: False dilemma hides the middle ground. Real choices are rarely 'this OR nothing.' Many families are great with no dog, no cat, no pet at all.

question: Dad says: 'if I let you skip ONE chore, you will never do ANY of them again.' What part of his worry is the slippery slope?
answer: He has not shown WHY one skip would mean a total chore strike from now on.
choices: He has not shown WHY one skip would mean a total chore strike from now on.
Most kids skip chores when their parents are not looking, so he should know.
Dad is correct that chores need to be done, but he is wrong about the future.
He should have a list of chores you skipped before he can make any new rules.
context: The slippery slope worry might be right OR wrong. The fallacy is using fear of the BOTTOM of the slope to skip the question at the TOP.

question: Lily says: 'EVERYONE in our class loves that movie, so it MUST be the best one.' What is the weak part of her reason?
answer: Lots of kids liking a thing does not prove it is the best out of all movies.
choices: Lots of kids liking a thing does not prove it is the best out of all movies.
Lily watched the movie alone, so she missed the whole class talking it over.
Class kids can change their minds at any time, so the count might be wrong.
Best movie is a guess that you can never really prove from a class only.
context: Bandwagon = 'lots of people agree, so it must be true.' But popular and BEST are two different things. Best needs reasons, not just a head count.

question: Greg says: 'a famous singer wears these shoes, so the shoes must be good for kids in school.' Why is this a weak kind of evidence?
answer: What a famous singer wears has little to do with what is good for kid feet.
choices: What a famous singer wears has little to do with what is good for kid feet.
Famous singers are paid to wear the shoes, so it is not really their own choice.
Most kids cannot afford the shoes that famous singers wear in their work videos.
Greg should have asked the singer to send a free pair to test on his own feet.
context: Appeal to authority works when the authority KNOWS the field. A famous singer's fame is in singing, not in foot health.

question: Your dad says: 'do not start smoking -- it hurts your health.' You say: 'but YOU smoke!' What did you skip past in his warning?
answer: Whether smoking is actually bad for you -- which is the real point he is making.
choices: Whether smoking is actually bad for you -- which is the real point he is making.
Whether dad is being a hypocrite for smoking while telling you not to do it.
Whether dad has tried to stop smoking before, or whether he means to try soon.
Whether mom thinks dad smoking is okay, or whether she has told him to stop.
context: Tu quoque (you-too) feels like a win, but it doesn't answer the actual point. Dad smoking might be bad AND his warning about smoking might still be true.

question: Theo went to one big city and met TWO rude people. He says: 'EVERYONE in that city is rude.' What is wrong with what Theo did?
answer: He took two people and used them to judge a whole city of lots of people.
choices: He took two people and used them to judge a whole city of lots of people.
Theo should have stayed longer and seen more parts of the big city he was in.
Most cities have a lot of rude people in them, so he is right about the place.
Theo should have asked other folks first if they had had any rude run-ins there.
context: Hasty generalization jumps from a SMALL sample to a HUGE claim. Two people in a city of millions is not enough to judge the whole place.

question: Sam says: 'that idea came from a kid I do not like -- so it is a DUMB idea.' What did Sam not bother to check before he judged?
answer: Whether the IDEA itself is good or bad, apart from where it happened to come from.
choices: Whether the IDEA itself is good or bad, apart from where it happened to come from.
Whether the other kid was trying to be funny when he had the idea in class.
Whether Sam knows the other kid well enough to say if he likes him or not.
Whether all of the kids in the class like the same idea as Sam likes today.
context: The genetic fallacy judges an idea by its ORIGIN -- where it came from -- not by its QUALITY. Even a kid you dislike can have a great idea.

question: Mom asks: 'did you do your homework?' You answer: 'but the dog needs a walk!' What is the dog-walk in this talk?
answer: A side topic you dropped in to draw mom away from the homework question.
choices: A side topic you dropped in to draw mom away from the homework question.
A way to be kind to the dog while you say sorry for not doing the work.
A clue that you do not understand the homework and need a help break first.
A reminder that taking care of pets is just as big a job as homework is.
context: A red herring is a side topic dropped into a talk to PULL ATTENTION AWAY from the real question. The dog might need a walk -- AND you still owe an answer.

question: An ad says: 'this drink is 100% natural, so it must be GOOD for your body.' Why is this a weak reason to drink the drink?
answer: Lots of natural things hurt us -- 'natural' alone is not the same as 'safe.'
choices: Lots of natural things hurt us -- 'natural' alone is not the same as 'safe.'
Most drinks have water in them, and water is natural, so all drinks are good.
Natural drinks have a worse taste than other drinks that come in bottles or cans.
Ad people are paid to use the word 'natural' and so the drinks may not be it.
context: Appeal to nature says 'it is natural, so it is good.' But poison berries are natural too. The word 'natural' is not a real measure of whether a thing is safe.

question: You have spent a whole hour on a puzzle. You see now it is missing pieces. You say: 'I have to KEEP going because I spent so long.' Why is this a weak reason?
answer: The hour you spent is gone -- staying longer cannot bring back any of it.
choices: The hour you spent is gone -- staying longer cannot bring back any of it.
The puzzle is missing pieces, so the box was probably broken from the start.
Your mom told you not to start any puzzle she does not check for missing parts.
An hour is not enough to do a big puzzle on your own without any helping hands.
context: The sunk cost fallacy uses time or money you ALREADY spent as a reason to spend MORE. But the past is past -- choose by what is BEST from here.

question: Your sister cries: 'if you do not give me the last pancake, you are MEAN!' Why is her tears not a real reason to give it up?
answer: Tears tell what she WANTS, not whether the last pancake is hers to claim.
choices: Tears tell what she WANTS, not whether the last pancake is hers to claim.
Sisters always get the last pancake at the table, so she is right to ask.
She should have eaten faster if she really wanted the last one at the end.
If you are kind in other ways, you do not have to give up your pancake today.
context: Appeal to emotion uses strong feelings to push you. Real reasons say WHY something is fair. Tears alone are about her feelings, not the question.

question: Ben says: 'this book is the best because no other book is as good as this one.' What is broken in his sentence?
answer: He used the SAME idea twice -- 'best' and 'no other as good' say one thing.
choices: He used the SAME idea twice -- 'best' and 'no other as good' say one thing.
He should have read at least one other book to compare it to before he said this.
Ben is a bit too young to know the real best book in the school library yet.
He should have asked the school librarian to make a list of best books for him.
context: Begging the question hides the conclusion INSIDE a premise. Saying 'best because no other is as good' tells us nothing -- it just repeats itself in fancier words.

question: Theo says: 'if we cut homework by 10 minutes, soon we will cut it all, then school itself!' What did Theo not show?
answer: Why a small cut would HAVE to lead to bigger cuts and then to no school at all.
choices: Why a small cut would HAVE to lead to bigger cuts and then to no school at all.
Why some homework is good to keep, even if a small bit gets cut next year.
Why ten minutes is the right amount to cut, instead of some other small amount.
Why he thinks teachers will not push back against the parents who want a cut.
context: Slippery slope works ONLY when each step is given. Saying 'this will lead to that' without showing HOW is just fear-talk, not a real reason.

question: An ad says: 'this kid's meal is FREE -- so a free meal is GOOD!' Then later: 'now you have a FREE day to do anything!' What word is being played with?
answer: 'Free' -- the first means no cost, the second means open to choose what to do.
choices: 'Free' -- the first means no cost, the second means open to choose what to do.
'Meal' -- the first kind is dinner, the second kind is what you have for lunch.
'Day' -- a day on a kid menu and a day in a week are not the same kind of day.
'Good' -- the ad uses 'good' in two ways but only one of them is the right way.
context: Equivocation slides between two meanings of one word in the same talk. 'Free' means a lot of things -- mix them up and the argument falls apart.

question: Coach asks Tim: 'why do you ALWAYS skip the warmup?' Tim has skipped only once. What is hidden in the way she asks?
answer: She treats 'always skip' as a given -- but it has not been shown to be true.
choices: She treats 'always skip' as a given -- but it has not been shown to be true.
She is being a bit too kind, so Tim feels okay to skip more warmups now.
She wants Tim to know that warmups are good for him before he plays today.
She is asking nicely so that Tim will be okay with telling her the truth.
context: A loaded question hides a guess. 'Why do you ALWAYS X?' takes 'you always X' as already true. Push back on the hidden guess before you answer.

question: A man on TV says: 'we should build a new park.' Another man says: 'he wore the wrong tie last week!' What is wrong with the reply?
answer: Wearing a tie has nothing to do with whether the park is a good idea or bad.
choices: Wearing a tie has nothing to do with whether the park is a good idea or bad.
He should have said why the tie was wrong before he made his own park reply.
Wearing a wrong tie is rude, so we should not listen to the first man at all.
The first man should have worn a better tie that day, or he should say sorry.
context: Ad hominem in politics is everywhere. Watch for: 'so-and-so is rude / dumb / bad,' with no answer to the actual idea on the table.

question: Anna says: 'we should turn off lights to save power.' Tim says: 'so you want us to live in the DARK like cave people?' What did Tim do?
answer: He took 'save power' and stretched it into 'live in the dark' -- much further.
choices: He took 'save power' and stretched it into 'live in the dark' -- much further.
He may be right that turning off lights all the time will hurt how we see at night.
He should ask Anna if her family has saved a lot of power so far this past year.
He thinks cave people are bad, so we should not be like them in any way today.
context: Always check the actual claim. Anna said 'turn off LIGHTS' -- not 'have NO light at all.' Tim turned a small idea into a big easy-to-knock one.

question: Sam says: 'there is a dragon in my closet.' Lily says: 'PROVE there is not!' What did Lily get backwards?
answer: Sam claimed the dragon -- HE has to show it, not Lily prove the empty closet.
choices: Sam claimed the dragon -- HE has to show it, not Lily prove the empty closet.
Lily should have asked first if the dragon has a name or a kind home in there.
Sam said it nice, so Lily should trust him until she has time to look in herself.
Both kids are wrong because dragons are not real and they should know this fact.
context: Shifting the burden of proof = pushing the work of proving onto the person who did NOT make the claim. The maker of the claim has to bring the evidence.

question: Sara says: 'no one has PROVED ghosts are not real, so they MUST be real.' What is the broken move in her reason?
answer: Just not having proof AGAINST a thing does not mean the thing is true.
choices: Just not having proof AGAINST a thing does not mean the thing is true.
She should look up the ghost stories online and use them in her own argument.
Lots of people say ghosts ARE real, so she should have used their words to start.
Sara is right -- if you cannot prove a thing is false, then it must be true today.
context: Appeal to ignorance says 'no one proved it false, so it is true.' But not having proof either way means the question is OPEN -- not that the answer is yes.

question: A boy notices that the sun rises every day right AFTER the rooster crows. He says the rooster CAUSES the sunrise. What is the goof?
answer: The two events happen in order, but ORDER alone does not show one causes the other.
choices: The two events happen in order, but ORDER alone does not show one causes the other.
The rooster crows because it sees the sun coming up, not the other way around.
The boy lives near a farm, and a rooster on a farm crows often during the day.
Roosters can crow many times in a day, so the rule of the boy is the wrong rule.
context: Post hoc, ergo propter hoc -- 'after this, therefore because of this' -- is a famous mistake. The rooster crows; the sun rises. Order does not equal cause.

question: Coach says: 'do not eat junk food -- eat fruit.' A player snaps back: 'I saw YOU eating chips!' What is the move called?
answer: Tu quoque -- the 'you too' reply that swaps the topic for the speaker's habits.
choices: Tu quoque -- the 'you too' reply that swaps the topic for the speaker's habits.
Ad hominem -- the move that goes after the person making the point at hand.
Straw man -- the move that twists the point into a worse and bigger one.
Red herring -- the move that drops in a side topic to draw the talk away.
context: Tu quoque is a sub-type of ad hominem. The 'you too' reply might be true (coach DOES eat chips). But coach's eating habits have not answered the point about fruit.

question: You like LOUD music while you do homework. Your sister likes QUIET. The Golden Rule says do for others what you would want done for you. How should you use it here?
answer: Ask what SHE wants -- the rule means treating others how THEY want to be treated.
choices: Ask what SHE wants -- the rule means treating others how THEY want to be treated.
Play your loud music because that is what you would want when doing homework.
Play no music at all in the home until your sister has gone to bed for the night.
Take turns hour by hour with loud and quiet so both of you get what you want.
context: A bully sometimes says 'I would want a punch, so I punch you.' That is not the rule. The real Golden Rule asks: what would they want? Not: what would I want?

question: A boy follows EVERY rule perfectly but he is mean to his sister. A girl breaks small rules but she is always kind. Who is the BETTER person, would you say?
answer: Neither is fully good -- both rules AND kindness matter, and each kid is missing one.
choices: Neither is fully good -- both rules AND kindness matter, and each kid is missing one.
The boy, because rules make a class run smoothly for the teacher to teach kids.
The girl, because kindness is the only thing that really matters at the day's end.
The boy, because his sister will probably grow up tougher from how he treated her.
context: Aristotle's virtue ethics says GOOD CHARACTER is about both -- doing the right action AND for the right reason. Rules without heart is half. Heart without rules is half too.

question: Your friend asks for math help. You do the WHOLE worksheet for her and she turns it in. Did you really HELP her -- or did you hurt her?
answer: You hurt her -- helping is teaching her to do it, not doing it instead of her.
choices: You hurt her -- helping is teaching her to do it, not doing it instead of her.
You helped a lot because she got the right grade and was very glad to thank you.
Neither -- she has to learn on her own and your work has nothing to do with her.
You helped her in a small way because the next quiz she will do on her own again.
context: Real help builds the other person up. Doing it FOR her means she still cannot do it tomorrow -- and the grade is a lie.

question: You make a promise to YOURSELF to read every night. No one would ever know if you skip. Does breaking it still HURT something?
answer: Yes -- it hurts your trust in yourself the next time you try to make a plan.
choices: Yes -- it hurts your trust in yourself the next time you try to make a plan.
No way -- a promise to yourself is only real when there is somebody to know it.
Only on school nights -- weekend promises do not really need to be kept by kids.
Yes a little, but if you do not break it twice in a row, it will not really matter.
context: Kant said duty is duty even when no one watches. Breaking a promise to YOURSELF makes self-trust thinner -- and self-trust is how you keep bigger promises later.

question: Your friend asks you to LIE to her mom to cover up a small bad thing she did. She is your best friend. Should you do it?
answer: Maybe not -- a friend who asks you to lie is putting you in trouble for HER act.
choices: Maybe not -- a friend who asks you to lie is putting you in trouble for HER act.
Yes -- a real best friend has your back and lies for you, so you should do hers.
No -- friends should never ask each other for help with anything that is wrong.
Yes -- so long as the lie is small and she did not do anything that was harmful.
context: A true friend does not ask you to do wrong on her behalf. Lying for her makes her act YOUR act -- and now her trouble is your trouble too.

question: Two kids play a fair coin-flip game. Sam wins three times in a row. Is the game UNFAIR because Sam keeps winning each time?
answer: No -- a FAIR way to choose can still give one side many wins in a row at random.
choices: No -- a FAIR way to choose can still give one side many wins in a row at random.
Yes for sure -- if Sam wins three times in a row, the coin is not really a fair one.
No way -- a fair game is one that always has a kind of balance between the two kids.
Yes a little, since the loser is sad and the game should let her win at least once.
context: Fairness can be about the PROCESS (a real coin flip) OR the RESULT (everyone wins some). These are different ideas. A fair process can give a one-sided result.

question: Your friend says a mean thing about you. She comes back the next day and says sorry. Should you let it go right away -- or wait?
answer: It depends -- a quick sorry is a start, but trust comes back over time, not in a day.
choices: It depends -- a quick sorry is a start, but trust comes back over time, not in a day.
Right away -- friends should forgive each other the moment a sorry is said out loud.
Never -- once a friend says a mean thing, the friendship cannot really be the same.
Wait at least a week -- you should make her wait so she can see what she did to you.
context: Forgiveness is a process. Saying 'I forgive you' is the first step. But REBUILDING trust takes time. Both pieces matter -- one without the other is not whole.

question: A kid jumps off a high wall without looking to see what is on the other side. Is this COURAGE, or is it something else?
answer: Recklessness -- courage faces a known danger; jumping blind is closer to a guess.
choices: Recklessness -- courage faces a known danger; jumping blind is closer to a guess.
Yes courage -- a kid who jumps is brave even if he does not know what is over there.
No, it is fear -- the kid is scared of the wall and just wants it to be over fast.
Yes courage -- the willingness to jump from a high wall takes a lot of guts to do.
context: Aristotle put courage as a mean between two ends: COWARDICE (too little) and RECKLESSNESS (too much). Real courage knows the danger AND chooses to face it.

question: A kid cheats on a test and gets a perfect score. He hurt no one, right? Why might his teacher disagree even if his test is great?
answer: Other kids worked hard for their score; cheating makes his look like theirs.
choices: Other kids worked hard for their score; cheating makes his look like theirs.
Cheating is wrong, so the teacher will be mad even if no one was really hurt.
The teacher has to give him a zero, so he hurt himself when she finds out today.
Most teachers do not really care about cheating as long as the grades are okay.
context: Cheating is rarely 'victimless.' It makes one student's grade dishonestly equal to the grades of kids who actually learned the work.

question: A man steals bread because he is hungry. The baker loses the money his bread cost to make. Both things are TRUE. What does this show?
answer: Hard cases hold TWO real harms at once -- a moral choice may not have a clean win.
choices: Hard cases hold TWO real harms at once -- a moral choice may not have a clean win.
The man was wrong -- stealing is always wrong, no matter what the kind of need is.
The baker was wrong -- a man should never lose his bread if a hungry man is there.
Both are wrong because they should have spoken about a trade or a way to share food.
context: Real ethics has to face dilemmas where both sides have a real claim. Hunger is real. Loss is real. Pretending one side is empty makes the question too easy.

question: Brother says: 'either I get a later bedtime, or my whole life is ruined.' What is hidden inside this kind of choice?
answer: All the OTHER ways his life can be good without a later bedtime to set it.
choices: All the OTHER ways his life can be good without a later bedtime to set it.
The fact that bedtime times are made by parents to help kids grow up well.
The truth that all kids his age go to bed late, so he should not be too sad.
The detail that brothers and sisters have the same bedtime in most families.
context: False dilemma cuts out the middle. Real life has many paths -- happy without late bedtime, sad with late bedtime. The two are not actually linked.

question: Dad says: 'if I raise your allowance, you will keep asking for more, then I'll be broke!' What did dad jump over?
answer: Every middle step between 'a raise' and 'broke' -- how each one would happen.
choices: Every middle step between 'a raise' and 'broke' -- how each one would happen.
The chance that you might use your money well and not ever ask for any more.
The chance that dad has a lot of money already, so a small raise will not hurt.
The chance that other kids get allowance and dad should just match what they get.
context: Slippery slope is sometimes RIGHT (one thing does lead to another). The FALLACY happens when no one shows the steps -- they just leap to the worst end.

question: Mom: 'why is your room a mess?' You: 'but the cat keeps stealing my socks!' What is your reply doing?
answer: Drawing mom's eye to a side topic so the question about the room slides past.
choices: Drawing mom's eye to a side topic so the question about the room slides past.
Telling mom an honest reason why the room is hard to keep clean for any kid.
Asking mom for help with the cat instead of doing the work in your own room.
Reminding mom that cats are part of family life and have to be cared for too.
context: Red herring is named after a smelly fish that hunting dogs would chase if dropped on the trail. The dogs lose the real scent. So do people in talks.

question: A child's doctor says vaccines are safe. Your friend says: 'but a movie star online said they are bad.' Whose word counts more?
answer: The doctor -- her training is in this; the star is famous for OTHER kinds of work.
choices: The doctor -- her training is in this; the star is famous for OTHER kinds of work.
Both equally -- a famous person and a doctor are both adults, so both can teach.
The movie star -- a regular person with a story is more trusted than a doctor.
Neither -- you have to do your own research before you trust anyone on any topic.
context: Appeal to authority is fine when the authority KNOWS the field. A doctor on a medical topic = good evidence. A movie star on a medical topic = weak evidence.

question: Eli plays ONE chess game and loses badly. He says: 'chess is the WORST game and no one should play it.' What is wrong with his rule?
answer: A single bad game tells you about THAT game -- not about chess as a whole game.
choices: A single bad game tells you about THAT game -- not about chess as a whole game.
Eli should have asked the other player for some tips before he made up his mind.
Chess is hard for new players, so Eli should have started with a simpler version.
He should have played a different game first and saved chess for when he is older.
context: Hasty generalization takes a small sample and shouts a big claim. ONE game is not enough to know what a player thinks of a game forever.

question: A news reader says: 'this new park plan will help kids.' Another person says: 'his hair is funny so I do not trust him.' Why is that a bad reply?
answer: Hair has nothing to do with whether the park plan will actually help any kids.
choices: Hair has nothing to do with whether the park plan will actually help any kids.
He should have said that the news reader is sometimes wrong about news things.
Funny hair is okay on TV, so the man should not have said anything about it.
News readers are not in charge of parks, so the plan does not matter to the public.
context: Going after the messenger's looks, voice, or feelings -- instead of the IDEA -- is ad hominem in everyday life. Kids see it all the time on news and social media.

question: Mom says: 'do the RIGHT thing.' Brother says: 'turn RIGHT at the corner.' Could a kid mix up these two meanings of 'right'?
answer: Yes -- one means good or proper; the other means a side opposite to left.
choices: Yes -- one means good or proper; the other means a side opposite to left.
No way -- a kid knows that mom means a moral thing, not a direction on the map.
Yes always -- words with two meanings are very tricky and kids cannot use them.
No -- mom should always use one kind of meaning when she talks to her kid today.
context: Equivocation slides between two meanings of a word in one talk. Most puns are fun uses of equivocation. The FALLACY is when the slide tricks a real argument.

question: Ben says: 'I read that idea in a kids' book, so it must be too SIMPLE.' What did Ben skip past in his judgment?
answer: Whether the IDEA itself is true and useful, no matter what book it came in.
choices: Whether the IDEA itself is true and useful, no matter what book it came in.
Whether the kids' book is at his reading level or whether it is too hard for him.
Whether his teacher wants him to read kids' books or adult books for this year.
Whether the book was a gift from his mom that she had picked just for him to read.
context: The genetic fallacy judges by ORIGIN, not by quality. A great idea in a kid's book is still great. A bad idea in a thick adult book is still bad.

question: A poll says 80 percent of kids think eating dirt is fine. Does the poll prove eating dirt is HEALTHY for kids? Why or why not?
answer: No -- many people agreeing is not the same as the truth about what is healthy.
choices: No -- many people agreeing is not the same as the truth about what is healthy.
Yes -- if 80 out of 100 kids think a thing is fine, it is probably fine for all.
Maybe -- but only if the poll asked kids who had tried eating dirt themselves first.
No -- but the poll does prove that kids today are bad at giving honest answers.
context: Appeal to popularity says 'most people agree, so it must be right.' But most people used to think the sun moved around the Earth. Popular and TRUE are different.

question: Mom asks: 'why do you always FORGET your lunch?' What is hidden in the way she asks the question?
answer: She is treating 'always forget' as already true -- not as a thing to find out.
choices: She is treating 'always forget' as already true -- not as a thing to find out.
She is asking nicely because she wants to know if you forgot your lunch this week.
She wants you to remember next time and forget the time before that you forgot it.
She is letting you off the hook by asking 'why' instead of asking 'how many times.'
context: A loaded question hides a guess. 'Why do you ALWAYS X?' carries 'you always X' as given. Push back on the hidden guess before you answer.

question: Ice cream sales go UP in summer. Pool drownings ALSO go up. Does ice cream CAUSE drownings -- or is something else at work?
answer: Something else -- summer heat causes BOTH ice cream sales AND more time in pools.
choices: Something else -- summer heat causes BOTH ice cream sales AND more time in pools.
Yes -- people who eat ice cream get a stomach ache and then sink in the cool pool.
Maybe -- the ice cream is cold and makes swimmers' muscles tighten up in the water.
No way to tell -- without a study, we just cannot know what causes drownings ever.
context: A 'lurking variable' (summer) can cause two things at once. Two things rising together may share a CAUSE, not have one cause the other.

question: An ad says: 'if you do NOT buy this lock, your house will be robbed!' What is the ad using to push you to buy?
answer: Fear -- it is making you scared so you reach for your wallet without good reasons.
choices: Fear -- it is making you scared so you reach for your wallet without good reasons.
Facts -- the ad is just telling you the truth about how the world really is today.
Logic -- the ad is showing you a step-by-step argument for why you need a new lock.
Authority -- the ad is using an expert who knows about safety to back up its claims.
context: Appeal to fear sells locks, cars, vitamins. It works because fear is loud and fast. Always pause: is there real evidence? Or just a scary picture?

question: A friend says: 'you are EITHER on my team, OR you are my enemy.' What is wrong with how the friend is thinking here?
answer: Most friends are neither full team members nor full enemies; they are friends.
choices: Most friends are neither full team members nor full enemies; they are friends.
Friends should always be team members for each other in any sort of contest.
The friend is right -- in life, you have to pick a side or other people will pick.
Being a friend means you owe the friend your full loyalty on every kind of thing.
context: Black-and-white thinking forces a world full of grays into two clean boxes. Most real things have lots of middle ground.

question: Rule: 'if it rains, the ground gets wet.' The ground is wet. Did it RAIN? Why might this guess be off?
answer: Many things wet the ground -- a hose, dew, a spill -- not only the falling of rain.
choices: Many things wet the ground -- a hose, dew, a spill -- not only the falling of rain.
Yes -- if a rule says rain wets the ground, then wet ground always proves the rain.
Maybe -- but rain is the most likely way the ground is wet on any normal sort of day.
Yes for sure -- a wet ground always means it rained sometime in the past few hours.
context: 'If A then B' does NOT mean 'if B then A.' If rain wets the ground, wet ground might be rain -- OR sprinklers, OR dew. This mistake is called affirming the consequent.

question: Sam says: 'my book has no mention of Mr. Smith, so he did NOT live.' What is the broken step in Sam's reason?
answer: A book that says nothing about Mr. Smith tells us nothing about whether he lived.
choices: A book that says nothing about Mr. Smith tells us nothing about whether he lived.
He should have looked at a different book that maybe had Mr. Smith in it for sure.
He should have asked his teacher about Mr. Smith before he said anything at all.
He should have written his own book and put Mr. Smith into it as a guess for now.
context: Argument from silence says 'X is not in this source, so X did not happen.' But sources often skip things. Silence is not evidence either way.

question: Each player on the team is FAST. So the team must be GOOD, right? Why might this guess be wrong?
answer: Fast players on their own may not work well TOGETHER -- a team needs more than speed.
choices: Fast players on their own may not work well TOGETHER -- a team needs more than speed.
Right -- if every player is fast, the team will be the fastest team on the field.
Wrong -- the team also needs slow players for balance, or the speed will be wasted.
Right -- every fast player adds up to a faster team than any team with slow players.
context: Composition fallacy says 'each part has property X, so the whole has X.' Each brick is light; a wall of them is heavy. The shift from parts to whole is not safe.

question: Socrates said: 'a life with no looking back is not worth living.' What did he mean by 'looking back'?
answer: Asking yourself why you do what you do, and whether your reasons hold up.
choices: Asking yourself why you do what you do, and whether your reasons hold up.
Studying for a test every night and then looking over your answers in school the next day.
Checking with your parents if your choices are okay with them before you make them.
Reading the works of great old thinkers so you can copy what they did in your own life.
context: An examined life turns thought BACK on yourself. What do I believe? Why? Would I act the same way if I really looked at the reason? That is the work Socrates did.

question: Plato told a story about people chained in a cave watching shadows on a wall. What did the shadows stand for in his story?
answer: Things we see and feel that we MISTAKE for the real, deeper world behind them.
choices: Things we see and feel that we MISTAKE for the real, deeper world behind them.
Pictures of what real life is like that the cave people had never gotten to see yet.
Animals on the wall that the cave people wanted to study before any of them got out.
Things the cave people drew themselves to amuse one another in the cave each night.
context: Plato's cave: the chained people think the shadows ARE the world. Until one is freed and steps out, he won't know that the real world is so much more.

question: Plato said the BEST rulers would be wise people who did NOT WANT to rule. Why did he link wisdom and not-wanting?
answer: Wanting power means you may USE it for yourself -- a wise person sees that danger.
choices: Wanting power means you may USE it for yourself -- a wise person sees that danger.
He thought people who want power are bad and will use it to harm those they rule.
He thought people who do not want it will not last long enough to actually rule.
He thought ruling is too boring for smart people to want and so they avoid it now.
context: Plato's worry: those most eager to rule are often the ones LEAST safe to trust with rule. The wisest sees the burden first; the ambitious sees only the prize.

question: Aristotle said HAPPY is not a feeling like 'fun.' It is much bigger than that. What was his deeper idea about happy?
answer: Living a full life of doing what is right and using your gifts well over many years.
choices: Living a full life of doing what is right and using your gifts well over many years.
Having a lot of money saved up so you can buy what you want to make yourself happy.
Feeling great every day from the moment you wake up to the moment you go to bed.
Doing one big great thing so you can look back on it and feel proud for many years.
context: Aristotle's 'eudaimonia' is closer to 'flourishing' than to 'pleasure.' It is what you would say of a WHOLE LIFE -- not of a single afternoon.

question: Aristotle taught that being GOOD is often in the middle -- not too much, not too little. What is the middle for being BRAVE?
answer: Between being a coward who runs from every danger and being reckless without care.
choices: Between being a coward who runs from every danger and being reckless without care.
Between being a quiet kid who never speaks up and being a loud kid who shouts a lot.
Between being a kid who plays sports too much and being one who never plays at all.
Between a kid who is too kind to other kids and one who is mean to many of them.
context: The Golden Mean: virtues are not the highest possible setting. Courage is between cowardice and rashness. Kindness is between coldness and being a pushover.

question: Epictetus said: 'some things are up to us, others are not.' Which of these is something a KID can control?
answer: How you act when you fail a test -- whether you try again or you give up.
choices: How you act when you fail a test -- whether you try again or you give up.
Whether the teacher gives you an easy test or a really hard test on that day at school.
Whether your parents have time to help you study for the test that you have on Monday.
Whether the kid next to you finishes the test fast or slow during class on a normal day.
context: Epictetus split life into two: what you control (your thoughts, choices, effort) and what you don't (other people, weather, what happens TO you). Peace comes from knowing the line.

question: Cicero, a Roman thinker, said the strong should help the weak --  not out of pity but out of DUTY. What did he mean by duty?
answer: What a person OWES because of who they are -- not just what they FEEL like doing.
choices: What a person OWES because of who they are -- not just what they FEEL like doing.
A long list of tasks that a person should do every morning and night each day.
A loud feeling of needing to help that takes hold of you when you see a person in need.
A way of helping that is the same for all people no matter where they live in the world.
context: Cicero's idea of duty (officium) was tied to your ROLE -- father, citizen, friend. Each role brings duties. Feelings come and go; duty stays.

question: Epicurus is called a 'pleasure' thinker. But he said the GREATEST pleasure of all was a simple thing. What did he prize the most?
answer: Good friends -- a small life with steady friends was the happiest life of all.
choices: Good friends -- a small life with steady friends was the happiest life of all.
The wildest parties he could go to with friends and lots of food and drink on the side.
A long life with a lot of money saved so he could have fancy meals to himself.
A house of his own with a quiet study and shelves full of books he loved to read.
context: Epicurus's 'Garden' was a small group of friends sharing simple food. The pleasure he prized most was the kind that lasts -- friendship, not feasts.

question: Augustine said 'love, and do what you want.' This sounds easy -- but it has a catch. What is the catch?
answer: Real LOVE will not let you do harm -- so 'what you want' is what love asks of you.
choices: Real LOVE will not let you do harm -- so 'what you want' is what love asks of you.
Love means feelings, so you can do whatever feels right at the time without too much thought.
Love is hard, so most of the time you cannot do what you want because love comes first.
Love changes a lot, so you have to ask each day what kind of love you really feel inside.
context: Augustine's idea: if your heart is RIGHTLY ordered (you love what is good), then doing 'what you want' will line up with right action. The work is in the loving.

question: Augustine asked: what IS time? He said: when no one asks, I know. When asked, I do NOT know. What was strange about this?
answer: We USE time every day -- but we cannot say clearly what it IS when pressed.
choices: We USE time every day -- but we cannot say clearly what it IS when pressed.
He thought time was made up by people and was not really a thing in the real world.
He had no good clocks back then, so it was hard for him to know any kind of time.
He thought time was a kind of motion or change that goes in only one direction.
context: Many deep things are like this: we use them all day but cannot define them when asked. Time, friendship, mind -- familiar in use, mysterious in thought.

question: Anselm gave a tricky argument: GOD is the GREATEST thing you can think of. Greater things must EXIST. So God must exist. Why did many people find this odd?
answer: He used a definition alone to prove existence -- many felt that was not quite fair.
choices: He used a definition alone to prove existence -- many felt that was not quite fair.
He used a really long proof and most people did not have the time to read it all.
He did not believe in God himself and so the proof he gave was not really his own.
He used the idea of a perfect island to prove islands exist, which is silly to say.
context: Anselm's ontological argument is one of the most debated proofs ever. Some say it WORKS, some say it sneaks the answer in. Either way it forced thinkers to dig hard.

question: Aquinas gave FIVE paths to think about God -- one from motion, one from cause, and more. Why did he give five rather than one?
answer: Different minds need different paths -- one proof may move you that another does not.
choices: Different minds need different paths -- one proof may move you that another does not.
He thought one path was not enough, so he had to give exactly five for the best.
He wanted to be fair to all kinds of people and so he made each one a special path.
He had five teachers, each one taught him a different path, and he used them all.
context: Aquinas's 'five ways' start from things we see (motion, cause, value) and reason up. He thought reasoning ABOUT God starts in this world, not in pure thought alone.

question: Aquinas said that even WITHOUT being told, all people can know some basic right and wrong. He called this 'natural law.' Why natural?
answer: It comes from being HUMAN -- not from any one book, country, or church teaching us.
choices: It comes from being HUMAN -- not from any one book, country, or church teaching us.
It is found in nature -- in the way trees grow and how birds choose where to build a nest.
Most people learn it by themselves at a young age, so it is not really taught at all.
It is the basic law that all old societies had and so we should keep it for the future.
context: Natural law: humans CAN see -- by thinking -- that murder is wrong, that gratitude is right, that promises matter. No revelation needed for these basics.

question: Abelard wrote 'Yes and No' -- a book that gave church arguments on BOTH sides of every big question. Some called him risky. Why?
answer: He showed students that great teachers had DISAGREED -- they had to think for themselves.
choices: He showed students that great teachers had DISAGREED -- they had to think for themselves.
He was too young to write a book about church teachings and so people did not trust him.
He had been kicked out of his school for being a rude student, so people did not read him.
He used a hard language that most readers of his day could not read on their own.
context: Abelard's 'Sic et Non' was a method of THINKING: line up the disagreement, then work out a careful answer. It made thinkers active, not just listeners.

question: William of Ockham said: when two ideas explain the same thing, pick the SIMPLER one. We still use this. What is it called now?
answer: Ockham's razor -- a rule of thumb to shave off ideas that are not needed.
choices: Ockham's razor -- a rule of thumb to shave off ideas that are not needed.
Ockham's spear -- a tool for picking apart any bad idea before it can spread to others.
Ockham's lamp -- a guide that shows what to do when you are not sure what to think yet.
Ockham's path -- a way of walking through a tough question step by step at your own pace.
context: Ockham's razor isn't a hard rule -- sometimes the more complex idea is right. But all else being equal, FEWER guesses beats MORE guesses.

question: Maimonides taught that we know more about what God is NOT than what God IS. Why this strange view?
answer: Our words come from things we know -- but God is not LIKE other things we know.
choices: Our words come from things we know -- but God is not LIKE other things we know.
He was Jewish and so he had different ideas about God than Christian writers had.
He was a doctor as well as a thinker, so he knew that we know nothing for sure.
He thought God was so far away that talking about God was always going to be hard.
context: Negative theology says: human words like 'good,' 'wise,' 'just' work between humans. Stretching them to God may say less than we think -- it is safer to say 'not X' than 'X.'

question: Boethius wrote his famous book in prison while waiting to die. He pictured a 'wheel of fortune' that lifts you high and crushes you. What did he learn from it?
answer: Real happiness cannot rest on what FORTUNE gives -- the wheel always turns again.
choices: Real happiness cannot rest on what FORTUNE gives -- the wheel always turns again.
He learned that life can be very bad and so it is better not to hope for much at all.
He learned that prisons are bad and we should not put people in them for any reason.
He learned that rich people are happier and so we should all try to get rich one day.
context: Boethius lost everything -- power, freedom, soon his life. His book asks: what is worth having that fortune CANNOT take? That is where real peace lives.

question: Avicenna asked us to picture a man FLOATING in the air, blindfolded, with no feeling at all. What would the man STILL know?
answer: That HE is -- the floating man would still know he exists, even with no other facts.
choices: That HE is -- the floating man would still know he exists, even with no other facts.
Where he is in the sky -- a man can guess his height from how cold the air around him is.
What time of day it is -- a person can tell day from night by changes in light over time.
Why he is floating -- a man can think his way to a guess about why he is in the air.
context: Avicenna's floating man is meant to show: the SELF is known to itself before any thing else. It anticipates Descartes' 'I think, so I am' by hundreds of years.

question: Descartes said: doubt EVERYTHING you can doubt, and see what is left. What was his goal in this strange exercise?
answer: To find ONE thing he could be SURE of, and then to build new knowledge from there.
choices: To find ONE thing he could be SURE of, and then to build new knowledge from there.
To prove that doubt is bad and that all old teachings should be kept for safety.
To show that smart people doubt everything and so we should all be more like them.
To find out who had taught him things that were wrong so he could correct them all.
context: Descartes wanted a SOLID floor. If I doubt everything that can be doubted, what is left? Answer: the doubter HAS to exist to do the doubting -- 'I think, so I am.'

question: Spinoza thought that God and NATURE were one and the same. Why did some readers find this exciting -- and others found it scary?
answer: It made the world divine -- but it also made God less like a person and more like all-that-is.
choices: It made the world divine -- but it also made God less like a person and more like all-that-is.
It said God was big and far away, so people could not really pray to him each day.
It said nature was bad and so we should not look at the world for any kind of beauty.
It said one substance is all there is, but it did not say what the one substance was.
context: Spinoza wrote: 'God or nature' (deus sive natura). For some, this dignified the world. For others, it dissolved a personal God into a chilly, all-pervading whole.

question: Locke said the mind of a newborn is like a BLANK SLATE -- no ideas yet written on it. What follows from this view?
answer: We learn EVERYTHING through experience -- ideas are not built into us at our birth.
choices: We learn EVERYTHING through experience -- ideas are not built into us at our birth.
Babies are very smart from the moment of their birth but they cannot speak about it.
We should write on our minds every day so that the slate stays clean and easy to read.
Babies have all the ideas they need, but they have to wait to learn how to use them.
context: Locke's empiricism says experience writes our minds. Education matters HUGELY because all we know -- math, music, manners -- gets written through living.

question: Hume noticed people would describe a fact ('this IS the way it is') and then suddenly say what we OUGHT to do. What is the leap?
answer: Saying what IS true does not tell you what SHOULD be done about it -- those are different.
choices: Saying what IS true does not tell you what SHOULD be done about it -- those are different.
Saying what IS today does not tell you what tomorrow will be like for the most part.
Saying what IS in one country tells you nothing about another country and its laws.
Saying what IS does not actually tell you whether it is good or bad, hot or cold.
context: Hume's 'is-ought gap' is one of the deepest moves in ethics. From 'people eat meat' to 'people SHOULD eat meat' is a leap. You need a SECOND premise about value.

question: The sun has come up every day for all of history. Hume asked: are you really SURE it will come up tomorrow? Why such an odd question?
answer: Past patterns do not PROVE the future -- they only say what has happened before.
choices: Past patterns do not PROVE the future -- they only say what has happened before.
Hume was a bad sleeper and he did not know what time the sun would rise tomorrow.
Hume thought the sun was small and was very close to the earth and could go away.
Hume thought science had not yet figured out the sun and what made it appear and go.
context: Hume's 'problem of induction' shows that all of our predictions REST on a guess: the future will be like the past. We CAN'T prove that guess. We just live by it.

question: Kant said: only do what you could wish EVERYONE in the world would do. How does this rule work on lying?
answer: If everyone lied always, no one would trust talk -- lying could not even WORK as a tool.
choices: If everyone lied always, no one would trust talk -- lying could not even WORK as a tool.
Lying is sometimes okay if it helps another person so you do not have to feel bad.
Lying is bad for kids but is sometimes fine for grown-ups, like at work or in court.
Lying is fine if no one finds out, so the rule does not really apply to most people.
context: Kant's test: can your rule UNIVERSALIZE? A lying-rule cancels itself -- it depends on people trusting talk, which lying destroys. So lying fails the test.

question: Kant said NEVER use a person ONLY as a means to your own goal. What does this rule out in everyday life?
answer: Using people only for what they can do for you -- as tools, not as full persons too.
choices: Using people only for what they can do for you -- as tools, not as full persons too.
Using money to buy things from people, because money makes them serve your needs.
Asking a friend for help with homework, because that uses her time to help you out.
Hiring a worker to fix your car, because workers are paid to serve the customers.
context: Kant says other people are 'ends in themselves' -- they have worth on their own. Hiring a worker is fine; treating her as just-a-tool with no respect is not.

question: Hobbes pictured life without any law or any rules as 'nasty, rough, and short.' Why was he so dark about life like that?
answer: Without rules, the strong take from the weak -- everyone fears everyone all the time.
