choices: Without rules, the strong take from the weak -- everyone fears everyone all the time.
Hobbes lived in a small town that did not have many laws, and life there was rough.
Hobbes did not really like other people and so he wrote down the worst of them.
Hobbes was sick when he wrote the book and so all his ideas came out a bit dark.
context: Hobbes lived through England's civil war -- he saw what life is like when order breaks. His dark picture argues FOR a strong government to keep peace and trade going.

question: Mill's 'harm principle' says government can stop people from HARMING others -- but not from harming THEMSELVES. Why this line?
answer: Each adult should run his own life as he sees fit, as long as he hurts no other person.
choices: Each adult should run his own life as he sees fit, as long as he hurts no other person.
Self-harm is small but harm to others is big, so only big things should be against the law.
Most self-harm is not really harm and so people should be free to do those things at home.
It is hard to stop self-harm and easy to stop harm to others, so we do the easier one.
context: Mill's principle is one cornerstone of liberty. Drinking? Up to you. Punching the neighbor? No -- you cross into HIS sphere. Freedom ends where harm begins.

question: Hegel said that ideas develop in steps: a CLAIM, then a COUNTER, then a deeper view that holds both. How does this work in talk?
answer: A first idea meets push-back; the best answer keeps what is right in BOTH and grows from there.
choices: A first idea meets push-back; the best answer keeps what is right in BOTH and grows from there.
A first idea wins out and the second idea simply goes away after being heard a few times.
Two ideas fight forever until one is the winner and is the right one for all of history.
All ideas are equal and so the new idea is just a different way of saying the old one.
context: Hegel's dialectic is one famous way of seeing INTELLECTUAL HISTORY: tensions get RESOLVED at a higher level. Real talks often work this way: two sides, then a deeper third view.

question: Nietzsche said some moral words ('weak,' 'humble,' 'meek') praise what was once SCORNED. Why did he find this strange?
answer: He thought those words flipped older values -- making the WEAK look like the GOOD.
choices: He thought those words flipped older values -- making the WEAK look like the GOOD.
He thought all moral words were strange and that we should not use any of them now.
He thought the words came from a foreign land and so they did not belong in his land.
He thought the words had no real meaning and so it was strange that people used them.
context: Nietzsche claimed Christianity flipped pagan values: instead of strength and pride, it praised meekness. He called this the 'revaluation of all values' -- and pushed back hard.

question: Schopenhauer thought all of us are pushed by a blind WILL inside us -- pushing us to want more and more. What did he see as the way out?
answer: Art, music, kindness -- moments when we step OUT of wanting and just look at the world.
choices: Art, music, kindness -- moments when we step OUT of wanting and just look at the world.
Hard work, school, and friends -- the normal ways most people get away from sad days.
Lots of money, a big house, and travel -- the ways grown-ups try to get away from it.
Religion -- mostly the kind where you give up everything and live alone in a quiet place.
context: Schopenhauer said wanting always returns -- get what you want, and you want the NEXT thing. The only rest comes when you stop wanting -- in music, in art, in pure compassion.

question: Marx said factory workers can feel that their work is NOT THEIRS -- they make a thing and it goes away with no link to them. What did he call this?
answer: Alienation -- the worker is cut OFF from his work, his fellow workers, even himself.
choices: Alienation -- the worker is cut OFF from his work, his fellow workers, even himself.
Wage slavery -- the worker has no choice but to work for the boss to feed his family.
Class war -- the workers and the bosses are always in a fight for who runs the factory.
Selfishness -- workers want more than they really need and so they keep being unhappy.
context: Marx's idea of alienation is one of his deepest moves. A craftsman who makes a chair and uses it is whole. A worker who makes one piece of a chair, then never sees it, is split.

question: Kierkegaard said real FAITH is taking a leap when proof is missing. Why is this scary -- and why might it also be brave?
answer: You commit your life to something you cannot fully prove -- that takes courage.
choices: You commit your life to something you cannot fully prove -- that takes courage.
It is scary because no proof means you could be wrong, and brave because you tried.
It is scary because faith is hard, but brave because faith means giving up free time.
It is scary because no one will help you, but brave because you face it on your own.
context: Kierkegaard against safe, easy faith. Real commitment, he said, is staked WITHOUT a safety net. If you can prove it, it isn't faith -- it's just a calculation.

question: Jefferson said some truths are 'self-evident.' One was: 'all men are created equal.' What does 'self-evident' mean here?
answer: A truth you do not need to PROVE -- it is clear once you really see what it means.
choices: A truth you do not need to PROVE -- it is clear once you really see what it means.
A truth that a few smart people know but most other people in a country do not.
A truth that comes only from the Bible or another book that some people read for it.
A truth that came to Jefferson in a dream and he wrote down on his paper that day.
context: Self-evident: not 'obvious to everyone' but 'so clear that you cannot deny it once you understand it.' Jefferson's claim grounded the new republic in MORAL TRUTHS, not power.

question: Emerson wrote 'self-reliance' -- TRUST yourself, even when the crowd disagrees. When does this become a real test for a kid?
answer: When all your friends say one thing and you really think they are wrong about it.
choices: When all your friends say one thing and you really think they are wrong about it.
When your parents ask you to do something hard and you have to do it on your own.
When you have to choose between two friends and one of them gets mad at you.
When the teacher gives a test and you have studied for many hours the night before.
context: Emerson is not saying 'do whatever YOU want.' He is saying: the loud agreement of a crowd is not the same as the TRUTH. Stand your ground when you have a reason.

question: Thoreau refused to pay a tax that paid for slavery. He went to JAIL for one night. Why did he think this was a moral act?
answer: He thought a bad law should be RESISTED in public -- with your body, not just your words.
choices: He thought a bad law should be RESISTED in public -- with your body, not just your words.
He was poor and could not pay the tax, so he had to go to jail for that day.
He had a fight with the man who collected taxes and they made him go to jail.
He went to jail to write about it later for a book, and so it was just for fun.
context: Thoreau's 'Civil Disobedience' shaped later leaders like Gandhi and MLK. The point: if a law commands you to do wrong, refuse -- and accept the cost openly.

question: William James said an idea's TRUTH lies in what it does -- the DIFFERENCE it makes if you act on it. Why call this 'pragmatic'?
answer: Pragmatic means tied to action -- an idea has worth by how it shapes what you DO.
choices: Pragmatic means tied to action -- an idea has worth by how it shapes what you DO.
Pragmatic means simple -- so the idea is only worth what a kid can use in a small way.
Pragmatic means money -- so the idea has to make a person richer to be worth a lot.
Pragmatic means fast -- so the idea has to be useful right away or it is not real.
context: James asked of every belief: what cash-value does it have? What changes in your life if you ACT on it? Beliefs that make no difference were, for James, empty.

question: Dewey said kids should learn by DOING -- not by sitting and listening. How does this work in a real classroom?
answer: Kids try a problem, fail, fix, try again -- they learn by living the work, not just hearing it.
choices: Kids try a problem, fail, fix, try again -- they learn by living the work, not just hearing it.
Kids should not have any teachers -- they should learn from doing things in groups alone.
Kids should be quiet for half the class and then they should get up and move for the rest.
Kids should write down what the teacher says and then act it out in plays later that week.
context: Dewey's progressive education isn't 'no rules.' It is HANDS-ON learning, with the teacher as a guide. You learn fractions by cooking. You learn ethics by living with classmates.

question: Douglass, a man born into slavery, said his SLAVE MASTER tried to keep him from learning to read. Why did the master fear this so?
answer: A slave who reads can think, plan, and SEE that slavery is wrong -- and then resist.
choices: A slave who reads can think, plan, and SEE that slavery is wrong -- and then resist.
A slave who reads might learn how to write letters to leave the farm without a pass.
A slave who reads would no longer want to work and the master would lose his money.
A slave who reads could send his master a long letter to ask for some kind of mercy.
context: Douglass's autobiography turned on this moment. The master let it slip that knowledge would 'spoil' a slave. Douglass realized: knowledge was the PATH out of slavery.

question: Confucius gave a Golden Rule too: 'do NOT do to others what you would not want done to YOU.' How is this different from the kind Jesus would later give?
answer: It is the same idea but in NEGATIVE form -- 'do not' instead of 'do for others.'
choices: It is the same idea but in NEGATIVE form -- 'do not' instead of 'do for others.'
It is more strict because it says 'do not' instead of saying the kinder way to do good.
It is more old because Confucius came first and so it must be the very best rule of all.
It is more soft because it is easier to NOT do something than to do something for kids.
context: Confucius's rule appears in the Analects centuries before the Sermon on the Mount. The negative form sets a floor (do no harm). The positive form sets a higher bar (do good).

question: Confucius taught that respect for PARENTS was the root of all other goodness. Why might he start with the home?
answer: If you cannot be good to those nearest you, you cannot be good to strangers far off.
choices: If you cannot be good to those nearest you, you cannot be good to strangers far off.
Parents had a lot of power back then, so respect for them was needed for safety.
Parents were strict, so Confucius wanted to make sure kids never spoke against them.
Parents were the only adults a kid knew, so they had to be respected for that reason.
context: Confucius's 'filial piety' (xiao) is not just rule-following. It is the early TRAINING ground for all wider virtues -- you learn to honor before you learn to lead.

question: Lao Tzu praised WATER -- it is soft, it flows around things, yet over time it shapes mountains. What lesson did he draw from water?
answer: Real strength is not in being hard or pushy -- the soft thing can outlast the hard one.
choices: Real strength is not in being hard or pushy -- the soft thing can outlast the hard one.
Water is everywhere, so we should be everywhere too if we want to be like water at all.
Water is clear so we can see through it -- we should be clear in everything we say too.
Water is the source of life on the earth, so we should drink as much of it as we can.
context: The Daodejing's 'water' chapters teach by image. Soft beats hard, low places gather more, yielding endures. The wise person is more like a river than a wall.

question: The Daodejing teaches 'wu wei' -- often called 'non-action.' But the wise person is still BUSY. What is the trick of wu wei?
answer: Acting in step with the moment -- no forcing, no straining, like flowing water.
choices: Acting in step with the moment -- no forcing, no straining, like flowing water.
Doing nothing all day -- the wise person sits quietly and lets others do the work.
Doing the easy parts first, and then taking long breaks before the next round of work.
Doing only what your boss tells you and not asking why -- just letting it go to him.
context: Wu wei is not laziness. It is action WITHOUT force -- like a skilled cook who slips a knife between joints rather than hacking. Effortless because in tune.

question: Mencius said: see a child about to fall into a well. Any person feels a JOLT of alarm. What did this prove about people?
answer: We have GOOD instincts built in -- pity for others rises before we even think about it.
choices: We have GOOD instincts built in -- pity for others rises before we even think about it.
Most people would save the child but a few would walk away and not help at all that day.
Children should not be left alone near wells because they cannot stay away from them.
Most people are bad and so the jolt of alarm is not really a good feeling at all.
context: Mencius argued human nature is FUNDAMENTALLY good. The jolt is not learned -- it is a seed all of us have. Bad people are those whose seeds were starved.

question: Every choice you make is made by a BRAIN that follows physical laws. So is your choice REALLY free, or is it locked in?
answer: Maybe both -- many thinkers say a choice can be free AND have physical causes at once.
choices: Maybe both -- many thinkers say a choice can be free AND have physical causes at once.
Locked in -- if the brain is made of cells and laws, the choice is just what cells do.
Totally free -- the brain is just a tool and the real you is something else entirely.
Cannot be answered -- science has not yet found a way to test what really happens here.
context: Compatibilism: a choice is FREE if it springs from YOU -- your wants, your reasons -- even if YOU have causes. Free will and physical causation may not be enemies.

question: You at age 6 liked one thing. You at age 12 like a very different thing. Are you still the SAME person, deep down?
answer: Yes -- memory, body, and ongoing story link the two yous, even with big changes inside.
choices: Yes -- memory, body, and ongoing story link the two yous, even with big changes inside.
No -- if your likes change, then YOU change, and there are many of you in your life.
Yes -- your body is the same, and that is the only thing that decides who is who.
No -- the kid at six is now gone forever and a new person sits in his place today.
context: Personal identity is debated. Many say: memory + body + a continuous story keeps you the SAME you, even when your tastes shift. Some philosophers disagree.

question: How do you KNOW your best friend feels happy when she smiles? You cannot get inside her head. What is the puzzle called?
answer: The 'other minds' problem -- you only know your own feelings, never another person's directly.
choices: The 'other minds' problem -- you only know your own feelings, never another person's directly.
The 'happy mind' question -- it asks if people are happy more often than they look like.
The 'mirror puzzle' -- it asks if your smile in the mirror really shows your own feelings.
The 'friendship test' -- it asks if you really know your friends are friends or not.
context: You see her face. You hear her words. You assume the inner feeling MATCHES. But you cannot ever directly check. We all live with this gap -- and most days it works fine.

question: Your hand HURTS when it touches a hot stove. The pain is FELT -- but is the pain the same thing as some nerve in your hand firing?
answer: Maybe not -- the FEELING of pain seems different from the cells doing what cells do.
choices: Maybe not -- the FEELING of pain seems different from the cells doing what cells do.
Yes for sure -- the cells firing is what pain IS, and there is nothing more to say.
No for sure -- the pain is in your soul, a thing your body cannot ever really touch.
Yes maybe -- but only if the cells fire at the right speed, or pain will not happen.
context: This is the 'hard problem' of mind. Brain stuff is OUT THERE for science to study. Feelings are INSIDE -- known from the first person. How they connect is still debated.

question: What if you LOST all your memories tomorrow? Would you still be YOU -- or would you become a new person without your past?
answer: Many would say still you, but a CHANGED you -- the body and habits link backward.
choices: Many would say still you, but a CHANGED you -- the body and habits link backward.
Totally a new person -- without memories, the old you is dead and a new one takes over.
Still you, no change -- memories do not matter at all to who you are at the deep core.
Half and half -- you would be the same in the morning but a new person by the night.
context: Locke linked identity to MEMORY. Lose memories and you lose part of yourself. But the body keeps going. Most thinkers today say: memory is a piece, not the whole.

question: Does your DOG have a mind like yours? She looks happy when you come home. She seems sad when you leave. What is the puzzle here?
answer: Her body shows feelings -- but we cannot directly check if she FEELS them inside like we do.
choices: Her body shows feelings -- but we cannot directly check if she FEELS them inside like we do.
She is a dog and dogs do not have any real feelings, just trained habits and rewards.
She has feelings just like a human does because she lives in the house and is family.
She might have a mind, but a small one, and she cannot use it for anything but eating.
context: Most people grant dogs SOME inner life -- pain, joy, fear seem real. But how RICH is their inner world? That is one of the open puzzles in philosophy of mind.

question: When you DREAM, things feel real. Then you wake up. How can you tell that THIS moment is not also a long dream?
answer: Hard to say -- the test we want would have to come from OUTSIDE both dream and waking.
choices: Hard to say -- the test we want would have to come from OUTSIDE both dream and waking.
Easy -- pinch yourself and if it hurts, you are awake; if not, you are in a dream still.
Hard -- so most of the time it does not matter, we just live and ask later in the day.
Easy -- in dreams, things are weird, and in real life, things are mostly normal for you.
context: Descartes pressed this. The 'feels real' test fails -- dreams also FEEL real. The famous answer 'I think, so I am' tries to find ONE thing the dreamer cannot doubt.

question: For thinkers long ago, KNOWING something meant three things: you BELIEVE it, it is TRUE, and you have a good REASON. Why three?
answer: A guess might be true by luck; a reason makes it more than just a lucky right guess.
choices: A guess might be true by luck; a reason makes it more than just a lucky right guess.
Three is a lucky number, so the old thinkers picked it for that one reason alone.
Three is the most pieces a kid can hold in mind, so it was easier to teach this way.
Three is what the church taught at the time and so all thinkers were forced to use it.
context: The classic 'justified true belief' (JTB) view of knowledge: belief + truth + reasons. A lucky guess hits truth but lacks the reason, so it isn't knowledge -- just luck.

question: Most of what you know comes from OTHER people -- not your own eyes. Why is trust in others important for any kind of learning?
answer: If you had to test every fact yourself, you would barely learn anything in a lifetime.
choices: If you had to test every fact yourself, you would barely learn anything in a lifetime.
Other people are smarter than you, so it is best to just trust them on all of the facts.
Other people have more time to test things, so they always do a better job than you do.
Other people get paid to know facts and so they have to give the right answer to you.
context: Almost ALL knowledge -- science, history, the news -- comes through chains of trust. The skill is not 'trust nothing' but knowing WHO to trust and how to spot a break in the chain.

question: Some things you are SURE of (your name). Some you are not (will it rain tomorrow). Why is it useful to know which is which?
answer: You act DIFFERENTLY when you are sure than when you guess -- you should know the gap.
choices: You act DIFFERENTLY when you are sure than when you guess -- you should know the gap.
Most kids do not know any of these things very well, so they have to ask others a lot.
If you are sure, then nobody can change your mind on the topic for any kind of reason.
Most things you know are sure, so the gap does not matter to you in your daily life.
context: Calibration -- knowing how SURE you are -- is one of the most useful skills. Acting too sure of a guess gets you in trouble. Acting unsure of a known fact wastes your time.

question: EVIDENCE supports an idea. PROOF nails it down for sure. What is one difference between the two in everyday life?
answer: You can have lots of evidence and still be wrong; PROOF, in theory, rules out all doubt.
choices: You can have lots of evidence and still be wrong; PROOF, in theory, rules out all doubt.
Evidence is for kids and proof is for grown-ups, so school does not really teach proof.
Evidence is found in books while proof is found in real life and so they are different.
Evidence is what a teacher gives you while proof is what a court gives in a real trial.
context: Outside math, real-world PROOF is rare. We mostly work with strong EVIDENCE -- many facts pointing one way. That is why honest thinkers stay open to being wrong.

question: Skepticism is doubting some claims. Why might a LITTLE skepticism be good -- but a LOT be bad?
answer: A little keeps you from being fooled; a lot stops you from acting on anything at all.
choices: A little keeps you from being fooled; a lot stops you from acting on anything at all.
A little is okay for kids and a lot is okay for grown-ups, with no in-between for anyone.
Lots of skepticism is great because it means you doubt things that are not really sure.
A little skepticism is just being lazy, so doubting nothing is the best path for most.
context: Healthy skepticism asks for evidence. Total skepticism freezes you -- you cannot act if you doubt EVERY claim. The skill is in knowing when to push and when to trust.

question: It is HARD to spot the wrong parts of your OWN side's arguments. Why might this be a danger for everyone -- and what can help?
answer: We love our own side, so we miss its flaws -- a friend who pushes back can save you.
choices: We love our own side, so we miss its flaws -- a friend who pushes back can save you.
Most people on your side do not really know much, so it is good to find new sides.
Our side is always right, so the danger is not real but it does feel real sometimes.
Our side does have some flaws, but they are small and not really that big a deal.
context: Confirmation bias makes us see our own side's weak points last. The check is HONEST feedback from someone NOT on your side -- not to convert you, just to keep you honest.

question: A senator argues against a tax cut by saying its supporters 'are in the pocket of big oil.' Even if true, what move has she made?
answer: A poisoning-the-well variant of ad hominem -- attacks motive without engaging the proposal.
choices: A poisoning-the-well variant of ad hominem -- attacks motive without engaging the proposal.
A valid call for transparency -- voters should know who funds which side, then judge.
A standard appeal to expertise -- senators are entitled to call out conflicts of interest.
A red herring shifting the debate; she should have made the connection explicit first.
context: Even with true motives, a proposal's merits are not settled by who supports it. Disclosure is legitimate; substituting disclosure FOR argument is the fallacy.

question: A debater claims his opponent's view 'leads logically to nihilism.' He never shows the steps. What pattern has he reproduced?
answer: Reductio by association -- attaching a feared label without supplying the deduction.
choices: Reductio by association -- attaching a feared label without supplying the deduction.
A genuine reductio ad absurdum -- valid if the conclusion really does follow.
A no true Scotsman move that redefines categories to exclude the opponent's view.
A pure appeal to consequences -- valid criticism if the consequence really is bad.
context: A real reductio walks through premises to an absurd conclusion. Skipping the walk and stamping the conclusion-label on the opponent is rhetoric, not reasoning.

question: A study finds gun control laws correlate with lower homicide rates across some states. A commentator concludes laws caused the drop. What confounders could undermine the inference?
answer: Demographics, urbanization, poverty rates -- any unmeasured factor common to both.
choices: Demographics, urbanization, poverty rates -- any unmeasured factor common to both.
Nothing -- correlation across states is direct evidence of causation between them.
Bias in the data collection -- studies of laws are always politically motivated.
Sample size alone -- if you add more states the correlation might disappear quickly.
context: Cross-sectional correlation is famously weak evidence for causation. Without controlling for confounders -- or better, longitudinal or quasi-experimental design -- the inference is fragile.

question: Bulverism (named by C.S. Lewis) presupposes an opponent is wrong, then explains WHY he is wrong by his psychology. What is the error?
answer: It substitutes a causal story about the opponent's belief for a refutation of the belief.
choices: It substitutes a causal story about the opponent's belief for a refutation of the belief.
It is a sound move when the psychology really does explain the opponent's view.
It is a form of straw man because it attacks a position the opponent never held.
It is appeal to authority when the explainer is a trained psychologist by profession.
context: Lewis: 'You must first show that a man is wrong before you start explaining why he is wrong.' Bulverism reverses the order -- the explanation poses as the refutation.

question: Galileo's foes were wrong about heliocentrism. So today's persecuted contrarians must be right too. Where does this argument break down?
answer: Being persecuted does not track being right; the reference class is mostly cranks, not Galileos.
choices: Being persecuted does not track being right; the reference class is mostly cranks, not Galileos.
Persecution is real evidence -- the establishment defends orthodoxy and silences truth-tellers.
The argument is fine for contrarian SCIENTISTS but not for contrarian non-experts on the same topics.
The argument confuses Galileo's geometry with later astronomy, which had different methods.
context: The Galileo gambit is appeal to a tiny tail of cases. For every Galileo, thousands of persecuted contrarians turned out to be wrong. Persecution is not evidence of correctness.

question: Equivocation in legal reasoning: a court rules 'the people' have a right; later, an opinion treats 'the people' as a collective. What is the danger?
answer: Different senses of one term in successive arguments can produce a chain that no single sense supports.
choices: Different senses of one term in successive arguments can produce a chain that no single sense supports.
Courts must always use the same term consistently, so equivocation is impossible in law.
Equivocation in law is fine when authorized by precedent; otherwise it becomes a fallacy.
The danger is purely stylistic -- the substance is preserved across the sense changes too.
context: Heller and later Second Amendment opinions debated whether 'the people' is collective or individual. A subtle equivocation across cases can build a doctrine that no single reading supports.

question: Survivorship bias: 'successful CEOs all wake up at 5am, so waking early causes success.' What dataset is missing from the inference?
answer: All the people who woke at 5am and did NOT become successful CEOs -- the failures.
choices: All the people who woke at 5am and did NOT become successful CEOs -- the failures.
Data on what time the CEOs went to bed; you need both ends of the day to compare.
Data on whether the CEOs work harder than others; the wake time is a proxy variable.
Data on CEO demographics; without controls for age and sex the claim is unfounded.
context: Sampling on the dependent variable hides the base rate. To test 'early waking causes success,' you need to look at early wakers in general -- not only those who succeeded.

question: Tu quoque often has TWO valid uses and ONE fallacious. Naming the valid uses tightens criticism. What ARE they?
answer: Exposing hypocrisy as character evidence, and exposing inconsistent commitments in argument.
choices: Exposing hypocrisy as character evidence, and exposing inconsistent commitments in argument.
Replying with anger, and rebuilding lost trust between the two debaters in real time.
Showing the opponent reading from a script, and quoting his unflattering past actions.
Returning the favor in kind, and ensuring no debater enjoys an unfair speaking advantage.
context: Tu quoque becomes fallacious when used to AVOID the original point. It is legitimate when (1) the inconsistency is itself the point, or (2) character is the topic.

question: Begging the question is sometimes confused with circular reasoning. What is the more precise distinction Aristotle had in mind?
answer: Begging the question takes a contested premise as obvious; circularity loops conclusion into premise.
choices: Begging the question takes a contested premise as obvious; circularity loops conclusion into premise.
There is no real difference -- the two phrases name the same logical move under two names.
Begging the question is about evidence; circular reasoning is about word order on the page.
Begging the question is informal rhetoric; circular reasoning is formal-logic vocabulary only.
context: Aristotle's petitio principii is broader than tight circularity -- it covers any argument whose premises won't be granted by anyone who doubts the conclusion.

question: The 'motte and bailey' tactic: defend an indefensible claim (bailey) by retreating to a safer one (motte). Why is naming it useful in arguments?
answer: Naming the move forces an opponent to pick one ground and stay there.
choices: Naming the move forces an opponent to pick one ground and stay there.
Naming any fallacy in a debate wins on style; the opponent cannot recover politely.
Naming it is harmful because it sounds academic and confuses listeners on each side.
Naming it lets you push the bailey claim as the correct view of the whole disagreement.
context: Coined by Nicholas Shackel. Activists, politicians, and intellectuals deploy it constantly. Insisting on which thesis is actually under debate is the cleanest counter-move.

question: Kant's first Critique argues that space and time are NOT features of things in themselves but forms of human intuition. What follows?
answer: We cannot know things as they are in themselves -- only as they appear to minds like ours.
choices: We cannot know things as they are in themselves -- only as they appear to minds like ours.
Space and time are unreal and so our experience is mostly an illusion of the senses.
Mathematics fails because spatial reasoning depends on a non-feature of the real world.
We can know the past but not the future because time runs in one direction only here.
context: Kant's transcendental idealism reshapes the question of knowledge. Phenomena (the world as it appears) are knowable; noumena (things in themselves) are not -- a hard limit.

question: Critics charged Mill's utilitarianism with reducing human experience to one metric. How did Mill himself defend the view in chapter 2 of his book?
answer: He distinguished higher pleasures from lower ones, judged by competent judges.
choices: He distinguished higher pleasures from lower ones, judged by competent judges.
He gave up on the single-metric idea and adopted a pluralist account of human value.
He argued the metric is fine because most pleasures really do reduce to bodily satisfaction.
He shifted the theory to rights-based reasoning and abandoned consequences as foundational.
context: Mill's famous line: 'better to be a Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied.' Quality of pleasure matters, judged by people who have tasted both. Critics say this is no longer pure utilitarianism.

question: Hegel argued the modern state secures freedom in a way no earlier form could. Where does he say the OBJECTIVE side of freedom lives?
answer: In institutions -- family, civil society, the state -- that give individual freedom durable form.
choices: In institutions -- family, civil society, the state -- that give individual freedom durable form.
In the subjective conscience of each citizen, holding herself to her own moral law.
In the marketplace, where individuals pursue interests and the state stays out of trade.
In private property alone, which protects each person from the demands of every other.
context: Hegel's Philosophy of Right traces freedom from abstract right through morality into 'ethical life' (Sittlichkeit). True freedom is not bare choice but life in well-formed institutions.

question: Nietzsche's 'death of God' is sometimes read as celebration. What did Nietzsche himself think the death meant for European culture?
answer: A coming crisis -- the foundations of values had collapsed, and Europe had not yet noticed.
choices: A coming crisis -- the foundations of values had collapsed, and Europe had not yet noticed.
A welcome liberation of human reason from millennia of clerical superstition and dogma.
An empirical claim that fewer Europeans attended church than in previous centuries on average.
A purely metaphysical claim about the actual non-existence of a divine being above the world.
context: The Gay Science §125: the madman in the marketplace. Nietzsche thought the loss of God removed the ground of all values. The hard work -- creating new ones -- had barely begun.

question: Schopenhauer's pessimism turns on a deep claim about the Will. What features of human striving did he argue make satisfaction impossible?
answer: Wanting is incessant -- attained ends produce new wants; intervals are boredom, not peace.
choices: Wanting is incessant -- attained ends produce new wants; intervals are boredom, not peace.
Wanting is hidden -- people do not really know what they want and so cannot get it ever.
Wanting is shared -- our desires are copied from others, so we never truly want for ourselves.
Wanting is unrealistic -- people want too much and so they are always going to fall short.
context: Schopenhauer: satisfaction is the brief lull between two wantings. The pendulum swings between lack (pain) and surfeit (boredom). His exits: art, asceticism, compassion.

question: Marx attacked the 'fetish' of the commodity in Capital. What specific illusion did he say the commodity form gives rise to?
answer: Relations between people appear as relations between things -- the social is mistaken for the natural.
choices: Relations between people appear as relations between things -- the social is mistaken for the natural.
Workers worship their products and lose interest in their families and other social relations.
Consumers buy more than they need because objects exert a mystical pull over the human mind.
Capitalists treat money as sacred and so the whole society becomes a kind of religious cult.
context: Marx's point: under commodity production, the human labor making things gets hidden BEHIND the exchange relations of the things. The social character of work appears as a property of objects.

question: Kierkegaard's three stages -- aesthetic, ethical, religious -- describe possible lives. Why is each later stage NOT just an improvement on the earlier?
answer: Each stage involves a leap -- a discontinuous choice -- not a gradual moral progress.
choices: Each stage involves a leap -- a discontinuous choice -- not a gradual moral progress.
Each stage is just one more option a person can pick, like flavors of ice cream at a counter.
The stages are arranged by age -- aesthetic for kids, ethical for adults, religious for old age.
The religious stage is for believers only; non-believers cannot have ethics or aesthetics either.
context: Either/Or pushes the aesthetic-to-ethical leap; Fear and Trembling pushes ethical-to-religious. No incremental ladder -- a person must JUMP, and reasons run out before the jump.

question: Hume's compatibilist account of free will redefines 'free' as 'uncoerced.' Why did Kant find this view inadequate?
answer: Kant wanted free will as a noumenal, self-legislating capacity -- not just absence of external chains.
choices: Kant wanted free will as a noumenal, self-legislating capacity -- not just absence of external chains.
Kant thought Hume was wrong on the empirical facts of how human choices actually work.
Kant rejected freedom entirely; for him, all human action is determined by prior causes.
Kant adopted Hume's view but used different words for it; the two thinkers basically agreed.
context: For Hume, 'free' = action springing from your wants, not from outside compulsion. Kant says this is too thin -- moral responsibility requires a deeper freedom to set one's own law.

question: Spinoza identified God with Nature ('deus sive natura'). Why did he insist this was NOT atheism, even though it denied a personal creator?
answer: He preserved divine attributes -- infinity, necessity, eternity -- and worship as intellectual love of nature.
choices: He preserved divine attributes -- infinity, necessity, eternity -- and worship as intellectual love of nature.
He thought the personal-creator view was a minor doctrinal point that didn't define theism.
He kept the word 'God' as a polite cover; his actual position was straightforward atheism.
He believed in many personal gods, each tied to a different attribute of one larger universe.
context: Spinoza's Ethics treats God as the single infinite substance with infinite attributes (thought, extension). Religious authorities still excommunicated him -- his God was unrecognizable to the orthodox.

question: Chalmers distinguished the 'easy' problems of consciousness from the 'hard' problem. What feature makes the hard problem so hard?
answer: Explaining WHY there is something it is like to undergo a brain process at all.
choices: Explaining WHY there is something it is like to undergo a brain process at all.
Explaining how the brain processes data fast enough to keep up with daily experience.
Explaining why some people pay attention and others do not while undergoing experience.
Explaining how memories form during conscious moments and persist when we no longer attend.
context: Easy problems: functions like attention, integration, reportability. These yield to neuroscience. The hard problem: why functional states are accompanied by EXPERIENCE.

question: Searle's Chinese Room argues that symbol manipulation alone is not understanding. The man in the room follows rules and passes for a Chinese speaker. What does this allegedly show?
answer: Syntax (rules) is not enough for semantics (understanding) -- so a computer cannot, on its own, understand.
choices: Syntax (rules) is not enough for semantics (understanding) -- so a computer cannot, on its own, understand.
Computers are slow at language and will never match human translators in real-time settings.
Symbol manipulation is too narrow; computers need to also process images and sounds together.
The man learns Chinese over time as he applies the rules; the room is a kind of slow tutor.
context: Searle's target was 'strong AI' -- the claim that running the right program just IS understanding. His thought experiment claims a syntactic engine, however good, lacks the inner semantics of mind.

question: Parfit argued personal identity is not what matters in survival. What was his reason for the demotion?
answer: What we care about -- psychological continuity -- can split or branch, while identity is one-to-one.
choices: What we care about -- psychological continuity -- can split or branch, while identity is one-to-one.
Identity is a legal concept and so it should not really be at the heart of any philosophy.
Bodies change over time and so identity is unstable, while what matters stays steady.
Identity is too vague to be useful and should be replaced with simpler everyday concepts.
context: Reasons and Persons (1984) used fission cases: a person's psychology branched into two equally continuous successors. Both can't be 'you' under identity, yet what you cared about is preserved in each.

question: Block split 'access' consciousness from 'phenomenal' consciousness. The split tries to sharpen the hard problem. What is the split itself?
answer: Access is information available for reasoning and report; phenomenal is what experience FEELS like.
choices: Access is information available for reasoning and report; phenomenal is what experience FEELS like.
Access consciousness is for everyday tasks; phenomenal consciousness is for art appreciation only.
Access is conscious; phenomenal is unconscious -- the two names label opposites in the mind.
Access consciousness is human; phenomenal consciousness is what animals have but cannot describe.
context: Block's distinction is contested but influential. Many functional theories of mind handle access well but say nothing about phenomenal -- the 'what it's like' that gives the hard problem its bite.

question: Functionalism identifies mental states with their causal roles. What is the standard worry that 'absent qualia' cases raise?
answer: A system could have all the right causal roles but no inner experience -- the qualia would simply be missing.
choices: A system could have all the right causal roles but no inner experience -- the qualia would simply be missing.
A system could become depressed if the qualia were dimmer than they normally would be for it.
A system might confuse its qualia with another system's, leading to misunderstandings everywhere.
A system needs more qualia than functionalism allows in order to count as a real conscious mind.
context: The thought experiment: imagine a being functionally identical to you (same causal map) but with no inner experience -- a 'zombie.' If conceivable, function and consciousness come apart.

question: Strawson's 'reactive attitudes' -- resentment, gratitude, anger -- offer a way past the free-will debate. What did he argue these attitudes show?
answer: Holding people responsible is a fact of practice; abandoning it on theoretical grounds is impossible.
choices: Holding people responsible is a fact of practice; abandoning it on theoretical grounds is impossible.
Reactive attitudes are unreliable and should be replaced with a calmer attitude toward all people.
Reactive attitudes are evidence against determinism -- they imply we already know we are free.
Reactive attitudes only matter for personal life, not for any decisions about public policy.
context: Strawson's 'Freedom and Resentment' (1962) sidesteps the metaphysics. The community of responsibility-attributors is the very fabric of human life; theory can't really dissolve it.

question: Wittgenstein's 'private language' argument goes after the idea that words for inner feelings get their meaning by inner pointing. What is the beetle-in-a-box image meant to show?
answer: If each person had a 'beetle' in a private box no other could see, the word 'beetle' could drop out of the language.
choices: If each person had a 'beetle' in a private box no other could see, the word 'beetle' could drop out of the language.
Each person should label their beetle so they can compare notes across the population over time.
The beetles are real but no one will ever know about them because they are private and hidden.
Beetles are placeholders for any private experience; the word 'beetle' refers to all of them at once.
context: The argument: meaning depends on public criteria and use. A 'word' that I assign by purely private ostension to a private sensation can't really play a meaning role -- there's no check on its use.

question: Burke's Reflections on the Revolution in France defended the old British way against French abstract reason. What did he see the French Revolution missing?
answer: Inheritance -- a constitution slowly grown is wiser than one freshly designed from theory.
choices: Inheritance -- a constitution slowly grown is wiser than one freshly designed from theory.
Strong leadership -- the French should have chosen one king to guide the rapid change.
Open speech -- the Revolution shut down debate and that was its great error in execution.
Material progress -- France was not yet ready economically for the kind of changes attempted.
context: Burke distrusted abstract reason in politics. Inherited institutions encode practical wisdom that no committee can match. The Revolution swept away that capital -- and replaced it with terror.

question: Hayek's 'knowledge problem' argues that central planners cannot do what markets do. What is the precise knowledge claim?
answer: Markets aggregate dispersed local knowledge no planner can collect; prices carry the signal.
choices: Markets aggregate dispersed local knowledge no planner can collect; prices carry the signal.
Planners are corrupt while market actors are honest -- it is a problem of character, not data.
Markets are faster than planners but not necessarily better; the trade-off is debatable now.
Planners lack the right tools because computer science is still too primitive to model trade.
context: Hayek's 'The Use of Knowledge in Society' (1945) is the classic statement. Markets are not merely an efficient allocator -- they are an EPISTEMIC institution. Prices condense knowledge no central mind has.

question: Sowell distinguished a 'constrained' from an 'unconstrained' vision in A Conflict of Visions. What is the core disagreement?
answer: Whether human nature is fixed (constrained) or perfectible by reformed institutions (unconstrained).
choices: Whether human nature is fixed (constrained) or perfectible by reformed institutions (unconstrained).
Whether government should be small or large -- a difference about administrative scale alone.
Whether human reason is reliable or unreliable -- a question about cognitive capacities only.
Whether morality is innate or learned -- a debate over the source of basic moral concepts.
context: Sowell's framework: from this one root, many surface disagreements grow. Trade-offs vs. solutions, experience vs. articulate reason, results vs. process -- each vision generates its own family of positions.

question: Rawls's veil of ignorance is meant to derive principles of justice fair to all. What feature of the parties behind the veil drives the result?
answer: They are rational, mutually disinterested, and ignorant of their own talents and social position.
choices: They are rational, mutually disinterested, and ignorant of their own talents and social position.
They are altruistic and so they pick principles that look out for everyone else first.
They are angry about historical injustice and so they pick principles that try to fix the past.
They are politically liberal in advance and so the veil mostly confirms their existing leanings.
context: A Theory of Justice (1971): rational agents who could be anyone in society, knowing nothing of their own place, choose principles that hedge against being worst-off. Result: equal liberties + difference principle.

question: Nozick's Anarchy, State, and Utopia raised the Wilt Chamberlain case against patterned theories of distributive justice. What was the point?
answer: Free voluntary exchanges shift any pattern; preserving the pattern requires constant interference.
choices: Free voluntary exchanges shift any pattern; preserving the pattern requires constant interference.
Wilt was a great athlete and so he deserved to be paid more than other players in the league.
Sports stars distort labor markets and so government must regulate professional salaries.
Patterned distribution works fine; Wilt is a special case who confirms the rule for everyone else.
context: Nozick: start from any pattern you prefer (D1). Let people freely give some money to Wilt to see him play. New pattern (D2) is no longer your preferred one. To restore D1, you must override consent.

question: Scruton defended the small-c conservative love of place, custom, and the dead. What did he call this love, and why does he say political life rests on it?
answer: Oikophilia -- love of home -- as the basis of civic obligation, since rights need a 'we' to anchor them.
choices: Oikophilia -- love of home -- as the basis of civic obligation, since rights need a 'we' to anchor them.
Patriotism -- love of country -- which is the same idea but at a much larger national scale.
Nostalgia -- love of the past -- which only emerges when present circumstances feel insecure.
Authoritarianism -- love of order -- which is unrelated to the smaller-scale civic attachments.
context: Scruton's How to Be a Conservative argues that liberal abstractions ('the autonomous individual') live as parasites on the very particular loves they discount. No 'we,' no rights to begin with.

question: Coleman Hughes argues against race-based policy in The End of Race Politics. What does he offer in its place?
answer: Color-blind law and class-based remediation -- targeting disadvantage without sorting citizens by race.
choices: Color-blind law and class-based remediation -- targeting disadvantage without sorting citizens by race.
Eliminate all public assistance because race-based policies have created cycles of dependence.
Adopt heavier race-based preferences because earlier remedies were not aggressive enough yet.
Replace race with ethnicity because ethnicity is more meaningful than the looser racial categories.
context: Hughes argues that race-conscious policy reinforces the categories it tries to dissolve. Class-targeted support helps disadvantaged people of every background without making race the master variable.

question: Tocqueville feared a new kind of despotism native to democratic societies. What did he predict it would look like?
answer: Soft administrative tutelage -- not a tyrant, but a vast benign power managing every detail of life.
choices: Soft administrative tutelage -- not a tyrant, but a vast benign power managing every detail of life.
A populist demagogue who would rouse the masses and then make himself dictator over them.
A military coup by generals who would tire of civilian dithering and impose a hard order.
Economic collapse leading to chaos and the rise of small warlords across the territory.
context: Democracy in America Volume II: the new despotism would not strike at men's lives but at their energies -- it would 'enervate' rather than break. A condition Tocqueville thought no past society had known.

question: Plato's Form of the Good is said to be 'beyond being' (epekeina tes ousias). In the Republic Book VI, what role does it play in knowledge?
answer: It lights the other Forms the way the sun makes visible things visible -- the ground of all knowing.
choices: It lights the other Forms the way the sun makes visible things visible -- the ground of all knowing.
It is one Form among others, slightly larger and more important than the rest of them.
It is the source of bodies and material things, not of knowledge or intellectual life.
It is identical with the soul; knowing it is just knowing oneself in a deeper way today.
context: The Sun analogy: the Good is to the realm of Forms what the sun is to visible things -- the source of being AND of intelligibility. Knowledge becomes possible because the Good shines.

question: Augustine's account of evil in the Confessions and elsewhere treats evil as 'privation of good' (privatio boni). Why does this matter for the problem of evil?
answer: It denies evil any positive existence -- nothing real that God created is itself evil.
choices: It denies evil any positive existence -- nothing real that God created is itself evil.
It says evil is unreal in some loose sense -- so people do not really suffer in the world.
It blames evil on the devil and other dark spirits, who exist apart from God's good creation.
It claims that what looks evil is actually good when seen from God's view of the whole.
context: Augustine inherited the privatio boni doctrine from Neoplatonism. Evil is missing-good, not a stuff. Critics ask whether this fits the visceral reality of evil; defenders say it explains its parasitic structure.

question: Aquinas's doctrine of analogy says words like 'good' apply to God and creatures neither in the same sense nor in fully different senses. Why this middle path?
answer: Univocal use levels God; equivocal use empties theology of meaning; analogy preserves both at once.
choices: Univocal use levels God; equivocal use empties theology of meaning; analogy preserves both at once.
Aquinas wanted to please everyone in the medieval debates and so he picked a middle position.
Analogy is just a fancy word for metaphor and so the position collapses into negative theology.
Aquinas thought ordinary language was too crude to talk about God and rejected words entirely.
context: Words shared between God and creatures must mean something connected (else theology is babbling) without meaning the SAME thing (else God is just a big creature). Analogy of proportion is Aquinas's solution.

question: Anselm's Cur Deus Homo argued the Incarnation was NEEDED given some premises about sin and pay-back. What is the heart of the argument he gave?
answer: Sin owes an infinite debt only God can pay; justice requires payment by a human; so God-man.
choices: Sin owes an infinite debt only God can pay; justice requires payment by a human; so God-man.
Anselm thought God simply chose the Incarnation, and necessity language is loose rhetoric here.
Anselm built on Augustine's view that God could have saved humans by direct decree alone.
Anselm argued that humans owed nothing because original sin was inherited and not chosen by them.
context: Anselm's 'satisfaction theory' was revolutionary. Critics across centuries challenged each premise. But the move -- deriving doctrine from carefully stated necessities -- shaped Western theology for 900 years.

question: Plotinus's One emanates Intellect, which emanates Soul, which shapes the world. Why is this NOT creation in the biblical sense?
answer: Emanation is necessary overflow from the One's own nature; creation is a free act of God.
choices: Emanation is necessary overflow from the One's own nature; creation is a free act of God.
Plotinus's One creates instantly without any process while the biblical God takes six days.
Plotinus's One is impersonal while the biblical God speaks and chooses what to make next.
Both views are basically the same -- Plotinus just uses different vocabulary for one event.
context: Augustine wrestled with this. The biblical doctrine of creation ex nihilo by free divine will differs sharply from Plotinian necessary procession. Christian theology had to redraw the metaphysics.

question: Maimonides's Guide describes God in the 'via negativa' (the way of saying what God is NOT). Why did he find positive terms wanting?
answer: Positive terms drawn from creatures fail to apply to an absolutely simple, transcendent being.
choices: Positive terms drawn from creatures fail to apply to an absolutely simple, transcendent being.
Positive terms are too long and the human reader cannot really track them across a sentence.
Positive terms come from religion while God transcends all religions; only philosophy works.
Positive terms divide God's attributes; only negative terms can keep his unity perfectly intact.
context: Maimonides argued that we cannot say what God IS, only what God is NOT -- not bodily, not finite, not divisible. Even 'good' and 'wise' have to be carefully chastened before applying to the divine.

question: Bayesian epistemology models belief as degrees of credence updated by evidence. What is the role of priors in this framework?
answer: They encode the agent's belief state before new evidence arrives -- the starting point for updating.
choices: They encode the agent's belief state before new evidence arrives -- the starting point for updating.
They constrain what evidence the agent is allowed to gather during the testing phase.
They give the agent's beliefs about which experiments to fund and which to reject going forward.
They specify the conclusion the agent intends to reach before any evidence has been examined.
context: Bayes's theorem updates priors with new evidence via likelihoods. Priors matter -- two agents with different priors confronted by the same evidence may end up with different posteriors. Disciplined disagreement is possible.

question: Zagzebski's virtue view defines knowledge as true belief out of one's own intellectual virtue. How does this avoid the Gettier problem?
answer: Lucky truth doesn't issue from intellectual virtue -- the cognitive achievement isn't credited to the agent.
choices: Lucky truth doesn't issue from intellectual virtue -- the cognitive achievement isn't credited to the agent.
It abandons truth as a goal and substitutes coherence; Gettier cases require coherent justification.
It treats knowledge as a social institution; Gettier cases are individual and so don't arise here.
It rejects justification entirely; Gettier cases all turn on justification of some kind or other.
context: Virtue epistemology shifts the focus from 'when is the belief justified?' to 'when is the truth an achievement of the believer's intellectual virtues?' Gettier-style luck severs this credit.

question: Hardwig argued modern knowledge rests on testimony in ways that cannot be broken down to direct seeing. What follows for the ideal of solo verification?
answer: It is impossible -- no single mind can verify even most of what an educated person rightly believes.
choices: It is impossible -- no single mind can verify even most of what an educated person rightly believes.
It is achievable in some narrow fields like pure math but not in the empirical sciences anywhere.
It is realized by experts in each field who can verify their own corner but trust on others' work.
It is achievable for any individual who is willing to spend enough years studying many subjects.
context: Hardwig's claim is unsettling for Enlightenment epistemology. The Cartesian solo verifier was always a fiction; in practice, science and learning are deeply social. We trust to know.

question: Goldman's reliabilism takes knowledge as belief made by a reliable process. What is the standard 'generality' problem his view runs into?
answer: Every belief is produced by many processes at different levels of description -- which one is THE one?
choices: Every belief is produced by many processes at different levels of description -- which one is THE one?
Reliability is hard to measure for individual beliefs without a long history of similar tests.
Reliable processes can produce false beliefs sometimes; the view needs a backup justification rule.
Reliable processes are different in different agents; the view needs to relativize knowledge to agents.
context: Your belief that the cup is red was produced by 'vision,' 'human vision in afternoon light,' 'your specific eyes today,' etc. Which process's reliability counts? The generality problem keeps reliabilism honest.

question: Plantinga's Reformed Epistemology argues that belief in God can be 'properly basic.' What does 'basic' mean here?
answer: Not inferred from other beliefs -- held directly, the way perceptual or memorial beliefs are held.
choices: Not inferred from other beliefs -- held directly, the way perceptual or memorial beliefs are held.
Simple in vocabulary -- a basic belief is one that uses no technical or theological words.
Compatible with reason -- a basic belief is one that does not contradict any scientific finding.
Held by most people -- a basic belief is one widely shared across cultures and historical times.
context: Classical foundationalism allowed only sense experience and self-evident truths as basic. Plantinga argued there's no principled reason to deny religious experience the same status. The move was philosophically explosive.

question: Closure principles in epistemology say: if you know P, and know P entails Q, then you know Q. Why is this contested by some epistemologists?
answer: Applied, closure seems to give you knowledge that 'I am not a brain in a vat' -- which feels wrong.
choices: Applied, closure seems to give you knowledge that 'I am not a brain in a vat' -- which feels wrong.
Closure makes knowledge gain too easy; you could derive all of math from any single fact.
Closure ignores the social character of knowledge and treats it as a private inference activity.
Closure conflicts with Bayesian updating because credences are not closed under deduction.
context: From 'I have hands' and 'having hands entails not being a handless brain in a vat,' closure gives 'I know I am not a handless brain in a vat.' Some reject closure to block this; others accept it and accept the consequence.

question: The free will defense (Plantinga) addresses the logical problem of evil. What is the structural claim?
answer: It is possible that any world with morally significant freedom contains some moral evil too.
choices: It is possible that any world with morally significant freedom contains some moral evil too.
Free will is more valuable than the absence of any evil and so God prefers the trade-off here.
Most evil comes from human choices and so God can be excused for not stopping each one of them.
God could prevent some evils but not all; the doctrine of omnipotence has to be qualified now.
context: Plantinga's response targets the LOGICAL problem (Mackie). It needn't be plausible -- just possible. If even one possible world with free creatures necessarily contains evil, the contradiction dissolves.

question: Divine simplicity holds that God has no parts and is identical with His attributes. What does this make of saying 'God is good' vs. 'God is wise'?
answer: Both predicates refer to the same simple divine essence -- distinctions are in our minds, not in God.
choices: Both predicates refer to the same simple divine essence -- distinctions are in our minds, not in God.
Both predicates refer to different parts of God so that God ends up having an internal structure.
The two predicates are incompatible because no being can be both good and wise at the same time.
The two predicates collapse into one another and so the language of theology becomes redundant.
context: Divine simplicity is among the hardest doctrines in classical theism. Critics ask whether it leaves God indistinguishable from a single property. Defenders (Augustine, Aquinas, Anselm) insist it preserves transcendence.

question: Rowe and Draper's 'evidential' problem of evil grants that God and evil are logically possible. They ask: does the AMOUNT of seemingly pointless evil make theism unlikely?
answer: Rowe argued some evils seem pointless even after every theistic explanation has been considered.
choices: Rowe argued some evils seem pointless even after every theistic explanation has been considered.
Rowe argued there is no evil at all in the world; what people call evil is just inconvenience.
Rowe argued every evil has a known good purpose; the perplexity is only in our limited view.
Rowe argued God is responsible for every evil directly; the doctrine of providence ensures it.
context: Rowe's 'fawn in the forest fire' -- a slow agonizing death no one sees. Theists reply with skeptical theism (we can't track God's reasons). The debate is now over WHETHER we can read 'no apparent point' as evidence.

question: Pascal's Wager has a structural flaw critics call the 'many gods' objection. What is the objection?
answer: If the wager works for one god, it works for any god with infinite reward -- and they conflict.
choices: If the wager works for one god, it works for any god with infinite reward -- and they conflict.
Pascal's wager works in principle but the math is wrong; the expected utility is undefined.
Pascal's wager assumes you can choose to believe, but belief is involuntary, not voluntary.
Pascal's wager works only for Catholics, not for any of the other Christian traditions today.
context: The structure -- bet on infinite reward whose probability you can't dismiss -- recurs for any religion. The wagerer needs an additional argument to single out one religion before the wager bites.

question: Anselm's ontological argument seems to derive God's existence from his definition. Gaunilo answered with a 'lost island' parallel. What was the charge?
answer: If the argument works, you could prove existence of any 'greatest conceivable' thing -- including absurd ones.
choices: If the argument works, you could prove existence of any 'greatest conceivable' thing -- including absurd ones.
Gaunilo argued Anselm's definition of God was incorrect; he wanted a different definition first.
Gaunilo argued the conclusion follows but only for Christians; Jews and others use different premises.
Gaunilo argued Anselm conflated greatest with biggest; the argument fails on size alone.
context: Anselm replied that 'God' is uniquely conceived as 'that than which a greater cannot be conceived' -- no analogous 'greatest island' applies, because islands have no maximal degree. The debate continues today.

question: Mencius and Xunzi disagreed sharply over human nature. What is the contrast in one line each?
answer: Mencius: human nature is good but easily corrupted; Xunzi: human nature is bad but trainable by ritual.
choices: Mencius: human nature is good but easily corrupted; Xunzi: human nature is bad but trainable by ritual.
Mencius: nature is fixed by heaven; Xunzi: nature is fixed by social class and not changeable.
Mencius: nature changes with age; Xunzi: nature changes by region in which one is born.
Mencius: nature is neither good nor bad; Xunzi: nature is good in some and bad in others.
context: Both were Confucians, but the wager was opposite. Mencius's optimism centers cultivation of inborn seeds. Xunzi's pessimism centers ritual training to straighten crooked timber. Both shaped East Asian thought.

question: Nagarjuna's Madhyamaka school rejected both 'things have inner essence' and 'nothing exists.' What is the middle way he taught between these two poles?
answer: Things exist conventionally and dependently, but lack inherent self-standing essence (svabhava).
choices: Things exist conventionally and dependently, but lack inherent self-standing essence (svabhava).
Things exist in some parts of reality but not in others -- existence varies across regions.
Things exist when observed and stop existing when ignored -- a kind of mind-dependence view.
Things exist only in the mind and the external world is a mere projection of consciousness.
context: Nagarjuna's 'two truths' doctrine distinguishes conventional (samvrti) from ultimate (paramartha) truth. Things function and matter conventionally; ultimately they lack the self-standing being naive realism assumes.

question: Confucius's 'rectification of names' (zhengming) holds that social disorder begins when words drift from what they should name. Why is this a political doctrine?
answer: If 'father' no longer names what a father owes, family fails; the same drift undoes the state.
choices: If 'father' no longer names what a father owes, family fails; the same drift undoes the state.
It is about education -- children must learn vocabulary before they can do anything else.
It is about courtroom argument -- judges must use words clearly when ruling on cases of law.
It is about language reform -- old terms must be discarded in favor of modern equivalents.
context: Analects 13.3: 'If names are not rectified, language will not accord with truth; if language does not accord with truth, affairs cannot be carried on.' Political life depends on stable meanings.

question: Zhuangzi's butterfly dream raises a question about identity. What did Zhuangzi himself draw from waking and wondering whether he was a man dreaming of a butterfly, or vice versa?
answer: The transition between states is real; perhaps the rigid distinction between identities is what's confused.
choices: The transition between states is real; perhaps the rigid distinction between identities is what's confused.
The dream shows that the man and the butterfly are exactly the same thing in two states.
The dream shows that the senses cannot be trusted to tell which state is the real one for you.
The dream shows that butterflies are wiser than men, and so we should aspire to be like them.
context: Zhuangzi's point is more playful than skeptical. The fluid 'transformation of things' (wuhua) is the deeper reality; identity boundaries we cling to may be the illusion to release.

question: The Daodejing's 'reversal is the movement of the dao' (fan zhe dao zhi dong) is a recurring theme. What political wisdom did Lao Tzu draw from it?
answer: Extremes invite their opposites; rulers should soften before they harden, yield before they break.
choices: Extremes invite their opposites; rulers should soften before they harden, yield before they break.
Rulers should reverse all their policies every few years to keep their subjects from being bored.
Rulers should walk backward through their gardens to remind themselves of where they have been.
Rulers should reverse the practices of their enemies to gain advantage in any kind of competition.
context: Lao Tzu's wisdom is dynamic. Things at extreme become their opposite. A wise ruler reads this rhythm and acts BEFORE the swing -- yielding, retreating, softening when others would clench.

question: Maya says, 'All my friends have phones, so I should get one too.' What is wrong with that as the WHOLE reason?
choices: What other people have doesn't show what is best for HER.
The friends have probably stolen their phones from each other.
Maya is simply not old enough to ever own such a device.
Phones are evil objects that destroy the souls of all kids.
answer: What other people have doesn't show what is best for HER.
context: This is the bandwagon move — assuming popularity proves a thing is right. The truth depends on Maya's situation, not the crowd's. Also called 'appeal to popularity.'

question: A boy says, 'Everyone is making fun of the new kid, so it must be okay.' Where is his thinking off?
choices: Crowds can be wrong — being cruel is cruel even when many do it.
The new kid actually deserves the teasing because of his shoes.
Group rules always work better than individual decisions and morals.
Making fun is fine as long as the teacher isn't in the room watching.
answer: Crowds can be wrong — being cruel is cruel even when many do it.
context: Bandwagon fallacy. 'Many people do X' is not evidence X is right. The size of the crowd doesn't change the action.

question: Sara hears, 'This song sold a million copies, so it must be good.' What is sneaky about that claim?
choices: Sales count how many bought it, not whether it is actually good.
A million is actually a small number for popular music sales.
Songs never sell — most streaming today is free for everyone.
Sara should not listen to popular music made by any artist.
answer: Sales count how many bought it, not whether it is actually good.
context: Popularity is not quality. Many things sell well because of marketing or trends, not because they are excellent.

question: A kid says, 'Lots of kids cheat on this teacher's tests, so cheating is fine.' What is wrong with the reasoning?
choices: What others do does not change whether YOUR action is right.
The teacher made the tests too hard, so cheating is justified.
Cheating is fine because the kid won't get caught this time.
Most kids actually do not cheat — the kid is exaggerating numbers.
answer: What others do does not change whether YOUR action is right.
context: Bandwagon defense. Ethics is about your own act, not the crowd's. The number of people doing wrong does not make it right.

question: Aiden argues, 'My YouTuber has 5 million followers, so he must be telling the truth.' Where is the flaw?
choices: Followers measure popularity, not whether the words are true.
Five million followers is too small to count as proof of trust.
YouTubers are paid for views, so they always say false things.
Aiden should follow only YouTubers with ten million or more.
answer: Followers measure popularity, not whether the words are true.
context: Popularity does not equal truth. A creator can be widely followed AND wrong about the facts at the same time.

question: 'Everyone is wearing baggy jeans this year, so they must be the best style.' What is wrong with that as a reason?
choices: Trends change — what is popular today is not always best.
Baggy jeans are objectively the worst clothing item invented.
Style is decided by famous fashion designers in big cities only.
The speaker should wear baggy jeans every day until next year.
answer: Trends change — what is popular today is not always best.
context: Bandwagon plus a side helping of trend-following. What is fashionable now will look silly later — that fact alone shows popularity is not quality.

question: 'My whole class is going to the dance, so my parents should let me go.' What is the WEAKEST part of that argument?
choices: The class going does not show the dance is right for ME.
The kid's class is actually too small to count as a real group.
Parents should let kids go wherever the school says is allowed.
Dances are universally good for every kid in every grade level.
answer: The class going does not show the dance is right for ME.
context: Bandwagon again. The crowd's plans do not change YOUR family's reasons. The argument should focus on the dance itself, not on who else is going.

question: Pia says, 'Half the school plays this game, so it must be safe.' What is she missing?
choices: Lots of people doing a thing does not prove the thing is safe.
Pia is mistaken — only a third of the school actually plays it.
The game has been tested by professional safety inspectors yearly.
Pia is too young and small to know what counts as safe for kids.
answer: Lots of people doing a thing does not prove the thing is safe.
context: Bandwagon meets safety claims. Many people can do something risky without realizing it. Popularity gives no real evidence about danger.

question: A girl says, 'It must be a real story — millions of people are sharing it!' What does that miss?
choices: Stories can spread because they're exciting, not because they're true.
Millions of people would never share a story if it was untrue.
Sharing means each person has verified all facts independently.
Only stories with proof get shared more than a million total times.
answer: Stories can spread because they're exciting, not because they're true.
context: False stories often spread FASTER than true ones because they're shocking. Popularity online is not evidence at all.

question: 'Nobody on the team thinks it's a foul, so it isn't one.' What is the trouble with that?
choices: The team agreeing does not change what actually happened on the play.
The referee should let the team decide all fouls by majority vote.
Teams know the rules better than the people in striped uniforms.
Fouls are made up by referees to slow down good winning teams.
answer: The team agreeing does not change what actually happened on the play.
context: Bandwagon over evidence. Group agreement is comforting but it doesn't replace looking at what actually happened.

question: Dad tells Lily not to leave dishes in the sink. Lily replies, 'YOU left dishes there yesterday!' What is wrong with her reply?
choices: Even if Dad did it, that doesn't make HER dishes okay to leave.
Dad is a complete hypocrite, so nothing he says counts as fair.
Lily is allowed to break the rule whenever she sees Dad break it.
Yesterday's dishes are way worse than today's dishes ever could be.
answer: Even if Dad did it, that doesn't make HER dishes okay to leave.
context: This is 'tu quoque' — the 'you too' move. It changes the subject. The original question (should Lily leave dishes?) doesn't depend on what Dad did.

question: Marco breaks a vase and says, 'My brother broke one last week!' Why is this NOT a defense?
choices: What his brother did doesn't change that Marco broke the vase NOW.
His brother should be punished first before anyone looks at Marco.
Two broken vases proves the family has cheap and breakable items.
Marco's brother is the one truly responsible for both of the vases.
answer: What his brother did doesn't change that Marco broke the vase NOW.
context: 'You-too' defense. Pointing at someone else's mistake doesn't undo yours. The question is still: what should Marco do about THIS vase?

question: When told not to interrupt, Beth says, 'But Sam interrupts all the time!' What is the flaw?
choices: Sam's behavior doesn't decide whether BETH should interrupt.
Sam's interrupting is much worse than Beth's interrupting today.
Adults should always punish Sam first before they punish Beth.
Interrupting is fine if there is at least one other person doing it.
answer: Sam's behavior doesn't decide whether BETH should interrupt.
context: Tu quoque. The right question is about Beth's own action. Sam can be wrong AND Beth can also be wrong — two separate issues.

question: A coach tells Theo to stop showing off. Theo replies, 'But COACH yells all game!' Why isn't that an answer?
choices: Pointing at the coach doesn't address whether THEO is showing off.
The coach should stop yelling first before correcting any player.
Showing off is allowed for any player whose coach also makes noise.
Coaches are supposed to set the example, so Theo wins this argument.
answer: Pointing at the coach doesn't address whether THEO is showing off.
context: Tu quoque dodges the question by accusing the accuser. It's a popular move because it FEELS like a defense — but it doesn't actually answer.

question: When caught lying, Reggie says, 'Adults lie too!' How is that NOT a good defense?
choices: Whether others lie has nothing to do with whether HE lied.
Adults lying is much worse, so kid lies should be ignored entirely.
Kids are always allowed to copy the bad habits they see in adults.
Reggie is too young to understand the harm that his lying causes.
answer: Whether others lie has nothing to do with whether HE lied.
context: Tu quoque. The question on the table is Reggie's lie, right now. Other people's lies are separate questions, even if also worth examining.

question: Jamie says we should eat less candy because sugar hurts teeth. Mike replies, 'Jamie is bad at math!' What's wrong with Mike's reply?
choices: Mike attacks Jamie, not the argument about sugar and teeth.
Jamie being bad at math means her claim about sugar must be wrong.
Only kids who are great at math are allowed to talk about teeth.
Mike should have attacked Jamie's reading score instead of math.
answer: Mike attacks Jamie, not the argument about sugar and teeth.
context: This is 'ad hominem' — Latin for 'to the person.' Attacking the person doesn't disprove their argument.

question: Mia argues recess should be longer. Tom replies, 'You can't trust Mia — she wears weird socks.' What's wrong?
choices: Tom attacks Mia's clothes, not her actual argument.
Mia's weird socks prove her recess ideas are silly.
